en: Preface to the *Fahua Wenzhu Zuyao*:

Originally, when the Tathāgata was on the stage of the Dharma-body, his tranquil illumination reached all capacities. With great compassion permeating his mind, he manifested in the world and expounded the Dharma.
The sudden and perfect realization of the One Vehicle cannot be expedited without the *Avataṃsaka*; the gradual ripening of the five flavors cannot be fully realized without the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Thus, when the Buddha-sun rose in the east, the great Bodhisattvas of the high mountains were first illuminated by its light; when the wheel of wisdom reached its zenith at midday, even the subtle virtues in the dark valleys were all bathed in its radiance.
Through the three turnings of the Dharma-wheel, the single rain fell, yet the capacities of beings naturally varied in their height and depth. The nine...

This illustrates how the One Vehicle (ekayāna) accords with or differs from various perspectives. (Regarding the three cycles: first, the Dharma-exposition for those of superior faculties; second, the parable-exposition for those of middling faculties; third, the exposition on past-life causes and conditions for those of inferior faculties.)

Regarding the nine metaphors: first, the metaphor of the lotus serves as the general overview; it generally illustrates the wondrous Dharma of both the "Original" (hon) and "Traced" (jaku) gates. Second, the eight metaphors serve as the specific details. These eight metaphors are: 1. The metaphor of the burning house, which illustrates that the three realms are not peaceful or secure. 2. The metaphor of the impoverished son, which illustrates that those of the Lesser Vehicle lack the merit and the wealth of the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. 3.

The metaphor of the medicinal herbs, which illustrates that all contaminated (sāsrava) wholesome deeds can eliminate evil, yet uncontaminated (anāsrava) goodness is supreme. 4. The metaphor of the conjured city, which illustrates the true emptiness and *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles, which defends against the errors of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) and wards off the enemy of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

5. The metaphor of the jewel in the garment, which illustrates the prince’s planting of conditions, sowing the seeds of the definitive cause for the One Vehicle. 6. The metaphor of digging a well, which illustrates how a Bodhisattva who merely studies various Mahāyāna sutras prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is like seeing only dry soil.

The water is still far away. If one hears and understands this sutra, it is like seeing wet mud; one is close to the water of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). The metaphor of the seven-tufted jewel represents the Middle Way and true reality, which is the primary tenet of the ultimate fruit. These seven preceding metaphors all illustrate the Trace Gate’s revelation of the provisional to manifest the real.

The eighth metaphor, that of the physician’s son, represents the Great Physician King who universally cures the illnesses of all sentient beings; this single metaphor alone illustrates the Root Gate’s revelation of the trace to manifest the root.

The general meaning is that while all three weeks of teaching consist of the single Dharma of true reality, the three types of capacities perceive it as high or low according to their own inclinations. All nine metaphors illustrate the principle of the One Vehicle, yet the differences in how conditions perceive it reside in the capacity and the conditions; the Dharma itself has no differentiation. (The explanation of the seven metaphors is derived from the *Dharmapada-saṃgīti-śāstra*.)

*Huālùn* (The Treatise on the Lotus): "The preceding [section] does not mention the lotus flower, and the subsequent [section] does not speak of digging a well; it merely employs the seven intermediate metaphors to establish seven antidotes. Jingxi remarked that while the first and second [metaphors] capture the intent of the sūtra, the others seem logically incomplete.

Now, following the sūtra, I shall supplement these with nine metaphors. It would be better to deviate from the *lùn* than to deviate from the sūtra. As for his exercise of provisional means (*upāya*), he entices beings to enter the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). As for his manifestation of traces, he causes them to reach the fundamental source.
The source of sources begins with the beginningless Vīci (the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, as explained in the *Nirmita-śarīra-parivarta*). The source within the traces arises from...

The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging—his traces and his origin, and the mutual manifestation of origin and trace—are boundless. Even if one traverses the atoms of the ultimate realm, his lifespan cannot be exhausted;

even if one exhausts all ink-drops, his temporal divisions are endless (as seen in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter). Since the Way of Origin and Trace has been clarified, the intent of this revelation is now understood.
Furthermore, regarding this single period of the Great Dharma, the ocean of wisdom has been fully drawn upon for its proclamation; the circulation through these two gates reaches its utmost extent.

He categorized and exhorted them with praise. This was truly because sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas; it is only due to their lack of awakening and ignorance that [the Buddha] desires to cause them to turn their faculties in a single thought-moment.
He did not merely instruct them two or three times, but rather, every verse and every phrase entered into the scope of bestowing predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

The Three Virtues and the Three Modes of Practice constitute the wondrous cultivation of the act of preaching the Dharma. (The Three Virtues are the Dharmakāya, Liberation, and Prajñā; these are the ultimate fruits of Buddhahood. The Three Modes are the rules for propagating the Dharma. The "Chapter on the Dharma Master" states:

"Enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat. The Tathāgata’s chamber is the heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s robe is the heart of gentleness and patience. The Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all dharmas.

Abiding therein with a mind free from indolence, one extensively expounds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly. The commentary states: "Entering the Tathāgata’s chamber means cultivating the compassion of same-nature (*samatā-karuṇā*)."

The Dharma-body virtue is to don the robe of the Tathāgata and cultivate the patience of quiescence; this is the liberation virtue. The sitting virtue is that the sitter and the seat are ultimately empty and still; this is the prajñā virtue. Thus, they are three in one and one in three—this is the threefold track for propagating the Dharma.
Therefore, the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter says: "Although the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he remains within the jeweled stūpa."
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma. How is it that you people do not strive diligently for the Dharma? This King of Sutras—[as the verse in the 'Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta' says:
'The definitive teaching of the Śrāvaka-dharma is the king of all sutras']"—is the fundamental basis of this single transformation and the ultimate proclamation of the five periods.

To receive, uphold, read, recite, explain it to others, and practice according to its teachings leads to the final attainment of Buddhahood. When a wise person obtains this, they should rejoice and feel fortunate."
It is all over. Could there possibly be anything further than this?

The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai personally received the transmission on the Sacred Peak; he attained wondrous enlightenment at Dàsū Mountain, realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, and manifested the *Pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*.
His illumination of the *Lotus Sūtra* was like the brilliant light descending upon a dark valley; his penetration of the characteristics of all phenomena was as if...
In his "Roaming in the Great Void" (Chángfēng zhī yóu tāixū), he first expounded the profound mysteries for ninety days to explain the title of the scripture;
next, he interpreted the chapters and verses to clarify the textual meaning. He further composed the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* to elucidate the sublime practice.

Thus, the Great Master used the Buddha’s mind to seal his own mind, and used his own *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to interpret the Buddha’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, like empty space merging with empty space, leaving nothing unperceived.

It is like pouring water into water; there is no distinct flavor between them. Among the masters before him, there were several renowned families of exegetes who were great pillars of the Dharma-gate, each famous throughout the world.
Yet, once the Master’s words emerged, they were like the bright sun adorning the heavens, causing all other lights to lose their brilliance.
Even in later generations, there have been those who did not understand the Master’s words, yet who nonetheless attained the Buddha’s mind—such instances occurred frequently.
I have composed this commentary separately; it is not without one or two new insights, yet these do not exceed the level of minor, peripheral details.

It is like adding a handful of earth to a high mound—it ultimately neither increases nor diminishes it. In my youth, while traveling on pilgrimage, I frequented lecture halls and personally attended upon many eminent masters;
thus, I gained a rough grasp of the essential principles of the Tiantai, Huayan, Faxiang, and Weishi schools. Later, I entered the Chan school and devoted myself exclusively to its practice.

I engaged in intensive investigation (*sanchou*). As for the various vehicles of the teachings, I set them aside on a high shelf. After another ten years had passed, once I had ceased my formal practice, I took up again the doctrines I had studied previously and read them.
Only then did I realize that they were originally the ancestral estate of my own house;

the title deeds were clear and distinct, without the slightest discrepancy. From that time forward, I redoubled my efforts in research, beginning first with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, studying it daily alongside the *Vimalakīrti*.
Old Master Lu kept Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra’s eyebrows knotted together, never parting from them for even a moment.
When he reached the age of sixty-four, he began compiling the essential passages of the commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, annotating them beneath the sutra text;

this resulted in one hundred and twenty fascicles, which were published for the world. By that time, he was already seventy years old. In the blink of an eye, he had unwittingly reached his eightieth year.
He visited once more. Reflecting upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he thought that it had remained an unfinished task; if he did not address it now, would he not be failing this life?
He then requested the *Wenju* and the *Ji* commentaries and began his study from the beginning.
On the first day of the tenth month of winter in the year of Jiashu, he took up his pen. He compiled only the Master’s correct interpretation of the Sūtra to enable others to...
The sections concerning "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" have been recorded; their correct meaning is already sufficient.
As for his flowing eloquence and the comprehensive, expansive development of his arguments, I have recorded only their essentials and cannot record them in full.

Furthermore, regarding the refutations of past views, which consist of long compositions spanning many pages—though they were indeed the necessary medicine and stone-therapy for that time, they are now like discarded hair-ornaments and thus need not be recorded. As for the topical outlines established prior to the sutra...

I have abridged and refined what was redundant and supplemented what was missing. Furthermore, regarding points where the principle is profound and subtle or the phrasing is concise and obscure, I have cited the *Jingxi Records* to provide brief explanations.
Moreover, concerning meanings not yet fully developed or my own humble views, I have ventured to add one or two observations.
This is done solely with the aim of adapting to the capacities of others, so that those of similar views and practice may find resonance.
I have therefore entitled this work *The Essential Compendium of the Textual Explanations of the Lotus Sūtra*. However, my old eyes are dim and my physical strength no longer suffices;

thus, there may well be errors and discrepancies. I hope that those of noble virtue will deign to examine it and not withhold their instructions, so that it may be corrected and circulated together for the benefit of all.
This is truly what I have long hoped for. This serves as the preface.

Written on the day of the winter solstice during the second month of the winter in the *Yihai* year of the Kangxi era, by the self-cultivating bhikṣu Daopai, in homage, recording the table of contents for the *Fahua jing wenju zuanyao*.

The Essential Compendium of the Text and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Venerable Guanding of Zhang’an during the Sui Dynasty;
spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Chen and Sui Dynasties.
Recorded by the Tang Dynasty Venerable Jingxi, Zhànrán;
compiled by the Private Disciple Bhikṣu Dàopài of Gǔshān, Fúmiàn.
△ Prior to the Sūtra, there are three sections. First, a brief explanation of the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*).
When the Great Master Zhizhe was about to expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
he first established five layers of profound meaning (*wǔchóng xuányì*) prior to the scripture to clarify the title and elucidate the great purport of the entire sutra—
namely, what is known as the "Ninety-Day Discourse on the Sublime. These are called the five layers.

These refer to name, essence, tenet, function, and the characteristics of the teaching. One relies on names to express the essence; through the essence, one realizes the tenet; based on the tenet, there is function;

and furthermore, the characteristics of the teaching are required to distinguish them clearly, so that the provisional and the real may have their proper destination and the coarse and the subtle may not be confused.
This sutra takes the dharma and its parable as its title; the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence; the cause and effect of the One Vehicle as its thesis;

the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith as its function; and the *amṛta* (clarified butter) as its doctrinal characteristic. Regarding the title consisting of one dharma and one parable: a wondrous name is inconceivable.
What is called "dharma" refers to the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses. This dharma...
This is precisely the wondrous. This wonder is itself the Dharma; they are non-dual and without distinction, and thus it is called "wondrous.

When the term "wondrous" is uttered once, both the relative and the absolute are simultaneously revealed. In terms of relative discourse and judgment, it transcends the three teachings and four periods.
In terms of absolute discourse and opening, it opens up the three teachings and four periods so that they all become the single reality. "Lotus" is a metaphor; it is a metaphor for the provisional.

These are the actual dharmas. The seed-pod is likened to the Real (the ultimate), and the flower is likened to the Expedient (the provisional). This is because the Subtle Dharma is difficult to understand, whereas it is easy to manifest through metaphors.
Furthermore, since the underlying intent is manifold, I have briefly modeled the Original and the Traces to form six analogies in total. First, the three analogies of the Gate of the Trace:
first, "flowering for the sake of the lotus," which is a metaphor for establishing the expedient for the sake of the real. As the Sūtra says: "Knowing the foremost quiescence..."
By the power of skillful means (*upāya*), although various paths are displayed, they are in reality for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle.

Second, the blossoming of the flowers and the appearance of the lotus illustrates the disclosure of the provisional to reveal the real; as the Sūtra says: "Opening the gate of skillful means, he reveals the true aspect.

Third, the falling of the flowers and the formation of the lotus illustrates the setting aside of the provisional to establish the real; as the Sūtra says: "Directly abandoning skillful means, he speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way."

Next are the three parables of the Essential Gate (Honmon). First is "the flower for the sake of the lotus. The lotus is a metaphor for the fundamental (hon), and the flower is a metaphor for the manifested trace (jaku).
The trace is suspended from the fundamental; the trace relies upon the fundamental. As the Sūtra says: "In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been as long as this."
However, in order to teach and transform sentient beings, he speaks thus: "I left home at a young age and attained *sambodhi*.

This is like the opening of the two flowers and the manifestation of the lotus, which serves as a metaphor for revealing the trace by manifesting the fundamental. As the sutra says: "All the world thinks that I have only now attained the Way;
yet since I became a Buddha, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*nayuta*) kalpas have passed. This is like the three flowers falling and the lotus becoming fully formed.
It is like discarding the traces to establish the foundation. As the Sūtra says: "The Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is thus;
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false. Therefore, first the wondrous Dharma is signaled, followed by the metaphor of the lotus flower.

This washes away the attachment to the provisional teaching of the "Transformation City" and discards the stagnant emotions of the "grass hut. It opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the wondrous principle of ultimate reality.

The assembly, having recognized these minor practices as virtuous, returns to the single vehicle (Ekayāna) of the vast and great. For those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties, all are granted the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa)—this being the intent of the section on the concealment of traces.

Furthermore, the skillful means (*upāya*) of Gayā are manifested to reveal the profound subtleties of the original ground. Through the increase of the Path and the decrease of births, their rank approaches that of Great Enlightenment.
Thus, the mission of a single lifetime of transformation reaches perfection in both principle and phenomenon. The analogy of the lotus flower is intended to convey this meaning.
[This concludes the meaning of the introductory section. Regarding the term *sūtra*: in the Western lands it is called *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Scripture" (*qijing*).

This means it accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings. It possesses four meanings: "pervasion," "gathering," "goodness," and "dharma. Specifically, it refers to the pervasive threading together of the meanings that ought to be taught;

the gathering and sustaining of those beings to be converted; its being unchanging throughout the three periods of time; and its being followed by a thousand sages alike. (The first explanation of the name is complete.)

Regarding "the two take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their essence": all phenomena do not transcend the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); this directly indicates that the true mark is taken as the primary essence.
Therefore, the *Ayuḥpramāṇa-parivarta* states: "It is not as those within the three realms see the three realms; it is neither like [them] nor different [from them].
If people within the three realms see the three realms as different, and those of the Two Vehicles see the three realms as like [them], [it is not so]."
The Bodhisattva views the three realms as both identical and different. The Buddha views the three realms as neither identical nor different, illuminating both identity and difference simultaneously.
Now, we take what the Buddha perceives as the true essence of the ultimate reality (dharmatā). This essence constitutes the skillful means and the ultimate truth for transforming others.
This is precisely the provisional and the ultimate of one's own practice. It is like a person inside a soiled garment who is actually a wealthy elder;

this is the essence of the provisional and ultimate of practicing for oneself and transforming others, which is identical to the provisional and ultimate of one's own practice. It is like the priceless jewel tied within the garment;
the provisional of one's own practice is itself the ultimate of one's own practice. To know all worldly ways of livelihood and governance is [the ultimate].
All phenomena are in no way inconsistent with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way;
how much more so could the provisional means of one's own practice not be the reality? (The second section, the determination of the essence, is concluded.)
Third, the One Vehicle’s cause and effect constitute the central tenet (*zong*). A "tenet" refers to what is essential. What constitutes this essence?

All immeasurable wholesome deeds are subsumed under the term "cause," and all immeasurable realizations are subsumed under the term "effect. It is like pulling the main cord of a net: there is no mesh that does not move.
Or like tugging a single corner of a robe (referring to the monastic robes): there is no thread that does not follow. Therefore, it is called the "essential tenet. However—
One must clearly and thoroughly understand all causes and effects. One does not even adopt the causes and effects of other teachings, much less those of other [worldly] causes and effects.
The causes and effects regarding the Buddha’s past practices elucidated in various sutras are all merely skillful means; they are not the essential core of this present sutra.
These are spoken with the underlying intent that the cause reaches the ultimate reality of long-term cultivation, and the fruit reaches the ultimate reality of long-term realization. It is thus.
This is the cause. Vertically, it stands upon the seven kinds of skillful means; horizontally, it encompasses the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms.

Initially practicing this cultivation of the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is called the Buddha-cause; that which is realized at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is called the Buddha-fruit. It can only be known through wisdom.
It is impossible to describe them in full. These causes and effects have been briefly cited merely as the essential tenets (the conclusion of the Threefold Mingzong).
Fourth, the function is to sever doubt and engender faith. "Function" refers to the power of application. The three types of provisional and real wisdom are all powers of application;

within these powers of application, they are further distinguished: the two wisdoms of one's own practice illuminate the principle, and because this principle is all-pervasive, it is called [the Name].
It is for the sake of power. The two kinds of wisdom that transform others discern the capacities [of beings]; this pervasive discernment of capacity is termed "function.

Indeed, the two kinds of wisdom for one's own practice are identical to the two kinds of wisdom for transforming others; the two kinds of wisdom for transforming others are identical to the two kinds of wisdom for one's own practice.

To illumine the principle is to discern capacity, and to discern capacity is to illumine the principle. It is like when Śākyamuni drew the bow of King Jñāruṇa to its full extent—this is termed [power].
This is its power. [It] pierces seven intermediate iron drums, penetrates one Iron Encircling Mountain, and passes through the earth to reach the water-wheel;

this is called its function. The powers and functions of the various provisional teachings are weak and slight, like the bows and arrows of ordinary people. Why is this? Formerly, those with the capacity for conversion received the two wisdoms of transforming others;
their illumination of principle was not universal, the faith they generated was not deep, and their doubts were not fully dispelled. Now, those with the capacity for self-realization...

They practice the two wisdoms, reach the ultimate realm of the Buddha, give rise to faith in the *dharmadhātu*, and increase the perfectly sublime path. They sever the fundamental afflictions and diminish the birth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-janman*).
This benefits not only those with birth-bodies (*janma-kāya*) but also those bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti-lābhin*); both types are benefited.
The Dharma-body and the final thought-moment after the Dharma-body—both types of Bodhisattvas likewise receive benefit. The power of transformation is vast and its profit profound;
this is indeed the efficacy of this sutra. (The discussion of the four treatises on function is concluded.)
The fifth is the *paramārtha-ghṛta* (the essence of clarified butter) as the characteristic of the teaching. "Teaching" (*śāsana*) refers to the words spoken by the Sage for those below him.

"Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the discernment of similarities and differences. How are they discerned? It is like the sun when it first rises: it first illuminates the high mountains [of those] who have planted thick roots of goodness.

Reflecting upon this teaching of the Sudden, one realizes that the Sudden teaching was fundamentally not intended for those of small capacity. Although those of small capacity were present in the assembly, they were as if deaf and mute;

this was truly because the Small could not endure the Great, and likewise because the Great was separated from the Small. This is precisely the *Avataṃsaka*, which, in terms of its Dharma, accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

Those of sharp faculties obtain great benefit; this is termed the "characteristic of the Sudden Teaching. Regarding the sequence of exposition, it is termed the "characteristic of the flavor of milk produced from the cow.

Next, it illuminates the deep valleys, where those of shallow practice gain partial clarity and achieve gradual understanding within their own respective stages; this is like the Tripiṭaka. The Tripiṭaka is fundamentally not intended for the Great [Vehicle].
Although the Great is present in the assembly, there are many *taṭabha* (ignorant) ones who do not recognize what is Small; this constitutes the separation of the Small.

The Great is hidden within the Small; according to the Dharma applied to the capacities of beings, this is called the characteristic of the gradual teaching. According to the sequence of exposition, it is called the characteristic of the flavor of curd.
Next, it illuminates the level ground, and its reflection appears in the myriad waters; it conforms to the squareness or roundness of the vessels and follows the movement or stillness of the waves.

He manifests a single buddha-field, yet makes it appear as pure or defiled according to different perceptions; he manifests a single body, yet makes it appear vast or minute according to different perspectives;
with a single voice he preaches the Dharma, yet beings understand it each according to their own kind—some feeling fear, some joy, some weariness and renunciation, and some the severing of doubt.

Because his supernatural powers are unique, there are those who see purity and impurity, hear praise and censure, smell the scent of *campaka* or non-*campaka*, and perceive flowers clinging to his body.

It does not cling to the body. Wisdom may be manifold or not manifold; this is like the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other Vaipulya sutras, which, by means of the Dharma, respond to the capacities of beings.
Yet these are still teachings of gradual progression. In terms of the sequence of exposition, they possess the characteristics of the flavor of "fresh butter" (*mantha*).

Furthermore, there is another principle: the great man benefits from its radiant utility, while the infant loses its visual clarity; those wandering at night crouch in concealment, while those engaged in labor achieve success.
Therefore, the text says: "It was only for the sake of the Bodhisattvas that he spoke of the reality of things; he did not speak these essential truths for my sake.

Although all three types of people studied together, the two vehicles attained realization, as fully described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. If we consider the Dharma applied to the capacities of the listeners, it still belongs to the gradual teaching (*anupūrva-vinaya*).
Regarding the sequence of its exposition, it is called the flavor of "matured butter" (*pakva-ghṛta*). Furthermore, there is another interpretation: it is like the sunlight shining universally.
High and low are all made equal and level. When measured with the *tugu* (earth-gnomon), the shadow neither shortens nor lengthens.
Whether they lower their heads, speak in small voices, are distracted, or possess only slight goodness, all shall attain the Buddha-way. No one is permitted to attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*) alone;

rather, all are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction. This is fully as described in the present sutra. If one summarizes this according to the Dharma and its application to capacities, it is named...
Regarding the gradual and perfect teachings (*anupūrva-paripūrṇa-yāna*), according to the sequence of their exposition, they possess the characteristics of the *amṛta* (nectar) flavor.

One should know that the analogy of the *Avataṃsaka* is identical in meaning to the *Nirvāṇa*. The analogies of the three sons, the three fields, and the three horses all refer first to the bodhisattvas and subsequently to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

The latter refers to the icchantika; thus, the noble and the ordinary are equal. Regarding the analogies of the three sons, the three fields, and the three horses: in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata has compassion for all sentient beings;

he can tame those who are untamable and liberate those who are not yet liberated. Sunakṣatra was the son of the Buddha when he was a bodhisattva; he had severed the fetters of the desire realm and attained the four dhyānas. For what reason did the Tathāgata declare him to be an icchantika who will dwell in hell for an eon?"

"One must not treat others [as if they were incurable]. Why not first expound the True Dharma for them, and afterwards become a bodhisattva? If you cannot save the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, how can you be called one of great compassion or one who possesses great skillful means? The Buddha said, "Good son," [the Buddha continued: "Good son."

Suppose, for example, there were a man who had three sons. The first son possessed a mind of faith and compliance, revered his parents, and was of sharp faculties and wisdom; he was fully capable of understanding all worldly affairs.

The foundation was level and the rafters were brilliantly adorned; their artistry surpassed that of humans, as if wrought by divine power and demonic craftsmanship, yet achieved with such speed.

The Master led the assembly to take up residence there, expounding the Dharma day and night. One day, a spirit addressed the Master, saying, "I, your disciple, have had the fortune to hear the Great Dharma;

I further wish to receive the precepts so that they may forever serve as the root of my bodhi. The Master immediately took up the incense burner, burned incense, and conferred the precepts upon the spirit.
Having completed the taking of the precepts, the deity received them with joy and faith. He prostrated twice, ascended into the air, and departed.
Thereupon, the deity’s majestic virtue spread clearly for a thousand *li*; those who looked upon him from near and far offered prayers, all of whom were filled with solemn reverence.

The Prince of Jin submitted a memorial requesting that a temple be built at Dangyang, stating that since this matter originated from the deity’s own mind, its principle transcends ordinary expectation and it should be granted an auspicious name. The Emperor approved his request and bestowed [the name].
His name was Yuquan. As the Master was about to return to Tiantai, the Prince of Jin requested that he remain at Qixia so that the populace might seek his counsel and resolution.

The Master firmly declined; the Prince did not dare detain him, and he thus departed. The people of Wu and Yue swept their lanes to welcome him, with banners and flowers lining the road in continuous succession.
Upon arriving in Kuaiji, he stayed at an ancient temple. One night, the bright moon shone upon his bed as he sat alone.

He was preaching the Dharma when someone posed a difficult question. The attendant Zhixi asked him at dawn: "I wonder what kind of causes and conditions you encountered during the night? The Master replied:
"In my first dream, a great wind suddenly arose and blew down a jeweled pagoda. Next, I saw a monk from India who said to me: 'The karmic conditions are like firewood;
the illuminating function is like fire; the auxiliary support is like the wind. When these three things are complete, [the light shines forth]...'"

The Way of transformation has now proceeded; at the summit of Mount Hua, we have mutually influenced one another. As my capacity for expedient means is nearing its end, my assistance on the sidelines shall also cease;
thus I inform you. This is the manifestation of the signs of death. I recall a dream from my youth that I should pass away in this very place;
therefore, I have always wished to return to the mountains. After my death, my remains should be interred on the southwestern peak. I entreat you to do so.
He fashioned a niche from stone and planted pines to cover it, erecting two white stupas so that those who saw them would give rise to the bodhicitta.
The following day, he set out on his journey; upon reaching Shicheng, he claimed to be ill and said to Zhiyue, "My end shall be here."

"There is no need to proceed further. This Stone City is the western gate of Mount Tiantai. Since this site for the future sacred image of the Great Buddha is excellent, you should apply your mind with focused diligence here at the very end.
Divide your robes, bowl, and requisites into two portions: one portion to offer to Maitreya, and one portion to provide for the *karmadāna*.
Having spoken thus, he lay down on his right side facing west, single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
When the recitation was finished, he ordered his attendant to chant the titles of the two divisions of the *Sūtra*. Having finished chanting the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he said:

"This Dharma-gate is the father and mother [of all teachings]; wisdom and understanding arise from it. Its fundamental and manifested aspects (*honji-suijaku*) are vast and great, subtle and wondrous, difficult to fathom.

For over forty years, I have harbored this within myself—whom else could I have known it? Only I alone am clearly enlightened; others cannot see it. I now lay down my chisel and sever my strings. At that, he passed away.
This day, having finished chanting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, [the Master] said: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land with lotus ponds and jeweled trees;
yet though it is easy to go there, no one does so. Even when the signs of the fiery chariot appear, if one can repent and recite the Name, one still attains rebirth there.
How much more so for those who cultivate through precepts and wisdom and possess the power of practicing the Way—truly, their efforts are not in vain. This was requested by the disciple Zhilang.
[The disciples] said, "We do not know with certainty what stage of realization the Master has entered, where he will be reborn after passing away, or whom we should take as our model and veneration.
The Master said, "You all are too lazy to cultivate roots of goodness, yet you ask about my merits—like the blind asking about milk. What benefit would there be in telling you the truth?
I shall now dispel your doubts for you. I do not lead a community; I must purify my six sense faculties. To benefit others, I must sacrifice myself; I shall simply ascend [to the Pure Land]."
"O you of the five ranks! My teachers and friends, along with those who attend upon Avalokiteśvara, have all come to welcome me.
The Prātimokṣa is your teacher; the four kinds of samādhi that I have constantly preached are your enlightened guides.
I and you have met through the Dharma; we take the Dharma as our kin. Transmitting and perpetuating the lamp of the Buddha—this constitutes our family. Furthermore, I admonish you:"
The *vinaya-dhara* said: "When a person's life is about to end, hearing the sound of bells and chimes increases their right mindfulness; let it be long and enduring until the breath is exhausted.
Why then do you strike the chime only when the body has grown cold? Having finished instructing the great assembly, he then chanted the names of the Triple Gem as if entering samādhi.
This was truly on the twentieth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era.
The fourth day, at the hour of Wei (2–4 p.m.). He was sixty years of age and forty years since his ordination.
Seated in meditative equipoise outside, ten days passed as monastics and laypeople rushed to him, wailing and circumambulating him in prostration as if they had lost their own parents.

As they were about to carry the reliquary shrine back to Fulong Mountain, continuous rain did not cease. The disciples offered prayers, beseeching the addition of divine power; no sooner had they lifted the sacred shrine than it responded.
The weather then cleared. Consequently, he erected a stupa on the southwestern peak of the monastery to enshrine [the relics], in accordance with his prior instructions.
Among his thirty-two dharma-heir disciples, those who attained the Dharma and practiced it themselves were beyond counting. He constructed thirty-six monasteries;
Xiqia, Lingyan, Tiantai, and Yuquan are known as the "Four Wonders" of the world. He also produced ten sets of the Great Tripitaka.
In five locations, he commissioned eight hundred thousand images made of sandalwood, gold, copper, and painted silk. He ordained fourteen thousand monks.

For thirty years, the Master wore only a single patchwork robe (*nāṃsa*), never changing it through either winter or summer. Whatever offerings he received, whether a single fruit or a single thread, [he accepted].

He dedicated everything to the assembly. Regarding all that he propagated, he did not keep any commentaries or treatises. Possessing unhindered eloquence, his words accorded with principle and were consistent with the scriptures.
When there was a great spiritual resonance, he would then personally compose works.

On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Daye era of Emperor Yang, coinciding with the anniversary of the Master’s death, the Attendant-in-Ordinary Lu Chengfang was sent into the mountains to ordain four [monks].
Nineteen monks were invited to perform a thousand-monk vegetarian feast. The Emperor opened the Master’s spirit-stupa to inspect it;

upon opening the inner chamber, no physical remains were found—there was only an empty seat and a vacant canopy. When the messenger returned with this report, the Emperor said to his ministers, "The Venerable Zhi was my teacher and previously displayed many miraculous signs.
In the first year of the Renshou era, I ordered Zhang Qianwei to go and observe him."
In the niche chamber, the Dharma-body sits upright as if entering meditative concentration. Now, when Lu Cheng arrives, the numinous form is no longer seen;
there is only an empty seat. That the Perfected One has attained the Way is not false; it is truly inconceivable.
The Biography of the Venerable Zhāng'ān Guǎngjìng of the Sui Dynasty:
The Master’s name was Guǎngjìng, with the courtesy name Zhāng'ān. He was a native of Zhāng'ān in Línhǎi; he was named after his place of origin out of respect for him.
At three months of age, he was able to follow his mother in reciting the names of the Triple Gem. At seven years old, he entered Cesheng Temple and became a *kū-ō* (crow-chaser) under Huizheng;
he memorized ten thousand words daily. At twenty, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Gifted with innate wisdom and understanding, he never forgot anything upon hearing it once.

During the Zhidu period of the Chen dynasty (under Emperor Houzhu), he visited Zhiyi at Xiuchan Temple, where he received instruction in the practice of contemplation (*guan*) and devoted himself to its profound study.

After a long time, he was suddenly granted formal certification (anujñā). Consequently, serving as an attendant, wherever the Master resided and whatever Dharma-gates were taught, Ānanda was immediately able to receive and retain them.
Just as the vast waters of the Buddha-Dharma flow into the heart of Ānanda, so too did it happen for the Master who received the wisdom of the Dharma.
In the first year of the Zhengming era, he followed Zhiyi to stay at Guangzhai Monastery in Jinling, where he listened to the lectures on the Lotus Sūtra.

(The *Wenju* states: "At the age of twenty-seven, he studied under [Hui]zhi at Jinling. In the summer of the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he received the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) at Jiangling.
In the summer of the fourteenth year, he received the teachings on the Perfect and Sudden *Zhi-guan* at Yuquan.

He compiled all of the Great Master’s lectures and expositions into more than one hundred fascicles of various major and minor works, which have been transmitted for ten centuries; this was due to the Master’s efforts.

In the tenth year of the Daye era of Emperor Yang, he composed the *Nirvāṇa Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) in two fascicles and its commentary (*shu*) in twenty fascicles. At that time...
At the end of the Sui dynasty, warfare broke out and bandits rose up in swarms. The Master himself recorded that he spent five years in total examining the sacred texts;
there was no year in which he did not witness the fires of war, and no month in which he did not see the clash of arms.

He subsisted on vegetables and water, and slept upon ice beds and snow blankets. Such was his toil and hardship. When the commentary was completed, he attempted to burn it with a fierce fire, but it would not catch. In his later years, at...
At the Chexin Vihāra in Kuaiji, he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, earning the praise of his contemporaries.

There were those who remarked that he surpassed Daolang and Guṇabhadra, and rivaled Fayun and Jñānagupta. In the commandery was Jiashang Jizang, who had previously composed commentaries and exegeses on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Upon hearing the Master’s teaching, he abandoned his lectures and dispersed his assembly; he prostrated himself to request instruction, deeply repenting his former delusions.

On the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he passed away at Guoqing Temple at the age of seventy-two and with fifty-two years of ordination seniority.
When he first manifested illness, a wondrous fragrance was present. As he approached death, he instructed his disciples, saying: "The *Maitreya Sūtra* states that the World-Honored One..."
He entered nirvana. He burned many varieties of incense, the smoke of which rose like clouds. "You should now burn much incense as well; I am about to depart," he said.

He then offered detailed final instructions, the words and principles of which were most earnest. Suddenly, he rose, joined his palms, and recited the names of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Pure Land.
He then passed away in an instant. Previously, in the first year of the Zhenguan era, his fellow student Zhi Xi had said at the time of his own death:
I was born in Tuṣita Heaven and saw the Master Zhizhe. On either side of the jeweled throne, rows of seats were all occupied by people, yet one seat alone was empty.
A celestial being there said, "Six years hence, the Dharma Master Ding will come to ascend this seat.
Calculating the years and reckoning the period, it was clear and not mistaken. On the ninth day of this month, he was interred on the southern mountain of the monastery. The Master resided there.
At Sheshing Monastery, he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* when a band of robbers suddenly arrived.

Seeing the monastery gates adorned with banners shining like the sun, and divine soldiers brandishing weapons over ten feet tall, the thieves were terrified and fled in total disorder. The Master would always recite the sutras and sit in meditative composure.

Celestial flowers frequently drifted down beside him. Among his writings are the *Eight Teachings: General Meaning* (*Bājiào dàyì*) and the *Distinct Tradition of the Wise One* (*Zhìzhě biéchuán*), each in one fascicle;
the *Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* (*Guānxīn lùn shū*) in two fascicles; the *One Hundred Records of Guoqing* (*Guōqīng bǎilù*) in five fascicles;

and the *Biography of Dharma Master Zhenguān* (*Zhēnguān fǎshī zhuàn*) and the *Record of Mount Nanyue* (*Nányuè jì*), each in one fascicle. The King of Wuyue requested the posthumous title of "Venerable Total Retention" (*Zǒngchí zūnzhě*).
The Biography of Venerable Zhànrán of Jīngxī of the Táng Dynasty:
The Master’s name was Zhànrán; his style name was Jīngxī. His surname was Qì, and his family had resided for generations in Jīngxī, Jìnlíng.

Because people of the time revered his Way, they adopted it as his style name. His family had practiced Confucian learning for generations; thus, his early studies were accomplished at a young age, even among the ranks of children.

He possessed a transcendent resolve to transcend the mundane world. At the age of seventeen (born in the second year of Jingyun of Emperor Ruizong’s reign; the fifteenth year of Xuanzong’s reign, corresponding to his seventeenth year), he traveled to Xishi to seek the Way.
There he met Fangyan of Jinhua, who transmitted to him the methods of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). This was in the eighteenth year of Kaiyuan.
He first studied under Zuoxi (at the age of twenty). When Zuoxi spoke with him, he knew him to be a vessel for the Dharma.
One day, he dreamed that he was wearing monastic robes and, supporting two wheels, was wading through a great river. Upon waking, he reported this to Zuoxi. Zuoxi said, "Ah!

Could it be that you shall use the two methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to ferry sentient beings across the abyss of birth and death? Thereupon, while still in the attire of a retired scholar (*chushi*), he received [the precepts].
Regarding the Way of Teaching and Contemplation: in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era, he first discarded his scholar’s robe and donned the *saṃghāṭī* (at the age of thirty-eight).
He subsequently visited Master Yì of Kuàijī to extensively study the Vinaya-piṭaka. After a long time, he expounded the *Zhìguān* (Cessation and Contemplation) in Wúmén.
After Zuoxi had passed away, the Master took up the secret treasury and alone propagated it in the southeast.

One day he said to his disciples, "The difficulty of practicing the Way—I have come to know it. Those of antiquity remained still to observe the return of all things and moved to respond to external objects;
they dwelt in neither state, thereby treading upon the Great Square. Those of the present age, however, are sometimes lost in emptiness."
Some are stuck in the notion of existence; they suffer from their own illness and their practice of the Way lacks vigor. As they seek to attain rectitude, whom but you would they turn to?
Thereupon, you grandly opened the wondrous Dharma, arraying the myriad practices alongside it, fully encompassing all phenomena so that they enter the unconditioned.
He used written characters to facilitate profound insight and guided speech through silence to return to the source.

Thus, he followed and expounded upon the transmitted teachings, composing a record consisting of several hundred thousand words. He provided annotated commentaries on the essential tenets of the three great works of his school.
The *Xuan-yi* has the *Shiqian*; the *Wenju* has the *Ji*; the *Mohe Zhiguan* has the *Fuxing*.
His writings are very numerous and are detailed in his biography. As for the Way of Tiantai and Zhang’an, it reached its full perfection under this Master.

During the Tianbao and Dali eras, the court issued three edicts summoning him, but he declined each time on the grounds of illness. The Master first resided at Lanling and once [stayed] with Jianghuai...
Forty eminent monks set out together to pay homage at Mount Wutai. Among them was Hanguang, a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra, who addressed his master, saying:
"Recently, while traveling to India with my teacher, I encountered a monk from India who said:

'I have heard that in the Great Tang there exists the legacy of the Tiantai teachings, by which one may discern the partial and the perfect, distinguish the heterodox and the orthodox, and clarify *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. It would be well to translate these.'"
When he heard that [the Dharma] had reached the Western Lands, the Master sighed and said, "It can truly be said that the Middle Kingdom has lost the Dharma.
(The "Middle Kingdom" refers here to India; the "four directions" refer to China. Later, he returned to Mount Tai, where he wore coarse robes and lived upon a single bed.
He instructed others through his own person, never wearying even in his old age. Amidst the times of great war and famine, his students became ever more numerous. As they gazed toward his hall...
He took the chamber as his refuge. On the fifth day of the second month in the third year of the Zhongzhong era, he manifested illness at Fulong.
He addressed his disciples, saying: "The Way has no fixed direction; nature has no substance. Whether one is born or dies, the underlying principle is one and the same.
I shall leave my bones upon this mountain, for tonight my retribution is exhausted. I wish to discuss the Way with you all before parting. Indeed, in a single thought..."
Mutual relativity is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The non-deficiency of phenomena is called the provisional (*prajñapti*). Neither identical nor different is called the middle (*madhyama*).
As mundane factors, they are the three causes; as transcendental factors, they are the three virtues. Like a burning wick, the beginning and end share the same nature;
like crossing the sea, the shallow and deep flow into one stream. Self-benefit and benefiting others consist in this alone. You should bear this in mind. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
He passed away at the age of seventy-two, the forty-third year of the Xianqing era. His disciples enshrined his entire remains in a stupa in the southwestern corner of the burial grounds of Zhiyi.
The Kings of Wu and Yue posthumously conferred upon him the title "Venerable Yuan-tong" (Perfectly Penetrating).
(The biography of Master Hong-chuan concludes. △ Subsequently, the general classification into three major sections follows.

Looking up with reverence to our Buddha, who responded to the various capacities and conditions of sentient beings, he established two modes of teaching: the "Scattered Flower" (Pṛṣṭapadā) and the "Stringed Flower" (Saṃghātapadā).

Those who compiled the scriptures transmitted them according to these teachings, while those who composed treatises expounded upon them based on the sūtras; yet neither followed a fixed structural format.

Ancient lecturers merely propagated the broad principles of the meaning without dividing the text into chapters and sections, following the precedent of Master Kumārajīva’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. If one were to employ this method exclusively...
[The Master] said: "Later generations initially did not understand how [the text] begins and ends.

Vasubandhu composed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*, dividing it into seven sections of merit for the Introductory Chapter (*Nidāna-parivarta*) and five sections of manifestation for the Chapter on Expedient Means (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*); the remaining chapters each have their own designated places.

Formerly, [Master] Ping of Hexi and [Master] Yao of Jiangdong adopted this principle to annotate the scriptural text; from that point on, it gradually became more elaborate, and at Guangzhai Monastery, it was further [expanded]."
Subtle. Thick mists shroud the Great Clarity (*taiqing*), causing the three luminaries to dim their brilliance; this is what those who seek the Way do not value. Tánluán said:

"Fine incense smoke rises, mingled with the dust of coarse grit. This is like being excessive or falling short; it is simply that among human sentiments, the orchid and the chrysanthemum each excel in their own beauty.
Those of later generations should not engage in disputes of right and wrong, for such things offer no benefit of the three virtues (*sanyì*).
The "one Way" and the "three benefits" refer to the three *siddhāntas*, such as the worldly and so forth; the "one Way" refers to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.

Only the three divisions of introduction, main body, and dissemination have been clearly distinguished by the Great Celestial [Kumārajīva], and are followed alike by both the ancients and the moderns.
This scripture consists of one fascicle and twenty-eight chapters.
The Great Master Zhi (Zhiyi) divided the text according to this [principle]: the first chapter is designated as the Introduction (*nidāna*);
from the "Expedient Means" chapter up to the nineteenth line of the verse on the "Distinction of Merits," comprising fifteen and a half chapters, is named the "Correct Teaching" (*bhūta-deśanā*);

from the verse following that until the end of the sutra, comprising eleven and a half chapters, is named the "Circulation" (*pariṇāmanā*). Furthermore, it can be divided into two parts at one time: from the "Introduction" chapter up to the "Peaceful Practices" chapter.
There are fourteen chapters. From the "Emergence from the Earth" up to the end of these fourteen chapters, the provisional is opened and the real is revealed according to the Trace Gate (*jìmén*).
Each of the two—Trace and Origin—has its own introduction, main body, and dissemination. In the Trace Gate, the first chapter serves as the introduction.

The *Upāya* (Expedient Means) chapter concludes with the bestowal of predictions upon those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); these eight chapters constitute the "Correct" section.

The Dharma Master [notes that] the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices) chapter concludes with the fifth chapter as the "Circulation" section. The "Emergence from the Earth" in the Original Gate concludes with Maitreya having already asked about this matter;

the Buddha now answers him. The first half of the chapter is titled the "Introduction. From "The Buddha addressed Ajita" onwards, it concludes with the nineteenth chapter, the *Funbetsukudoku-hon* (Chapter on the Distinction of Merits).
The verses of practice are called the "Correct Teaching" (zhengzong). From the end of these verses through the end of the sutra, eleven chapters and a half constitute the "Circulation" (liutong).

The first three sections combine two gates to form the "Correct Teaching. Furthermore, the subsequent portion is divided into the two gates of "Traces" (ji) and "Essence" (ben), each consisting of three parts.

This section clearly elucidates the principles of the provisional and the real, and the original and the manifested, through two gates, so that the structural connections may be distinct and the beginning and end may be understood.

Now, based on this, we shall interpret the text. First, it asks: "How can there be two introductory sections in a single sutra? The answer is: "The *Avataṃsaka* gathers assemblies at every stage; the *Āgama* does likewise in every chapter;

and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* entrusts [the teaching] both before and after [its main body]. None of these contradict [the principle of a single sutra]; thus, one sutra has two [introductions]."
What prevents [the inclusion of] the introduction? Why are the five meanings not established in the present "Root Gate"? It is because the Root Gate is not the primary beginning.

The "Trace Gate" consists solely of the single section on the circulation [of the teaching], meaning it contains the exhortation to uphold [the Dharma] but lacks the entrustment, because the preaching of the Dharma has not yet concluded.
This is merely the meaning of "existence" and "non-existence. (The general judgment of the three sections of the major outline is concluded. (The first three segments of the sutra are concluded.
△ First, the title of the chapter is presented; second, the text of the sutra is explained. Now, for the first [part]:
The Preface to the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, Chapter One.
The title of the sutra has been briefly explained as before; now the title of the chapter shall be explained. Regarding the term "Preface" (序), there are three meanings: namely, sequence.

The five matters, such as the "Preface" (由), are placed at the beginning of the sutra to establish the sequence. The six auspicious omens of the emission of light constitute the opening of the inspiration;
this is the Preface (由序). The questions and answers that resolve doubts serve as the prologue to the main exposition;

this is the Narrative (述序). Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the "Preface" (序). As for "Chapter" (品), the Sanskrit term is *varga*, which is translated here as "chapter. It refers to a category of similar meaning.

A "chapter" (*p'in*) is so named because [the contents] are gathered together in one place. Sometimes the Buddha himself proclaims a chapter, as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (The Brahma’s Net Sutra on the Ground of the Mind).

Sometimes it is established by the compilers, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Sometimes it is added by the translators, as when Kumārajīva translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* into ninety chapters.
Now, this "Chapter on the Original Acts of Bhaiṣajyarāja" was proclaimed by the Buddha; [the following] "Ghoṣadatta... [is not].
Avalokiteśvara and others are the compilers; the translators have not heard [of them] at the beginning of the various chapters, hence it says "the first.

△ Next, the explanation of the scriptural text has two parts: first, clarifying the four modes of interpretation: 1. causal conditions (nidāna); 2. according to the teaching (yathā-śāsana); 3. original and manifested traces (honji-suijaku).
Fourth, the Contemplation of the Mind. From the beginning with "Thus" (evam) to the end with "and then withdrew" (vyavalokayati sma), all [passages] are explained through four intentions;

however, I shall now record them briefly—sometimes three, two, or one—valuing the attainment of the meaning rather than burdening the reader with excessive script. Question: If it is to be brief, then let there be only one.
If it were not for these four [extremes], why would this be so? The answer is: if it were too extensive, it would cause wisdom to regress;

if it were too concise, the meaning would not be comprehensive. I shall now speak with moderation, so that the meaning may be easily understood. As for "causes and conditions" (*nidāna*), they are also called "stimulus and response" (*ganying*).

If sentient beings lack the capacity (*indriya*), they will not perceive even what is near. Through the power of the roots of goodness of compassion, there is a stimulus that leads to spontaneous communication. Thus, the path of stimulus and response intersects. Therefore...

This is explained by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), according to the fourfold intention (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*). Regarding the teaching (*yāna*): in establishing teachings according to the capacities of beings, there are naturally differences in provisional and ultimate, shallow and deep.
This present sutra opens up the previous four flavors so that they all return to the *amṛta* (the "ghee" of the highest truth), causing one to see the moon and forget the finger [pointing at it].

Therefore, I shall explain this by means of the abbreviated teaching (*yōkyō*). Regarding "original" (*hon*) and "trace" (*jaku*): long-term accomplishment is the original; short-term accomplishment is the trace.

As for the intermediate original and trace, they are mutually related through successive stages. Here, we discuss only the opening of today’s trace to reveal the original of the initial accomplishment.

Therefore, I explain this by means of the "root" (the fundamental) and the "trace" (the manifestation). As for "contemplating the mind": if one pursues the traces, the traces are vast and one merely exhausts oneself;
if one pursues the root, the root is sublime and its sublimity is beyond limit. This is like counting another's treasures while having not even half a coin of one's own.

One should instead contemplate the height and breadth of one's own mind, thereby striking a resonance with the infinite response of the Sage. When the capacity is perfected, it leads to a spiritual response, whereby one attains one's own benefit. Thus, I employ [this method].
This is an explanation through the contemplation of the mind (*citta*). However, each of the preceding four teachings possesses its own dharma-gate for the contemplation of the mind;

after their revelation and clarification, they all converge in the Perfect Vehicle (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). Their essential principle is the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), namely, the mind of a single momentary thought.
The "three thousand" are fully present; they are precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Furthermore, there is the meaning of "each possessing" and "mutually possessing.

To take even a single phenomenon as an example, it is the vast totality of the dharma-realm. Through mutual possession and individual possession, through mutual fusion and mutual inclusion, they are intermingled yet not confused, distinct yet not divided.
Unity and multiplicity are sovereign, without obstructing one another. Thus, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "The student..."
Even if one knows that the inner mind possesses the three thousand [worlds] (in the sense of individual possession), one does not know that my mind pervades those three thousand worlds.

It is likewise for each of those three thousand worlds to mutually pervade one another (in the sense of mutual possession). [Regarding "each of those": it refers to each respective Buddha and each respective birth; thus, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings all possess both the meaning of individual possession and the meaning of mutual possession.]
It is like the jewels in Indra’s net, mutually penetrating, harmoniously integrated, and infinitely layered.
Yet, the reason this single thought-moment is able to be thus is that cultivation arises entirely from the nature, and cultivation is itself entirely the nature. Therefore, Siming said:
"The inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm acts as my single thought-moment; likewise, it functions with its entire essence as the nine realms of sentient beings."

To act as the Buddha (the Buddha-realm), to act as the support (the receptacle world), and to act as the correctness (the world of the five aggregates). This constitutes one fascicle of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).

To these are added the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), totaling sixteen moments of mind. Thus, they comprise thirty-four moments of mind. In the case of Śrāvakas, the delusions of vision and thought are severed sequentially, both before and after [the path of vision]. Although Pratyekabuddhas sever the delusions of vision and thought instantaneously, their residual habits are not yet exhausted. Therefore...

In all cases, one may not yet discuss the thirty-four moments of mind; it is only when the Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka reaches the foot of the King of Trees, and both cultivation and realization are fully exhausted, that one may then discuss them. Thus, one comes to know the mundane and the supramundane.

The general and specific characteristics: awakening to the mundane world is the realization of suffering and its origin; awakening to the supramundane is the realization of the path and its cessation. One is also able to awaken others.

are those who, through the Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others, universally manifest only the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*, sitting upon a lotus pedestal and receiving the office of a Buddha.

The Dharma-realm is without discrimination; this is precisely the meaning [of the passage].
