Therefore, each of the thirty-two marks is boundless, which constitutes the 'Exalted Form' (zunte) and is also the Dharma-body. Thus, the Dragon Girl’s praise says: 'The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks.

Regarding the three aspects of origin (*hon*) and manifestation (*soku*): one Buddha is the origin, while the three Buddhas are the three manifestations (this refers to the essence and function within the origin). In the middle, he manifests...
The manifestations—repeatedly proclaiming arising and proclaiming ceasing—are all *traces* (*ji*). Only the four Buddhas of the Original Ground (*ben-di*) are all the *root* (*ben*).
(In the traces, both essence and function are traces; in the root, both essence and function are the root. Regarding the explanation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*):

contemplating the mind produced by causes and conditions as first empty, then provisional, and finally the Middle is partial awakening (*bian-jue*). Contemplating the mind as simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously the Middle is perfect (*yuan*) awakening.
This concludes the fourfold explanation of "Awakened" (Buddha). First, the explanation of "Abiding" (*sthita*) by way of causes and conditions:

there is that which abides, the act of abiding, and the place where one abides. The place where one abides is the royal city of this Sahā world. That which abides refers to the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) remaining in the world without yet passing away; this is the world itself.

Furthermore, "abiding" refers to proceeding toward the ten paths of wholesome action and dwelling within the four dhyānas; this is the person. Furthermore, "abiding"— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "Furthermore, 'abiding'".)
"Those who abide" refers to abiding in the three samādhis; this is the counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*). Furthermore, "abiding" refers to abiding in the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi];

this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Next, regarding the classification by teaching: the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka develops true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) through the gate of analytical negation and abides in the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha of the Shared Teaching develops true outflow-free wisdom through the gate of essence and abides in the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

The *p'an* (separate) Buddha enters and abides in the secret treasury through the gate of sequential progression (*anupūrva-mukha*). The *yuan* (perfect) Buddha enters and abides in the secret treasury through the gate of non-sequential progression (*ananupūrva-mukha*).
In the abiding of the former three Buddhas, both the subject (*neng*) and object (*suo*) are coarse; in the abiding of the latter one Buddha, both the subject and object are subtle.
This present sutra concerns the perfect Buddha, who abides in this subtle dwelling. Regarding the three aspects of origin and trace (*benji*): the Buddha of the Tripitaka...
They should enter *nirvāṇa*. Yet, out of compassion, they manifest traces and dwell in this world in their birth-bodies (*janmakāya*).

The Universal Buddha (*sambhogakāya*) fulfills his vows and, through compassion, assists remaining habitual tendencies to deliver sentient beings and perform buddha-works. Both the Distinct and Perfect Buddhas are permeated by the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) through compassion;

because they pity sentient beings, they manifest responses throughout the *dharmadhātu*. One should know that these four types of buddhas abide in the dwelling of the fundamental Buddha; because of their compassion, they abide therein.
The royal city of the Sahā world maintains its majestic deportment in the world; this is called "abiding by traces. Regarding the four ways of contemplating the mind:
one contemplates abiding within an object—whether it be the object of impermanence, or the objects of emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle Way.

Because one abides within these objects by means of the dharma of non-abiding, it is called "abiding" (the term "non-abiding" applies to all four teachings; from the perspective of coarse cognition, one speaks of "abiding," yet in reality there is no such thing. If situated within the Perfect Teaching, it becomes the absolute beyond all relativity).
The fourfold explanation of the dwelling is concluded. 1. Explanation of Rājagṛha by way of its causes and conditions: In India, it is called Rājagṛha-kāla.
"Rājagṛha" means "King’s Abode" (Wángshè); "kāla" means "city. The name of the country is Magadha, which means "Non-Harming" (Bùhài).
When there are those with offenses, they are sent into the Śīrṣavana forest; there is no law of corporal punishment or execution. It is also...
It is named Magadha; this is translated in Chinese as Tiānló (天羅). It is the name of the king who founded the kingdom, and the country is named after its ruler.

Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain is translated as "Numinous Vulture Peak" (Língjiù). Both former and later Buddhas all resided upon this mountain. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Arhats would dwell there; when the Dharma perishes, Pratyekabuddhas will dwell there;
and if there are no Pratyekabuddhas, spirits and deities will dwell there. Next, regarding the classification by teaching: during the Semblance Dharma (Saddharma-pratirūpaka),...
The *Jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts) states: "The entire great assembly perceives things differently.
Some see the Śāla forest as being entirely composed of earth, sand, grass, wood, stones, and cliffs; others see it as pure and adorned with the seven treasures;
some see this forest as the place where the Buddhas of the three periods of time have traveled; and others see this forest as being inconceivable."
The true dharma-body of all Buddhas should be understood through this principle. As the four views differ, so too do that which is inhabited and that which inhabits.

Regarding the three aspects of the fundamental and the manifested: the fundamental resides on the mountain of Great Nirvāṇa endowed with the three virtues, while the manifested dwells at Vulture Peak.

Furthermore, there is a Vulture Peak for both the fundamental (hon) and the trace (jaku). Regarding the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, it says: "Constantly dwelling on Vulture Peak" refers to the fundamental;
"manifesting appearance and disappearance" refers to the trace. Regarding the interpretation of the mountain through the four contemplations of the mind (*kanjin*):

if one contemplates that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is insentient like a mountain, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like the spirit, and the other three aggregates are like the vultures, then contemplating this Vulture Peak as impermanent is analytical contemplation (*keshikan*). Contemplating this...

"Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) is emptiness; this is the contemplation of the essence (*tattva*). "Contemplating the Gṛdhra" is the wisdom-nature as the *vidyā-hetu* (enlightening cause); this is the adornment of wisdom.
"The Vulture" is the accumulation of conditions as the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause); this is the adornment of merit. "The Mountain" is the *dharmatā* as the *samyag-hetu* (correct cause).
These three dharmas are unmoving and are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). Abiding therein oneself, one also uses it to deliver others. As the subsequent text says: "The Buddha himself..."
"Dwelling in the Mahāyāna" refers to the two contemplations of the Distinct and the Perfect (the fourfold explanation of the Buddha dwelling in Rājagṛha is thus concluded).

Regarding "in the middle": the Buddha dwells in the Middle Way without abiding; ascending to the heavens, appearing as the sun at midday, descending to the central kingdom, and passing away at midnight—all these symbolize the Middle Way.
Now, being situated in the mountains, he preaches the Middle Way. (This concludes the first explanation of the four phrases beginning with "Thus have I heard.")

The matter is concluded). △ Second, the explanation of the fifth assembly, those who hear and uphold [the Dharma], has two parts: first, the listing of the assembly; second, the summary. The listing of the assembly has three parts:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas; second, the assembly of bodhisattvas; third, the assembly of devas, nāgas, and others. Most sūtras follow this pattern.

The ancient [commentary] states: "There are matters and there are meanings. As for 'matters,' this refers to the proximity or distance of physical traces. Śrāvakas have forms that have emerged from the mundane net; their traces are near to those of the Tathāgata.

Since they realize the sūtras, they are considered proximate, and thus are listed first. Deva-mānuṣas have forms whose vehicles and attire differ; their traces do not consist of service and attendance.

Since they realize the sūtras only distantly, they are considered remote, and thus are listed later. Bodhisattvas have forms that are not constrained by formal decorum; their traces have no fixed location."
Since they are neither the same as the laity nor different from the monastic community, they dwell between them.

This meaning is that while *śrāvakas* delight in *nirvāṇa* and gods and humans are attached to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), each being partial to one side, the Bodhisattva neither delights in nor is attached to either; dwelling in the middle, they seek the ultimate principle.

Thus, they exist in the space between the two. The intent of the *Śāstra* is also like this. Now, regarding the first group, the assembly of *śrāvakas*, there are two parts: first, the assembly of *bhikṣus*; second...

Regarding the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are first two categories: first, those with many acquaintances; second, those with few acquaintances. Regarding the first, there are again three parts: first, citing examples to clarify the number;
second, clarifying their ranks and extolling their virtues; third, listing their names and providing a conclusion. Now, the first [part].
Together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus.
"With a great assembly of bhikṣus" indicates their general category; "twelve thousand" specifies their number.
"Shared" (*sādhāraṇa*) means having a common purpose. The *Śāstra* explains "shared" through seven points:

namely, one time (the world-truth), one place (the world-truth), one precept (the person-truth), one mind, one view (the remedial-truth), one path, and one liberation (the ultimate-truth). "Great" (*mahat*)—in Sanskrit, *mahā*;
here it is translated as "great," "many," or "superior. It refers to one whose capacity and measure are revered, such as a celestial king (*devendra*).
It is called "Great" because it is revered by great beings; it is called "Victorious" because it transcends the ninety-five types of heterodox paths;
it is called "Much" because it universally knows both internal and external scriptures, and furthermore, because its numerical count reaches twelve thousand.
Moreover, when examining the nature of the mind directly within this [teaching], it is vast and expansive like space, and is thus named "Great. It simultaneously negates both extremes.
He enters the ocean of quiescent extinction; therefore, he is called "Victorious" (*jina*). He simultaneously illuminates the two truths, containing and integrating many things;

within one mind are all minds; therefore, he is called "Many. *Bhikṣu* is the Qin (Chinese) term for "mendicant" (*yācaka*). It destroys afflictions, is able to maintain the precepts, and terrifies Māra, among other qualities. This single Indian name contains these four meanings.
Since there was no corresponding term in the Qin language to translate it, the original designation was retained. [The character] *bu* (怖) means "to fear" or "to terrify."
As for "Māra," Māra delights in birth and death. This person has left the household life and further transforms others so that they all depart from the three realms;

this runs counter to Māra’s intent, and thus Māra uses his power to restrain him, causing him instead to be bound by the five fetters. He does nothing but grieve and fear; therefore, he is said to "frighten Māra.
As for "destroying evil," those who have left the household life must necessarily destroy the seven evils of body and speech; therefore, he is said to "destroy evil. As for "mendicant" (bhikṣu):

Regarding this: there are three lawful ways for a householder to sustain their life—first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, service. For those who have left the household life, the Buddha did not permit these;

rather, they sustain themselves solely through begging. With their own bodies at ease, the Way is preserved, and they bring benefit and merit to their donors; therefore, they are called "mendicants" (bhikṣu).

These three meanings are mutually constitutive; this is precisely the meaning of *bhikṣu*. From the initial reception of the precepts, through the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one already possesses the three meanings of "one who destroys evil," "one who terrifies Māra," and "a mendicant.
It is not that these apply solely to the final moment of mind. According to the Sūtra masters, they merely praise the *bhikṣu* in his final state.
Regarding the term "assembly" (*saṃgha*): the Sanskrit word is *saṃgha*, which is translated here as "harmonious assembly. [An assembly consists of] one person, two persons, or three...
Individuals are not called the *saṃgha*; only when there are four or more people is it termed the *saṃgha*. In matters, they are harmonious and there is no division into separate groups;

in the Dharma, they are unified and there is no divergence in principle. The Buddha was constantly accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people, though in various sūtras the number is sometimes indefinite.
As for the "twelve thousand" mentioned in this present sūtra, these were originally twelve thousand bodhisattvas who manifested as such.
There are twelve thousand śrāvakas. As for "contemplating the mind," one contemplates the twelve *āyatanas*.

Each *āyatana* contains the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), and each realm contains ten realms, thus making one hundred realms. Within each realm are the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), thus making one thousand suchnesses.
Since each *āyatana* contains these one thousand suchnesses, the twelve *āyatanas* constitute twelve thousand dharma-gates. II. Explaining the Stages and Praising Their Virtues.
"All are Arhats" (up to) "having exhausted all fetters of existence, they have attained mastery of the mind.
"Arhat" is a stage of illumination. "With all outflows extinguished" is a praise of their virtues. Regarding "Arhat," some say it has no direct equivalent, yet it contains three meanings:
first, the meaning of non-arising, because they do not undergo further existence; second, the meaning of slaying the enemy, because they have severed [the defilements].

Because they have exhausted all views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa), this is the third meaning of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat): being capable of serving as a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra). This is the intent of both the Separate (Bie) and the Shared (Tong) Teachings.
As for the Distinct (Bie) and Complete (Yuan) Teachings, it is not merely the killing of the thief; one also kills that which is not a thief. That which is "not a thief" is Nirvana.

This, too, must be refuted. This is the meaning of "slayer of thieves" (the term "not a thief" refers to those who still derive their name from the Two Vehicles; if they are [still considered] thieves even in relation to the Perfect and Distinct [teachings], they must therefore be refuted).

Non-arising does not arise from arising, nor does it arise from non-arising. Being untainted is non-arising (taking the unconditioned as proof; arising exists outside the realms, whereas non-arising is arising, and thus it does not cause further birth).

It is not only that which is worthy of offerings, but also that which provides offerings (providing for what is appropriate is called "providing offerings," such as when a Buddha manifests as a practitioner to deliver offerings to forest-dwelling bhikṣus, etc.).
For one who contemplates the mind: the contemplation of emptiness is *prajñā* (wisdom); the contemplation of the provisional is *vimukti* (liberation); and the contemplation of the Middle is...

This is the Dharma-body. Furthermore, from the contemplation of entering emptiness through the provisional, up to the contemplation of the Middle Way, one slays the thief of ignorance and does not give rise to the mind of the two extremes.
To make offerings to such a person is equivalent to making offerings to the World-Honored One. The Vaipulya Sūtra says:
"To offer to the Buddha and Mañjuśrī is not as good as providing a single meal to sustain the body of one who practices the Vaipulya. This sūtra also speaks of both reviling and praising.

The Buddha replied: "The merit and demerit of [merely] slandering or praising the Buddha are still light. However, the demerit and merit of slandering or praising one who upholds this sutra are extremely grave.

Why is this? The Buddha has no thought of food; having long since departed from the eight winds (aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ), he is neither benefited nor harmed by them. But for one who upholds this sutra, to bestow upon them material gifts preserves their physical body and sustains their karmic life, while giving rise to the Dharma-body and increasing their life of wisdom—therefore, it is beneficial.
To slander such a person causes them grief, affliction, and regret, and may lead to the loss of their excellence."

When that time comes, it can no longer be remedied; thus, there is great loss. The two phrases "all outflows are exhausted" and "there are no further afflictions" praise the virtue of being a slayer of thieves.
The phrase "having attained one's own benefit" praises the virtue of being a Worthy One (Arhat).
The causes and effects of the three realms are all termed "other," while the merits of wisdom and abandonment are all termed "one's own benefit.

Because one is fully endowed with this personal benefit, one becomes an Arhat (Worthy of Offerings). The two phrases, "having exhausted the fetters of existence" and "attaining mastery of mind," praise the virtue of non-arising.
"Existences" refers to the twenty-five places of birth. "Knots" refers to the twenty-five causes of birth.

When the mind is sovereign, wisdom is necessarily sovereign; one who is fully endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom is a person of "liberation through both. △ Third, listing the names and providing a summary.
Their names are Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (and so on, up to) the Great Arhats.

First, their names are listed; twenty-one venerable ones are briefly cited. Although all the Buddha’s disciples were fully endowed with manifold practices, they concealed their perfect capabilities and each was designated by a name based on a single virtue.
This was done merely to accommodate those who had particular inclinations.
Kauṇḍinya is his clan name; it translates as "Fire-Vessel" (Agnikula). He was of the Brahmin caste, and his ancestors served the sacrificial fire, from which his lineage derived its name.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, as for those who are broad-minded, compassionate, and widely learned, Kauṇḍinya is the first to have received the flavor of the Dharma" (this is according to the *loka-siddhānta*).
Indeed, when one lies in a long sleep through the vast night, no one can awaken them; yet the sun...
Before the light has emerged, the morning star appears first. Kauṇḍinya was the first to attain the wisdom of non-arising; he is like the morning star at the beginning of all luminosity.
Among the intellectual luminosities of all people, none preceded Kauṇḍinya; in breaking through darkness, nothing surpasses the morning star.
In the extinction of the darkness of all people, none preceded Kauṇḍinya; therefore, he is named Ajñāta (The One Who Knows). (This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*. Great!
The son entered the mountains to study the Way. His father, the king, dispatched five men to follow and attend him: two were from his mother’s kin and three from his father’s kin.
Two of them held that sensual desire was purity; three held that asceticism was purity. While the Prince was practicing austerities, [the five men remained with him].
The two men abandoned him and departed. The Prince abandoned his ascetic practices and accepted food, drink, ghee, and warm water; the three men again abandoned him and departed.
When the Prince attained the Way, he first preached the Four Noble Truths to the five men. Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya was the first to declare his understanding.
Therefore, he is named Ājñāta (One Who Has Fully Understood). [Supplementary Note: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"At that time, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha: 'I am now the elder among this great assembly, and alone have I earned the name of "Understanding.

This was because I realized the two characters "guest" (*āgantuka*) and "dust" (*rajas*) and thereby achieved fruition. World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who stays at an inn, either lodging there or eating there.'"
Having finished the evening meal, one packs for the journey ahead and finds no leisure to remain settled. If one were truly the host, there would be no reason to depart.
Reflecting thus, "not remaining" is called being a guest, while "remaining" is called being the host; therefore, that which does not remain is defined by the meaning of being a guest.
Furthermore, it is like after a fresh clearing of rain, when the clear sun rises in the sky and its light enters through a crack in a wall, illuminating all things within the void.

There are characteristics of dust (*rajas*). The substance of dust wavers and moves, while empty space (*ākāśa*) is tranquil and still. Reflecting in this way, that which is clear and still is called "space," and that which wavers and moves is called "dust.
That which wavers and moves is given the meaning of "dust. The Buddha said: "It is so. The guest is dust; the host is space.

These are the Four Noble Truths. The guest is suffering (*duḥkha*); dust is the origin (*samudaya*). The host is the path (*mārga*); space is cessation (*nirodha*'). Formerly, the Great Master Zhiyi faced west and prostrated himself, seeking to behold the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Because he could not obtain it, he departed from here.
Mahākāśyapa—this is translated as "Great Kauruṣya," also translated as "Radiant Wave," and also translated as "Drinker of Light. His name was Piṇḍola;
his wife's name was Bhadrā. His family was immensely wealthy, ten thousand times richer than King Bimbisāra. The sixteen...

The kingdom had no neighbors with whom it could form an alliance; fearing that it might incur the punishment of a superior king, it reduced its plowing by one furrow, using only nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of oxen and golden plows.
Furthermore, a sutra states: In that household there were woolen cloths (*karpāsa*), even the lowest grade of which was worth a hundred thousand taels of gold.
If these were driven into the ground seven feet deep with nails, the cloth would not be pierced or torn, remaining exactly as it was. [This was] entrusted.
Dharmākara said: After the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the golden images and stupas became worn and damaged. At that time, there was a poor woman who obtained a gold bead by begging.

She requested a craftsman to fashion it into a thin plate. The goldsmith was delighted; once he had finished polishing and restoring the Buddha image, he made a vow to remain a lifelong celibate couple.
For ninety-one kalpas, throughout their lives among humans and in the heavens, their bodies were always golden in color and their minds always experienced [bliss].
Because he was joyful, when the gods requested the compilation of the scriptures, they praised him, saying: "The Elder has already eliminated desire, anger, and pride;
his form is like a pillar of purple-gold, majestic from top to bottom and incomparably sublime; his eyes are clear and pure like a lotus."

He abandoned his family estate and his golden-hued wife to leave the household life. He took a priceless robe and cut it into pieces to make a saṃghāṭī of four folds, which he offered to the Buddha as a seat.
Having made such threefold offerings, he was without peer in the world. The Buddha bestowed upon him the paṃsukūla-cīvara;
this robe is the great robe of the Great Sage, yet it is also very coarse and heavy. Therefore, Kāśyapa said: "I have received it..."

Regarding the Buddha’s robes, one should maintain the perception of them as the Teacher and the perception of them as a stupa; they must never be used as a pillow for the head, much less as a cover while lying down.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that among those who practice the twelve *dhūta* ascetic practices within the Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost.
In Sanskrit, *dhūta* means "to shake off"; it refers to shaking off twelve kinds of faults. The first is dwelling in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage).
1. Dwelling in seclusion, one avoids the fault of clamor and bustle. 2. Constantly practicing alms-gathering, one avoids the faults of eating within the monastic community and accepting invitations.
3. Practicing sequential alms-gathering, one avoids the fault of selective picking. 4. Adopting the practice of eating only once a day, one avoids the fault of excessive seeking.

Fifth, moderation in eating, which avoids the fault of craving flavors. Sixth, not drinking fruit juices, honey-water, or similar beverages after midday, which avoids the fault of seeking sensory desires.
Seventh, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), which avoids the fault of desiring fine garments. Eighth, possessing only the three robes (*tricīvara*), which avoids the faults of increase or decrease.
Ninth, dwelling among burial mounds (*śmāśānika*), which avoids the fault of the inverted attachment to permanence and pleasure. Tenth, staying under trees (*vṛkṣamūlika*).
10. One who dwells in a secluded place is free from the fault of fear. 11. One who sits in the open air is free from the fault of craving for trees. 12.
One who always sits and does not lie down is free from the thieves of affliction. These are explained in detail as in the *Dvādaśadhūta-sūtra*.

Five are rules concerning the dwelling place, five are rules concerning food, and two are rules concerning clothing. When the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he entrusted them with the True Dharma Eye.
He concealed it and entrusted its transmission and preservation to others, commanding that it never be allowed to be interrupted; thus he became the first patriarch of India.

Furthermore, having transmitted the golden-threaded *saṃghāṭī* robe and completed the entrustment of the Dharma to Ānanda, he took this robe and entered into meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda, awaiting the descent of Maitreya.
Uruvilvā: this translates as "Pumpkin Grove. ○ Nadi: this translates as "River" or also as "Stream. ○ Gayā: this translates as "City.

These three brothers were all non-Buddhist practitioners who worshipped fire. The circumstances [of their conversion] appear in the *Śrī-mālā-devī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (Ruiying jing) and various Vinaya texts.
Regarding the interpretation according to the teachings (*jiao*), the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: Uruvilvā...
Nanda is foremost in being able to protect the fourfold assembly and provide them with the four requisites so that they lack for nothing; he is the most preeminent.

Nadi is foremost in having a tranquil mind and subduing all fetters through diligence. Gaya is foremost in skillfully teaching and transforming others by contemplating all phenomena and remaining entirely without attachment.
These constitute the instructional intent within the stage of curd. If one proceeds further toward birth...
Regarding ghee (*sarpis*): one should then feel shame for the small and aspire to the great; this principle may be understood by analogy.

If it transforms into clarified butter (*pakvasarpis*), one should then diligently attend to one's duties and receive the teachings. If it transforms into the finest cream (*sarpirmaṇḍa*), it is like receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood within such a sutra.
Śāriputra—this is translated as "Son of the Body" (Shenzi) and is also called "Pearl" (Zhuzi). His name, Upatiṣya, manifests his father's virtue;
it is translated as "Discourse on Meaning" (Lunyi). He was foremost in wisdom. At the age of sixteen, he had thoroughly mastered all the classics and texts of Jambudvīpa.
There was no field of learning with which he was not proficient. Among the sixteen great nations, he was peerless in debate;
throughout the five regions of India, he was considered the foremost. He served the brahmin Śāriputra as his teacher, and Śāriputra mastered all the brahmin’s arts and sciences.
One day, he saw the bhikṣu Aśvajit, whose dignified deportment was orderly and composed. Consequently, he inquired about the Master’s Dharma. Aśvajit replied: "All phenomena arise from conditions."

"Birth. Therefore, the causes and conditions, these phenomena, their objects, and their exhaustion—thus my Teacher has spoken. Upon hearing this once, he immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
He came to the Buddha’s presence and, within seven days, thoroughly mastered the ocean-deep depths of the Buddha-dharma. It is further said:
Fifteen days later, he attained arhatship. He became the attendant to the Upādhyāya Rāhula and the teacher to Kauṇḍinya.
Among the assembly of Śrāvakas, he was the disciple on the right side. When Devadatta split the Saṃgha and led away five hundred bhikṣus, Śāriputra went to convert them, and they all returned.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states that Śāriputra is the mother who gave birth to the fourfold assembly, while Maudgalyāyana is...
The foster mother’s son, Śāriputra, asked Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: "Virtuous one, what is your name? How do those who practice the holy life address you? He replied:
"My father's name is Pūrṇa and my mother's name is Maitrāyaṇī; therefore, those who practice the holy life address me as 'Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra'.
Śāriputra praised him, saying: "Excellent, virtuous Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! As a disciple of the Tathāgata, you possess wisdom, eloquence, and intelligence."
He is resolute, secure, and fearless; he has attained great eloquence and obtained the banner of the Deathless (amṛta).

Having realized the Deathless for himself, those who encounter him obtain great benefit. Fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) should wrap their robes around him and carry him upon their heads like a crown.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "Venerable one, what is your name? How do fellow practitioners address you? He replied: "My father’s name was Upatiṣya."
"Tiṣya, my mother’s name was Śārī; therefore, I am called Śāriputra. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra sighed and said:
"Now, while debating with the disciples of the Buddha, he does not know [the answer]. He debates with the second World-Honored One and does not know.
He debates with the General of the Dharma and does not know. He debates with those who have turned the wheel of the Dharma and again with the disciples who turn it..."
To debate without understanding—if I were to know this Venerable One, I would not be able to answer even a single phrase, let alone such a profound discourse.
Excellent, excellent! To be a disciple of the Tathāgata is such a thing that one should wrap one’s robe around one’s head as a crown.

When the Buddha spoke a single phrase, Śāriputra took it as his fundamental basis; for seven days and seven nights he uttered the lion’s roar, producing ever more diverse phrases and diverse meanings.
How could it ever be exhausted? This is especially true since the Buddha has spoken so extensively; how then could the wisdom and eloquence of Śāriputra ever reach its end? Regarding the teaching:

the wisdom of the Tripitaka consists of the ten knowledges of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Having severed the fetters and realized the truth, he assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation.
The *Śāstra* refers to him as the "Great General on the Right. As for the wisdom of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika*), it is as described in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

He speaks of himself as a *mahāsattva* because he has destroyed such views as the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a Buddha (*buddha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of awakening (*bodhi-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana-dṛṣṭi*); for this reason, he is called a *mahāsattva*. This wisdom differs from the initial teaching.
From the very beginning, it is like hearing that when a cow eats the grass of patience (*kṣānti-tṛṇa*), it immediately produces clarified butter (*ghṛta*). If one is able to consume it...
All illnesses are eliminated, and all medicinal herbs enter therein. To cultivate this practice is precisely the wisdom of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Regarding "Original and Traces" (*benji*): the Original resides in the True Reality (*shixiang*), taking the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its mother.
Wisdom arises from the objective realm; the realm is the body, and wisdom is the child. Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Trace manifests as the body of the five flavors.
Son, wishing to transform the foul blood of afflictions into the wholesome milk of virtue, you manifested as a teacher of external paths and a great master of treatises;
wishing to boil that milk into curd, you manifested the wisdom of the Tripiṭaka and served as a second Buddha;
wishing to extract butter from the curd, you displayed the small while concealing the great and accepted the humiliation of Vimalakīrti; and wishing to refine that butter into clarified butter...

Clarified butter (*ghṛta*) comforts and benefits those who practice the same *brahmacarya*. Regarding the teachings received in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he desired to extract the matured butter (*navanīta*) to produce the finest cream (*sarpis*).

At the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he attained awakening and received his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). All of these were external manifestations within his traces (*tyakti*), while his fundamental ground (*mūlabhūmi*) remained secret;

yet in reality, this has been so for a long time. As for the contemplation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*): through the three contemplations within a single mind, one encompasses all wisdom. Thus one contemplates.

Because the mind is itself emptiness, one attains the wisdom of curd. Because one contemplates that the mind is itself provisional, one attains the wisdom of the two types of clarified butter (*sarpis*) as well as worldly wisdom.
Because one contemplates that the mind is itself the Middle Way, one attains the wisdom of the finest clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
This is called, within the contemplation of the mind, the single wisdom that is all wisdom, all wisdom that is single wisdom, and neither single wisdom nor all wisdom.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana is his clan name; it is translated as "Praise and Recitation. In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is translated as "radish. Paramārtha states that *mudgara* is translated here as "pea";
both of these items were favored by ancient seers (*ṛṣi*), and thus he took them as the names for his lineage. The *Śāstra* says:
"Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent and wisdom, while Maudgalyāyana was held in high regard for his noble spirit and refinement; their intellectual arts were thus complementary."
In comparison, their virtuous conduct is mutually identical. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Among my disciples, as for those who possess the supernatural power of levitation and can fly to the ten directions, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost. The *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 41, refers to him as the "left-hand disciple."
Five hundred followers of a non-Buddhist teacher used incantations to attempt to move the mountain. After one month had passed, the mountain began to wobble.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "If this mountain moves, much harm will be done. He then sat cross-legged in mid-air at the summit of the mountain, and the mountain returned to its place, unmoved.
The non-Buddhists said to one another, "The mountain of our doctrine has moved; we calculated that it would surely shift by now. Why is this?"
"An-gu (Ānanda) has returned to his former state; this must surely be the work of a śramaṇa.

Recognizing the weakness of his own powers, he has taken refuge in the Buddha-dharma and caused immeasurable people to leave the household life in accordance with the True Dharma. Jīvaka—this is translated as 'Solid Life'—was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When a disciple of Maudgalyāyana fell ill, Jīvaka traveled there by means of his supernatural power to inquire after him. He encountered various devas leaving the gardens to play."

The deities remained in their chariots without alighting, merely joining their palms in reverence. Maudgalyāyana stopped them, whereupon the monk Daoyi said, "The devas enjoy such pleasures that they are so preoccupied they have no leisure to look at one another.
Venerable One, what do you seek? He then explained his purpose for coming in detail. The deity replied:
Fasting was the essential requirement. Maudgalyāyana released him, and the chariot was finally able to move forward.

Śakra, having won the battle against the asuras, constructed the Hall of Victory, a seven-jeweled pavilion of extraordinary splendor. Its beams, pillars, and structural joints were each capable of accommodating a single thread;
though they did not touch one another, they were able to support each other. Such is the wondrous power of celestial merit. Maudgalyāyana then flew away.
They went. Śakra, leading Maudgalyāyana, went to view the hall. All the celestial maidens were ashamed to be seen by Maudgalyāyana;
they all hid and fled, refusing to come out. Maudgalyāyana thought that Śakra was attached to pleasure and did not cultivate the root of the Path.

He immediately manifested a transformation in which the Hall of Victory was set ablaze, collapsing in a brilliant conflagration. Thereupon, he extensively expounded impermanence to Śakra, who rejoiced. Later, the hall...
He stands solemnly, without the color of ash or smoke. In the past, he once assisted a pratyekabuddha by shaving his head, washing and dyeing his robes, and sewing his *kāṣāya*.
He made a vow to attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). As for his fundamental reality (*honjaku*):

fundamentally, he dwells in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), able in a single thought-moment to respond universally throughout the ten directions, manifesting in various ways to perform the work of a Buddha. Out of compassion, he appears as a trace-manifestation (*e*).

This constitutes the supernormal power of the five flavors, which leads one to enter the ultimate. Regarding the contemplation of the mind: when contemplating the single mind, suddenly all minds appear;
when contemplating all minds, suddenly no minds exist. Since the mind is neither existent nor non-existent, one penetrates to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Mahākātyāyana is translated here as "Textual Ornament" (*vyañjana-alaṃkāra*). It should also be called "Fan-rope" (*śaṅkha*) or "Fine Shoulder.
All these are names derived from his clan. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In skillfully discerning meanings and expounding the teachings of the Way, Kātyāyana is foremost.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* says: "There was a non-Buddhist who held the view of annihilationism, asserting that there is no other world."
In this world, there are ten rounds of questions and answers. The non-Buddhist says, "There is no other world.
The Buddha replies, "If there were no other world, there would be no tomorrow. Again he asks, "I see people die and not return; how can you say they undergo suffering?"
"Therefore, we know there is no other world. He replied, "Suppose a criminal is being detained; would he be able to return? He asked again, "If one were born in heaven, why would they not return?
"Therefore, we know there is no other world. He replied, "It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine and managed to get out."
"Would you be willing to enter the latrine once more? He replied, "Furthermore, one day in heaven corresponds to a hundred years here.

Having been born there for only three or five days, I have not yet had the leisure to turn my heart toward it. Even if someone were to turn their heart toward it, by the time they did so, you would already have passed away;

how then could they know of it? He asked again, "I have seen the cauldrons used to boil sinners, with their lids sealed tight; even when I waited, I saw no spirit emerge. Thus I know there is nothing else."
The worldling replied: "When you sleep during the day, does a person standing by your side see your spirit depart? He asked again:
"I have flayed the skin of the dead, cut their flesh into pieces, and crushed their bones, yet I could not find their spirit. Therefore, I know there is no other world. The other replied: "..."
"It is like a child splitting firewood: if one splits it inch by inch, how could fire ever be obtained from it?

He asked again, "I weighed a dead person and found him heavier; if the spirit had departed, he should have been lighter. If no spirit departs, then there is no other world. He replied, "It is like iron combined with fire:
when the iron has fire, it is light; when the iron loses its fire, it is heavy. When a person is born, they possess a spirit..."
"Light [is the state] when one loses consciousness at death; it becomes heavy. He asked again, "I have seen those on the verge of death who, conversely, seek for their spirits but cannot find them.
Therefore, I know there is no other world. He replied, "It is like a person who, turning around, seeks the sound of a conch shell—could he ever obtain that sound?"
He asked again, "Although you have refuted me repeatedly, I have held to this for a very long time and cannot let it go. He replied, "It is like a person gathering hemp:
first seeing the hemp, they take the hemp; next they discard the hemp and take the bark; next they discard the bark and take the fibers;
next they discard the fibers and take the cloth; next they discard the cloth and take the silk; next they discard the silk and take the silver; and finally they discard the silver."
Take gold; abandon the inferior and take the superior. Why would one not be able to abandon [the inferior]? He asked again: "It is not only I who speak thus;
all people also speak thus. Why do you claim that I am wrong? He replied: "Two merchants encountered a ghost. The ghost assumed the form of a human being and said to them:
'The road ahead has abundant rice and sufficient grass; why do you carry these [heavy loads]? One merchant then—"
They discarded their provisions for the journey; both man and ox became hungry and were subsequently devoured by ghosts.
One merchant said, "If you obtain fresh rice and fodder, you may discard the old rice and fodder; then neither man nor ox will be eaten by ghosts. The others spoke falsely.
It is like a ghost’s deceptive words: "If you do not accept my words, it will be like discarding old rice and grass; now that you have obtained the new, why do you not discard the old?
He asked again, "I cannot abandon them; if you urge me, I become angry. He replied, "You are like a pig-herder who encounters excrement on the road and carries it back on his head.
While on the way, he meets rain, and the sweat from his brow soils his head. A bystander [says to him]..."
He caused [the pig] to be abandoned. Yet, instead of reflecting, he became angry with the other, saying, "Because you did not raise the pig, you have caused me to abandon it.

Thus he turned his anger upon the one who had offered the advice. In this manner, through successive stages of analysis and refutation, the various arguments were extensively expounded until the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) was subdued.

He then praised him, saying, "Venerable sir, when you spoke previously, I already understood; however, desiring to hear your wisdom and eloquence, I repeatedly raised objections and challenges. Well done!"

How wondrous is this sublime teaching! Kātyāyana was likewise skilled in discussing the characteristics of the meanings [of the Dharma]. As stated in the Vinaya: he was well able to teach and transform others so that they would take refuge in the precepts;

he caused a butcher to receive the "night-precept" and a lecher to receive the "day-precept. When they later received their retribution, each saw the signs of their former pleasure during the day or the night, respectively (and so forth).
Regarding the interpretation according to the teachings (*yàojiào*), it relies upon impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

To refute the views of nihilism and eternalism is the doctrinal meaning of the Initial Teaching (Śrāvaka-yāna). To refute the views of nihilism and eternalism by relying on emptiness, non-existence, and non-apprehensibility is the doctrinal meaning of the Shared Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna).

To refute the views of nihilism and eternalism by relying on the dhāraṇīs and the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), observing capacities and illuminating the conventional while administering medicine according to the disease, is the doctrinal meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Bodhisattva-yāna). [This continues] by relying on the ultimate reality (bhūtatathatā)...
"Existence and non-existence" refers to the refutation of the views of annihilationism and eternalism;
this is the doctrinal meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*). *Aniruddha* is also called *Aniruda* or *Aniruddha*; these are all transcriptions of the Sanskrit sound with the "shē" (奢) initial.

This translates as "Free from Poverty" (*apagata-daridra*) or "As One Wishes. He was the younger cousin of the Buddha. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that he was [the disciple of] Puṣya Buddha.
During the age of the Final Dharma, when the world was plagued by famine, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Liṭṭha who went begging for alms but returned with an empty bowl, having gained nothing.
A certain poor man, seeing this, felt deep compassion and said to the noble one, "Could you accept some millet? He immediately offered him what he himself was eating.

After the Pratyekabuddha had eaten, he performed the eighteen miraculous transformations. Later, as he went out to gather more millet, a rabbit leaped up and embraced his back; [the Buddha] transformed it—
He became a dead man. Having no companion, he was able to escape; waiting for the darkness, he returned home. When he cast himself upon the ground, he immediately became a golden man.
As he pulled out his fingers, they grew back accordingly; as he used his feet, more emerged. Though one took them, they were inexhaustible.

When wicked men and evil kings came wishing to seize him, they saw only a corpse, yet what they beheld was entirely composed of gold and jewels. For ninety-one kalpas, his karmic retribution was fully satisfied.
Therefore, he was named Aṅgaṇa (The One Without Poverty). After he had left the household life, wherever he went, people were filled with joy upon seeing him;
whatever they desired, it was no different from being in their own homes. Anuruddha practiced with such diligence that for seven days and seven nights his eyelids did not blink.

Sleep is the nutriment of the eye. If one does not sleep for seven days, the eyes lose their luster. Once the physical eyes have failed, the Buddha directed him to seek the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
By fixing the mind upon its object—the pure matter (*rūpa*) derived from the four great elements—this vision arises across half the head, penetrating both internal and external obstructions.
He saw both light and darkness clearly. Addressing the Brahma King, he said, "I see Śākyamuni’s great trichiliocosm as if looking at a fruit in the palm of my hand.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost among those who possess the divine eye that penetrates all vision.
Regarding the classification of teachings: this refers to ordinary persons and non-Buddhists who develop the divine eye based on worldly dhyāna; it does not refer to the untainted (anāsrava) reality.

The Abhidharma-piṭaka (Tripiṭaka) perspective holds that the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) inherent in the essence of phenomena gives rise to the various meditative practices (*saṃskāra*), and based on these practices, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is produced.

The perspective of the Shared Teaching (Pāramitā-yāna) holds that based on mundane wholesome roots (*prākṛta-kuśala-mūla*), the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is produced; based on dhyāna, the divine eye is produced; based on the Truth (*tattva*), the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) is produced;

based on the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) is produced; and based on the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) is produced. The perspective of the Distinct Teaching (Vaipulya-yāna) holds that [the eyes are produced] based on the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
He develops the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The divine eye is itself the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*);

this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). Kapphiṇa (in Chinese, *Jié bīn nà*) is translated as "Lunar Mansion" (*nakṣatra*). His parents prayed to the lunar mansion of Kṛttikā and were blessed with a son; therefore, they named his physical body after that lunar mansion.
When this bhikṣu first left the household life, he had not yet seen the Buddha. Just as he was heading toward the Buddha’s location, he encountered [an event] at night.
It was raining, so he took lodging in the room of a potter and used grass as his seat. Later in the evening, another bhikṣu arrived following him and also sought lodging;
the first bhikṣu immediately pushed his grass over to him and sat on the bare ground. At midnight, they questioned one another:
"Where do you intend to go? He replied, "I wish to see the Buddha. The latter bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for him, and he suddenly attained the Way.
The bhikṣu who followed later was none other than the Buddha himself; the account of this may be verified in the Āgamas.

Because he shared a room with the Buddha and thereby beheld the Dharma-body, he was named according to the place where he attained the Way; thus he is called Kapphiṇa. Vaiśravaṇa held a parasol and followed behind Kapphiṇa.
Vaiśravaṇa is the presiding deity [of the constellation]; since the presiding deity serves him, the star-constellation does likewise. This is comparable to...

The Buddha was skilled in divining the constellations and clearly understood diagrams and images; he attained renown through his mastery of these arts and was named Kapphiṇa. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Within my Buddha-dharma, the bhikṣu Kapphiṇa is foremost among those who skillfully know the stars, the moon, and the sun. Regarding the teaching:
he dismantled the house of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and objects (*viṣaya*), and together with the Buddha, took up residence in the chamber of ultimate truth (*satya*). Third.

The meaning of the *Zangjiao* (Treatise on the Storehouse): To realize that the abodes of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are themselves empty is to dwell together with the Tathāgata in the chamber of the True Truth (*satyadharma*).
The meaning of the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching): To discern that within the chambers of the ten dharma-realms of sense organs and objects, one attains the vision of the Buddha in all of them.

The meaning of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching): Within the chamber of a single sense organ and object, one immediately sees all chambers and sees all Buddhas. The meaning of the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching)...
Ājñātakauṇḍinya—this is translated as "ox-chewer. In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he is called the "Ox King" (*go-rāja*). The *Ekottarika Āgama* refers to him as "Ox Footprint.
In five hundred past lives, he had previously been an ox king; after eating, an ox always engages in "empty panting," which was his residual karmic retribution.
He had not yet attained full mastery. He was constantly chewing with his mouth open, so those of the time called him "the Ox-Chewer.

Among those who delight in the heavens and do not delight in the human realm, the Bhikṣu Goṣṭhika is foremost. It is further said that people merely observe outward form and do not know of one's virtue;
if one smiles at an Arhat, one incurs sin. Because he wished to avoid being ridiculed by others, he always dwelt in the heavens, for the devas recognize virtue.
He laughed at his appearance. While he was still in heaven, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa assembled a thousand great arhats and dispatched a junior monk as a messenger to summon Kauṇḍinya.
Kauṇḍinya asked about the Buddha and his preceptor; they replied that both had passed away.

He then said, "When the Buddha appeared, I appeared; when the Buddha remained, I remained; now that the Buddha has passed away, I have passed away. Kauṇḍinya Bhaṭṭi then bowed his head in prostration.

Ritual: To the Wondrous Assembly, the Great Virtuous Sangha of the Foremost Rank. Hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall follow him, just as when a great elephant departs, the calf follows.
Regarding the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*): dwelling in the heavenly garden demonstrates good; the ox-chewing demonstrates evil. This is the intent of the Tripiṭaka:
that one attains the Way even with a body that chews like an ox, showing that what appears evil is not truly evil; thus, while residing in the heavenly garden, one may still chew like an ox.

To demonstrate what is wholesome and unwholesome is the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). To demonstrate the wholesome and unwholesome within and beyond the realms is the intent of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
To demonstrate the true reality (shixiang) of the wholesome and unwholesome is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Revata is also called Revatī; this translates as "Constellation" (nakṣatra), or "Room-constellation" (śravaṇa), or "Provisionally Combined.

The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* refers to him as "Ever-Making-Sound. His parents sought a son from the constellations, and having obtained him through their invocation, they named him after the constellation.
Although he left the household life, he still retained his original name. Regarding "Provisionally Combined," the *Śāstra* states: "Emptiness..."
He stayed overnight in a pavilion and saw two ghosts contending over a corpse. He informed them that whether they judged according to principle or contrary to principle, neither would escape harm;
therefore, he answered according to the facts. The larger ghost tore off its hands and feet, while the smaller ghost took the corpse to replace them.
Having finished eating, he wiped his mouth and departed. As for the one who constantly made sounds, he harbored doubts about this matter:

"Is this my own body that I see being pulled out with my own eyes? Or is it another body that follows me in walking and staying? Thus, filled with uncertainty and hesitation, whenever he encountered someone, he would ask, "Do you see my body?
For this reason, he was said to be "one who constantly makes sounds. The monks said, "This person is easy to deliver," and spoke [to him].
He said: "Your body was originally the remains left by another; it is not yours. At these words, he immediately attained the Way. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Among those who sit in meditation and enter samādhi with minds free from distraction and confusion, the bhikṣu Revata is foremost. Regarding the provisional teaching (*yìjiào*), this refers to the analytical deconstruction of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as not being one's own possession.
According to the intention of the Tripiṭaka [Teaching], this means realizing that the five aggregates are fundamentally not one's own. This is the Shared Teaching (*tōngjiào*).
The meaning of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*) is that one discerns that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the ten dharma realms are none of them "mine.

The meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*) is that one realizes the five aggregates are neither "mine" nor "belonging to another," thereby perceiving the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the aggregates. As for the practice of contemplating the mind, it means contemplating the mind while recollecting the Buddha.
He saw the Buddhas of the ten directions as numerous as stars observed at night.
Pindola Bharadvāja—this name is translated as "Residual Habit"—had been a Brahmin for five hundred lifetimes, and his residual habits remained prominent.

As he crossed the Ganges, he shouted, "Hey! Little slave-girl! Stop your flow! The deity of the Ganges split the river into two channels because of this. The deity went to report the matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha ordered him to perform repentance. [Vatsa] immediately joined his palms and said, "Little maid, do not be angry. The great assembly laughed at him; he repented, yet continued to revile them.

The Buddha said, "His habitual practice has been such as this; truly, he has no prideful mind. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, regarding those who sit in austerity under trees and avoid neither wind nor rain, the Bhikṣu Vatsa is foremost.
Regarding the interpretation of the teaching (*yǎojiè*), it is because he has extinguished arrogance that he is without pride. This is according to the Tripiṭaka.
The general sense refers to both pride and the absence of pride. The specific sense refers to the mind that discriminates between the high and low of the ten dharma realms.
The ultimate sense refers to the sovereign self who is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma.
Bakkula is translated here as "Good Appearance" (Śubhadarśana), or "Magnificent Form," or "Greatly Flourishing. His physical appearance was upright and handsome; thus he is called "Good Appearance.
He was one hundred and sixty years old, yet remained free from illness and untimely death. He possessed five reports of non-death:

once his stepmother placed him on a roasting pan, then in a cauldron, then in water, then among fish, and finally he was split by a blade; in all these instances, he did not die. Formerly, he had maintained...

Because he observed the precept against killing, for ninety-one kalpas his life was never cut short prematurely. Because he once gave a single *harītakī* fruit to the Sangha, his body has always been free from illness.

While he was able to uphold even a single precept, adorned by four, maintaining them firmly without transgression even at the cost of avoiding neither water nor fire, other people, though they may observe the five precepts, mostly violate them. His body delighted in tranquility, and he dwelt alone.
He lived in seclusion and took no pleasure in the midst of crowds. His eyes did not delight in colors such as black and yellow;
his ears did not delight in hearing worldly sounds; his nose did not smell worldly fragrances; his tongue never spoke even a word or two for the sake of others;
and his mind was always in meditative concentration, without distraction. King Aśoka paid homage to the various stūpas of the arhats, and next he arrived at that stūpa.
And he spoke in verse: "Though one may personally discipline their ignorance, it brings little benefit to the world. [The *Ekottarika Āgama* says:
"By giving a single coin, a cowrie shell flew out from the stupa and landed at the king's feet. The ministers were struck with wonder, thinking:
"Even for one who is secluded and has few desires, such power still remains even in his stupa. Thus, the *Ekottarika Āgama* says: "[Regarding] longevity..."
Their lifespan is extremely long; they never meet an untimely death. They always delight in dwelling in seclusion and do not remain amidst the crowds.

For those of the *Kula* [or *Kula*] class, this is the foremost [method]. Regarding the provisional teachings: the *Tripitaka* (Śrāvaka) teaching involves extinguishing clamor to enter the truth; the *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teaching involves finding tranquility within clamor itself.
To depart from the two extremes and enter the Middle Way is the distinct tranquility; to be the middle within the extremes is the perfect tranquility.

For one who contemplates the mind, the nature of the mind is the Middle Way—simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle. This is the contemplation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Mahākauṣṭhila—translated as "Great Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. From the beginning, he had always excelled his sister in debate;

however, once she became pregnant, he could no longer defeat her in discussion. Realizing that the one she carried was wise, he thought: "If even her borrowed eloquence is thus superior, how much more so will it be once [the child] has emerged from the womb?"
He immediately abandoned his home and traveled to South India, where he studied eighteen sūtras. The people of the time mocked him, saying, "It will be difficult to master these over many lifetimes;
one cannot hope to achieve this in a single life. He sighed deeply and said, "At home I was surpassed by my sister; on the road I am held in contempt by others.
He vowed never to stop his studies, and finding no leisure even to trim his nails, the people of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail). Having completed his learning, he—
He returned home and asked where his nephew was. People said, "He has become a disciple of the Buddha.

At this, he became greatly arrogant and thought, "My nephew is only eight years old, yet his fame resounds throughout the five regions of India. What kind of spiritual arts does that śramaṇa possess to have seduced my sister's son?
He went straight to the Buddha’s dwelling and meditated for a long time, but not a single dharma entered his mind. He said to the Buddha, "All dharmas are..."
"Patience. "Patience" has the meaning of "settling. This refers to saying that one can destroy all dharmas so that they do not find rest;
therefore, it is called "not being patient with all dharmas. The Buddha asked: "Do you see this patience? This falls into a position of double defeat.
If I see patience, I have already stated previously that there is no patience with anything. If I see no patience, I have no means to surpass the Buddha.
He immediately lowered his head and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. When Śāriputra fanned the Buddha, he heard his uncle’s discourse and attained the fruit of Arhatship.

According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); when confronted with difficult questions, he was able to answer them, becoming foremost among those skilled in debate.
The Southern Heavenly King, Virūpākṣa, constantly came to attend upon him. As for the contemplation of the mind: contemplating the mind as being empty is itself concentration. It is...
"Jia" (假) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), by which one adorns the mind.
Nanda is also called Gopāla-Nanda; this translates as "Good Joy" (*Sukha-nandana*) or "Delightful.
Some say he is Upananda mentioned in the Vinaya. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the bhikṣus..."

The monk entered the three-month *varṣā* retreat. He told a cowherd to stay nearby and have him deliver milk, curd, clarified butter (*sarpis*), and other provisions every day until the end of the three months.
The king, feeling great compassion for him, ordered that he be allowed to see the Buddha.
Thereupon, he consulted with his companions, saying, "I have heard that the Omniscient One is the son of King Śuddhodana; he was born in the royal palace."
"Do you know anything of the matter of tending cattle? He then entered the Bamboo Grove, sat upright, and questioned the Buddha.

The Buddha explained for him the eleven matters and so forth, as detailed in the second record of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Consequently, he resolved his mind to leave the household life and attained the fruit of *aśaikṣa*.
He was named after his original occupation, hence "Tending Cattle. As for the name "Sukha-nandī" (Joyful in Goodness), it was given based on his initial aspiration for the Way. Regarding...

Regarding "teaching": the *śrāvaka* (Tripitaka) teaching holds that there is joy in phenomena (*dharma*), but no joy in principle (*tattva*). The meaning of the Tripitaka is that joy in phenomena is itself joy in principle. The meaning of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika*) is the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

The Separate Teaching (*vaibhāṣika*) is the Abode of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*). The Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*) is as follows: The Tripitaka [teaches] that there is joy in phenomena, but no joy in principle. The meaning of the Tripitaka is that joy in phenomena is itself joy in principle. The meaning of the Shared Teaching is the Stage of Joy. The Separate Teaching is the Abode of Joy. The Perfect Teaching is... [as above].
Sundarananda. "Sundara" is translated here as "lovely" or "handsome. "Nanda" is as explained previously. His lineage is as described in the section on Aniruddha.

He was born on the ninth day of the fourth month. He was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha. His appearance and bearing were exceptionally distinguished and far superior to those of the world;

The *Śāriputraparipṛcchā-vinaya* states: In Magadha there was a naked ascetic who was highly intelligent; the people of the country called him "the Wise One.
