He requested to leave the household life, and Nanda immediately ordained him. According to the provisional teaching, there is the joy of the Dharma within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
According to the meaning of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, there is no joy in ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). According to the intention of the Tripiṭaka [Hīnayāna], mundane joy is itself true joy.

According to the intention of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), from the joy of the Dharma common to all, there arise mundane joy, the joy of the Dharma of the Middle Way, and the joy of the Distinct Teaching (*pratipakṣika-yāna*). According to the intention of the Distinct Teaching, this very joy of the Shared Teaching fully possesses all forms of joy of the Dharma.
The meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is as follows:
Pūrṇa, according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, my father’s name was Pūrṇa and my mother’s name was Maitrāyaṇī. Fellow practitioners of the holy life call me "Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
This name is derived from the two conditions of my parents; therefore, I am called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Thus it is said.
This person was well-versed in both internal and external scriptures; there was nothing he did not know. Because his knowledge was complete, he was further named Pūrṇa (Full).
He was exceptionally skilled at expounding extensively and analyzing the principles of the teachings, such that among the sons of Pūrṇa, he was the foremost.

As the subsequent text states: "Among those who preach the Dharma, he is the most preeminent. The term "preeminent" (prathama) refers here to the syllable *pūrṇa*. Desiring to return to his native land to benefit others, he departed.

The Buddha said, "That land is corrupt and evil; what will you do? He replied, "I shall practice patience. If they revile and insult me, I shall consider myself fortunate that they do not strike me with their fists.
When they strike with their fists, I shall consider myself fortunate that they do not use wooden staves. When they use wooden staves, I shall consider myself fortunate that they do not use blades.
When they use blades, I shall consider myself fortunate to be free from the poisonous vessel of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). This is how one practices."
Because patience is fulfilled, it is called "fulfillment. As stated in the *Saptasārayāna-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Seven Chariots), it was praised by the Great Wise Śāriputra:
"All fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) shall wrap their robes around their heads and carry you upon them; whoever sees you will obtain great benefit.
This is the praise of fulfillment, and thus it is called "fulfillment. Regarding the teaching, it refers to the diligent analysis of phenomena and the deeds performed.
The stage of "Already Accomplished" (Kṛtāvin): the vows of the Tripiṭaka are fulfilled; one realizes that the essence is emptiness and attains realization within the dharma of emptiness.

The vows of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) are fulfilled; the Dharma-eye is perfected. The vows of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna) are fulfilled; one dwells in the Secret Treasury. The vows of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) are fulfilled. As for "Original and Traces": [text continues].
His original vow has long been fulfilled; his manifested trace is that of being foremost in preaching the Dharma, demonstrating to sentient beings the nature of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Regarding the contemplation of the mind, as in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one contemplates the person, the practice, and the principle as spiritual friends (the person is a Buddha, a Bodhisattva, or an Arhat; the practice is the path of the six perfections and the factors of enlightenment;
the principle is the *dharmatā* and the limit of reality).
Subhūti, this name is translated as "Born of Emptiness. At the time of his birth, all the family’s granaries, treasuries, baskets, chests, and vessels were entirely empty.
When he consulted a diviner, the diviner declared it auspicious; because he was born from emptiness, he was named "Emptiness-born" (Kūṭadanta), and is also called "Auspicious" (Śubha).
He always delights in dwelling and roaming in secluded forests, stone caves, and places of silence. As for the practices he cultivates: [text continues]

Emptiness is the foundation. One constantly enters the samādhi of emptiness and abides in the *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention) to protect sentient beings, ensuring they do not give rise to obstructions.

When there is aversion toward practice, one abides; when there is aversion toward abiding, one practices. Regarding the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*), the wisdom of the emptiness of form arises through the cessation of form.

According to the intent of the *Tripiṭaka* (Hīnayāna) teaching, the wisdom of the emptiness of the substance of form arises. According to the intent of the *Shared* (Prajñāpāramitā) teaching, the wisdom of emptiness arises from the wisdom of existence, and from the wisdom of emptiness [arises]... [wisdom of existence].

Conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). From conventional wisdom arises middle wisdom (*madhya-jñāna*); this is the meaning according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*). When emptiness gives rise to wisdom regarding existence, that is also conventional wisdom and middle wisdom;
this is the meaning according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
Ānanda, this is called "Joy" (Nanda), or "Untainted. King Śuddhodana had hoped that his son would become a Golden Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakravartin) to rule over his ancestral realm.
Suddenly, [the prince] abandoned the kingdom and renounced kingship; the king’s grief was nearly overwhelming. Then a Māra came to deceive him, saying, "Your son is already dead.
The king wept and said, "The words of Asita were false, and the auspicious signs have proven fruitless. Furthermore, another deity came and said:

"Your son has attained Buddhahood. The king’s doubts remained unresolved; however, shortly thereafter, a message arrived confirming that during the night, heaven and earth had shaken violently and the Prince had become a Buddha.
The Great King was filled with immense joy. King Pāṇḍuvāsa announced, "A son has been born," and the entire kingdom rejoiced.
Consequently, he was named Nanda (Joy). This was the name given by his parents. Ānanda was handsome; all who saw him were delighted. *Madhyama Āgama*...
Hanchun said: "When the fourfold assembly hears what Ānanda says, whether much or little, there is none who does not rejoice.
When he wishes to ask a question, he first clears his throat, and the great assembly all rejoices.

If the fourfold assembly observes his silence, or his walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, his gestures and instructions, his advancing, retreating, moving, or turning—all bring them joy. On the eighth day of the twelfth month, Ānanda..."
On this day, the Buddha was born on the day he attained enlightenment. He had served the Buddha for twenty-five years.
Inferring from this, the Buddha was fifty-five years old and Ānanda was twenty-five. At that time, the Buddha sought an attendant; five hundred [monks] volunteered, as previously described.
The assembly exhorted Ānanda, and Ānanda complied. All five hundred were filled with joy. Maudgalyāyana conveyed Ānanda’s three vows.
The Buddha said, "Anticipating censure and seeking to avoid receiving food and clothing, he desires his own benefit and seeks to enter and exit at no fixed time.
The Buddha approved and permitted it. The Buddha said, "Ānanda excels the attendants of the past.
While those past attendants understood only after hearing the teaching, now before the Buddha has even spoken, Ānanda already understands the Tathāgata’s intention—whether this is required or not."
He was able to know them all; therefore, he entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda, and the Tathāgata rejoiced.

The Four Heavenly Kings each offered a bowl to the Buddha, which the Buddha stacked and pressed together so that they merged into a single bowl. The four rims remained distinct, yet this bowl was exceedingly heavy.
Ānanda was filled with joy and bore [the teachings] without weariness. The seventh fascicle of the Madhyama Āgama states: "Ānanda attended the Buddha for twenty-five years;
of the eighty thousand *khandhas* he heard, he recited them all without omission, never asking for a single phrase to be repeated."
With the power of mindfulness, he was filled with joy. Ānanda followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, and nāgas;

though he saw deva and nāga maidens, his mind remained free from defilement or attachment. Although he had not yet exhausted all residual thoughts, they could not stain him. All devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits were without exception filled with joy.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as he sat upon the lion throne, the great assembly led by Kāśyapa praised him, saying: "His face is like..."
The pure full moon, with eyes like blue lotuses—the waters of the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma—flowed into Ānanda’s heart.
He made a vow to sit and enter *nirvāṇa*, fearing that if he remained, the Licchavis might harbor resentment, yet fearing that if he advanced, King Ajātaśatru might harbor resentment.

Within the Ganges River, he entered the *Vāyu-vega* (Wind-Swiftness) *samādhi* and divided his body into four parts: one for the devas, one for the nāgas, [one for the yakṣas, and one for the humans].
One at Vaiśālī and one at Ajātaśatru. King Aśoka paid homage to the stūpa of Ānanda and offered ten million taels of gold, praising it in verse:
"Able to uphold and maintain the Dharma-body, the lamp of the Dharma thus abides; I call to mind the flourishing ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom."

Therefore, he established the supreme offerings; he retained what he had heard extensively; his mouth uttered subtle and wondrous words praised by the World-Honored One and beloved by devas and humans.

According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Ānanda was foremost because he knew the proper time, understood things clearly, was free from doubt regarding whatever he encountered, remembered without forgetting, possessed vast and extensive learning, and was capable of receiving and upholding the teachings. Regarding the classification of the teaching, he is the "Joyful One."
Ānanda is the Tripitaka. Worthy Ānanda is the Penetrating. Treasury-Ānanda is the Distinctive. Sāgara Ānanda is the Perfect.
Rāhula—this means "obscuration. When the Prince sought to leave the household life, his father the King would not permit it, despite his earnest entreaties.
The King said, "If you have a son, I shall permit you to leave the household life. The Bodhisattva pointed to his consort’s womb and said, "Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.
Because he remains in the womb for six years, he is called 'Obstructing' (Rāhu).

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated that Rāhu’s original name was Asura, who is able to obstruct the sun and moon with his hand; translating this literally, one should say "obstructing the moon. The Buddha said, "I..."
"The Dharma is like the moon; this child obstructs me from leaving the home life immediately. He has obstructed me in life after life, yet I have been able to renounce him in every birth;
therefore, he is called 'the obscuration. After the Buddha had left the home life, Yaśodharā became pregnant. All the Śākyas were enraged, asking, 'By what cause did this come to be?
They wished to punish her and kill her, and an evil reputation filled the roads. The noble lady Gopikā testified on her behalf, and the situation was slightly alleviated."
She cast the fire-pit into a blaze and made this great vow: "If I have committed an injustice, let mother and child perish together;

if these are truly the remains of my son, may the heavens bear witness. She then embraced her child and threw them into the pit. The pit was transformed into a pond, and a lotus flower emerged, cradling their bodies.
Only then did the King and the people of the land cease to doubt. Later, when the Buddha returned to his homeland, Yaśodharā commanded Rāhula to offer service and joy to the Buddha.
"Joyful Ball! Although Rāhula is but a child, he has directly offered this to the Buddha amidst the great assembly. Yaśodharā has thereby stilled the slander;
for it was because of having a son that the slander arose, and thus it is said to have been a 'covering obstacle. The Grandfather King is filled with joy;

though he has lost his son, he has gained a grandson who shall become a Golden-Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakravartin). What cause for regret could I have? I only hope that as he grows up, he will obtain the divine treasures."

When she arrived, the Buddha requested that she leave the household life, but her father the King would not permit it. Yaśodharā went up to a high tower, and Maudgalyāyana flew through the air to fetch her.
The Buddha ordained her as a renunciant and entrusted her to Śāriputra to be his disciple. Having thus left the household life, she...
He also lost his royal throne; therefore, it is called "obscuration. Later, when he practiced the Path with diligence yet failed to attain realization, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Have you taught others concerning the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)? He replied, "I have not. "You should teach others," [the Buddha said].

After he had finished teaching, the Buddha asked again, "Have you taught the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*)? Have you taught the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*)? The Dharma is the gateway for attaining the Path."
"If you wish to attain the Way, you should preach the Dharma for others. Having extensively expounded the Dharma, he subsequently attained the Way.
Once he had attained the Way, his views and cravings were all eliminated, and his births within the three realms came to an end.

The Buddha commanded the four great arhats not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to wait until his own Dharma was completely extinguished; for this reason, they remain in the world and have not yet entered nirvana without remainder.
[The character] "pan" (槃). Second, the summary states: Regarding those "known by all," some say that "knowing" (*jñā*) is simply consciousness (*vijñāna*);

others say that hearing the name is "knowing" and seeing the form is "consciousness"; yet others say that seeing the form is "knowing" and seeing the mind is "consciousness. As for the fundamental and the trace: [text follows].

In essence, he acts as a teacher of the full syllables for sentient beings; in his provisional manifestation, he acts as a teacher of the half-syllables (the preceding section on the many teachers is concluded). II. Few Teachers.
Furthermore, there were two thousand individuals, both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Next, the assembly of those with little knowledge is listed. Regarding these two thousand, both *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa*, the passage merely cites their status to clarify their number.
He did not praise their virtues, nor did he list their names; he referred to them merely as "those with little learning.
The holy and the ordinary were severed from social ties, and there was no distinction made between those of great learning and those of little.

Specifically, those who aspired to the lofty and admired the distant were led by means of great learning, while those who concealed their names, hid their virtues, and practiced humility were led by means of little learning. Thus, he acted in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

Therefore, there are various [distinctions]. One must not lose sight of the fundamental principle due to the traces of quantity or magnitude. Regarding those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):

within the Tripiṭaka, there are eighteen types of persons in training and nine types of persons beyond training; furthermore, in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), all five stages are termed "in training."

The sixth stage (*bhūmi*) is designated as "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Furthermore, within the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa*), the nine stages are designated as "training" (*śaikṣa*), while the Buddha-stage is "beyond training.
Within the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*viśeṣa* and *pariniṣpanna*), one clarifies training and beyond-training either by way of effort and non-effort, or by way of being complete and incomplete.

(Regarding the eighteen types of persons in training in the Tripiṭaka, see the commentary on the sixth fascicle of the *Śikṣānanda-śāstra* [Zhi guan]. Regarding the two sections on the stages of training and beyond-training in the Shared Teaching: the former concerns the Two Vehicles, while the latter concerns Bodhisattvas; furthermore, the former concerns the three [vehicles]).

Regarding the shared stage of the vehicle: subsequently, this concerns the solitary bodhisattva. Within the Distinct and Complete teachings, there is also a twofold judgment: first, "with effort" and "without effort," which refers to the stages prior to and after [the first] ground; second, "possessing" and "not possessing," which refers to Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment.

Entering for the first time into the state of being without effort may also be termed "beyond training" (aśaikṣa), yet this is only a partial attainment; therefore, it is further distinguished by its full perfection. Regarding origin and trace:

the Dharma-body Great Being abides in the stage of completion within the learning and beyond-learning of the "full-syllable" (pariniṣpanna) teaching, while sentient beings should be adorned with the dual [aspects] of the person beyond learning in the "half-syllable" (aparinispanna) teaching.

It is like a tree. Contemplating the Middle Way, one does not rely on the two extremes; this middle itself is the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). To be able to contemplate in this manner is called "learning" (*śaikṣa*).

If we clarify the number [of elements] according to the gate of contemplation: contemplating that a single mind possesses the ten dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), and discussing these realms and suchnesses in relation to one another, they comprise two thousand [elements].

*Ni* is a general term for women in India. She originally dwelt in the dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom), and in her manifested traces, she served as the mother of the thousand Buddhas.

Mother. She who gave birth to the Teacher. The *Mahāpratītyasamutpādānuśaṃsā-sūtra* (*Dà bà'ēn jīng*) states: "The Buddha’s maternal aunt, Gautamī, sought to leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha did not grant her permission. Her heart was filled with regret and resentment; she was overcome by grief, sorrow, and distress.
She immediately departed from the Jetavana Monastery, her eyes brimming with tears of lamentation. When Ānanda saw her, he addressed the Buddha, saying: 'This woman, Gautamī, is the mother of men.'"
The Tathāgata’s physical body was nurtured by suckling and nourishment until he attained Buddhahood today.
Thus, a mother has a great debt of gratitude toward the Tathāgata; since the Tathāgata permits all people to enter the Buddha-dharma, how much more so should he permit women?
The Buddha said: "If women were permitted to enter the Buddha-dharma, the True Dharma would gradually become faint and diminish."
"For five hundred years, therefore, [entry] was not permitted. Ānanda addressed the Buddha again, saying, "All Buddhas of the past were accompanied by the fourfold assembly;

why is it that the World-Honored One alone is not so? The Buddha told Ānanda, "If Gautamī loves and delights in the Buddha-dharma and is able to practice the eight rules of respect, she shall be permitted to enter the Buddha-dharma. Having heard these words, Gautamī—
Her heart was filled with great joy. The Tathāgata then proclaimed for her the Eight Rules of Respect.
Gautamī said, "World-Honored One, please do not worry; I shall ensure they are practiced. Even at the cost of my life, I shall never let them fall away."

(The Eight Rules of Respect are: 1. A bhikṣuṇī, even if she has been ordained for a hundred years, must pay homage at the feet of a bhikṣu who has been ordained for only one summer. 2. She must not revile or slander a bhikṣu. 3. She must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu. 4. She must receive full ordination from the Saṃgha. 5. If she commits a fault, she must confess it before the Saṃgha. 6.

"Treasure-Palm" (Baozhang): Holding this treasure of the Truths to benefit both oneself and others, he is thus called "Treasure-Palm. Regarding the "Medicine King" (Yaowang):

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that he made a vow to provide offerings to all one thousand four Buddhas when they first attain enlightenment during the Bhadrakalpa, and to attend them when those Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa.

I shall build stupas for all of them. During the sufferings at the end of the kalpa, I shall protect and deliver them all. Amidst the calamities of war, weapons, pestilence, and disease, I shall act as a great King of Physicians;
only then shall I become a Buddha. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said, "From this day forth, I shall name you 'Agnidatta' (Fire-Purified).

You, Bhaiṣajyarāja, shall later become a Buddha, namely the Tathāgata Roca. [Regarding "Fire-Purified": this name was established from his burning of his own body. In this text, worldly governance is used to represent supramundane governance. ... [Brave] ...
As for "Generosity" (Dāna): it bestows the world-transcending Dharma-treasure universally upon all sentient beings without weariness; therefore, it is named "Courageous Generosity.
As for "Jewel Moon" (Ratnacandra): the Three Truths realized are venerable like jewels, and the Three Wisdoms that realize them shine perfectly like the moon.

Therefore, he is named Jewel Moon (Ratnacandra). As for Moonlight (Candraprabha): the three perfect and subtle wisdoms can eliminate the feverish afflictions of delusion, just as moonlight is cool and dispels darkness;
therefore, he is named Moonlight. As for Full Moon (Pūrṇacandra): the three wisdoms are perfectly luminous.
It is without deficiency or diminution, just like the full moon; therefore, it is named "Full Moon.
○ As for "Great Power," the realm of wisdom and its object are merged in profound harmony, possessing great power and function; therefore, it is named "Great Power.

○ As for "Immeasurable Power," by means of this great power and function, it universally responds to all conditions and universally uproots all sufferings; therefore, it is named "Immeasurable Power. ○ As for "Transcending the Three Realms," by means of one...

Through the three contemplations of the mind, one transcends the two kinds of birth and death—those of the *pariccheda* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative)—and is therefore said to "surpass the triple world.

(From "Vīradatta" to "surpassing the triple world," these seven stages of Bodhisattvas have not been verified in the textual passages of the sutra; they remain missing and unresolved. Here, based on the annotated outline and drawing from supplementary notes, I provide a brief explanation.
*Bhadrapāla* means "Good Guardian" (*śubharakṣita*) or "Worthy Guardian. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Cintāmayī-bhūmi-sūtra*) states: "If sentient beings hear his name..."
One who is thus shall certainly attain *sambodhi*; therefore, he is named "Well-Guarded" (*Sugupta*). As for the "contemplative understanding," it is the correct contemplation of the Middle Way;
because it is the foremost among all virtues, it is called "Well-Guarded. ○ Maitreya means "The Kind One" (*Maitrīputra*) in this language.
The *Siddhivigraha-paripṛcchā* states: "If sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the Samādhi of Loving-kindness;
therefore, he is named Maitreya. The *Bhadra-avidvat-sūtra* states: "When the king saw the elephant trainer taming an elephant, compassion arose within him; from this, he received the name Maitreya."
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "He made a vow to protect sentient beings during the kalpa of swords and fire. As for the contemplative understanding:
the Middle Way’s correct contemplation is precisely unconditional great compassion (*nirālambana-mahāmaitrī*).

By the power of the roots of goodness of this compassion, all mental factors are caused to enter into the dharma of great compassion of identical substance, thereby departing from all that is unwholesome; thus he is named Maitreya. Furthermore, it says: "Maitreya is his clan name."
His name is Ajita, which translates as "Unconquered" (or "Without Superiority"), as explained in the subsequent text. ○ As for "Jewel Accumulation" (Ratnakūṭa):
it refers to the accumulation of the jewels of the threefold wisdom within a single mind. ○ As for "Guide" (Śāstṛ):

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Cintaviṣaya-sūtra*) states that one gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings who have fallen into wrong paths and leads them into the right path without seeking any reward; therefore, he is called a "Guide. Regarding the contemplative interpretation, there are three [aspects].
Observing wondrous wisdom, he guides all practices so that they do not fall into the two extremes, leading them all into right contemplation; therefore, he is called the "Teacher.
(The section below, "In this way," concludes the enumeration [of the second assembly, the Bodhisattvas]. △ Third, the assembly of devas, nāgas, and others, in eight parts:
first, the assembly of devas of the desire realm.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (up to) came together with his retinue of thirty thousand devaputras.
As for Śakra Devānām Indra, he is also called Indrā or Candrā; this translates as "The Able One. He acts as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"Trāyastriṃśa" translates as "Thirty-three. There are eight cities on each of the four sides, centered upon the city of Sudarśana.
Together they number thirty-three and dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. "Sumeru" is translated here as "Anming" (Peaceful Brilliance).

It is composed of four precious substances and is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* in height and breadth. Because he is the lord of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), he is listed first.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 40, states: A certain bhikṣu asked the Buddha, "For what reason is he named Śakra Devānām Indra? The Buddha replied:
When he was formerly a human being, he practiced sudden giving and was capable of acting as a lord;
therefore, he is named Śakra Devānām Indra. Why is he named Puraṃdara? Because when he was formerly a human being, he gave gifts repeatedly.
Why is he named Maghavat? Because of his name when he was formerly a human being. Why is he named Sahasrākṣa? Because when he was formerly a human being, this...
Because he gave robes as an offering, why is he named Kauśika? It is because of his clan name from when he was formerly a human.
Why is he named Śacīpati? Śacī is the wife and pati is the husband. Why is he named Sahasranetra (Thousand-Eyed)?

Because when he was formerly a human, he was intelligent; while sitting at one time, he contemplated, examined, and weighed a thousand kinds of meanings, and for this reason he is called "Thousand-Eyed."
The Eye. Why is he named Indri? Because he is the lord of the thirty-two heavens.
According to the third fascicle of the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra on Necklaces), the name of the Heavenly Lord is Kauśika. Regarding the gate of teaching: within the Āgamas, Śakra is an Anāgāmin;

in the Prajñā [Pāramitā] scriptures, those who pose difficult questions regarding Prajñā from the ten directions are all called Śakradevendra. Within the Separate and Perfect [teachings], Śakra is explained...

Huan Yin attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; his internal realization was peerless. After two thousand twenty-four kalpas beyond the Bhadrakalpa, he will become a Buddha named the World-Honored One Without Attachment (Anāsa).
Regarding his original and manifested traces: the ten stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) and the ten abodes (*vihāra*) constitute thirty [stages].

The ten stages constitute one; Equal Enlightenment constitutes two; and Wondrous Enlightenment is the sovereign. Together they dwell in the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-dhātu*) and collectively partake of the nectar of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
this is the fundamental reality. To reside upon the summit of Mount Sumeru is the phenomenal trace. For those who understand through contemplation of the mind:
practicing the ten wholesome acts oneself, exhorting others to do so, and rejoicing in them—these thirty wholesome acts are all empty, all provisional, and all middle. This is precisely [the truth].

This is the thirty-third contemplation gate. (Regarding those who together partake of the nectar of immortality: the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Four Reliances," states: "It is like the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where there is the wondrous nectar, the medicine of non-death.")
This is analogous to the principle [applying] from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward. ○ The three deva-sons, Candraprabha and the others, are internal ministers, like high officials (*qingxiang*).
Alternatively, it is said they are the deva-sons of the Three Luminaries. Candraprabha is the deva-son Ratnaśrīcandra; Mahāsthāmaprāpta should be [likewise identified].

Puxiang (Universal Fragrance) is the Celestial Son Mingxing (Star Brightness). Xukongzang (Space Treasury) should be manifested as him. Baoguang (Jewel Light) is the Celestial Son Baoyi Ri (Jewel-Mind Sun);

Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara) should be manifested as him. This is the explanation in terms of the fundamental and the trace. Regarding the contemplative interpretation: the three contemplations are the three wisdoms;
the three wisdoms are the three lights. The three wisdoms arise from the three truths; the truths are the "Heavens" (tian), and the wisdoms are the "Sons" (zi)—the bright moon.

[The sections on] the "Equalization of the Original and the Traces" both appear in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. ○ Regarding the Four Great Heavenly Kings: they are the external ministers of Śakra, like military generals.
They dwell upon four mountains of precious substances, which are half the height of Mount Sumeru and twenty-four thousand *li* in breadth.

In the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, here translated as "Holder of the Nation" (*Chíguó*) or alternatively as "Peace for the People" (*Ānmín*). He dwells on the Golden Mountain and commands two classes of spirits: the Gandharvas and the Kumbhāṇḍas.
Next is South Vīrūḍhaka, which is translated as "Increase" or "Liberation. He dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and leads two classes of spirits:
the Pretas and the Kumbhāṇḍas. Next is West Vīrūpākṣa, which is translated as "Non-Excellent Retribution," "Evil Eyes," or "Diverse Speech.
He dwells on Mount Rūpya and leads two classes of spirits: the Poisonous Dragons and the Piśācas.
In the north is Vaiśravaṇa, which is translated here as "Various Hearings" (Zhǒngzhǒngwén) or also as "Much Hearing" (Duōwén). He dwells on Mount Crystal and leads two classes of spirits:

rākṣasas and yakṣas, each leading two types of spirits. Because he prevents them from harassing people, he is called a World Protector (Lokapāla). Regarding his fundamental nature and manifested traces:
fundamentally, he is one of the Four Kings of Purity, Joy, Self, and Permanence, who protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma so that outsiders cannot seize it.
The branches and leaves are cut down and destroyed. King Nitya (Eternity) protects the eastern pair of trees, Nitya and Anitya;
King Sukha (Bliss) protects the southern pair of trees, Sukha and Asukha; King Ātman (Self) protects the western pair of trees, Ātman and Anātman;

and King Śuddhi (Purity) protects the northern pair of trees, Śuddhi and Aśuddhi. The trunk and branches are metaphors for eternity; the flowers are metaphors for the self; and the fruit is a metaphor for... [the result].
Joy. The luxuriant foliage is a metaphor for purity; by protecting these flowers and fruits, one is constantly able to benefit all sentient beings.

Thus, his traces manifest as the Four Heavenly Kings who protect the world. For those who practice through contemplation and understanding, the wisdom that contemplates the Four Noble Truths is itself the Four Heavenly Kings.
Under each Truth, the removal of the two delusions of craving and views constitutes the protection against the eight types of craving and views. Next, above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is...

Yāma (Candramas) is translated here as "Good Time" (Sukālana). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls it "Sublime Good. It is located three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* from Trāyastriṃśa.

Above Sukālana is Tuṣita, which is translated as "Sublime Foot" (Miaozu). Its distance from Yāma is as great as the distance [from] the previous level; that it is not listed [separately] is merely an abbreviation. Why?
Because the inhabitants of the lower heavens are dull-witted, while those of the higher heavens are attached to pleasure; yet even they still know [the Buddha] will come.
How much more so for one who is neither attached nor dull-witted—would such a person not come? ○ *Īśvara* is the fifth [heaven]; *Maheśvara* is the sixth.

[In these heavens, there are those who] manifest the five desires for themselves (*svayaṃ-nirmita-pañcakāma*) and the five desires manifested by others (*para-nirmita-pañcakāma*), and so forth. Some say that this refers to Maheśvara at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This, however, should not involve leaping directly to that level. For the practitioner who contemplates the mind, entering into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is *Īśvara*.
Contemplation: Entering therein is the contemplation of Great Sovereignty (Maheśvara). △ Second, the assembly of devas of the Form Realm:
Brahmā, the King of the Sahā World (up to) together with his retinue of twelve thousand sons of gods.
*Saha* is translated here as "Endurance" (*kṣānti*). The sentient beings of that land are habituated to the ten non-virtuous actions and are unwilling to renounce them;
because the land is named after its inhabitants, it is called "Endurance. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Why is it called Saha?
Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and all afflictions, it is called the Land of Endurance. It is also called 'Mixed,' for it is a mixture of the nine realms of existence."

Jū (Residence). ○ *Brahmā* (梵): This is translated here as "Free from Desire" (*vītarāga*). Because he has severed the fetters of the lower realms and ascended to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), he is named "Free from Desire.
He is also called "Highly Pure" (*viśuddha*). ○ *Śikhin* (尸棄): This is translated as "Crest" (*śikhā*). Furthermore, in foreign lands, fire is called *jyotis* or *śikhin*.
This king originally practiced the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) and destroyed the afflictions of the Desire Realm; thus, his name was established based on that virtue.
This is his name. However, since the sutra mentions both Brahmā-rāja and Śikhin, it appears as though there are two individuals. According to the *Śāstra*, Śikhin is indeed the king;
thus, the present sutra cites his rank to reveal his name, likely referring to one person alone. He dwells in the intermediate stage of dhyāna.

Internally there are applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and externally there is speech. One who possesses sovereign mastery is a *rāja* (king); one who practices meditation alone is a *brahmakāyika* (Brahma-follower);

one who adds the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) is a *rāja*. In the first dhyāna, there are the Brahma-multitude (*brahmapārṣadya*), the Brahma-ministers (*brahmapurohita*), and the Great Brahma (*mahābrahman*).

Here, by citing the king, all [the other classes] are included. Regarding "radiance" (*ābhā*): this refers to the second dhyāna. Herein are the Limited Radiance (*parīttābha*), the Immeasurable Radiance (*apramāṇābha*), and the Radiant Light (*ābhāsvara*).
Sound. ○ In the third dhyāna, there are Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity), Apramāṇaśubha (Immeasurable Purity), and Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity).
○ In the fourth dhyāna, there are Ghanavat (Dense Body), which is likewise without obstruction; Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light); also Puṇyaprasava (Birth of Merit) and Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit);

Āsaṃjñisattva (Non-percipient Being), as well as Āsaṃjñika (the state of non-perception). Furthermore, there are the five Anāgāmins: Avṛhā (Not Afflicted), Atapa (Not Tormented), Sudarśana (Good Vision), Sudṛśa (Good Appearance), and Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form). It is also...
Maheśvara is Mahesvara. The scriptural text is abbreviated and incomplete; it merely says "etc. This refers to these various devas.
One should reflect upon this according to the teaching gates of the fundamental and the trace, and the contemplation of the mind. △ Third, the assembly of dragons.
There are eight dragon kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Nanda is named "Joy," and Upananda is named "Good. These brothers constantly protect Magadha, causing rain to fall at the proper time.
The kingdom never suffered years of famine. King Bimbisāra held a great assembly once every year; when the common people heard of it, they all rejoiced, and from this it derived its name.

It was here that Maudgalyāyana brought [the dragon] under subjugation. As for the explanation of its fundamental and provisional traces: fundamentally, it dwells on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);
provisionally, it resides within the ocean. As for the explanation through contemplation: the three contemplations are precisely the Middle Way, from which the joy of the Dharma arises. ○

Sāgara is named after his dwelling in the ocean; as referred to in the *Avataṃsaka*, he was formerly said to have been named after his country, but in reality he dwells in the great ocean of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), appearing only in the track of the vast sea. ○ Hayaśīrṣa (Andhaka) means "Many-Headed" or "Jewel-Famed";
he dwells within the waters, fundamentally abiding in the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms), while his traces manifest as having many heads.
"Guan" (the cheekbone) refers to entering the provisional [reality] through the cheekbone; it signifies the discernment of immeasurable dharma-gates. ○ *Takṣaka* (德叉迦):
This is translated as "Manifesting Poison," also as "Many Tongues," or "Raining Tongues. He fundamentally abides in the dharma-gate of unhindered eloquence in joyful exposition.
The traces manifest as many tongues. ○ Anavatapta (阿那婆達多). It is named after its lake; this is translated as "Without Heat" (無熱). The *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 18, states:
"On the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a lake named Anavatapta. Within the lake is a hall where five [beings] dwell;
it is named after the lake. The Dragon King constantly resides therein. The dragons of Jambudvīpa have three afflictions."
First, hot winds and hot sands strike their bodies, burning the skin, flesh, and marrow, causing them great suffering.

Second, fierce evil winds suddenly arise and blow their palaces away, stripping them of their jeweled ornaments, garments, and the like; their dragon forms then manifest, causing them great suffering.
Third, when the dragons are enjoying themselves, the garuḍas enter their palaces, seize the newly born dragon offspring, and devour them.

It is filled with fear and the torment of feverish affliction (*paritāpa*). This lake is free from these three calamities; yet if a bird conceives the thought of going there, its life immediately ends.

Therefore, it is named the Lake Without Feverish Affliction (*Anavatapta*). Its original abode is the state of coolness, permanence, bliss, self, and purity (*śītalā-nitya-sukha-ātma-viśuddhi*); its manifested dwelling is this Cool Lake.

Those who contemplate it employ the wondrous wisdom of the three contemplations (*trividhā-pratyavekṣā*) to purify the clamorous defilements of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*) and escape the scorching sands of the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*).

○ Maṇas: This is translated as "Great Body," or alternatively "Great Mind" or "Great Power. When the asuras pushed back the ocean and submerged the city of Priyadarśana, this dragon coiled its body to block the seawater.
It fundamentally dwells in the dharma-gate of the Boundless Body; its manifested trace is the Great Body.
As for "contemplation," it refers to the Middle Way’s correct contemplation; its nature is vast and expansive. ○ Utpala: This is translated as...

The Black Lotus Pond (*Daisè Rengechi*). A dragon dwells therein; it is named after this pond. Originally, he resided in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* (Lotus Samādhi), and his manifested trace now abides in this pond.
For the observer, the three contemplations (*sankan*) are themselves the cultivation of the cause, and the cause is the lotus flower.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that the dragon protects the realm for the various devas. When the asuras raise their armies and advance to fight with the dragon, one thus knows [the significance of its role].
They are governed by the devas. △ Fourth, the assembly of kinnaras.
There were four kinnara kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
They are also called *Candāla*; this is translated as "doubtful spirit. They resemble humans but possess a single horn, and are thus termed "neither-human-nor-non-human" (*amanuṣya*).

These are the Dharma-music deities of the Heavenly Emperor who dwell upon the Ten Jewel Mountains. Their bodies bear extraordinary marks, and they immediately perform music when the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
The various devas play stringed instruments and sing, while the *pañcaśikha* praise the Dharma-gates. In older translations, they were called *Dharmakinnara*.
The *Catur-āryasatya* is performed by Miaojin; the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda* by Dajin; and the *Ṣaṭ-pāramitā* by Chijin.
Chijin performs all three together. This refers to the performance of the four dharma-teachings.

Abiding in the inconceivable, without arising from or entering the meditative absorption of cessation, he remains in tranquil meditation with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses, entrusting his traces to strings and pipes in song and chant.
The Ten Powers. As for "contemplating," it means contemplating that voice and sound are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle, in accordance with the Three Truths;
this is precisely the praise of the Buddha. △ Fifth, the Gandharva assembly.
There are four Gandharva kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
"Gandharva" is translated here as "Fragrance-Smeller"; they take fragrance as their food and are also called "Fragrance-Body," for fragrance emanates from their bodies.
These are the deities of the secular music of the Heavenly Lord. "Music" refers to acrobatic feats such as pole-climbing and tumbling.

"Musical sounds" refer to drums, cymbals, strings, and wind instruments. "The beautiful" refers to the most excellent among the acrobatic feats; "the beautiful sounds" refers to the most excellent among the stringed and wind instruments.
(Note: "Pole" [幢] refers to the supporting pole, which is a wooden staff; "tumbling" [倒] refers to acts such as aerial somersaults. △ Sixth: The Assembly of Asuras.
There are four asura kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
As for "asura," this is translated as "no-wine" (*amṛta*). They gather flowers from the four continents and ferment them in the great ocean;

yet, through the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor does not change. Because they have sworn to sever anger and jealousy, they are called the "Gods of No-Wine. They are also called "The Ugly."
Master Mitiān said: "Zhìliàng (質諒) means straightforward faith. This spirit is deceitful and crooked;
its name does not correspond to its nature. There are two types: those subsumed under the realm of ghosts dwell on the shores of the great ocean;
those subsumed under the realm of animals dwell at the bottom of the great ocean. ○ Pózhì (婆稚) means 'the bound,' or 'bound in five places.'"
Five evil objects are bound around his neck so that they cannot be removed; hence he is said to be "bound" (*bǐfù*) or "possessing bonds" (*yǒufù*). He is bound by Śakra Devendra.

Fundamentally, he is bound by the five fetters (*pañca-bandhana*) against Māra and non-Buddhists; it is merely for the sake of this manifested form that he appears thus. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

The Most Victorious One (Jinsheng). As for the Contemplator (Guanzhe), by means of the wisdom of the three contemplations, he binds the delusions of the five abodes and enters into the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

○ Kharaskandha—this is translated as "Broad Shoulders" (Guangjiānqiè) or "Evil Aggregate" (Èyīn). Regarding the one who causes the ocean waters to surge, the original text says "Precious Brocade" (Bǎojǐn).

This refers to the fundamental abiding in the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, which compassionately bear the burden of sentient beings; thus, in his manifested trace, he appears as Broad Shoulders. As for the Contemplator:
The three contemplations are able to overturn the great ocean of birth and death of the five abodes. (The "Correct Text" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*). ○ Vemacitra:
This is translated as "Pure Mind," and also as "Various Doubts. When the waters of the sea produce a sound, it is named Vemacitra;
he is the father of Śacī. The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven are born in this land..."
There was a woman who entered the ocean to wash away her impurities. She fell into the mud and transformed into an egg. After eight thousand years, a girl was born from it;
she had one head short of a thousand, and twenty-four hands. While this girl was playing in the water, the essence of the water entered her body.
After eight thousand years, a boy was born from her; he had twenty-four heads and one hand short of a thousand. The sound of the waves upon the ocean sea is called *Vīṇā*.
Mācika begot Śacī from a Gandharva woman. By the karmic power of Śakra, her father was made to dwell in a palace of the seven jewels and she was taken as his wife.
Later, she slandered her father, leading to a military conflict. She crossed the waters of the Jambū River with her feet and attacked Sudarśana with her hands;
yet, by the power of the Prajñā-mantra, Śakra could not be harmed. The original text says "Yanju" (Kāyotsarga). Original.
"Zhě" (者): Form and mind are fundamentally pure; this name is given to their traces. "Guān" (觀): To contemplate correctly the Middle Way is itself the pure mind. ○ Rāhula:
This is translated as "Obstructing-Holder," for he obstructs and holds the sun and moon. He belongs to the species of animals.
His body is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* long, his mouth is one thousand *yojanas* wide, and his body is adorned with precious jewels. [He] contemplates the celestial maidens.

In the celestial gardens, if the people of the four continents filially support their parents and make offerings to śramaṇas, the various devas, possessing great power, will rain down swords from above in the sky.
If they do not act thus, the devas enter their palaces and do not emerge. Furthermore, the sun emits light that dazzles their eyes so that they cannot see;
when they raise their palms to shield themselves from the sun, the people of the world all say it is a solar eclipse.
The eclipsing of the moon is likewise. Sometimes it makes a great sound; people of the world say it is the roar of a celestial beast.

When it causes fear in the sun and moon, it doubles the size of its body and breathes upon them with its breath, causing the sun and moon to lose their radiance. They come to complain to the Buddha, and the Buddha says to Rāhu:
"Do not swallow the sun and moon! Rāhu’s limbs trembled and his body broke out in cold sweat; he immediately released the sun and moon.
By the power of the sun and moon, the power of sentient beings, the power of the Buddha, and through various causes and conditions, they could not be harmed.

Long ago, there was a Brahmin who was intelligent and practiced extensive giving; he loaded four thousand carts with food and gave it away in the wilderness. There was a Buddhist stūpa [where] an evil...
When the city was being consumed by fire, he used four thousand chariots to carry water and extinguished the flames to save the stupa.

Rejoicing, he made a vow, wishing to obtain a great body that would be the foremost in the desire realm. Because he lacked right faith yet delighted in fighting and loved war, and because he took pleasure in giving, he was born in the City of Radiance as Rāhu, the King of the Asuras.
