Furthermore, the number of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas is like the sands of the Ganges; though they seek it together with a single mind, they likewise cannot know it.

This is because those who have attained non-retrogression through the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) have severed the delusions within the realm of desire (the mundane world), and therefore do not know it. Even those prior to the stages of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) possess some realization.
The non-retrogression of stage, the non-retrogression of practice, and so forth—these too are unknown [to others]. (End of Section 48).

△ The fifth section, consisting of one line and a half, is a verse summarizing the aforementioned difficult-to-understand Dharma. The Buddha alone is able to know the realm of true reality (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, [the passage] from "Again, he addressed Śāriputra" up to "The Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise" concerns the "outflow-free and inconceivable.
This summarizes the preceding essential points and sets forth the realm where the provisional and the real abide.
The single phrase "the most profound and subtle dharma" summarizes the first point mentioned above: "the rare, unprecedented, and difficult-to-understand dharma. I have now [attained it].
This possesses three phrases. It reiterates the verse above: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom [this]. This clarifies that the paths of all Buddhas are identical;
they are equally ultimate. Therefore, it says: "Only I know these marks; so too do the Buddhas of the ten directions. To explain the "inconceivable":
it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), which, though possessing not even a hair’s breadth of existence, can rain down all manner of treasures. Such is the true mark (*dharmatā*).
It gives birth; it is able to give birth to prajñā. (The twenty-third line and a half concludes the verses on the praise of ineffability.
(The first seventeen lines and a half conclude the verses on the prose section. △ The final three lines and a half constitute the verses on the brief exposition of the three as manifesting the one.

The text has two parts: first, a brief opening that reveals the three as one; second, the raising of doubts and the request for clarification. Regarding the brief opening and revelation, there are two sections.

The first half-verse praises all Buddhas for revealing the reality (*tattva*); the subsequent verse praises Śākyamuni for opening the three vehicles. These merely clarify one aspect each. Now, the first [section]:
"Śāriputra, you should know... [up to] 'the words of all Buddhas are not different.
This means that the Buddhas' methods of transformation are identical. The following two phrases exhort one to have faith."
The latter two lines—“In the distant future, the World-Honored One’s Dharma must speak the truth”—reveal the reality itself.
That people were moved by their former attachments and gave rise to present doubts, wondering, “Could it be that a Māra has become a Buddha? was precisely due to hearing these words.

Since the Buddha speaks words of suchness and exhorts one to have faith, why turn back to doubt? To prevent those who might give rise to slander because of such doubt, it is necessary to provide this exhortation.
Believe me. △ Next, the verse explains Śākyamuni’s revelation of the three vehicles. The text is divided into three parts. First, one line explicitly clarifies the revelation of the three:
"I have caused those among the assembly of śrāvakas, as well as those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, to be released from the bonds of suffering and to attain nirvāṇa."
This is intended to clarify that the Two Vehicles are not [the ultimate]. Therefore, it says, "those who have attained nirvana. Furthermore, another interpretation is:
"I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and attain nirvana" refers to the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the Six Perfections. How is this known?

By practicing the conduct of the Six Perfections, one is indeed freed from the bonds of the four realms of existence, yet one has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; only after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and a hundred kalpas does one finally attain nirvana.

"Attaining" (*pan*) means "to reach" or "to arrive. Furthermore, regarding the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*): because one first causes others to cross over, it is said, "I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering";

because one subsequently attains the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), it is said, "one attains *nirvāṇa*. By inferring through this meaning, one knows this refers to the vehicle of the six perfections.
Moreover, by inferring through the number [of verses], the following line says: "The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, shows..."

Regarding the teaching of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*): if this were not indicated, on what basis would one establish "three"? One should not count the two vehicles twice to constitute the three vehicles.
Next, the half-line verse correctly clarifies that the three vehicles are expedient means (*upāya*).
The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifests the teachings of the three vehicles.
The next two lines clarify the intent behind establishing these three:
"Sentient beings are attached everywhere; he leads them so that they may attain liberation."
The mind is a provisional guide, for it leads one away from all suffering;
it is not the ultimate reality, but merely a gateway of skillful means (the first section, the brief revelation, is concluded). II. Raising Doubts and Entering the Request.

Because they heard that the three vehicles are skillful means, attachment was shaken and doubt arose (these śrāvakas, having heard that the three vehicles are skillful means, thus doubted the skillful means; furthermore, having heard that the ultimate truth must be taught, they thus doubted the ultimate truth). The text is as follows:

Two: First, the narration of the doubt; second, the formal request for a resolution. The narration of the doubt is further divided into two: first, the narration by the sūtra compiler; second, the actual arising of the doubt.
The former [the compiler’s narration] is divided into two: first, the narration of the doubt of the twelve hundred [disciples].
At that time, within the great assembly were various śrāvakas, numbering up to twelve hundred people. Next,
[the text] describes the doubts of the fourfold assembly,
as well as those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had resolved their minds upon becoming śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

The preceding statement that "the three vehicles are all expedient means" addresses the expression of doubt specifically regarding the two vehicles because their attachments were heavy and their doubts were deep;

thus, they were singled out. However, when reaching the subsequent section where doubts are presented, it says: "Those seeking Buddhahood, the various bodhisattvas, numbering approximately eighty thousand, also all had doubts.
From this, we know that those of all three vehicles harbored doubts, and it was merely the two vehicles that were specifically mentioned.
△ Second, the actual arising of doubt, which has two parts: first, doubting the Buddha; second, doubting the [Buddha’s] wisdom.
Each forms this thought: (up to) "that which no śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha can attain."
For what reason is the skillful means (upāya) so earnestly praised? This constitutes a general doubt regarding the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.
Consequently, it is said: "The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound"—this doubts the real wisdom (bhūtajñāna).

"That which is spoken has an intention difficult to discern"—this doubts the provisional wisdom (saṃvṛtijñāna). Because one hears that the speech of all Buddhas is without difference, one must indeed speak of the truth.
Indeed, from this, doubt arises. Why? Because in the past, the Buddha taught that the wisdom of the three vehicles is identical in its realization and not different;
there is only the matter of whether residual habits have been exhausted or not. Now, he suddenly praises the two kinds of wisdom of the Tathāgata as being beyond my reach.
Therefore, they doubt the Buddha’s two types of knowledge. △ Second, they doubt what they themselves have attained:
"The Buddha has taught the meaning of a single liberation (up to this point), yet now we do not know where this meaning leads."
From the Buddha’s teaching on the single meaning of liberation, we have also attained this Dharma.

We previously harbored doubts as to whether the noble paths of the three vehicles that we had realized were truly the definitive means of transcendence, and whether by cultivating these principles we would likewise reach nirvana.
Now, hearing that all of these are merely skillful means, we do not yet know which one is the ultimate reality; therefore, it is said that we do not understand the meaning of this.
[The section on] "The Destinies" (gati). This follows the previous refutation of the three as being merely skillful means (*upāya*), which gave rise to this doubt.

(1) The narration of the doubt is concluded. △ Second, the formal request for a definitive resolution. The text contains three requests and two refusals; regarding the former, there are three instances of refusal.

The Buddha, foreseeing that those who would benefit from the three successive cycles [of teaching] could not do so simultaneously, therefore suppressed him three times to wait for his third request. Regarding the first request, it is divided into two parts.
First, the prose; second, the verses. The prose section is twofold: first, the presentation of doubts.
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the minds of the fourfold assembly were filled with doubt... (up to)... now the fourfold assembly all have doubts.
△ 2. The formal request:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter—[extending to]—this profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
△ 2. Within the verse section, there are eleven lines of verse, divided into six parts. The first two lines of the text praise the reality of the doubt.
[The Buddha] said: "Wisdom. At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has long since preached this Dharma."
△ Second, three lines. These verses express doubt regarding provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
[The text] says: "I have attained such [wisdom]... that which all Buddhas have attained.
△ Third, three lines. These clarify that the members of the Three Vehicles and the fourfold assembly harbor doubts.
"O Arhats free from outflows... (up to) I pray that the Buddha will explain this for us.
This first line consists of three parts: the first phrase clarifies the Arhats; the second phrase clarifies the Bodhisattvas. Since it speaks of "nirvāṇa," why mention Bodhisattvas?
The previous statement, "those who have attained nirvāṇa," refers here to the term "and" (*ji*). In this context, "and" (*ji*) refers to these Bodhisattvas.
They seek nirvana for themselves and also for others; thus they differ from the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Knowing this, one recognizes them as bodhisattvas.
The latter two lines clarify the pratyekabuddhas: the two groups of renunciants and the eight classes of beings, etc., are all those with the capacity for the Middle Vehicle.
△ The fourth section, consisting of one and a half lines, clarifies the doubts of Śāriputra.
[This is] the path practiced by all the assembly of śrāvakas.
△ Fifth section: Clarifying the doubts of the Buddha’s sons.

"The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth, with palms joined, gaze up at him in expectation. We pray that you will utter a subtle and wondrous sound, and at this time speak for us according to reality."
△ The sixth section, consisting of two lines, provides a general clarification of the shared inquiry and request.
From "The devas, nāgas, spirits, and so forth" up to "desiring to hear the complete path":
generally, verses can be inferred from their prose counterparts; if they do not correspond to the verse, they are considered prose expansions. Regarding the meaning:
As this is not urgent, I have not troubled myself with detailed textual analysis and have thus abbreviated it. Next, the two types of cessation are explained;
fearing that [the audience] might be startled or doubtful, at that time the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: “[... all the gods and humans in the world will surely be startled and doubtful.”
△ Second, Śāriputra proclaims his own sharp faculties from former lives; therefore, he requests again.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha once more (until) and spoke in verse:
"O Dharma King, Supreme Honored One, please speak; do not hesitate. In this assembly there are immeasurable multitudes who are capable of respectful faith.
△ Next, the Buddha stopped him three times, in order to protect those with overweening pride.
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra (and so on), and spoke these verses once more:
"Stop, stop; there is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. Those with overweening pride will certainly not show respect or faith upon hearing it."
△ Third, Śāriputra describes how his wisdom brings great benefit. This section consists of two parts: first, the prose narrative.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] "...bringing peace and security for a long night and providing much benefit."
△ Next, the verses.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings... [omitted] ...then gives rise to great joy."
(1. Briefly opening the three to reveal the one and resolving doubts through inquiry concluded). △ 2. Extensively opening the three to reveal the one, severing doubt and engendering faith.

This consists of three cycles, comprising eight chapters in total. First, from this point until the end of the second fascicle, ending with the verses on dedicating toward the Buddha-way, constitutes the cycle of the Dharma-exposition for those of superior faculties.
Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Śāriputra, I... [the cycle for those of middling faculties begins].

From "Now there is no further doubt or regret" below, up to the bestowal of the prophecy, there are four chapters; these constitute the completion of the teaching through parables for those of medium faculties.

The three chapters beginning with the Parable of the Phantom City constitute the completion of the teaching through causes and conditions for those of inferior faculties; they are also termed the "Practice of Principle and Phenomena."

Question: The three cycles [of the *Lotus Sūtra*] are for those of the three faculties. How is it that one cycle universally possesses all three explanations? If that were so, then a single explanation should possess all three faculties. Answer:
The Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*) does not merely accommodate those of the highest among the middling; there are also those of middling and inferior faculties.

Because it proceeds from the primary [teaching] to the secondary, it is said to "accommodate the superior" alone. The same applies to the other two cycles. (The intent of the answer is to grant that each [cycle] possesses all three faculties; the Dharma-exposition...)

Within the discourse on the Dharma, three [faculties] are primary; the remaining two are likewise so. It suffices to speak of the three faculties to encompass all nine. Regarding the principle of prioritizing the principal over the secondary: among the superior faculties, the "superior-superior" is the principal, while the "middle-inferior" is secondary.

One should also say: "In full discussion there are three, but for the time being we speak only of the superior. If one accords with those of superior faculty, all three superior types are included; however, the superior is predominant and constitutes the principal, while the middle and inferior are abbreviated and secondary. The same applies to whether the three middle and inferior faculties are considered principal or secondary. Indeed, the minds of sentient beings are unstable;
encountering adverse conditions, they turn from sharpness to dullness, and encountering favorable conditions, they turn from dullness to sharpness.

Those with sharp faculties had encountered Buddhas and heard the Dharma in previous lives; thus, they were able to transform their inferior or middling capacities into superior ones, attaining awakening through the direct teaching of the Dharma.

Some transformed their inferior capacity into a middling one, attaining understanding through the parables. Those with inferior faculties did not transform at all, only reaching realization after the three turnings.

Such transformations of the faculties are illustrated by the analogy of cutting wood with three types of axes: the sharp one cuts once, the middling one twice, and the dull one requires three blows. This illustrates the difference in sharpness.

The name "dull" is not lost; the place where the wood is cut is the same. (As for the analogy: the blade is like the root; the wood is like delusion; the trigger is like the grasping; the Buddha causes it to be cut.)

Receiving the teaching is like hearing the Dharma; wielding the axe is like applying contemplation; the wood being cut is like realization; and having been whetted is like transformation. Because the encounter with the whetstone differs, there are those who are sharp and those who are dull. Question: Do the three faculties enter the first stage?
Question: Are there those who are sharp and those who are dull? Answer: When the essence of true cultivation is manifested, there is no gradation of difference. Question:

If that is so, for those from the first stage (bhūmi) upward, when they further give rise to cultivation through conditions (pratyaya-bhāvanā), is there still superiority or inferiority? Answer: For those who occupy the same level, there is no longer any distinction of victory or defeat.
Since the essence of true cultivation is harmoniously integrated, how could there be any difference?
Question: In the sūtras, it is frequently explained that bodhisattvas possess superior faculties, pratyekabuddhas middling faculties, and śrāvakas inferior faculties.

If it is said that bodhisattvas have superior faculties, should they not all attain awakening through the Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā), pratyekabuddhas all attain understanding through the parable-exposition (avadānadeśanā), and śrāvakas all attain awakening through the exposition of causes and conditions (nidānadeśanā)? However, in the sūtras, generally speaking...

The classification into three faculties (*indriya*) pertains to their realization; however, from the standpoint of ultimate meaning, this is not necessarily so. In the present sutra, we see only that the *śrāvakas* attain understanding, while no mention is made of the *pratyekabuddhas*.

Since *pratyekabuddhas* possess middling faculties, and having encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, they are included within the category of *śrāvakas*, attaining awakening according to their faculties;
therefore, they are not separately designated as "Pratyekabuddhas. Thus, Śāriputra’s verse of request says: "That..."
Regarding those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha—monks and nuns—one knows from this passage that pratyekabuddhas are included within the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, the "Dharma Master" chapter states: "Monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen."
Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka or those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha—do they not also attain liberation through conditions?

The traditional view holds that bodhisattvas possess superior faculties, yet this does not mean they are necessarily sharp-witted; rather, they are considered superior because their mental dispositions are more easily transformed.

Although their original aspiration was to seek Buddhahood, once they have practiced for more than three hundred kalpas, they immediately seek proximate fruits. This doubt is easy to resolve for those of the three faculties.

Bodhisattvas all attain understanding through the teaching of the Dharma. Those of superior capacity may do so through a brief exposition; those of middling capacity may do so at the beginning of a detailed exposition;

and those of inferior capacity are equal to Śāriputra. Now, it is clarified that the term "bodhisattva" is inclusive: as long as one has resolved upon the Great Mind (mahācitta), one is entirely a bodhisattva.
Why must they necessarily possess sharp faculties? Furthermore, since even Śāriputra was still young, how could [the others] have attained [realization] from the very beginning?

At the beginning of the Zhou dynasty, [the Buddha] had already attained awakening. If this is so, for what purpose does the *Lifespan Sūtra* (Shouliang) state that there are various bodhisattvas who, at each successive stage, attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and resolve their minds on enlightenment (*bodhicitta*)? The traditional explanation says: they awaken within the context of the Lifespan.
All these are the Dharmakāya; [it is said that] one increases the Path and diminishes births. Now it is said that this is not so.
There were six hundred and eighty *koṭi-nayuta* of people, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Since these people have only now attained this patience, one should know that prior to this attainment of longevity, they were not yet the Dharmakāya. Therefore, one knows that the realization of a Bodhisattva cannot be restricted [to a single stage].
This was at the beginning of the first cycle.
Question: If the awakening attained by Bodhisattvas extends from the beginning to the end, then the awakening attained by those of the Two Vehicles should likewise reach the latter stages. Answer:

Once the three cycles have definitively established the natural affinity between father and son, they are all designated as Bodhisattvas; even if their awakening occurs later, they share the same name.
The Bodhisattva awakens.
Question: If the three vehicles awaken equally, for what reason do we see only the Śrāvaka attaining realization, while the other two do not? Answer:

It is explained that when no Buddha appears in the world, one is called a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer). When one hears the Buddha teach the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, one is called a [Śrāvaka].
Regarding "Awakening": once they have entered among the ranks of the Śrāvakas and attained realization and understanding, they do not emerge separately; the general meaning is thus evident.

Since Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, and others all possessed the spiritual capacity (*gotra*) of the Middle Vehicle, the realization of the Śrāvakas therein also encompasses that of the Pratyekabuddhas, making it unnecessary for them to emerge separately.
Furthermore, among the fourfold assembly, there are those who have resolved upon the mind of a Pratyekabuddha; such individuals [attain this realization].
Awakening is precisely not a single state. As stated in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding": "He secretly dispatched two men to pursue and seize [the son] to bring him back. This is its meaning.

If a bodhisattva does not yet fully comprehend this, it is because the teachings for śrāvakas do not clarify the attainment of Buddhahood; whereas this present sutra opens the path for returning to the Great Vehicle.
Fearing that his own understanding might be erroneous, he therefore recounts his realization before the Buddha; a bodhisattva does not act in this manner. Thus...
There was no comprehension. Furthermore, there were two aspects to his intention: first, the Bodhisattva’s original intent was to seek Buddhahood;

even if he held divergent attachments, they were slight, and since he would ultimately attain Buddhahood, he had no anxiety that he might fail to do so. Now, having heard the teaching of the three turnings, [he has attained realization].

However, because this correctly establishes the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it does not require a formal acknowledgment of understanding (*prativedha*). There are texts in various places concerning the two bodhisattvas’ realization of the Great [Vehicle].

As for the two vehicles attaining Buddhahood, this begins with the present teaching; as it was transmitted according to its essential points, the bodhisattvas’ acknowledgment of understanding has been abbreviated.
It may exist in the Sanskrit original; it is simply not recorded in the Chinese translation due to abbreviation. Question:
If all have equally attained understanding, why do the śrāvakas receive predictions [of enlightenment], while we do not see the pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas receiving such predictions?

This also has three meanings. First, it clarifies that in the past, when the two vehicles entered the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), they were unable to resolve their minds toward enlightenment. Why? Because...

Because they have received their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), and now that they have awakened to the Great [Vehicle], they rejoice in this specific decision; therefore, the kalpa and the land are recorded for them.

When Bodhisattvas resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood, their practice reaches fulfillment of its own accord; thus, they do not rejoice in seeking Buddhahood with haste, nor is the prediction granted prematurely.

Furthermore, it is a constant teaching that predictions are granted to Bodhisattvas at various points throughout the preceding instructions. This has been translated according to the essentials, as previously stated.

"Yun" (Clouds). [Addendum by Zhen: Regarding the successive essential transmissions, the phrase "as previously stated, etc. refers to the first of these three points: bestowing upon the *śrāvakas* the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their kalpa and land. This is indeed the essential point. Bestowing predictions upon Bodhisattvas is a constant teaching and not what is urgent here.

Furthermore, in the section on the circulation of the *jī-mén* (Trace Gate), both Devadatta and the Dragon Girl are granted predictions; how can one say they were not? This is as cited in sequence below. Second, the two Bodhisattvas also have individual predictions. Are Devadatta and the Dragon Girl not recipients of predictions?
Moreover, the "Dharma Master" chapter states: "Those who seek the state of a *śrāvaka*..."
Pratyekabuddhas, those seeking the Buddha-way, and others of such kind—all have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the presence of the Buddha;
I have bestowed upon them all the prediction that they shall attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Is this not, indeed, a bestowal of predictions for all?

The followers of the three vehicles had never before received the prediction of the eight marks; therefore, their kalpas and lands were recorded. As for the Bodhisattvas, they had already previously...

Commentary: Therefore, it is not reiterated here. Such a prediction of a shallow and mundane attainment has already been achieved at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and is not what a Bodhisattva delights in.
What a Bodhisattva aspires to is precisely the prediction of the ultimate, wondrous enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Thus, in the *Ayuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta*, from the initial generation of the mind until the attainment [of Buddhahood] in a single lifetime, the wondrous cause is fulfilled and the supreme fruit is suddenly perfected; this is the bestowal of the Dharma.
The Prediction Concerning the Body. What is meant by "unpredictable" (avyākṛta)? Question:

If a small awakening corresponds to the Great [Vehicle], one should likewise receive the prediction of the Dharma-body; why then is the prediction of the eight phases (aṣṭalakṣaṇa) bestowed? Answer: The eight phases are that which should be predicted.
Since they are what should be predicted, it is known that there must be a fundamental basis for them. This is intended so that all beings may know and hear of it together.

Because they have formed the conditions for future connection, they are merely granted a prediction (vyākaraṇa). Furthermore, if these followers of the two vehicles were to hear [of the Buddha’s] lifespan, it would be equivalent to wasting their remaining lives;
thus, they receive the prediction of attaining the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Furthermore, this clarifies the distinction between those who depend on time and those who do not. Those who did not awaken prior to this point and must necessarily attain awakening through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are said to "depend on time.

Those who have already understood the teachings prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are said to "not depend on time. Why is this so? Because the Buddha possesses two modes of teaching: the manifest and the secret.

If one were to discuss the manifest teaching, before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the followers of the Two Vehicles had not yet awakened to the Great Way; it was only [through this sūtra] that they were required to...
The five flavors must be matured through refinement, and their convergence occurs at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore it is said:
"Because the time for preaching had not yet arrived," and now, "this is precisely that time; I shall definitively preach the Mahāyāna. This refers to "waiting for the time.

If we discuss the Esoteric Teachings (*guhyamantra*), they do not necessarily require the maturation of the five flavors before converging at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; since there were those who entered [the path] prior to that point, they are called "not waiting."

At that time, this is a general judgment regarding what is timely and what is untimely. If one considers the three cycles (*san-zhōu*), these likewise involve waiting for the opportune moment or not waiting for it.
Regarding the two gates of the Trace and the Origin (*jì-běn èr mén*), there is likewise the waiting for the opportune moment or not waiting for it;

this is precisely the meaning behind the fact that there are those who attain awakening and entry at different times, either before or after [the three cycles]. (Supplementary note: Those who attain realization and receive the teaching either before or after the three cycles do so by waiting for the opportune moment. Those who secretly attain it before or after, rather than being counted within the three cycles themselves, do so without waiting for the opportune moment. Furthermore, regarding the Trace...)
The provisional gate awaits the [proper] time; the original gate does not await the time.

Question: There is a certain type of faculty that is neither secret nor manifest and is not subsumed within either of the two periods; should this not be considered a case of missing the [right] time?
"Will they never attain awakening? He replied: "In other sutras, this may be called a loss of opportunity; however, this present sutra is not so.
Although these people do not awaken during either the secret or the manifest periods, and although they conceive the thought that they have attained parinirvāṇa, within that land..."
Because they have heard this sutra, there is no loss of time; it is simply that they are waiting for the time of that land. Question:
The five thousand who rose and departed must have lost their opportunity. Answer: These individuals will surely receive benefit as those who propagate the sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.

Question: During the first week, Śāriputra made the request on behalf of the fourfold assembly with the three capacities; during the second week, it was requested by those of middle and lower capacities.
Why, then, do you say that the Buddha taught the Dharma in three weeks specifically for each of the three types of capacity?

Answer: That phrasing is not appropriate. The request was universal, and the teaching was likewise universal. However, those of superior capacity possess sharp wisdom and attain awakening upon hearing the Dharma; those of middle capacity remain at a middling level.

One attains awakening through hearing analogies. Those of inferior faculties abide at the lower level; they attain awakening upon hearing three [analogies]. You should follow the meaning; why would you follow the literal words? Question:
The past lives are matters of the past; are the Dharma and the analogies not matters of the present and future? Answer: There is no such text in the sutras; it is a matter of interpretation.

It should be understood in this way. Drawing the three back to the one: when the three are viewed from the perspective of the one, the one is precisely what is appropriate. To cite a concrete matter as an analogy is to make it manifest.

Judging the latter in light of the former, it should be as you have asked. (Supplementary note: Regarding the meaning of the distinctions among the three cycles, there are ten types of analytical examination in the *Wenju*.)

As the text says, "The defilements of sentient beings are heavy"—this refers to this very point. The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) takes the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-saṃyojana*) as its essence.

The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) takes the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-saṃyojana*) as its essence. The turbidity of life-span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) takes the continuous maintenance of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) as its essence.
As for the characteristics: the four turbidities (kaṣāya) increase and intensify, gathering together at this time. Hatred increases and intensifies, and weapons arise;
greed increases and intensifies, and famine arises; delusion increases and intensifies, and pestilence arises.

Because these three calamities arise, afflictions flourish twofold, various views become increasingly fierce, and coarse and debased form and mind, evil reputations and foul names, destroy years and diminish lifespans—these are the many turbidities.

They converge and clash like rushing waters in a dark torrent; wind and waves surge and swell, while fish and dragons thrash about, such that not one can find any reliance. It is time that causes this to be so.
It is like when, at the beginning of a kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven fall to earth, and the earth causes them to have desires.

It is like when those from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Rough and Harsh Garden (Karkaśavana), and the garden gives rise to a fighting mind. This is called the characteristic of the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (the turbidity of the age). [The phrase "like rushing waters in a dark torrent" refers to turbid water. Regarding "Ābhāsvara" and so forth...]

When the world was first formed, this deity descended for the first time; that is, the first heaven of the second dhyāna. Upon first descending to the human realm, his body possessed radiance and he was still able to fly. He had no male or female organs and required nothing to eat.

This continued until he began eating forest creepers, *bhūmiparpaṭaka* (earth-crust), and eventually rice and so forth. At that point, male and female organs appeared, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Kalpas" of the *Abhidharmakośa*. The earth itself is an adverse condition (*pratyaya*); it is spoken of in terms of these conditions, hence the statement that it causes such things to arise.

The mention of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and others is likewise an illustration, further clarifying that desires and evils arise from the earth. Outside the city of Śakra, there are four parks: Caitraratha, Pāruṣyaka, Miśraka, and Nandana. When the gods wish to go to war, they take their various weapons from the Pāruṣyaka park; when they need vehicles, they go to the Caitraratha park.

Just as one enters the Nandana Grove and gives rise to joy, so too does the birth of desire within the realm of desire arise. As for the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): the ocean of greed receives all flowing streams yet is never satiated;
the venomous serpent of anger drinks poison and agitates all worlds; the darkness of ignorance is more stubborn and dull than lacquer or ink;
pride looks down upon others with haughty disregard and insults them without measure; and the net of doubt lacks faith such that the truth cannot be told. This is called the turbidity of afflictions.
Regarding the "impurity of views" (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya): to perceive what is not a person as a person, or what is not the Path as the Path;
the sixteen types of false views, the sixty-two [views], and so forth—these are like a net and resemble a dense forest, entangling and distorting one so that one cannot escape.

This is the characteristic of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). As for the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*): they grasp at form and mind to establish a single sovereign self, like sticky glue to which nothing does not adhere.
Wandering through the six realms of existence, they undergo birth everywhere—being called poor or short, or named rich or tall;

this is the characteristic of the turbidity of sentient beings. As for the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kāṣāya*): one is born in the morning and perishes by evening; one emerges by day and sets by night.

Waves roll and smoke swirls; in a mere instant, nothing remains. This is the characteristic of the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). Though the characteristics of turbidity are numerous and cannot be fully described, as for their sequence:
afflictions and views constitute the root. From these two turbidities, sentient beings are formed;
from sentient beings, there arises the continuity of life. The passage of time through these four is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

Regarding the discernment [of these matters]: Question: If the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) constitute such a great obstacle, why is it that those who hear the Dharma within the *Avataṃsaka* have not yet eliminated these turbidities?

Answer: This should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, there are those with sharp Mahāyāna faculties but heavy obstacles; because their faculties are sharp, the heavy obstacles cannot obstruct them.

These are the individuals in this land who first hear the Mahāyāna within the *Avataṃsaka*. Second, those with... [faculties... (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end of the second proposition.)

First, those with sharp faculties and light hindrances, such as those in the pure lands of other directions who hear the Mahāyāna. Second, those with sharp faculties and heavy hindrances, such as Śāriputra and others in this land who hear the Mahāyāna only after their defilements have been removed.

Third, those with dull faculties and light hindrances, such as those in the pure lands of other directions who hear the Mahāyāna. Fourth, those with dull faculties and heavy hindrances, such as Śāriputra and others in this land who hear the Mahāyāna only after their defilements have been removed.

Question: Do the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) obstruct those of the Lesser Vehicle? Answer: This is discussed from the perspective of the Lesser Vehicle and should be analyzed through four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).

First, when one’s faculties are sharp and the obstacles are light, the obstacles cannot hinder; Śāriputra is an example of this. Second, when one’s faculties are sharp and the obstacles are heavy, the obstacles likewise cannot hinder; Aṅgulimāla is an example of this.

Third, when one’s faculties are dull and the obstacles are light, they also do not constitute an obstruction; Upāli (Panthaka) is an example of this. [Fourth, when one’s faculties are dull and the obstacles are heavy...]
Obstructing what is weighty constitutes an impediment; such is one who does not hear the Hīnayāna and cannot attain liberation.

This was Caṅkumāra (translated as "Manifest in All Worlds"), the son of a Brahmin whose mother was Bhadrā. Having lost his father at a young age, he was twelve years old when he was fully endowed with physical strength, human characteristics, and wisdom. He studied under the Brahmin Maṇibhadra, through whom he mastered the four Vedas.

On one occasion, while his teacher had briefly accepted an invitation from the king, he left Caṅkumāra behind to guard the house. The Brahmin’s wife was young and beautiful; she conceived a lustful attachment toward Caṅkumāra and approached him, grasping his garment. Caṅkumāra said: "O Virtuous One, now..."

"She is my mother. How could you, in such a venerable position, commit an unrighteous act? My heart is filled with shame and terror; I have cast off my clothes and fled far away. The wife, overcome with shame, hanged herself with a rope.

Before her feet had even left the ground, Maṇibhadra returned home from his business and saw his wife suspended there. He cut the rope with a knife and cried out at the top of his voice, "Who has done this? The wife replied, "It was Lokāntika. Desiring to commit an unrighteous act, he forcibly oppressed me and caused me to do this. Maṇibhadra already knew that this man possessed great merit.

Having reflected upon this, he said to Lokāntika, "You are an evil man! You have brought disgrace upon one who is worthy of honor. You are no longer a true Brahmin; you must kill a thousand people to expiate your sin."

The world, appearing to obey his command, immediately killed one thousand people. He returned and prostrated at the feet of his teacher. The teacher spoke again, saying: "You must kill another thousand people; with a finger from each person, you shall make a garland to crown your head. Only then will you become a true Brahmin.

Aṅgulimāla then killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people, lacking only one finger. Seeing his mother, he intended to kill her as well. The World-Honored One appeared before him; he set his mother aside and sought to kill the Buddha. The Buddha manifested himself as if moving away to avoid him. The world, appearing to speak a verse, said: "Stop, stop, Great Śramaṇa!"

"Prince of King Śuddhodana, I am Aṅgulimāla; now you must pay the tax of one finger. The World-Honored One replied with a verse: "Stop, stop, Aṅgulimāla! I shall grant you the tax of the sword of wisdom. I abide at the limit of non-arising, yet you do not perceive it."

Finally, the World-Honored One spoke a verse to Aṅgulimāla, saying: "Come, Aṅgulimāla! Leave the household life and receive the Three Refuges. Aṅgulimāla replied with a verse: "This vehicle is the Mahāyāna; it is called the Unobstructed Wisdom. Therefore, on this day, I take refuge in the Tathāgata.

The World-Honored One then exclaimed: "Excellent, Aṅgulimāla! Welcome, Bhikṣu! He immediately became a śramaṇa, his deportment complete, just like a long-standing bhikṣu. At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions dispatched great bodhisattvas, saying:

"Now Śākyamuni Buddha is battling the Great Dharma General, subduing the Great Lion, and delivering immeasurable multitudes. Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla asked the Buddha: "The Tathāgata says: 'I abide in the limit of non-arising; I abide in the ground of liberation.'"

"How is it that you still dwell in this Sahā world? I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions. The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla: "You should go together with Mañjuśrī to the ten directions, each passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

In each of those worlds, ask the Buddhas about this same matter. You shall depart from here like a king of geese. Each of those Buddhas will reply: 'Śākyamuni Buddha is indeed my own body. When you return, they will explain it for you.

Aṅgulimāla and Mañjuśrī immediately returned to their own land and related the aforementioned events in detail, requesting the Buddha to provide an answer. The Buddha then said: "Aṅgulimāla, the limit of non-arising in nirvāṇa is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is precisely nirvāṇa and non-arising."

...and so forth. This sutra consists of four fascicles and was translated by Guṇabhadra during the Liu Song dynasty; here, however, I have recorded only its general outline. (○ The bhikṣu Panthaka lacked the faculty for extensive learning. The Buddha had him recite the two characters "zhāo" (broom) and "sǒu" (broom).

He would forget "zhāo" when reciting "sǒu," and forget "sǒu" when reciting "zhāo. One day, while reciting them together, he uttered the word "zhāosǒu" (broom). Suddenly his mind opened wide, and he realized the fruit of Arhatship.)
Question: There are those who hear both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, yet these teachings are neither contained within the *Avataṃsaka* nor within the Tripiṭaka.
Why is this so? Answer: This is based on the four teachings (*catur-deśanā*). Within each teaching, one makes a fourfold distinction according to the gates (*dvāra*).

For those with sharp faculties who are averse to [the view of] lightness, they enter by hearing the gate of "neither empty nor existent. For those with sharp faculties who are averse to [the view of] heaviness, they hear "both empty and existent."

The "gates" (mukha) refer to entry. For those of dull faculties who are hindered by light [afflictions], they enter through hearing the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). For those of dull faculties who are hindered by heavy [afflictions], they enter through hearing the gate of existence (*bhava*).
The four gates of the two teachings are distinguished according to the Hīnayāna; the four gates of the two teachings are distinguished according to the Mahāyāna.
These can be understood through careful analysis.

If one discusses cause and effect, there are two causes and three effects (the two causes refer to afflictions and views; the remaining three are effects, encompassing both the environment and its inhabitants).

If one discusses persons and dharmas, there is one person and four dharmas (the "person" refers to sentient beings; the "dharmas" are the remaining four). If one discusses the three obstructions, there are two that are obstructions of retribution.

Second is the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "Karma lies between them" (the two results refer to the life-span of sentient beings; the two afflictions include views as well, since they are also designated by the term "affliction";
that "karma lies between them" means that afflictions moisten karma, and karma is able to summon retribution; hence it is said "between them").

The treatise discusses the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Sentient beings are the provisional designation of causal aggregation; life is the provisional designation of continuity;

and relative dependence is the provisional designation of mutual relativity (as can be understood from the section on sentient beings). [In the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, this is the "Gate of the Three Provisional Designations. Regarding "relative dependence can be known": this refers to kalpas, afflictions, and views. Kalpas involve the relativity of long and short; afflictions involve the relativity of adverse and favorable conditions;

views involve the relativity of existence and non-existence. If discussed comprehensively, each possesses all three provisional designations. Both the primary and secondary retributions are, without exception, formed through these three provisional designations. Here, however, we proceed according to specific distinctions and speak of them separately; therefore, they are addressed individually.]

Question: Since you have spoken of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), what are the five clarities? Answer: By analogy with the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, the heterodox three poisons constitute the five turbidities, while the orthodox [three poisons] constitute the five clarities.
In the pure lands of other directions, there are no heterodox three poisons; thus, the obstacles of the five turbidities are light.

This meaning can be understood (when it says "the three poisons are truly absent," it refers to pure lands in other directions such as the land of Akṣobhya, where there are indeed women, yet because there is no lustful desire, one instance serves as the standard for the rest; all similar cases may be recognized by analogy).
△ Third, the explanation of the commentary on the text.
From "Śāriputra, during the period of the turbidity of the kalpa" up to "the One Buddha Vehicle is distinguished and taught as three.

(The third section, the explanation of the five turbidities and the completion of the teaching of provisional means. △ Fourth, the text that distinguishes the false and encourages the true, in two parts. First:

Distinguishing the True from the False. Second, resolving doubts through exemptions. The first [section] is further divided into two: first, if one does not hear and know [the teaching], one is not a true disciple;
second, if one hears but does not believe and accept it, one becomes conceited (adhimāna). Now, the first [point]:

Śāriputra, as for my disciples (up to) those who are not pratyekabuddhas, they follow the Teacher’s Dharma and succeed to the transmission of the lamp, just like the disciples of the world. If they do not hear and do not know the Teacher’s True Dharma, then there is no Dharma to which they can conform.
What, then, would constitute being a disciple? In the past, the Tathāgata spoke of three [vehicles] for the sake of the five turbidities.

By following [this path], you shall attain Nirvana; to hear it and to know it is what defines one as a disciple. Now that the five corruptions have been removed, I have preached the One for your sake.
For what reason do you neither hear nor know it? "Not hearing" means not hearing the teaching of the One.
"Not knowing" means not knowing the practice of the One. This is not the truth, which is to say it is not the principle of the One. Such a person is not a disciple; they are not a human being.
First. △ Second, failing to believe and accept upon hearing [the teaching] results in the formation of overweening pride (adhimāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra... (up to)... if one does not believe this Dharma, such a thing is impossible.

Regarding those who develop pride through lack of faith: this is to urge them toward faith. Why? You claim for yourself that you are in your final birth (*caramabhavika*), yet your remaining lifetimes are still immeasurable;
you are not, in fact, in your final birth. You claim for yourself that you have reached the ultimate goal, yet two hundred *yojanas* still remain;
you have not, in fact, reached the ultimate goal. To claim to have attained what one has not attained—is this not overweening pride (*adhimāna*)? A true Arhat is one whose turbidity has been removed.
Their faculties are sharp. Knowing that [their realization] is not ultimate, they believe in the true Dharma; though they are not yet in their final birth, they do not give rise to overweening pride.

Knowing it is not ultimate, they place faith in the ultimate; this is precisely faith in the oneness of principle, which is free from the pride of superiority, and thus constitutes the oneness of practice.
To have faith is to believe in the teaching; this constitutes the unity of the teaching. To be a disciple of the Buddha is the unity of the person.
△ Second, the opening of exceptions and the resolution of doubts, which is further divided into two parts. First, the opening of exceptions.
Aside from after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning [of this sutra] are difficult to find.
Aside from after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one does not fall into overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Why is this?

After the Buddha’s passing, it is clarified that good people are difficult to find and the profound sutras are difficult to understand; yet, one still does not fall into overweening pride. If the Buddha were in the world, he would correctly expound this.
If one does not believe in or accept the sutras, they are not a true Arhat and have developed overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

If it were the case that one could only become an Arhat after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, then those who cling exclusively to provisional sutras and do not believe in the perfect Dharma would be permitted to be considered as having overweening pride.

Furthermore, even though the Buddha has entered nirvāṇa, this sutra still remains; if one does not believe in or accept it, should that not indeed be overweening pride? Thus, [the teaching] is opened up.
[This is] excluded. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, although this sutra exists, those who can understand its textual meaning are difficult to encounter.
Even if Arhats do not believe or understand it, they may be permitted [to remain so], provided they are not characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*). △ Next, the resolution of doubts.
If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma.
However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can interpret the sūtras are difficult to find. As for those who have attained arhatship, do they enter parinirvāṇa forever?

The commentary explains: although this person conceives the thought that they have attained nirvāṇa, after their life has ended, they are reborn in another land beyond this realm where they encounter another Buddha and hear this sutra;
they then attain definitive understanding. The ninety-third fascicle of the *Śāstra* (Treatise), in its explanation of the "Chapter on Certainty," states:
"When an Arhat receives a body from a previous existence, that body must necessarily perish. [He] dwells...
"In what place is the Buddha-way fully realized? The answer is: "The Arhat has exhausted the causes and conditions of the outflows within the three realms and will no longer be reborn therein.
Beyond the three realms, there is a pure buddha-field where even the name of affliction does not exist.

It is in the presence of a Buddha in that land that one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and fully realizes the Buddha-way. This is immediately supported by the *Lotus Sutra*, which states: "There are Arhats..."
If one has not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, yet claims to have attained nirvāṇa, I shall explain this matter in other lands:
"You shall all become Buddhas. Since the treatise (*śāstra*) has already cited the sūtra as proof, I shall now interpret the sūtra by means of the treatise.

Master Nanyue said: "The 'other Buddhas' are the four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratiśaraṇāni*). When Arhats encounter them, they hear the sūtra and attain definitive understanding. Furthermore, Arhats practice...
Through the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions and they preach this sutra for one; thus, one immediately attains definitive understanding.
Furthermore, if an ordinary practitioner repents with utmost sincerity, they will see the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching for them, and likewise attain definitive understanding.
(The fourth section, "Distinguishing the False and Upholding the True," is concluded. △ Fifth, clarifying that there is no falsehood in order to stop the slanderous minds of others.
"Śāriputra, you all should with one mind believe and understand [up to] the single Buddha-vehicle.

This passage has three parts: first, the exhortation to believe that Śākyamuni’s teaching is the true word; second, from "All Buddhas, Tathāgatas... onwards, the exhortation to believe in all Buddhas.
"Third, 'There is no other vehicle remaining' below concludes that [the teaching] is not in vain (the first part, the prose exposition of the Dharma, is finished).
△ Second, the verse recitation consists of one hundred and twenty-one lines, divided into two parts: first, four lines and one phrase, which versify the aforementioned promise to answer;
second, one hundred and sixteen lines and three phrases, which versify the actual response. Regarding the aforementioned promise to answer:"
Three [aspects]: namely, the favorable, the admonitory, and the discriminative. Here, I shall not recite the favorable, but shall recite only the discriminative and the admonitory.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (up to: Śāriputra, listen well.

[This covers] the first three and a half lines of verse. Regarding the five thousand who withdrew above, they possessed overweening pride (*adhimāna*), self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and lack of faith; these four groups all had them in common.

However, among the two monastic orders, many cultivate the Way and attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet they mistakenly claim these are the fruits of sainthood and give rise to one-sided overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Among the laity, those who boast of their own excellence often give rise to the pride of self (*asmimāna*). Women possess shallow wisdom and frequently develop deviant views;

those who do not perceive their own faults have their minds shrouded by three kinds of loss. By concealing their flaws and extolling their virtues, they are unable to engage in self-reflection; such people are devoid of a sense of shame (*ahrīka*).

If one perceives one's own faults, such a person is a monk possessed of shame (*hrī*). Regarding those who have deficiencies in the precepts: a failure in the *vinaya* discipline is termed a "deficiency" (*chidra*);

a failure in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with the Path is termed a "leakage" (*srotas*), because of the absence of the Path, concentration, and so forth. Consequently, evil thoughts arise within.
Like jade containing flaws, because one lacks the *saṃvara* (restraint), external actions of body and speech reveal these flaws like jade showing its blemishes;

thus, by concealing one's offenses, one merely gains self-satisfaction, which is called "guarding and cherishing. One of small wisdom does not possess the knowledge of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or those in training (*śaikṣa*), but possesses only worldly, minor wisdom;
they falsely claim that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) to be without outflows (*anāsrava*). Being the smallest among the small, it is called "small wisdom. It is like dregs.

Regarding "husks": because they lack the moisture of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), they are like dregs; because they lack the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are like husks.

These five thousand [monks] and others possess mundane meditation like dregs and possess literal textual understanding like husks; they cling to the words and lose the essential meaning, like husks that contain no grain.

Furthermore, the analogy of dregs and husks illustrates their lack of great spiritual capacity (*indriya*); the analogy of branches and leaves illustrates that they are not excellent vessels. All [of this applies].
They shall not be employed; therefore, they must be dismissed. The two lines, "This assembly is without branches or leaves," eulogize the aforementioned purity of the assembly.
The line, "Śāriputra, listen well," eulogizes the aforementioned exhortation and permission—the exhortation to listen attentively.
△ The subsequent one hundred and sixteen lines in three stanzas eulogize the aforementioned direct answer. This is further divided into two parts. First, from "By all Buddhas... [the text continues].
Below "The Dharma Attained" (*prāptadharma*), there are seventy-three lines and one phrase, which versify the chapters on the four Buddhas.
Second, from "From now on, I too am likewise" (*ataḥ param aham apy evam*) downward, there are forty-three and a half lines, which versify the chapter on Śākyamuni above.

Within the first section, there are further four parts: the first consists of thirty-four lines and three phrases, which versify the chapter on the various Buddhas above; the second has two... [text breaks off].
Seventeen and a half lines [of verse] eulogize the section on the Buddhas of the past. The third [section] consists of six and a half lines, eulogizing the section on the Buddhas of the future.

The fourth consists of four and a half lines, eulogizing the section on the Buddhas of the present. Now, regarding the first [section], within the chapter on the various Buddhas, the text is divided into five parts.
The first five lines and three phrases eulogize the Buddhas' employment of skillful means (*upāya*). The second [part] consists of thirteen...
[The Buddha] proceeds. The second verse praises the Buddhas for manifesting the reality. The third section, comprising four and a half lines, praises the exhortation to believe as mentioned above.

The fourth section, comprising nine and a half lines, sets forth the five turbidities. The fifth section, comprising two lines, praises the non-falsity mentioned above. Now, regarding the first two [sections], the first four lines and one phrase praise the employment of skillful means (*upāya*).
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" (extending to) the *Upadeśa* Sūtras.
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" refers to attaining the various provisional dharmas through the cultivation of the path.

The section beginning with "immeasurable power of skillful means" is a verse summarizing the aforementioned "innumerable skillful means" and the various causes and conditions through which the various dharmas are expounded. [The next phrase concerns] the minds of sentient beings.
"Mindfulness" refers to the preceding verse on preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Within this verse, the characteristics of such appropriateness are extensively set forth;
that is, illuminating the capacities of the nine dharma-realms and teaching the seven expedient means. Since the "nine" and "seven" cannot be definitively fixed, it is said to be "various.

To be appropriate to their desires, one should employ the *loka-vyavahāra-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint); to be appropriate to their dispositions, one should employ the *pudgala-vyavahāra-siddhānta* (the individual standpoint).

The person-siddhānta (the standpoint of the individual) accords with the suitability of one's evil karma; the therapeutic siddhānta (prātipakṣika-siddhānta) should be applied accordingly. "Arising" refers to the manifestation of aspiration, which is termed *smṛti* (recollection/attention).
The diversity of dharma-gates is termed "various" (*nānā*). What was practiced in the past is termed "nature" (*prakṛti*). Present delight is termed "desire" (*chanda*).

Alternatively, habitual practice may form one's nature, and a formed nature may give rise to habitual practice. Regarding wholesome and unwholesome karma, the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*) are transmitted in succession as wholesome or unwholesome (and so forth).
The Buddha, through his skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), illuminates the various expedient means, dispositions, and desires;

he then employs various causes, conditions, and parables according to what is appropriate for each, preaching the ninefold and twelvefold divisions of the scriptures, as explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

The *Zhong* (Middle) [Āgama] states: "As for the ninefold division of the scriptures (*navāṅga-śāsana*), these nine categories of Dharma were taught for the sake of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). From the twelvefold division of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), nine categories of *sūtra* emerge, omitting the Mahāyāna Vaipulya, the Vyākaraṇa, and the Avidhura-svayambhāṣita.
The Upadeśa is here translated as 'treatise' (*upadeśa*). The remaining names are easily understood. The verse on the twelve divisions says: "Prose (*gadya*), verse (*geya*), and the Vyākaraṇa;

the Udgata, the Avidhura-svayambhāṣita, the Nidāna, the Avadāna, as well as the Itivṛttaka, the Jātaka, the Vaipulya, the Adbhutadharma, and the Upadeśa—these together constitute the twelve names. This is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 33. △ Second, one and a half lines conclude the provisional bestowal of the means.
[The Buddha] thought:
"Those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings (down to: for them he preaches nirvāṇa).

The mind conceives immeasurable and boundless evil. When in the realm of animals, they alternately devour one another with their bodies and alternately oppress and afflict one another with their minds.
When in the realm of hungry ghosts, their bodies are like burning mountains and their minds are like boiling cauldrons;

their false views are rampant, and they are stubborn, foolish, and ferocious. When in the human realm, their body, speech, and mind constantly perform unbeneficial acts, bringing suffering upon themselves through their own toil.

With body, speech, and mind, they constantly contemplate things that are not beneficial, thereby entangling themselves. While in the heavens, they become addicted to and defiled by the six sense objects;
they indulge in wanton play and do not hear the True Dharma, thus blocking the source of merit. This is called the long duration of birth and death for sentient beings.
What is the short duration of birth and death for sentient beings? When in the hells, they are able to take up a single thought-moment of a tranquil mind.
Regarding the precepts: when in the state of an animal, one is able for a single thought-moment to settle the mind and take refuge in the Triple Gem;

Transforming [them] into recitation and study; practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) with few words. This is what is meant by the "shortness" of the birth and death of sentient beings. (Regarding "practicing the holy life with few words":

Here, "square" refers to being like a square object, which remains fixed in its movement and stillness; having died here, one is certain to be born in the heavens. What is the "circular" birth and death of sentient beings?

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Aggregate" (*skandha*) is a name for the world (*loka*). Life-force (*āyus*) maintains the continuity of the aggregates, entering into the world from the initial stage of thin curd (*dadhi*) up until old age and death;

when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) receives a body, during the first seven days there is no transformation or differentiation. During the second seven days, there is the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), like thin curd. During the third seven days, it is like thick curd.

In the fourth week, it is like solidified butter. In the fifth week, it is like a lump of clay. In the sixth week, it is like a mass of flesh. In the seventh week, five blisters arise from that mass of flesh:

the head, hands, and feet. In the eighth week, there are again five blisters: one for the head, two for the shoulders, and two for the wrists. In the ninth week, twenty-four blisters continue to arise;
four blisters form the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, while twenty blisters become the [twenty] fingers and toes.

The ten fingers appear; at the seventeenth transformation, the abdomen manifests. Gradually, the skin and bones separate, producing various extraordinary signs. Seven hundred tendons and seven thousand vessels arise.
According to the required characteristics, they are colored by a specific wind: if white characteristics are required, they are colored by the white wind;
the same applies to all other winds. Because of the fragrant wind, [the body] is peaceful and upright; because of the foul-smelling wind, [it becomes otherwise].
Lacking peace and security, one becomes ugly, perverse, and deviant. After emerging from the womb and consuming the five grains, eighty thousand types of parasites arise within the body.

The text is divided into three parts. First, regarding the passage "I observe with the Buddha-eye," this verse describes the Buddha’s capacity for vision. The Buddha abides in the stage of the Dharma-body;

If their faculties are dull and their defilements heavy, he discards his jeweled necklaces and appears as an old man.

The Buddha, like one startled, entered the burning house and skillfully taught the three vehicles; this was merely to discern their capacities at that time, which is why he said, "I observe with the Buddha-eye.

If he were observing material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), he would employ the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); if he were discerning the faculties and capacities [of sentient beings], he employs the Buddha-eye.
One should apply the Dharma-eye. Why then say that he sees with the Buddha-eye? The Buddha-eye is all-pervasive and perfect; it mentions the superior while encompassing the inferior.
Furthermore, the four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye, and are all termed the Buddha-eye.

Regarding "the sentient beings of the six realms" below, the second section contains two lines, three phrases, and four characters, clarifying the five turbidities seen therein. This verse concerns the turbidity of sentient beings.

The line "Poor and lacking in merit and wisdom" praises the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the age). "Entering the perilous path of birth and death, with continuous suffering that does not cease" praises the *jīva-kaṣāya* (the defilement of lifespan).
"Deeply attached to the five desires" praises the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of afflictions).

"Not seeking the Buddha of Great Power" praises the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (the defilement of views); for by seeking after non-Buddhist paths and failing to seek the True Dharma, one falls deeply into false views.
Seeking to abandon suffering while remaining within suffering—this verse correctly describes the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Alternatively, it is said that those who desire to escape suffering by performing the "five heats" (*pañca-tapana*) instead obtain the retribution of suffering. The concealment of the Three Vehicles is a transformation for the sake of skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: first, one wishes to contemplate the Middle Way;

Finally, one wishes to contemplate "that which is identical to emptiness" (*kong*); because the skillful crossing of "that which is identical to emptiness" is also not attained, one then contemplates the analysis of skillful means.

The term "Exemplification" (Upamā) refers to the teaching of parables. It skillfully enables those of middling and inferior capacities to obtain the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*; therefore, it is called the "Parable Chapter.

Regarding the first principle (*paramārtha-siddhānta*), that which is neither born nor extinguished is the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). Regarding the interpretation according to the teachings: the Buddha’s original intention was to praise the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). They cannot keep up with others. The Bodhisattva drives an ox to carry others out of the fire; therefore, he is called a Mahāsattva. This is an analogy from within the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

Furthermore, those of the three vehicles develop the aspiration [for enlightenment] recently; their engagement with principle is shallow and their wisdom is weak. They sever the delusions common to all realms, yet they cannot exhaustively reach the ultimate limit;

To exhaust the source and fully realize one's nature: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that "the two vehicles are like fireflies, while bodhisattvas are like the light of the sun.
This is an analogy from the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). Furthermore, as soon as they first see my body and hear what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it.
