For those who have not yet entered, for more than forty years, I have employed various skillful means to assist in revealing the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Today, in this royal city, I shall definitively proclaim it.
The Mahāyāna universally causes all beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom, so that not a single person is left to attain extinction alone.

As it is now, so it was at the beginning; as it was at the beginning, so it is now. There is no duality and no distinction. Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence can understand upon hearing it, so as not to cause the Tathāgata to give rise to weariness or distress. Furthermore— (The Lotus Sūtra is the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is the Lotus Sūtra.)—no duality and no distinction.
Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence can understand upon hearing it, so as not to cause the Tathāgata to give rise to weariness or distress. Also—

There is no need for further analogies. It is precisely because those of middling and inferior capacities move their attachments and give rise to doubt, lingering at the crossroads, that they require today’s analogy of the great vehicle to obtain benefit.
This is called the analogy within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). (Supplement: *The Avataṃsaka* [teaches] that phenomena are themselves reality;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* [teaches] that worldly appearances are eternally abiding. Both equally clarify the Buddha-wisdom, yet there is a difference in the beginning and end of their pedagogical methods. Fearing that those who are deluded might not understand this, the Great Master [Zhiyi] himself reconciled them, saying: "As it is now, so it was at the beginning; as it was at the beginning, so it is now.")

Now, there is neither duality nor distinction. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* constitute the beginning and end of the Tathāgata’s great transformation in a single day; they are ultimately equal. Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"If one can receive [the teaching] within the *Avataṃsaka*, there is no need to wait for the Deer Park to open the One into Three. Those in later generations who distinguish between the superiority and inferiority of these two sutras not only fail to understand the Buddha’s mind, but also fail to understand the mind of the Great Master Zhiyi."

The analogies for the fundamental and the trace (*honjaku*) regarding the contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*) can be understood accordingly; they shall not be recorded here again (the analogies for the fundamental and the trace are fully explained within the section on the "Names," using the three metaphors of the lotus. As for the analogy for the contemplation of the mind:

emptiness is like the white ox, the provisional is like the complete parts, and the middle is like the body of the chariot; when these reach the stage of the perfect fusion of the three in one, this is the perfect contemplation of the mind). First, the headings of the chapters have been presented.

△ Next, the scriptural text is explained. In the preceding chapter, the discourse on the Dharma consists of five sections: 1. the discourse on the Dharma; 2. the acceptance and understanding; 3. the confirmation; 4.
the bestowal of predictions; and 5. the rejoicing of the fourfold assembly. The first section, the discourse on the Dharma, has just concluded, while the remaining four are not yet finished.
Because the text of the preceding chapter is extensive, it is appended here following the title of the "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta). ○ Now, the first [section]:

Section Two: Maitreya’s Comprehension. This section consists of his receiving what he has heard and articulating his understanding. In the prose, the reception and the understanding are explained in conjunction;
in the verses, the reception and the understanding are presented separately. Hence, it is called the "Section on Comprehension. The text has two parts: first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler;
second, Maitreya’s own statement. The first part is divided into two: first, internal comprehension.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy;

internal understanding dwelling in the mind is called "joy," while joy manifesting in physical form is called "leaping. Having heard the wondrous Dharma from the Wondrous Buddha, he was filled with delight.
Having attained wondrous understanding, if one encounters even a single joy, one still rejoices; how much more so when the three joys are fully present—how could one not leap for joy?
The text says: "Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy, and my inner and outer selves are in harmony."
This brings about joy; this is the "Worldly Śākya. Furthermore, he changed from being a minor to a major, abandoned his poor affairs and grass hut to inherit the estate of a wealthy family.
The text says: "Today I know for the first time that I am truly a son of the Buddha; therefore, I rejoice."

This is the explanation for humans. Furthermore, both sorrow and regret are simultaneously dispelled, and doubts and difficulties are likewise eliminated. Internal and external hindrances are cleared away until all is vast and luminous.
As the text says: "I have attained the exhaustion of outflows; hearing [the Dharma] has also removed my grief and affliction. Therefore, I rejoice."
This is the explanation by way of antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Furthermore, regarding that which a Son of the Buddha ought to attain, he has already attained it all.

As the text says: "Abiding within true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha. This is the explanation by way of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). As for the explanation by way of origin and manifestation (*honji-suijaku*):
Śāriputra attained Buddhahood long ago and is named Suvarṇanāga. In his manifested traces, he assists Śākyamuni as his right-hand disciple of wisdom.
Beginning with those from external paths, he uproots their heterodoxy and leads them to the correct path. He first manifests the joy of the flavor of milk to benefit ordinary beings;
next, he manifests the joy of the flavor of curd to benefit sages and saints; and next, he manifests the joy of the flavors of fresh and refined butter to benefit [others].
The Bodhisattva now acts as the finest cream (sarpis), entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision with joy and benefiting those who study the Buddha-way.
Such joys as these are all produced by means of his traces. △ Second, external deportment.
He immediately rose and joined his palms, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance.

Regarding the description of the external demeanor: "immediately rising and joining the palms" signifies the physical body's understanding. Formerly, the provisional and the real were two, like two palms that do not join;
now, understanding that the provisional is itself the real is like the joining of the two palms. As for "facing the Buddha": formerly, the provisional was not the cause of Buddhahood.
In truth, this is not yet the fruit of Buddhahood. Now, by understanding that the provisional is itself the real, one accomplishes the cause of the Great Perfect Circle.

Since the cause must inevitably lead to the fruit, it is said that "with palms joined toward the Buddha, gazing up at the Honored Countenance. This signifies the understanding of the Real; for the Real is the realm of the Buddha and is not a method of expedient means.
Gazing up at the Honored Countenance with no other thoughts represents the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as one’s mental understanding rests upon the Real.

This also constitutes the understanding of the provisional (*upāya*). While the person himself presides over the provisional, he also understands the ultimate (*paramārtha*); these are presented alternately from one perspective each. △ Second, Śāriputra’s own declaration.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The first part [the prose] is further divided into three: first, the heading for the three joys;
second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first [the heading].
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy; I have attained what I have never had before.
Now, from the World-Honored One, I designate my own body as the Buddha-body; therefore, it is called 'joy of the body. Having heard this Dharma-sound, I rely upon it."
Having heard [the teaching] from the Buddha’s own mouth, they rejoice; thus it is called "joy of the mouth.
Having attained what was never before experienced, they understand the Buddha’s intent through their own minds; thus it is called "joy of the mind. This marks the three types of joy.
Second, the explanation clarifies past failings and reveals present attainments, which is threefold. First, it clarifies the failure of not having seen the Buddha in the past.
Why is this? (Up to: They have lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
Formerly, when the Buddha conferred the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattvas, they were not included in that matter; their perception of the Buddha’s meaning was distant.
Since they did not see the Buddha, they lacked physical joy. As for those who hear such a Dharma as this, it is like when the sun shines upon a high mountain: there are those who hear it secretly.

"Meaning" (yi) refers to those who are like the deaf or mute, unable to hear such a Dharma. It simply means that within the Vaipulya teachings, hearing the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna is no different from what is heard now;
therefore, it is said that "one hears such a Dharma. As for "receiving a prediction" (授記):

Furthermore, within the Vaipulya sūtras, they receive predictions of enlightenment for bodhisattvas, while the followers of the two vehicles are excluded from this matter; thus, they feel profound personal distress.

In the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra*, they hear the praise of the great and the disparagement of the small; internally harboring doubt while externally feeling contempt, this is what is termed "feeling distress."
"To lose all knowledge and vision" means to lose the vision of the Buddha-eye and to lose the knowledge of the Buddha-wisdom.
△ Second, clarifying the loss resulting from not hearing the Dharma in the past:
"World-Honored One, we have always dwelt alone in mountain forests and beneath trees... (omitted)... this is our own fault, not the World-Honored One's."
Truly, because I dwell in the mountain forests while my mind clings to inferior paths, I have not heard the Dharma; thus, I lack the joy of speech.
My constant solitary dwelling is merely a place for contemplating my own faults. Those who enter together into the nature of reality (dharmatā) are precisely those who have emerged from their errors.
While clinging to the single principle of that which is entered, one harbors doubts regarding the gateways of the Three Teachings. Since the single principle is identical, it is I who have erred.
Regarding knowledge and vision: since the three teachings differ, yet the Bodhisattvas receive their predictions (vyākaraṇa), it follows that the Tathāgata is partial, which constitutes a fault.

Now, recounting this error, one says "I repent. To say "this is our own fault" means: because we were deluded regarding the provisional (upāya), what concern is this for the principle or the teaching?
Because we were confused regarding the real (tattva), what concern is this for the Buddha’s partiality? Thus, recounting past errors, one looks upward in gratitude and apology.
"Thus, the Tathāgata draws upon [the faults of] others to take refuge [in his own virtues]. (Supplementary Note: Regarding those who enter the *dharmatā* together:

the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the *dharmatā* is truly eternal and transcends mental conceptions; even the followers of the Two Vehicles can attain this. It is not for this reason that they are called World-Honored Ones. Rather, it is because of their profound and unimpeded wisdom—[as indicated by the first two lines of the verse]. The latter two lines clarify that while the followers of the Two Vehicles realize the limited truth (*pratisaṃvid*), they do not yet possess unimpeded wisdom.

Only by emerging from emptiness into the provisional (*upāya*) can they purify Buddha-lands, transform sentient beings, and fulfill Bodhi. Upon reaching this point, Śāriputra finally realizes his error and acknowledges his own faults. △
The three types of clear knowledge (trividyā) eliminate the fault of lacking understanding.
Why is this so? From [the beginning] until the end of day and night, one constantly reproaches oneself.

This is truly because without waiting for the causes to be explained, there can be no real understanding; furthermore, because one does not recognize the skillful means (upāya), there is no provisional [understanding].
"Understanding. Because there is no [object] to be understood, there is no mental joy. Since the past loss has been made manifest, the present attainment reveals itself spontaneously.

"Without waiting for an explanation of the cause" means one reproaches oneself for not understanding the reality (*tattva*). "Not understanding the skillful means" means one reproaches oneself for not understanding the provisional (*upāya*).
These two meanings of "the cause" are: first, not awaiting or depending upon what precedes (as in the *Avataṃsaka*); second, not abiding in or awaiting what follows.
(The Lotus Sūtra): First, it illuminates the high mountains, clarifying the wisdom of the three truths; this is the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

Because I was waiting for this [teaching] in opposition to that [previous one], I did not accept it, thereby losing it at the outset (explaining the non-acceptance of the *Avataṃsaka*). "When the Buddha-dharma has long endured, one must surely proclaim the truth";
I did not wait for this [time] (explaining the non-waiting for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*). Between the two pillars, I hastily took the lesser [vehicle].

"Unable to comprehend the true power" [Supplement: It is said that when one first hears the Buddha-dharma and immediately accepts it with faith, yet seeks realization through mere contemplation, this is Śāriputra describing his own fault—namely, seeking realization midway, like harvesting peas too early.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If one sees the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and enters the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one can no longer give rise to the bodhicitta. For example, lotuses do not grow on high ground or dry land; they grow only in the moist mud.

Likewise, those who see the unconditioned dharma and enter the stage of certainty will ultimately be unable to produce the Buddha-dharma. It is only within the mire of afflictions that sentient beings can give rise to the Buddha-dharma. Why? Because this is the path of learning."*]

This is a stage, not a stage of realization. In the eighth stage, the Immovable Bhūmi (*acalā-bhūmi*), of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattva realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Because of this Bodhisattva’s power of original vows, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, personally appear before him, bestowing three empowerments and seven exhortations, granting him immeasurable gateways for the arising of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*).

If the Buddhas did not grant these gateways for the arising of wisdom to this Bodhisattva, he would at that moment enter ultimate *nirvāṇa* and abandon all activities for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because the Buddhas grant such immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of wisdom, the intellectual activity produced in a single thought-moment exceeds by a hundredfold, even up to a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* times, all the practices cultivated from the first aspiration up through the seventh stage.

His portion does not equal even one grade; it is precisely the same as this [case]. However, the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan) represents the Perfect and Sudden [teaching], while the *Tripiṭaka* at the Deer Park is different. △ Third, the conclusion establishing the three joys, in two parts.
First, [he] bound [his mind].
Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, he attained a swift and profound peace.
From the Buddha, he experienced joy in his body; hearing the Dharma, he experienced joy in his speech; and by severing all doubts and regrets, he experienced joy in his mind. △
Second, accomplishment.

Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha. Born from the Buddha’s mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma, having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma—I now know I am truly a son of the Buddha.
This is being close to the Buddha; it is the completion of the body. Born from the Buddha’s mouth, it is the completion of the mouth.

It is accomplished. It is born through transformation from the Dharma; this is the formation of the mental continuum (*citta-saṃtati*). Interpreting the text in this manner, when the words are exhausted, the principle is revealed. (The initial prose section concludes).
△ Second, the verse commentary (*gāthā-paṭala*) consists of twenty-five and a half lines, divided into three parts:
first, the indication of the three joys; second, the explanation of the three joys; third, the concluding summary. Now, for the first part, one line indicates the three joys.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before. My heart harbors great joy, and the net of doubts has been entirely cleared away."
"Recite 'I have heard,' and you shall also attain Buddhahood," meaning that one has personally heard it from the Buddha. △ Second, twenty-two lines of verse explain the three types of joy.
This is further divided into three parts; first, one and a half lines of verse praise the joy of seeing the Buddha.
"Since ancient times, I have relied upon the Buddha’s teaching... [up to] "...hearing it also removes sorrow and affliction.

The prose section clarifies the loss of knowledge and vision, while the verse section clarifies not losing the Mahāyāna. The preceding discussion on loss is remote, whereas the discussion on the verses concerns attainment;
these are presented in mutual contrast. △ The second section consists of eleven lines, which versify the aforementioned failure to hear the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two [sections]. The first consists of nine lines. The verse above states that because he is at a great distance, he does not hear.
"I am situated in a mountain valley" (extending to) "causing the assembly to reach the place of enlightenment."
Regarding my constant [contemplation] throughout day and night: saṃsāra is the night and nirvāṇa is the day.
Is this because nirvāṇa exists within saṃsāra, or because it exists outside of saṃsāra? When awakening is attained, both doubts are simultaneously dispelled.
Furthermore, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are the night; when this doubt is removed, it is called "day. At the time of sunrise, both doubts are simultaneously dispelled.
Furthermore, there are two types of people in the world: first, those who begin their studies in the Mahāyāna; second, those who practice the Hīnayāna before entering the Mahāyāna.
When comparing their respective approaches, those who enter directly are inferior. For example, those who enter from the Abhidharma are superior. The Bodhisattva should also act in this manner.

Regarding those who enter through the *Avataṃsaka*, the path of transformation would be too weak; those who enter by means of the refinement of the five flavors are superior. The second section consists of two lines.
These verses praise the attachment to false positions, which is why they do not hear the Dharma. Attachment to false views is the clinging of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*);
attachment to fixed positions is the clinging of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Both fail to hear the Dharma.
"I originally held false views" (up to) "attained nirvāṇa.
△ Third section, nine and a half lines. This verse praises the joy of having attained wondrous understanding of the mind;
now one realizes for oneself (up to) "claiming it was the work of Māra."

The preceding section clarified that [the aspiration] does not depend on external causes and did not explain the skillful means. In this verse, it clarifies that one obtains the causes and further explains the skillful means.
Hearing that one shall become a Buddha is the cause; hearing that the Way of the five Buddhas is identical is the skillful means. These mutually manifest two aspects.
The chapter on the Five Buddhas is precisely the summary of the text (the second explanation of the three joys is concluded). △ Third, Two.
The practice is half-finished; the preceding verse concludes [the section].
Having heard the Buddha’s gentle voice (up to) "he teaches and transforms all bodhisattvas" (the second section on receiving understanding is complete).
△ Third, the Section on Confirmation. Above, Śāriputra personally recounted his attainment of awakening.
Now, the Tathāgata’s exposition and interpretation are not false. This passage consists of three parts: first, his former teaching of the Great [Vehicle];

second, his intermediate forgetting and taking up of the Small [Vehicle]; third, his returning to teach the Great [Vehicle] once more. Thus, by citing the former teaching of the Great, he describes the conditions for seeing the Buddha;

by describing the intermediate forgetting and taking up of the Small, he describes the conditions for experiencing sorrow and regret upon hearing the Dharma; and by describing the returning to teach the Great, he describes the realization [of awakening].
The explanation is not in vain; it fulfills the three preceding points. Now, first:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra... [up to] "...I have used skillful means to guide you, so that you have been born into my Dharma."
Regarding the "Unsurpassed Path," the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* enumerates seven types of unsurpassedness and explains them in two layers. The first explanation is as follows:

first, the unsurpassedness of the body, which refers to the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); second, the unsurpassedness of upholding [the Dharma], which refers to benefiting oneself and others.

Third is the unsurpassed perfection of the three: namely, life, views, and precepts. Fourth is the unsurpassed wisdom: namely, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Fifth is the inconceivable unsurpassed:
namely, the six perfections (*pāramitā*). Sixth is the unsurpassed liberation: which is able to destroy the two obstacles.

The seven types of unsurpassed practice refer to the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*) and the Brahma-conduct (*brahma-caryā*). To explain them in sequence: unsurpassed in body is called the "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*);
unsurpassed in upholding [the teachings] is called "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*); unsurpassed in fulfillment is called "Reaching the Other Shore" (*pāramitā*);
unsurpassed in wisdom is called "All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñā*); unsurpassed in the inconceivable is called an "Arhat"; and unsurpassed in liberation is called...
The Great Parinirvāṇa is the practice of the Unsurpassed; it is named Samyaksaṃbuddha. The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra*, fascicle thirteen, states:
"The Way should be pure; turbidity is not the Way. The Way should be single-minded; manifold thoughts are not the Way.
The Way should be contented; much desire is not the Way. The Way should be respectful; arrogance is not the Way. The Way should restrain the mind; negligence is not the Way."
Non-Dharma is not the Way; the Way ought to be radiant. Self-concealment is non-Dharma; the Way ought to be continuous. Non-practice is non-Dharma; the Way ought to be awakening.
Delusion and folly are non-Dharma; the Way ought to be transformative instruction. Arrogance and stinginess are non-Dharma; the Way draws near to virtuous friends.
Practicing evil and non-ways—through such various [teachings], they clarify the Unsurpassed Way. Now, this sutra takes perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) as the Unsurpassed Way.
Whether partial or sequential, these are all discussed in other sutras. (Regarding "this sutra takes perfect penetration as the Unsurpassed Way":

this refers to the Way of the Perfect Unsurpassed School, which is named the Unsurpassed Way. Each instance of the unsurpassed possesses the supremacy of all paths. As for "whether partial or sequential," the partial refers to the *zang* and *tong* [teachings], while the sequential refers to the *bie* teaching. Long night.

"Those who followed me to receive instruction, although they had not yet shattered ignorance despite my great transformation in the past, did so while within a mind shrouded by the darkness of delusion.
Even though the 'cause of penetration' was distant, it was nevertheless not extinguished; how much more so now that true awakening has been attained—how could it be in vain?

Therefore, by citing their former instruction, I demonstrate that my vision of the Buddha is not erroneous. (Regarding the phrase "Although in the past there was great transformation," etc.: within the realm of existence, ignorance had never been shattered; hence it is called "the darkness of delusion. If one practices the Perfect [Teaching] from the very first moment, even if...)

Before the destruction of the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), a single phrase heard is planted as a seed within consciousness and is never lost throughout eternal kalpas. When one looks from darkness toward light, even that darkness is not erroneous; how much less so regarding true awakening? As for those who are deluded by darkness, this refers to the stage prior to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Although the six sense faculties have not yet destroyed ignorance, they resemble the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), and are thus termed "not dark. Regarding my using skillful means (*upāya*) to cause beings to be born within my Dharma, there are two ways of drawing this out:

if they were previously transformed by the Great [Vehicle] and now give rise to great understanding, this belongs to the first meaning; if it is to cause them to escape the evil realms (*apāya*), [this belongs to the second].
The provisional [teaching] uses the small [vehicle] as an introduction; this is the second meaning. △ Within the second [section], there is the forgetting and grasping of the small.
Śāriputra, in the past I taught you to set your aspirations on the Buddha-way (up to the point where) you then claimed for yourself that you had already attained *nirvāṇa*.
From the time I first instructed you to set your resolve upon the path to Buddhahood, you have now entirely forgotten it.

This occurred because midway through your journey, you abandoned the Great Vehicle and practiced the Lesser Vehicle; this is what is meant by "having entirely forgotten the way midway. Furthermore, you claimed for yourself that you had already attained *nirvāṇa*, which is likewise an instance of having entirely forgotten.
Because you forgot your great vow and instead practiced the Lesser Vehicle, you have come to experience sorrow and regret, and thus you have been able to hear the Dharma.
It is not in vain. △ Third, returning to explain the Great [Vehicle]:
"I now wish to cause you to recollect... [the teachings] for instructing bodhisattvas and which are protected by the Buddhas."
I now wish to cause you to recollect your original vow; this is precisely to affirm that your attainment of understanding is not in vain.
First, provisional teachings were bestowed to establish the minor virtues of the interim stage; later, the ultimate truth was revealed to fulfill the great mind of your original vow.
(The third section, "Affirmation," is concluded. △ Fourth Section: Bestowal of Prophecy. The preceding self-proclamation has been sealed by the Buddha.
For this reason, he bestows a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). If one has attained great understanding and knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha, what need is there to wait for a prediction?

There are four intentions behind the bestowal of a prediction: first, that which was not previously predicted for the two vehicles is now to be predicted; second, to encourage those of middling and inferior capacities who have not yet awakened by means of the prediction;
third, to cause those who hear it to form karmic connections; and fourth, to fulfill their original vows. It is for these reasons that he bestows the prediction. [There is more...]
The Verses on Practice. The long prose section consists of ten parts. First, regarding the time:
"Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed..."
△ Second, the cause of practice:
making offerings to several tens of billions of buddhas, upholding the true Dharma, and fully perfecting the path practiced by bodhisattvas.
△ Third, the attainment of the fruit.
He shall attain Buddhahood and be named the Tathāgata Padmaprabha (Flower Radiance), up to:

Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. Although the ten titles are very numerous, I shall record but one kind: because he is without falsehood, he is named Tathāgata; because he is a field of merit, he is named Arhat (Worthy of Offerings);

because he knows the dharma-realm, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha (Rightly and Fully Enlightened); because he possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge, he is named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct); because he does not return again... [he is named Anāgāmin].

He is named Sugata (Well-Gone). Because he knows the realms of sentient beings, he is named Lokavid (Knower of the World). Because there is none equal to him, he is named Anuttara (Unsurpassed One). Because he tames the minds of others, he is named Puruṣa (Great Being).
Because he serves as the eye for sentient beings, he is named Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām (Teacher of Gods and Humans).

Because he knows the three groups (1. the group of those fixed in rightness; 2. the group of those fixed in error; 3. the group of those who are not fixed), he is named Buddha. Possessing these ten titles, he is named Bhagavat (this is translated here as "World-Honored One"). △ Fourth, the lands.
The name of the land is Vimala (up to: along its sides there are rows of trees made of the seven treasures, which always bear flowers and fruit).
△ Fifth, the preaching of the Dharma:
The Tathāgata Padmaprabha (up to: by virtue of his original vow, he preaches the Dharma of the three vehicles).
The commentary on the meaning states: This is analogous to Śākyamuni; therefore, it says "likewise. The passage beginning with "Śāriputra" below serves to resolve a doubt. The doubt is as follows:
As clarified above, the Buddha appears in the five turbidities because he has no other choice and thus teaches the three vehicles as a skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, if the land of the Buddha Flower-Light is pure to such an extent, why does he also transform beings through the three vehicles? The resolution is: It is by virtue of his original vow.
Therefore, regarding the original vow: according to the *Mahākaruṇā-gaṇḍa-vaipulya-sūtra*, Śāriputra once practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas;
when a brahmin begged for his eyes and he was about to retreat from the path, he made a vow that on the day he attained Buddhahood, he would open the gates of the Three Vehicles of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Amitābha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss likewise employs the Three Vehicles to transform and guide sentient beings. This is truly due to the power of his compassionate vows.
Profound and weighty. Those who are taken up [by this teaching] and attain birth while still carrying their karmic burdens cannot enter gradually without relying on the Three Vehicles.

Generally speaking, within the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages—whether pure or impure—those who practice the three [vehicles] are many, while those who practice in a single, unified way are few.
△ Sixth: The Name of the Kalpa.
The kalpa is named Mahāratnavyūha (Great Jewel Adornment), because in that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels.

One who cannot be moved by the violent winds of the four inversions is called "hidden" (*yin*). Being serene and beyond all burdens, one is said to have "attained liberation.
Sentient beings are not like this; they are scorched by fire. Yet the Tathāgata, out of compassion, is still inflamed by the fire of concern for them; therefore, he says "even though" (*sui*).
Regarding the scriptural statement "the gates that are burned," it is now asked: if the teaching constitutes the gate, is this teaching itself burned or not?
The response is: the gate of the teaching is not burned. The Buddha’s teaching serves as the gate that enables those who are to be burned to pass through;

since the person being passed through is burned, the gate that enables them to pass through is metaphorically called "burned. This is like when a person inside a gate dies, and the gate is said to have met with misfortune.
The gate is truly not subject to decay. He asked again: "If that is so, then the teaching is eternally abiding and is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
If it were otherwise, why would it not burn? Now, I explain that it is not so. For a gate consists of both the constituent parts (*avayava*) and the emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Without the parts, there would be nothing to designate the gate; without emptiness, there would be no means to pass through. The parts may be reduced to ashes, but emptiness cannot be burned. The teaching possesses the capacity for expression."
That which is expressed (*abhidheya*) must not be that which expresses (*abhidhāna*); otherwise, there would be no teaching. If it were not that which is expressed, how could one emerge?

That which expresses may be impermanent, but that which is expressed is not, in turn, impermanent. Because one attains the expressed meaning from beneath the teaching, it is called "emerging in peace.
Because that which expresses perishes, it is called "the door that is burned. One does not [emerge] through the door that is burned.
By what means can one emerge in peace and security? It is by relying upon the verbal teachings and acceding to that which they express.
As the Great Sūtra says: "Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is permanent. To explain it in this way is like [escaping] through the door of the burning house.

If it is the teaching-gate of impermanence of the Hīnayāna, one emerges from the door of the burning house; if it is the teaching-gate of eternal abiding of the Mahāyāna, [one emerges through the gate of permanence].
"Letters themselves are liberation. This teaching is itself the principle. By realizing that there is no burning within burning, one attains peace and emerges safely.
If one proceeds by means of the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), one emerges through the gate of that which is burned.

If one proceeds by means of ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), one realizes the nature of that which is burned and emerges safely. Therefore, one cannot emerge by first making a garment, a basket, or a desk; only later—
To expel them by means of impermanence is precisely this intended meaning. △ Fourth, the extensive description of the fire previously seen serves to further explain the sense of alarm and dread.
Thus, the sons within the burning house (up to) do not feel weary or distressed in their hearts and have no intention of seeking escape.

This passage generally clarifies that sentient beings lack wisdom. Within the burning house, those who delight in and cling to play and sport—where "play" (*hī*) refers to attachment to views and "sport" (*khi*) refers to attachment to craving;
furthermore, being immersed in the four views is called "play," while squandering one's merit and reputation is called "sport. Attachment to craving is likewise so described.
Being immersed in the five sensory objects is called "play," while returning empty-handed with nothing gained is called "sport"; thus they die in vain after having lived in emptiness.
Yet they feel no revulsion or detachment, like children at play. To neither perceive nor know [the fire] is called "non-perception" (abodha).
Not understanding that fire is a phenomenon of heat is called "ignorance" (ajñāna). Since one does not know the heat of the fire, one does not fear injury to the body;
this is called "not being startled. Because one does not consider the severing of life, one does not feel terror. Thus, sentient beings do not perceive the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) at all.

There are the eight sufferings. Being ignorant of the four inversions and the three poisons, and thus failing to recognize delusion, how could one worry that delusion might invade the Dharma-body and wound the life-force of wisdom?
In this way, they are not awakened to suffering, do not understand its origin, and are not startled by the wounding of the Path.

One does not fear their loss or extinction. Because one has not heard the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, one lacks the wisdom born of hearing; this is called "not awakening. One fails to attain the wisdom born of reflection;
this is called "not knowing. One fails to attain insight; this is called "not awakening. One fails to attain the insight born of contemplation; this is called "not knowing.
Upon seeing the truths, one is startled into realization; through contemplation, one develops weary detachment and dread. Furthermore, one does not awaken to present suffering, nor does one know it.
Regarding future suffering, the subsequent passage states: "One undergoes manifold sufferings in the present and will subsequently undergo the sufferings of the hells and so forth.

This is precisely that meaning. As for "that which oppresses the body," it refers to the group of the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*). As for "the mind" (*citta*), it refers to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the sovereign mind-king.
Since the three consciousnesses—the sixth, seventh, and eighth—take the mind as their root, the sixth consciousness may also be designated as "mind. Thus, [it is said] "the body..."

Though oppressed by the eight sufferings, their minds feel no weariness or distress. Because their minds feel no weariness or distress, they do not loathe the suffering of impermanence nor are they troubled by the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Having no intent to seek liberation, they do not cultivate the Path to seek cessation.

Now, it is said that the burning house is fundamentally a metaphor for the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*): "reveling" represents the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*), and "playing" represents the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*).

They do not perceive it, they do not know it, they are not startled, and they are not terrified. This is like the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). When fire comes and presses against their bodies, the pain is so acute that it cuts to the very core;

this is like the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*). Their minds feel no weariness or distress, and they lack the intention to seek escape; this is like the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). This corresponds to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāyāḥ*).
(The first elder’s analogy of seeing the fire concludes. △ Second: The analogy of abandoning the stool and using the carriage. This is an analogy for...
The "Great" above refers to the primary self initially seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), while the "Small" below refers to the seventeen lines and a half of verses.

This is divided into two parts: first, six lines and a half, which employ the Great [Vehicle] but find it unsuitable; second, from "Then he recalled the Buddhas of the past" onwards, eleven lines of verse, which employ the Small [Vehicle] and find it suitable.
The first section, employing the Great [Vehicle] and finding it unsuitable, is further divided into two: first, employing the gate of exhortation (*praśaṃsā-mukha*).

The preliminary preparations. Second, the section on the method of admonition and preparation. This consists of three parts for each of the two [methods]: first, the preparation; second, non-acceptance; third, relinquishment.
Regarding the three aspects of the method of exhortation: first, the analogy for the application of the Mahāyāna through the method of exhortation—contemplating this matter for twenty-one days.
Second, clarifying that the sons do not accept it, which is analogous to the lack of spiritual capacity (*anabhijñatva*) in sentient beings regarding their various faculties.
[The beings are] dull-witted. How can they be saved? Third, [the Buddha] relinquishes [his efforts]. This is like ceasing the transformation [of beings] when there is no receptive capacity above;
"I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana. Now, this is the first [instance].
Śāriputra, this elder thought thus... (up to) "...if he were to carry [the child] out of the house on a small table.

Regarding "body, hands, and so forth," the text provides an analogy for the downward extraction, explaining this metaphor by means of the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Here, the body represents the bearing of the burden through supernormal faculties, while the hands represent the lifting up through wisdom; this relies upon the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Thereupon, there are supernormal powers. Based on the wisdom of the virtue of knowledge, there is the preaching of the Dharma. Through the power of knowledge and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), one is able to accomplish the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This knowledge and abandonment, in turn, enter through the two gates of exhortation and admonition; "exhortation" refers to the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals).
The admonition is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint). These two *siddhāntas* serve as skillful means for the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).

When the Tathāgata first wished to employ the gate of exhortation to suit the capacities of sentient beings, intending to cause them to practice all that is good and thereby achieve the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and omniscience, sentient beings were unable to bear it. He then intended to employ the gate of admonition.

He commands that all evils be not committed so as to realize great *nirvāṇa*. Yet sentient beings are unable to endure this; lacking the capacity [for such teaching], his transformative activity ceases.

Thus we know that the application of mindfulness regarding the Mahāyāna consists merely of the two *siddhāntas* of exhortation and admonition, which are nothing other than wisdom and cessation, and meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*). (The four teachings on good and evil.)

Each [section] contains its own exhortations and warnings (here, these are summarized according to the Perfect Teaching). Thus, the preceding passage states: "Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings by means of this. This is precisely that meaning.
The previous praise of the elder for his advanced age is a metaphor for wisdom and cessation (*jñāna* and *prahāṇa*).

Wisdom and cessation are themselves the strength of the hands and body. Regarding the "garment-bag" (*yīkè*) and the "small table" (*jǐ'àn*), the Tripiṭaka Master said: "The garment-bag is a foreign [term]."
A vessel for holding flowers; it is presented to high-ranking persons for them to store [the flowers] therein. Now, taking this to form a textual analogy:

if I were to use only the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhibala*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*) to praise the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśanabala*) and his fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), sentient beings would be unable to attain deliverance through these.
The power of spiritual transformations is the body; the power of wisdom is the hand, as previously stated.
It is said that knowledge and vision are likened to a garment-bag; fearlessness is likened to a small table; and the ten powers are likened to a desk.

The Tathāgata mobilizes these three dharmas through his supernormal powers and proclaims these three dharmas through his wisdom. When there are no receptive vessels, he ceases his transformative activity. (Supplementary note:

Regarding the garment, the tool, the table, and the desk—concerning the literal objects, these are the implements for escaping a house on fire; concerning the dharmas, they are the dharma-gate of the true mark of the One Vehicle. Concerning the strength of the hands and body—concerning the literal person, this is the one who can use the garment, the tool, the table, and the desk; concerning the dharma, this is the Tathāgata.)

Regarding his supernatural powers and wisdom: the reason he does not employ them is that the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle is subtle and wondrous, difficult to comprehend; thus it is said to be "narrow and small," meaning it is difficult to emerge from [samsara]. Furthermore, the sons were young and ignorant, attached to their play-grounds, and were unwilling to come out.

Therefore, he abandons them. By using the three vehicles to entice and lead them, he acts in accordance with their capacities and in a fitting manner. △ Second, clarifying that the sons do not accept [the gifts] is an analogy for the aforementioned lack of capacity.
Furthermore, he reflects that this house has but a single door, [extending] to the point of being attached to the place of play.
It has but one door, and moreover, it is narrow and small. The meaning of "door" is as explained above; now it shall be further clarified.

"One" refers to the One Principle (ekayāna); it is the Single Path of Purity (*ekamārga-viśuddhi*). As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is ever thus: the Dharma-King has but one Dharma. All those who are unimpeded give birth from the One Path and transcend suffering. "Door" refers to...

The True Teaching. It is "one" because it universally penetrates all that is to be penetrated; since its principle is pure and without admixture, it is called one. Because this principle is capable of universal penetration, it is called a "gate.

Because it is subtle and wondrous, difficult to know, it is called "narrow and small. As for the "Teaching": if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle, only the Single Buddha Vehicle;
therefore, it is called one. Because this teaching is capable of universal penetration, it is called a gate. This teaching is subtle and wondrous.

Ordinary beings do not know the point of departure; this is because they do not understand skillful means (*upāya*). They do not know the point of entry; this is because they do not understand reality (*tattva*).

Those of the Two Vehicles, having heard [the teaching], have a slight knowledge of the essential way of departure, yet they never know the entry. Although Bodhisattvas know the departure for themselves, they likewise do not know the entry.

Excluding those on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), none know both the entry and the departure. As the preceding passage states: "If one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle..."

Sentient beings are submerged in suffering and are unable to attain self-realization through instruction; because they lack the capacity for such discourse, it is said that their faculties are narrow and small.
However, those of superior faculties cultivate the perfect cause through their own practice, following the great and direct path without hindrance; therefore, it is called "one."
They have practiced the bodhisattva path until reaching the site of enlightenment; therefore, it is called a "gate.

However, because their wondrous practices are difficult to perform and their skillful means lack the capacity [to lead others], it is described as "narrow and small. This clarifies that for twenty trillion buddhas, they were taught the unsurpassed path.
Those whose roots of goodness in the Mahāyāna are feeble are called "infants. If, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, they instead give rise to slander and revilement, this is called "having no discernment.
Regarding those who are attached to places of play: the former [section] clarified weak goodness, while this clarifies strong evil;

that is, at the time of the cause, they are deeply attached to views and craving, and at the time of the fruit, they are deeply attached to the primary and secondary [worlds]. They are attached to the six sense objects in the desire realm, and to the form realm...

They are attached to the flavor of dhyāna; they are attached to the meditative concentrations of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As the preceding passage states: "Sentient beings have dull faculties;
attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance, they are incapable of hearing the Mahāyāna. △ Third, relinquishment: these two lines are pointed out as the skillful guidance of relinquishment.
Or they may fall and be consumed by fire.
There are two ways of falling: first, those who are immature fall because they remember their former playgrounds; second, those who possess no consciousness at all.
Holding onto things without firmness leads to falling. First, this is a metaphor for being attached to the five desires and thus falling into the three miserable realms.
Second, it is a metaphor for those whose goodness is weak and who lack discernment; by slandering and毁 (ruining) the Mahāyāna, they likewise fall into the three miserable realms.

Therefore, one must let go and abandon them. (The first section using the gate of exhortation is concluded. △ Second, using the gate of admonition has three parts. First, using the gate of admonition through the Mahāyāna to terrify and cause [them] to...
"Come forth!
I shall speak to you of things that cause fear... (until) ...fully inform your children: 'Come forth quickly!
This is the characteristic of the remedy, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: the four foundations of mindfulness are the Mahāyāna, because they are ungraspable."

Therefore, it differs from the Hinayana. Since he has become attached to places of play, he speaks of terrifying matters to enable him to escape the fires of the five turbidities that burn the house of the five aggregates;
these should be abandoned. If one dwells in attachment for long, one will surely sever the roots of goodness; hence it is said.
"Do not let them be burned or harmed by fire. △ Second, they were unwilling to believe or accept [his words].
Although the father felt compassion and exhorted them with kind words, [they asked], "What is the house? What is the loss?"
Those who are neither startled nor afraid do not give rise to hearing or reflection, as explained above.

They fail to recognize that the eight sufferings and the five turbidities can burn away their roots of goodness, just as one who does not recognize fire. They do not recognize that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are instruments of suffering, just as one who does not recognize a house [as being on fire].
They do not know the cause for losing the Dharma-body, just as one does not know what it is that has been lost. Part Three.
"Relinquishing. These two phrases refer to relinquishment.
[The child] merely runs back and forth in play, looking only at its father.
Turning away from light toward darkness is like running east and west; dwelling in and returning from birth and death is as swift as galloping. Within this, [delusion] arises.
He views his father’s affection as mere play. Although [the father] employs the two gates of admonition using the Mahāyāna, the son refuses to accept it;

therefore, it is said that he merely looks upon his father (the first section on "Discarding the Couch" concludes). △ Second, the Parable of the Chariots. This illustrates the eleven lines of verse from the passage:
"Recalling the past Buddhas and the power of their skillful means. Here, the small vehicle is used to match what has been attained. In the preceding text, there is...

Fourth: Now there are likewise four analogies. First, the analogy of the three carts intended for use, which illustrates the aforementioned recollection of past Buddhas who also performed transformations through the three vehicles.

Second, the analogy of the father knowing the preferences of his children's former hearts, which illustrates the aforementioned moment when, at the time of such reflection, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared.
Third, the analogy of praising the three carts, which illustrates the aforementioned actual bestowal of the three [vehicles].

Having mounted [the vehicle] and reflected upon these matters, he proceeded directly to Vārāṇasī. Fourth is the analogy of fulfilling the son’s wish, which illustrates the aforementioned undertaking, practice, and realization;
this is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. Now, for the first [analogy]:
At that time, the elder had this thought: [omitted] ... so that his sons might be spared from this harm.

The merit of the Great Vehicle transformation serves as the father’s life; the great goodness of sentient beings serves as the sons’ lives. If great goodness is exhausted, then the sons’ lives are severed.
When the sons’ lives are severed, the transformative merit is also nullified, and thus the father’s life is severed. This refers to what was previously called "suffering and pain."
"Cease! You are still not dead. Now, to say that one "will certainly be burned" implies the reality of death.
In the preceding passage, it was said that one safely emerged from the burning gate; now it is said that if one does not exit in time, one will certainly be burned.

What is the meaning of this? That which previously emerged was the emergence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). What is now said regarding "not emerging at the proper time" refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) being identical to the illness.
When sentient beings possess goodness, the Response-body emerges at the proper time; when the goodness of sentient beings is severed, [it does not emerge].
If he did not manifest at the appropriate time through his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), both would have been consumed by the fire.
Now, wishing to manifest the response-body as is fitting and cause it to appear at the proper time, I shall now employ skillful means; that is, I wish to exercise expedient power.
△ Second, the parable of the father knowing the son’s previous inclinations.
The father knew the prior inclinations of his sons (up to: ...and that their hearts would surely delight in them).

He knew their former practice had been limited to the small [vehicle], thus he knew their prior inclinations; he knew that their dispositions and desires differed, thus he knew each had their own particular preferences.

Furthermore, one knows that sentient beings have previously practiced the Great [Vehicle], yet their practice of the Great has not been profound; this is called "weakness in the Great. For example, Śāriputra regressed from the six stages of mind;
because he was weary of old age, sickness, and death, he was received by means of the Small [Vehicle]. This is called "strength in the Small.

To know that they originally practiced the Great is called "knowing the prior mind"; to know that they are currently weary of old age and death is called "each having their own preference" (the regression from the six minds is according to the intent of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*).

Śāriputra, while at the sixth stage of the ten abodes, was caused to retreat from the bodhicitta by a brahmin’s request for his eyes; this is considered "great weakness. That he realized the fruit of arhatship is considered "minor strength.

△ Third, the praise of the rareness of the three vehicles, which serves as a parable for the aforementioned three turnings of the wheel of Dharma—namely, the exhortation, the demonstration, and the realization.
And he addressed them, saying: "These toys which you find so delightful are rare and difficult to obtain.
If you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later" (First turning). "Such various carts—goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts—are now outside the gate;
you may play with them as you wish" (Second turning). "You should all come out quickly from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall provide it all."
Regarding the phrase "bestowing upon you" (the third proof of turning):
it should be shown as being placed at the beginning; yet, following the sequence of the sūtra, first encouraging and then showing would also be without fault.

In the context of the proofs, the words "bestow upon" (*yǔ*) signify that while one is correctly abiding in one's own realization, one also causes others to realize it; therefore, it is called "bestowing. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
The Wheel of Dharma has been turned three times throughout the great trichiliocosm; that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure. △ Fourth, the analogy of fulfilling the son’s wish:
this illustrates the aforementioned receiving, practicing, awakening to, and entering [the truth]. The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words.
By the power of skillful means, he preached for the sake of the five bhikṣus; this is called "turning the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the sons, having heard their father speak of the rare and precious playthings, vied with one another to exit the burning house.

The preceding verse was originally concise; now the illustrative matter is expanded. This expansion clarifies the cultivation of causes leading to the fruit by explaining the meaning through six phrases. (Regarding the statement that "the preceding verse was originally concise":

the original illustration merely stated, "This is called turning the wheel of Dharma," and so forth. Regarding the expansion to six phrases: the "worthy" (*ārya*) stage is combined into four, and the stages of "seeing" (*darśana*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) are treated as two. The reason for combining the "worthy" stage is that the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are identical.)

Therefore, they are treated as one. *Uṣmagata* (Heat) and *Mūrdhan* (Summits) are both subject to regression; therefore, they are treated as one. *Kṣānti* (Patience) does not exit meditative observation; therefore, it is treated as one. *Laikāgrya* (Supreme Mundane Dharma) is unsurpassed; therefore, it constitutes its own category. Because the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) differ, each is treated as one.

This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (*Āryapudgalanirdeśa*) of the *Abhidharmakośa*; here, it is merely briefly clarified. 1. "Accordance with one's wishes" refers to the teaching being commensurate with the capacity of the four foundations of mindfulness;

this is the wisdom arising from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). "Vigorous acumen" is precisely the wisdom arising from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*). The mind of reflection moves through deliberation, which is the application of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). These two mutually push and pull one another.
"Zhě" (者): To investigate the four noble truths and suppress the delusions of views; when right and wrong have not yet been decided, it is called "mutual interaction.
This enters the stage of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) and belongs to the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*. "Sān jìng" (三競): To compete for the attainment of the supreme truth.

This is the stage of *kṣānti*. Competing to attain the supreme truth, one first contemplates the thirty-two truths, competing to advance toward the true path, and subsequently contracts the contemplation to advance [further].

This is the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma of suffering). Regarding the stage of receptivity (*kṣānti-avasthā*), one first contemplates the thirty-two aspects of the Four Noble Truths. There are sixteen aspects for each of the upper and lower realms; when these are combined, there are thirty-two. Under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one contemplates it as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self.

Under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), one contemplates it as origination, cause, condition, and production. Under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one contemplates it as cessation, extinction, tranquility, and detachment.

Under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one contemplates it as path, correctness, practice, and vehicle. These constitute sixteen aspects. In the two upper realms, because they share the same meditative level (*ekabhūmi*), the Four Noble Truths are treated as a single set; thus, one likewise contemplates sixteen aspects. This constitutes the joint contemplation of thirty-two aspects across the upper and lower realms. As for the method of contemplation, within the stage of receptivity, there are three distinct levels: inferior, medium, and superior. This refers to the inferior receptivity.

First, one contemplates the Four Truths of the Desire Realm and cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). Then, by analogy, one contemplates the Four Truths of the two higher realms and cultivates the sixteen aspects. Together, these constitute thirty-two aspects, which are termed the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). The objects of contemplation for the "middle patience" (*madhya-kṣānti*)—the eight truths (four truths each) of the three realms, comprising thirty-two aspects—are the same as those for lower patience.

However, within this stage, there is the distinction between the reduction of objects (*ālambana-hāni*) and the reduction of aspects (*ākāra-hāni*). Specifically, while a reduction of objects necessarily entails a reduction of aspects, a reduction of aspects does not necessarily entail a reduction of objects.

The "aspects" refer to the sixteen aspects; the "objects" refer to the four truths that serve as the objective spheres. There are seven cycles of reducing the objects and twenty-four cycles of reducing the aspects; this is termed the stage of middle patience. Finally, only one aspect of the Desire Realm, together with its corresponding object—the Truth of Suffering—is retained; this is termed the stage of "upper patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Therefore, it is said to be "contracted."

Contemplating the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) refers to the "Patience for the Dharma of Approaching Suffering" (*duḥkhābhisamaya-dharmakṣānti*). This is briefly explained as in the *Jizhu* (Collected Notes) on the *Sijiaoyi* (Outline of the Four Teachings); it is explained extensively in the *Xuanyi Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning).

The fourth, "commonality," refers to the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*), wherein one contemplates the same single truth (the Truth of Suffering), and thus does not differ from the four contemplations of the Patience for the Dharma of Suffering. The fifth, "running forth," refers to...

Entering the Path of Seeing consists of fifteen moments of mind. One swiftly perceives the principle (Regarding "swiftly perceiving the principle in the fifteen moments of the Path of Seeing": following the moment of the Supreme Mundane Dharma, the True Knowledge of the Patience regarding Suffering arises;

with respect to each of the eight truths, eight patiences and eight knowledges are produced, totaling sixteen moments of mind. According to the *Paryāya* school, the first fifteen moments are designated as the Path of Seeing and constitute the first fruit. From the sixteenth moment onward, it is the Path of Cultivation, which constitutes the positions of the second and third fruits).
The "sound of nirvana" mentioned above refers to the attainment of a portion of nirvana within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

The "striving to emerge" refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); it is the striving to emerge from the three realms, achieving the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), and exhausting all afflictions of cultivation before finally emerging from the burning house.
This corresponds to the aforementioned verse and the distinct designations for the Dharma and the Sangha of the Arhat. Contemplating the mind.
"Understanding" refers to the Middle Way’s correct contemplation, directly observing the true reality (*dharmatā*). When the mind and its phenomena correspond, it is called "fulfilling one's wishes.

Because the objects are boundless, the contemplation is likewise boundless; this is called "courageous. Because the objects sharpen the acuity of the mind, it is called "keen. Thus, the mind and its objects mutually refine one another.
The mutual pushing and shoving of names refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*). Their rapid engagement with objects is called "racing together in competition.
As they traverse all the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), there is nothing that is not the true nature (*dharmatā*);

this is called "leaving the burning house" (the second analogy of abandoning the stools and using the carts is concluded). △ Third, the analogy of equally bestowing great carts upon the sons. This illustrates the aforementioned [teaching].
The True Aspect. This text consists of four parts: First, the parable of the father seeing his sons escape danger and rejoice.

This illustrates the preceding passage: "I then had this thought: for what reason has the Tathāgata appeared... until now I am joyful and fearless," which serves as the basis for the one line and one verse of the gāthā.
Second, the parable of the sons requesting vehicles. This illustrates the preceding passage concerning the awakening of the capacity for the Mahāyāna: "I see the sons of the Buddha..."
1. Those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way, numbering immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis, all come to me;
this is based on the two lines of verse [from the Lotus Sūtra]. 2. The parable of equally bestowing great chariots upon the sons is based on the three phrases from above:
"Among the bodhisattvas, he directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the unsurpassed way. 3. The sons' joy upon obtaining the chariots...
The Parable of the Joyful One. This parable illustrates how the aforementioned Bodhisattvas, upon hearing this Dharma, have all cast off the net of doubt.

It is based on the single verse stating that the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas. In the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition, it first clarifies the arousal of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) and subsequently explains the removal of obstacles.

The Buddha’s joy and fearlessness are now illustrated in this parable: first by clarifying the avoidance of peril, and subsequently by clarifying the seeking of the carriage. If [the text] were complete...
The *Pāda-śāstra* (Foot Commentary) states that one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, there are those for whom obstacles are removed first and the capacity [for awakening] is subsequently aroused, such as the four great śrāvakas, who had their obstacles removed within the Tripiṭaka, yet only at the end of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* did their great capacity first arise.

Second, there are those whose two obstacles have not yet been removed when the capacity for the Mahāyāna is aroused, such as the various assemblies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who were able to enter [the path].

Regarding "the Buddha’s wisdom": the remaining two phrases are as explained above (the "above" refers to: when one's own obstacles are immediately removed and the spiritual capacity is immediately aroused—as when the *Ananta-artha* was preached and those of the Two Vehicles realized their fruits and their great capacity was aroused;

whereas when one's own obstacles have not yet been removed and the Mahāyāna capacity has not yet been aroused—as with the five thousand who withdrew from their seats). The "Expedient Means" chapter clarifies the Buddha’s joy and fearlessness.
In this context, the sons are filled with joy; because the sons are joyful, the father is also joyful. They become of one mind.
This is now the first analogy: the father’s joy upon seeing his sons escape from danger.
At that time, the elder saw that his sons had safely emerged [from the fire] and was filled with joy and exultation.

Being freed from calamity involves two meanings: namely, the freedom from calamity itself and the resulting joy. If the sons had not yet been freed from the calamity, the father would have been filled with anxiety;
once they were able to escape the fire, his mind became at ease. Therefore, being freed from calamity and feeling joy constitute a single analogy.
Because the son rejoices, the father also rejoices; this is analogous to the joy of the Buddha. "In the middle of a crossroads" is a direct metaphor for the Four Noble Truths.
The distinct contemplations of the Four Truths are called the "four crossroads. The convergence of the Four Truths at the vision of the truths is like the junction of intersecting roads.

Although the delusions of view have been eliminated, the delusions of mental cultivation still remain; thus, it is not yet called an "open space. When the mental cultivation within the three realms is exhausted, it is called [an open space].
In the open space, they abide in the fruits [of the path] without further progress; hence it is said they "sit. They are not constrained by the afflictions of views and thoughts;
hence it is said they are "serene. They conceive the thought of peace and security in nirvāṇa; hence it is said they are "joyful. △ Second, the parable of the sons requesting the carts.
At that time, each of the sons addressed their father, saying [up to] "we pray you will grant them to us at this time.

The subsequent verse says: "We pray you will grant us the three kinds of precious chariots. Although the text does not contain the character for "request" (*suo*), according to the meaning of this petition, it clearly implies a request for the chariots.
This is analogous to the arousal of the capacity for the Mahāyāna mentioned above. The *Huìyì* (Exegesis on the Meaning) states: "The three chariots serve as metaphors."
Regarding the fruit-positions of the three vehicles: it is for the sake of seeking the fruits of the three vehicles that one departs from the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Once having departed from the triple world, there is in reality no fruit of the three vehicles to be realized.

Furthermore, through the censure of the Vaipulya sūtras and the refinement of the Prajñāpāramitā, this present sūtra explicitly declares that these skillful means (*upāya*) are not ultimate. Therefore, [the disciples] earnestly requested three times, which is called "seeking the carriage," referring to the past.
The three provisional [teachings] that were previously granted are precisely the invitation to this one reality; therefore, it is called the "arousing of the Mahāyāna capacity.
One must know that during the Vaipulya period, [the teaching] was repeatedly met with setbacks, and because they did not understand what was being said, there was the "mechanism of capacity.

When it reached the Prajñāpāramitā period, the teaching was transferred and the treasury was entrusted, yet because they themselves did not yet know whether they had attained it or not, there was the "rope of sentiment. Now, regarding the Dharma...
The Flower Assembly. To speak thus and request three times is to further seek it verbally. △ Third, the Parable of Equally Bestowing Great Chariots.
This has two parts: first, marking the two chapter-headings; second, expanding upon the questions of the two chapters. Now, the first: marking [the headings].
Śāriputra, at that time the elder bestowed upon each of his sons an identical great carriage.
"Bestowed upon each of his sons" indicates that the sons were equal; "an identical great carriage" indicates that the carriages were equal.
Why? Because the sons were equal, their minds were equal. This is like the fact that all sentient beings equally possess the Buddha-nature. This is the Buddha-nature.
Because they are the same; they are equally sons. Regarding the "second chariots being equal," it is because they are equal in terms of the Dharma; there is nothing that is not the Buddha-Dharma.
This is an analogy for how all dharmas are the Mahāyāna. Because the Mahāyāna is the same, they are equally great chariots.

As for saying "each was given one," this means that each followed their own original practice of the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, and the immeasurable dharmas, according to what they had previously cultivated.
He reveals the ultimate truth. Because their former habits differ, he says they are "each" [given something]. Since all belong to the Mahāyāna, he calls them "great vehicles.

(The passage below, however, uses "sons" and so forth to resolve doubts regarding the "vehicles" and so forth. If it speaks of "vehicles" and so forth, why are they given "each"? It is because their former practices were different and their respective positions were not uniform. Yet, what is taught here is none other than the One Vehicle. Why is this? If one person were not included, they could not be called "sons" and so forth.

Furthermore, since it refers to their "original practice," it should encompass all dharmas; if even a single thing were not bestowed, it could not be called "giving each" and so forth. Therefore, whether matter or mind, adverse or favorable, the environment or the inhabitants, practice or principle, cause or fruit, self or other, delusion or awakening, small...)

Great! O Wisdom and Merit! Thus we know that the equal distribution is merely to open up for them the three vehicles and the six paths; there is nothing that is not the One Suchness. Therefore, in each and every suchness, all are universally encompassed, universally endowed, and universally entered. Among all sentient beings, who lacks their share of the four directions of the site of enlightenment?

Who does not possess the great vehicle with its various means of crossing over? It is simply because they await the time and await the conditions that it is so. Thus, until this day, one only speaks of "each being given. II. Extensively explaining the two chapter-headings. This has two parts: first, extensively explaining the vehicle; second, extensively explaining the mind.
Regarding the extensive explanation of the vehicle, there are again two parts: first, extensively explaining the substance of the vehicle; second, the explanation.
Regarding the origin of the chariot: within the description of the chariot’s body, there are three parts. First, the height and breadth are described; second, the white oxen are explained;
third, the attendants are clarified. Now, for the first:
the chariot is high and broad, adorned with various jewels (extending to) the placement of the vermilion pillows.
The provisional designation of a "chariot" possesses the characteristics of height and breadth. For example, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are profound and far-reaching:

horizontally, they encompass the very limits of the Dharma-realm; vertically, they penetrate to the source and bottom of the Three Truths. Therefore, it is said to be "high and broad. As for "adorned with various jewels":
The myriad practices are like its adornments. The surrounding railings are like *dhāraṇī*, which upholds all virtues and wards off all evils.
The bells suspended on all four sides are like the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) used to transform those below. The spread canopy is like the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*);
among all virtues, compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are supreme, universally covering all beings. The various rare and precious jewels...
As for its adornment, it is the myriad genuine virtues that adorn this compassion. The Great Sūtra states:
"If compassion is fully endowed with the ten powers and the fearlessnesses, it is called the Tathāgata’s compassion. Within this compassion, one practices giving and so forth.

The "interlacing jeweled cords" are a metaphor for the Four Great Vows, which strengthen the mind of great compassion. The "hanging flower tassels" are a metaphor for the Four Means of Integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that delight and move sentient beings are also like the exquisite wreath of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

The layered arrangement of a graceful mat symbolizes the cultivation through contemplation, refinement, and habitual practice, as well as all the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), which are thickly spread and soft.

The placement of a crimson pillow is like an external headrest for a carriage; when the carriage is driven and moving, it requires this support to remain upright wherever it goes—this is a metaphor for being active while simultaneously [abiding in stillness].
Stillness is movement within stillness. It is like one who rests their body and head while inside a carriage;
this is a metaphor for the *ekavyūha-samādhi*, which brings rest to all wisdom and all practices. "Dan" (丹) means vermilion light, which is a metaphor for the non-discriminative Dharma.
Next is the white ox.
The carriage is drawn by white oxen, their coats pure and clean, and its speed like the wind.
That it is drawn by white oxen is a metaphor for untainted *prajñā* (wisdom), which can lead one through the objects of the Truths and bring all myriad practices to completion.

Upon reaching *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), one declares that this form is fundamentally pure; it is thus associated with original purity and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Its essence is endowed with myriad virtues, like skin that is full and abundant.
It is unstained by afflictions (*kleśa*), like a complexion that is clean and bright. Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the white oxen.

Within the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the two periods of good are fulfilled like skin that is full and abundant, while the two periods of evil are exhausted like a complexion that is clean and bright. The four [right bases of power]...

The "satisfactions of mind" (iddhipāda) accord with the practitioner’s heart, just as a physical form may be beautiful. The "tendons" are a metaphor for the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), in the sense that they provide the basis for arising.

The "strengths" (*bala*) are a metaphor for the five powers (*pañcabala*), in the sense of their function to crush and subdue. Walking with even steps is a metaphor for the equality of concentration and wisdom;
