it also serves as a metaphor for the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) being harmoniously balanced. "Moving as swiftly as the wind" refers to proceeding within the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
One swiftly arrives at *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). △ Next, the retinue is explained:
furthermore, one is attended by many servants who guard and serve one.
These "servants" are a metaphor for the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), which can adapt and conform to others, providing service and carrying out instructions. The multitude...

Māras, external paths, and those of the two vehicles with their minor practices all follow the functional application of expedient wisdom; thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says, "They are all my attendants.

Furthermore, the supernatural powers of the stage of fruition can employ and direct things at will, which is precisely what constitutes being a servant. △ Second, explaining the reason for possessing the chariot.
Why is this so? This great elder possesses immeasurable wealth, and all his various treasuries are completely full.
Because the Tathāgata’s state of fruition is perfected in merit and wisdom, he is said to possess "immeasurable wealth. Regarding the phrase "various treasuries are full":
these are the treasury of practice, the treasury of principle, and all phenomena tending toward *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, and so forth; that which does not transcend these tendencies.

This refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* in terms of practice (*caryā*). All phenomena—aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth—do not transcend this "course" (*gati*).
This clarifies the *tathāgatagarbha* in terms of principle (*nyāya*). Practicing this course for oneself is called "pervasion" (*pūrṇa*); transforming others is called "overflowing" (*abhyudita*).

Fulfillment of ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) is called "pervasion"; fulfillment of expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) is called "overflowing. Entering the Middle Way is called "pervasion"; illuminating both simultaneously is...
Therefore, it is called "overflowing. It is not merely that the storehouse is large; rather, everything is filled to overflowing. What dharma is not the Mahāyāna?
Thus, the wealth of the Mahāyāna Dharma is immeasurable. (The first section, "The Broad Vehicle," etc., concludes. △ Second, "The Broad Mind," etc. This passage has two parts.
First, the broad mind; second, the explanation. Regarding the first:
he forms this thought, "My wealth and possessions are limitless; I shall give them to each person individually and should not treat them with partiality."
Regarding the phrase "with an impartial mind" and so forth: their wealth is immeasurable, and these sons are without distinction; therefore, his mind is impartial.
If one were wealthy but not a son, or a son but poor, then equality would not be possible. Now, the number of these great seven-jeweled chariots is immeasurable.
Whether in teaching or practice, all are the Mahāyāna; this is what is meant by "abundant wealth.

To give to each without making distinctions means that one does not alter their original training, yet reveals the reality. For example, Śāriputra opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through wisdom and was endowed with all Buddha-dharmas;
Maudgalyāyana opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through meditative concentration and was endowed with all Buddhas [dharmas].

The Dharma is thus for all other persons as well. Furthermore, in the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, the various distinct names—such as the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path—all reveal the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This applies likewise across all phenomena;
therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable. △ Second, the explanation.
Why is this? Because if these goods of mine were distributed throughout the entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted; how much less so for my sons? First, explaining "abundant wealth":
if it suffices to provide for an entire kingdom, how much more so for the sons? This is like the analogy of a great round cause that encompasses both good and evil;
how much more so the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Next, explaining "the sons and others": if even those who are not his sons are sufficiently provided for, how much more so his own sons?

It is like the Buddha, who still delivers even those with whom he has no karmic connection; how much more so his own children with whom he does share such a connection? (The section on the "Broadening of the Mind" concludes).
△ Fourth, the Parable of the Sons Receiving the Carts and Rejoicing. This illustrates the aforementioned stages of receiving, practicing, awakening, and entering.
At that time, the sons each mounted a great carriage, attaining what they had never experienced before and which was not what they had originally hoped for.

Originally they sought rams, deer, and water buffaloes, intending only to escape the realm of birth-and-death (*bhavāgra*); now they have obtained white oxen, exhausting even the realm of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

This exceeds their original expectations—how could they not be filled with joy? (Supplementary note: Master Li Tsao-pa’s verse says: "All sentient beings are the golden realm; pure and stainless, their wisdom is indestructible.")

The jewel of wisdom lies within the inner garments of sovereign mastery; yet, wishing only to remain in perpetual poverty, one stays outside the gate. The vast and precious vehicle stands at the crossroads, guided by Mañjuśrī and supported by Samantabhadra. The plump, white oxen possess immense strength, traversing everywhere in a single thought without contraction or expansion.

Unable to enter such a precious vehicle, one merely delights in diligent toil and stands before the gate, unaware that one’s own body dwells eternally within it—thus neglecting the constant teaching that "I am not equal [to this].

(The third analogy, the Bestowal of Great Chariots, concludes. △ Fourth, the Analogy of the Elder’s Lack of Deception. This illustrates that the Dharma King does not speak falsely. It consists of three parts.
First, the question; second, the answer; third, the praise. Now, for the first:
"Śāriputra, what do you think? (up to: Could there be any falsehood in this?"
Regarding the Buddha’s question: Originally, only three [options] were permitted, yet now he grants one. Is this not false?
[The Buddha] asked about falsehood in order to lead Śāriputra to realize the truth. △ Second, the answer, which is twofold: first, avoiding the charge of falsehood.
Second, not contradicting one's original intention and not being false; each of these is threefold. First, the non-falsity of escaping calamity: first, the brief statement.
Śāriputra said, "No, World-Honored One" (up to) "...preserving his body and life is not a falsehood."
△ Second, the explanation. Why is this?
If one preserves both body and life, it is as if one has already obtained objects of play and enjoyment. To explain:
life is weighty and the body is light. To preserve the body and escape the fire is to have already obtained a great treasure that saves one’s precious life; how could this not be so?

One should realize that [the teaching] is entirely within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) regarding the fivefold Dharma-body; having entered the life of wisdom in emptiness, one has already attained what was formerly cherished. How much more so, then, the skillful means for rescuing suffering from the burning house—how could this not originally belong to the Great [Vehicle]?
△ Third, the analogy of the three bonds.
How much more so for those who, through skillful means, rescue others from that burning house,

liberating them from the fires of the eight sufferings and preserving their bodies composed of the five aggregates— this alone is already a great treasure, let alone [the salvation of] twenty thousand *koṭis*.
At the place of the Buddha, the life-force of Mahāyāna wisdom is perfected through the fulfillment of causes; as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are revealed, how could this be false?
△ Second, not contradicting one's original mind, in three parts: first, the heading.
World-Honored One, if this elder had not even given the smallest single chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood.
This constitutes the chapter on how the initial declaration did not deviate from his original intention. Originally, he knew there were no three [kinds of carts]; his intent was to prevent slander.

As for "not slandering," it means he did not deviate from his original intention. (Regarding "not deviating from his original intention": this describes the elder’s original purpose. Whether small or large, both possess the original intention. The "Great Original" is the true original; the "Small Original" is not the original. He permitted the small.)

If he did not give [the small amount], there would still be no contradiction; how much less so when he gave such a great [position]? How could this possibly contradict his original intention? If he had promised a small amount of wealth and gave only a small amount, it would not be false; how much less so when he gave a great position, which far exceeds what was previously [promised]? How could this possibly contradict his original mind? One can know with certainty that the Tathāgata’s original teaching was not a minor one.

Thus, as for wealth, one is merely freed from the poverty of the *bhavāgra* (segmented existence); as for position, one transcends the lowliness of the two deaths (*dvimaraṇa*). Since both meanings are fully provided, what contradiction could there be? △ Second, the explanation.
Why is this? It is because the elder first formed this intention (up to) "for these reasons there is no falsehood.
He originally knew [the children] were not small; his intention was to prevent them from being harmed. Since there was no cause for harm, they did not fall into evil retribution.
Not giving them small carts does not contradict his original intention. △ Third, the conclusion by way of analogy.
How much more so for the elder, who knows his own wealth to be immeasurable and desires to benefit his sons by giving them all equal great chariots;
knowing his own wealth to be immeasurable and desiring to benefit his sons, he gives them all equal great chariots, exceeding what they originally expected.

Therefore, it is not in vain. The preceding chapter concludes by stating that "skillful means for deliverance" is analogous to the power of the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
The subsequent chapter concludes by stating that "immeasurable wealth" is analogous to the power of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) and eloquent exposition (*pratibhāna*).
Because the former concerns the [son] and so forth, it is not in vain; because the latter concerns wealth and so forth, it is not in vain. △ Third, the description and praise.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.
There are two 'excellent' [statements], which describe those two as not being false. Question: Why does the Buddha not himself state that they are not false?
Answer: The Buddha permitted three [vehicles] and one; he himself spoke of this as difficult. Śāriputra’s explanation is not false, and it is easy to take as authoritative.
(The fourth section, the parable of the elder without falsehood, concludes. The first section, the opening of the parable, concludes. △ Second, the application of the parables.
This applies both the general and specific parables mentioned above. First, there are six points for applying the general parable, all of which are now applied here. (Minor [details follow].)
This is not in sequential order. Here, for the first time, the first Elder is combined with the aforementioned [section on] names, stages, titles, virtues, deeds, and so forth;
therefore, it says, "The Tathāgata is also like this."
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this (up to) being fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means and wisdom, possessing immeasurable virtuous titles.
To briefly cite ten meanings, it is as explained above. Regarding "all worlds" (*sarvaloka*):
while the previous passage spoke of kingdoms, cities, and villages, here it is directly stated as "all worlds" to provide a comprehensive reference.

The *sahabhū* (co-resident), *śeṣa* (residual), *vipāka* (fruition of retribution), and *svabhāva* (essential) [bodies] are all places that are the fruition of the Buddha’s wondrous form and wondrous mind;
yet he universally responds to those in all three locations. Regarding "all fears" and so forth, this combines with the preceding praise of internal and external virtues.

Internally, although he is advanced in years and in decline, his realization and penetration are vast—just like the Tathāgata’s wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*). Thus, regarding all fears, he is without...
"Clearly exhausting all [defilements]" corresponds to the aforementioned "declining old age," manifesting the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

"Accomplishing immeasurable knowledge and vision" corresponds to his advanced years, manifesting the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). "Powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth" correspond to the aforementioned "external virtues," which are immeasurable riches.

The power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhibala*): by deeply cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is able to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This corresponds to the aforementioned field. The power of wisdom (*prajñābala*):
wisdom necessarily illuminates its objects, just as a body requires a dwelling place. This corresponds to the aforementioned house.

Being fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*) corresponds to the aforementioned various attendants. △ Second, corresponding to the aforementioned five hundred people. As stated above: "Now I am also like..."
It is so. Because it brings peace and security to sentient beings; peace and security are precisely compassion (*karuṇā*).
With great kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion, one is always free from weariness and constantly seeks virtuous deeds to benefit all.
Compassion is the foundation of transformative teaching. All beings belong to the five realms of existence and are constantly enveloped by compassion.
This includes the previous five hundred people. △ Third, including his family: Because of compassion, he was born into the burning house of the triple world.
Thus they are born into the triple world, this dilapidated and ancient house of fire.
△ Fourth, combining with the sixth [section] above, "Sentient Beings with Whom He Has a Karmic Connection": those who were previously close correspond to the thirty sons mentioned above.
There are the faculties and inclinations of the three vehicles.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings.
△ Fifth, "Peaceful Security" (An-yin) combined with the above: in contrast to the dharma of insecurity, a fire suddenly breaks out.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death; sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; the darkness of ignorance and delusion; and the fires of the three poisons.
△ This concludes the third section of the first fascicle, which proclaims the Buddha-way through various Dharma gates.
They are taught and transformed so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The teaching (*śāsana*) can express the principle (*tattva*); by investigating the principle, one gives rise to practice, and thereby attains *bodhi*. Thus, we know that the teaching and the principle function together.

This corresponds to the preceding analogy of "there being only a single gate. If one expounds [the teaching], it should be made intelligible from beginning to end; each point must be clearly presented.
Compare this with the parables in the "Expedient Means" chapter; later sections shall follow this same method (the six general parables are now concluded).

△ Second, the application of the specific parables. There are four specific parables: first, the application of the parable of seeing the fire; second, the application of the parable of abandoning the stool and using the cart;
third, the application of the parable of bestowing the great carts equally; fourth, the application of the parable of being free from falsehood. First, the application of seeing...
There are four analogies for fire. First, combining with the aforementioned "I," I observe and see with the Buddha-eye.
Here, by using the single character "see" (jiàn), it combines with the first [analogy], the eye that is able to see; this is the Tathāgata’s tranquil illumination.
The eye of wisdom is able to see this. △ Second, combining what has been seen: the fires arise from the four directions.
All sentient beings [suffer] the various kinds of suffering such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, up to and including these various sufferings.
In this context, the eight sufferings are clarified as fire. Four of these sufferings correspond to the text. "Clinging and seeking" refers to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;

subsequently, one undergoes the sufferings of the hells, as well as those of the heavens and the human realm, which are the sufferings of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Separation from the beloved and meeting with the hated" are as explained in the text.
These eight sufferings arise from the four aspects of the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). △ Third, combining the fires seen above serves as a metaphor for all [sufferings].
The sons are neither aware nor cognizant;
sentient beings are submerged within it (up to: though they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as an affliction).

Because they do not contemplate suffering and its origin, they do not feel weary of it. Because they do not contemplate the path and its cessation, they do not seek liberation. Though they encounter great...
They do not regard suffering as a calamity; their minds do not feel revulsion toward it, nor do they have the intention to seek its cessation.
△ Fourth, corresponding to the above, they give rise to alarm and fear.
Śāriputra, having seen this, [the Buddha]... (until)... causes them to sport therein.
Fourth, combining with the third, it gives rise to alarm and fear: "Although I am able to escape safely from this burning gate, my mind [remains troubled].
That which uproots such suffering and distress is the power of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
that which bestows immeasurable bliss is the power of Great Loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). (The first section, the parable of the elder seeing the fire, concludes. △ Second.

The application [of the analogy] consists of two parts: abandoning the small table and using the carriage. First is the application of abandoning the small table; next is the application of using the carriage. Regarding the first, the abandonment of the small table:

the preceding text contained both exhortation and admonition; here, we apply only the exhortation, not the admonition, because exhorting toward the good inherently constitutes admonishing against the evil.
Rebuking evil is equivalent to exhorting toward good. The preceding exhortation consists of three parts: the preliminary proposal, the lack of receptive capacity, and the cessation of the teaching.
Now, for the first:
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata again had this thought... [until] sentient beings cannot be delivered by means of this.
It is intended to represent a body, hands, and a robe-sleeve (*kaṭhina*). "Supernatural power" (*ṛddhi-bala*) corresponds to the strength of the body;
"wisdom-power" (*prajñā-bala*) corresponds to the strength of the hands. Praising the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision corresponds to the robe-sleeve;
the powers and fearlessnesses correspond to the small table (*mañca*). If the Buddha first appeared and immediately employed this [representation], sentient beings would be unable to comprehend it.
They have attained deliverance. △ Second, those lacking the capacity do not accept the exhortation.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings [from "to" ... how could they possibly understand the Buddha’s wisdom?
Precisely because the obstacles of the five turbidities are heavy, they have not yet escaped the fires of birth and death and the like; thus, they cannot enter the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna.
Therefore it is said: "How could they possibly understand the Buddha’s wisdom? This single phrase corresponds to the previous point that there is only one gate, which is moreover narrow and small.
△ Third, this corresponds to the previous point of relinquishing [the teaching] and ceasing transformation due to a lack of receptive capacity. Otherwise, it would not be so.
Or they shall fall, to be consumed by fire. This passage contains no words of relinquishment, yet the intent to cease the work of transformation is very clear.
There are two parts to the text concerning the cessation of transformation: first, it restates the three preceding metaphors and applies them accordingly.
"Śāriputra, it is like that elder (up to) 'and then gave each of them a precious great chariot.
This restates the preceding parable to correctly apply it to the cessation of the teaching. The subsequent two parables are cited to supplement the establishment of the cessation of the teaching.
"Although his body and hands possessed strength, he did not employ them"—this restates the preceding parable of how the father’s physical strength failed to save his children.

This corresponds to the Tathāgata likewise ceasing his great transformation (*mahādharmadeśanā*). However, from "but with earnestness" (*yǐnyíqín*) downward, it cites the analogy of bestowing the three vehicles.

Following that, from "each respectively" (*jiù ránhòu gè yǔ*) downward, it cites the analogy of equally bestowing the great vehicle. △ Second, the formal correspondence regarding the cessation of the transformation.
The Tathāgata is also like this. Although he possesses powers and fearlessness, he does not employ them.

These sixteen characters precisely correspond to the analogy of "ceasing transformation" (the first correspondence, ending with the simile of relinquishing). △ Second, the correspondence of the analogy of using the vehicle to rescue and save.
The preceding section has four parts; herein there are likewise four. First, the correspondence to the three aforementioned provisional measures.
It is like a carriage.
Yet, by means of wisdom and skillful means, he rescues sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world.
△ Second, this combines with the above to show that [the Buddha] knew his sons' prior inclinations.
For their sake, he preached the three vehicles: the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha vehicle.

△ Third, combining the above to praise the rarity of the three carts. Above, there was the exhortation, the demonstration, and the realization; now these are likewise combined, though not in their original order, beginning first with the demonstration.

And he spoke these words: "Do not take pleasure in dwelling within this burning house of the triple world (the Truth of Suffering). Do not crave coarse and inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
If you become attached through craving, you will be consumed by fire (the Truth of Origination). You must quickly depart from the triple world."
"You shall attain the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle (the two truths of cessation and the path).
These three carts mentioned above are now outside the gate. You who are within this burning house should quickly come forth! The triple world is shown as the truth of suffering;
do not crave its coarse and wretched things, nor give rise to attachment and the like—this shows the truth of origination. [Come forth] quickly!"
It causes them to exit the triple world and demonstrates to them the path of cessation (*nirodha-mārga*).

This "path of cessation" indicates that beyond the triple world there are the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) resulting from wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*); thus, it causes them to quickly exit the triple world so that they shall attain the three vehicles.
The three vehicles take this very path of cessation as their essence. △ Second, the proof.
I now guarantee this matter for you (up to the point where it says): "The Tathāgata uses these skillful means to entice and advance sentient beings.
Second, this corresponds to the above, meaning that one will certainly attain realization; it is not in vain. △ Third, this corresponds to the above praise of the rarity of the chariot.
This is an exhortation. He further speaks these words: "You should all know... [until] you shall thereby attain immeasurable peace and happiness.
These Three Vehicles are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas; they are the ritual methods for guiding sentient beings, and are thus praised by all the Sages. To attain [this]—

The arising of knowledge constitutes mastery. The attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) constitutes freedom from fetters. "My births have been exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence" is called being without dependence.
"What was to be done has been accomplished; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established" is called being without seeking.

Regarding the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*): the faculties are the five faculties; the powers are the five powers; awakening refers to the seven factors of awakening; and the path refers to the eightfold noble path.

The Path; Dhyāna; the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*); liberation (*vimokṣa*); the eight liberations; and the samādhis—the three samādhis.

These aforementioned dharma-gates encompass both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). These fruits of the Three Vehicles are all comprised of the outflow-free faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*).
"Immeasurable peace and happiness" refers to realizing true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and nirvāṇa, and being free from...

I see that by permanently extinguishing all afflictions such as views of existence and non-existence, one attains immeasurable peace and bliss; hence it is said, "one attains immeasurable peace and bliss.
△ Fourth, combining this with the preceding analogy of the son’s wish: above there were four stages—true, similar, and so forth; now, combining them, there are likewise four.

This is a general summary above followed by a specific analysis below; for each of the three vehicles, four [categories] are established, all of which draw upon the preceding parables to provide a detailed application.
Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings (up to) who, seeking ox-carts, emerge from the burning house.
Regarding those who possess the nature of wisdom within: having habitually practiced the aspiration for the Three Vehicles in past lives, they have perfected the wisdom-nature of the Three Vehicles;

therefore, the Buddha bestows upon them the teachings of the Three Vehicles. That there is wisdom within, and that they subsequently hear the Dharma from the Buddha and accept it with faith, corresponds to the aforementioned hearing of the father’s description of the playthings, which satisfied their wishes;
this corresponds to the aforementioned "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). With diligent and earnest application...
"Advancing" (*jin*) refers to earnestness; it corresponds to the first [of the three types of wisdom], which is the courageous and sharp application of thought and wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

"Vigorous effort" (*vīrya*) corresponds to the second, "pushing and clearing away. "Pushing" means reasoning (*tarka*), and "clearing away" means removing evil. Because evil is removed, there is "purity" (*jing*); because principle is clarified, there is "advancing" (*jin*).

This corresponds to the third, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). "Desiring to emerge quickly from below" corresponds to the third [of the three types of exertion], "racing together in competition"; this is called "fame" (*śabda*).

Regarding the "Hearing Vehicle" (*śrāvaka-yāna*): this corresponds to the fourth stage above, emerging from the burning house. The practice of the three vehicles all possesses these four [stages]. Now, as for the *pratyekabuddha* who seeks natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*):
a *pratyekabuddha* is one who practices through the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*). While they hear the Dharma from others to a small degree, they mostly infer its meaning on their own;
therefore, they are compared to a deer. A deer does not rely on humans. "Natural" means that [wisdom] arises from the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
This gate enters [into the realization]. This gate exists inherently; it was not created by Buddhas, devas, or humans, and is thus called "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
Because it is not heard from another, it is further named "spontaneous wisdom. The Bodhisattva is titled the "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*);

this is distinct from the Two Vehicles and is indeed the Buddha-wisdom. When a Bodhisattva contemplates this while cultivating the causes, it carries the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s simultaneous operation.
(Above, the second section combining [the parables] on abandoning the carts and using the analogy of the carts is concluded). △ Third, combining the analogy of the equal bestowal of the great carts.
The preceding text contains four parts: first, escaping the peril; second, seeking the carts; third, the equal bestowal; and fourth, rejoicing.

Now, we shall briefly omit the combination of "seeking the carts" and "rejoicing," but combine only "escaping the peril," which by its meaning also encompasses "seeking the carts," and combine "the equal bestowal," the meaning of which is as follows:
Furthermore, there is joy. Now, the two parables concerning the exemption from calamity and so forth are presented together; subsequently, these two parables are combined as a pair.
First, the pair is presented:
"Śāriputra, it was like that elder who [bestowed] great chariots upon his sons."
"Like that elder," and below, the exemption from danger is cited; "considering his own wealth," and below, the equal bestowal is cited.
△ Next, the two are combined together. First, the exemption from danger is combined.
The Tathāgata is also like this... [attaining] the bliss of nirvāṇa.

The "gate" has both the sense of entering and the sense of exiting. If the triple world is the house and the five aggregates are the dwelling, then by being deluded regarding form and mind, one enters into form and mind;
this is precisely the gate of birth and death for entering the house. If one acts as an "exitor," it is now said that—
The Gate of Buddhism. To emerge from the suffering of the triple world is precisely to receive the principles of both the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings.
Taking these teachings as the common gateway, one initiates the holy practices of the three vehicles, emerges from the suffering of the triple world, and attains the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

△ Next, regarding the "Equal Bestowal": first, the superior bestowal is indicated by two chapters; second, those two chapters are explained in detail; finally, the meaning of "possessing the vehicle" is elucidated.
Because the current text is incomplete and slightly disordered, it is briefly divided into five parts. First, combining with the preceding section, this explains the reason for having the chariot:
"At that time, the Tathāgata had this thought... up to "...the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers and the fearlessnesses."
The preceding passage states that his wealth is immeasurable and his treasuries are overflowing. △ Second, combining this with the aforementioned "vast and equal mind":
"All these sentient beings are my children... [and] I shall bring them all to extinction through the same extinction as that of the Tathāgata."
Above it was said, "My wealth and possessions are inexhaustible; it is not fitting that I should provide inferior, small carts.

Now it is said, "I shall not allow anyone to attain extinction alone; I shall cause all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata. Is this not indeed in accord with the principle of an impartial mind?
△ Third, this accords with the previously stated topical heading on the impartial mind.
These sentient beings who have escaped the three realms—this refers to what was said above regarding "giving each son an equal [gift].
△ Fourth, this combines with the preceding heading of the chapter on the "Equal Carts":
[the father] gives them all the various implements for enjoyment, such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and other [attainments] of the Buddhas.
△ Fifth, the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is correctly joined above;
all are of one characteristic, of one kind, praised by the Noble Ones, and capable of producing the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss.

Combining all these—the height and breadth, up to the servants and attendants—they constitute a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*); this is the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*).
This single kind is the *prajñā* of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*). It is able to produce pure and wondrous bliss;

this bliss is the absence of suffering, and is called the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). These three virtues are high and broad, fully adorned, and encompass all qualities; this is called [the Dharmadhātu].
Mahāyāna. This corresponds to the analogy of the great carriage (the third section, concluding the correspondence regarding the equal bestowal of great carriages upon all sons).

△ Fourth, the correspondence with the analogy of not being in vain. The preceding response consists of two parts: first, preserving one’s life and body; second, not contradicting one’s original intention.
Now, we only correspond to "not contradicting one’s original intention," which simultaneously encompasses "preserving one’s life and body. This is further divided into three sections. First:
The citation of the analogy:
"Śāriputra, it is like that elder... [up to] ...without the fault of falsehood.
△ Next, the application of the meaning explains how this does not contradict his original intention.
The Tathāgata is also like this... (until) thereafter he delivers and liberates them solely by means of the Mahāyāna.
△ Third, the application by way of analogy. This applies the preceding analogy to demonstrate that [the teaching] is not in vain.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom (up to) distinguishing and teaching three [vehicles].
This is just as a wealthy elder, knowing his own riches to be immeasurable, desires to benefit his children and thus grants them three [options] while ultimately bestowing one;
it is not false. This explanation differs slightly from the previous one; the former intention was to enable the children to escape.

The intention was not fixed upon the three [vehicles]. Having already enabled them to escape, he did not withhold it, nor was it a deceptive fabrication. Now it is clarified that when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, his original intent was to preach the Mahāyāna;
however, because those of small wisdom were attached to the triple world, he used skillful means to entice and lead them.
Once they had escaped, he restored to them the Mahāyāna, which accords with their original aspiration; therefore, it is said that he is able to bestow the Mahāyāna upon sentient beings.
The Dharma, however, they were not yet able to receive in its entirety. Had they been able to receive it within the *Avataṃsaka*, it would have already been fully bestowed;

there would have been no need to wait for the opening of the Deer Park to divide the One into Three. Because they were unable to receive it, [the Buddha] employed the power of skillful means regarding the Single Buddha Vehicle.
The threefold distinction is explained in three ways based on sentient beings; this was not the Buddha’s original intent.

Therefore, by using this explanation, it is established that there is no contradiction with his fundamental mind and that [the teaching] is not in vain. Previously, Śāriputra asked: "I pray that you will explain its causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly."
Now, for this reason, I reply: because these causes and conditions cannot be fully encompassed, I have explained them through three distinct categories (the initial prose section concludes).
△ Second, the verse section consists of one hundred and sixty-five lines, divided into two parts.
The first part contains one hundred lines, which versify the second analogy within the preceding prose text. The latter part contains sixty-five lines, which expand upon...
This clarifies the methods for understanding the sūtra and encourages faith in its circulation. In the prose above, there is both an opening analogy and a concluding application;

the verse commentary likewise has two parts. First, there are sixty-five and a half lines of verse for the opening analogy; second, there are thirty-four and a half lines of verse for the concluding application.
The first part also has two sections: first, there are thirty-three lines of verse for the general analogy; second, there are thirty...
The two and a half verses provide distinct analogies, while the summary verse encompasses six intentions; within those six, four are explicitly versified and two are implicitly included.
The verse on the house also includes one gate, and the verse on the five hundred people also includes the thirty sons.
Now, the first line clarifies the elder.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"For example, there was an elder."
The verse praises his titles; that is to say, it simultaneously names his achievements and extols his virtues. Since he possesses the virtue of leading others, one knows his conduct and reputation.
Because he is universally revered by the state and its cities, one also knows his internal and external qualities; both his age and virtue are high.
Internally, this corresponds to *Bhagavān* (the Blessed One), which refers to his title; thus, one knows he is fully endowed with wisdom, abandonment, compassion, and all myriad virtues. △ First.
The two or three lines consist of one verse. This verse illustrates the metaphor of the house, which is divided into two parts. The first line illustrates the house itself: "There is a great house.

Regarding "a great house," this refers for the time being to the triple world (*tridhātu*) within a single direction; hence it is called "one. △ The next two or three lines provide a detailed exposition.
The "body of the house" refers to the fact that the house is ancient (up to the point where it is) filled everywhere with various impurities.

This explains the characteristics of what is burned by the light; thus, one knows this verse refers to the body of the house. The three realms have been without beginning, hence they are "ancient. It is not...

Because that which is currently created is for the sake of the past, it is impermanent, base, and called "suddenly ruined. It is also said: the head is the palace, the belly is the hall, and the back is the house;
the continuous succession of moments, being impermanent, is called "perilous. One interpretation states: the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is the hall and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the house;
not escaping falling [from them] is called "perilous. The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) supporting [the body] is the pillar; past karma is...
It serves as the foundation and steps. It is also said that the two feet are the pillars and roots, while being subject to the transitions of the three marks is called "crumbling decay.
Consciousness acts as the structural framework, serving as the beams and rafters; being destroyed by various sufferings is like being tilted over.

It is also said that the spinal column is the beam and rafter, and the pelvis is the foundation and steps; at the time of old age, it becomes dilapidated and ruined. As for the walls, one explanation says: [text continues].
The four great elements are the walls; the skin is the plaster coating. The four modes of deportment being improper is like collapsing foundations.

The five consciousnesses being dull and not presiding over their respective objects is called "disorderly falling away. It is also said: the walls are dilapidated and cracked, just as the skin becomes wrinkled and decayed.
The vigor of youth, bright and pure, is like the fresh plaster applied at first; the decrepitude of old age, withered and exhausted, is like the later peeling and falling away. [The hair...]
The beard and hair grow old and decay; they all fall out like thatched roofing tiles falling in disarray.

The sinews and bones become weak and frail, and the joints can no longer support one another, like rafters and eaves that have shifted and fallen apart. Regarding "the surrounding enclosures are bent and curved," the Master Yin explains:

because the thirty-six constituent parts further obstruct and partition one another, it is called "surrounding enclosures. Because the intestines coil and twist, it is called "bent and curved. This is not merely a matter of impermanence.
That which is transmuted also possesses impurity, suffering, and so forth; thus it is said that "impurities and filth are pervasive.

What is now called "surrounding obstructions" refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), and "crookedness" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Because the six consciousnesses take the six sense organs as their basis, the apprehension of objects is difficult and obstructed; hence they are called "crooked.

Because the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) universally defile the six sense organs, it is said that "impurities and filth are pervasive. [This concerns] the contemplation of the mind through causes and conditions. Both...

The two commentaries (the *Yin-yuan guan-xin* and the other commentary) state: "The 'head palace' and 'abdomen hall' refer to the contemplation of mind (*guanxin*). The 'form hall,' 'desire house,' and so forth, refer to causes and conditions (*yin-yuan*).
From the passage beginning with 'life-root' (*minggen*) onwards, all refer to the contemplation of mind. △ Third: Half-verse of five hundred people.
There were five hundred people dwelling therein.
This is an analogy for those with the faculties and dispositions of the Three Vehicles being encompassed by the five destinies; it also serves as an analogy for obtaining thirty sons.
△ The fourth section consists of twenty-nine lines of verse, which directly eulogize the outbreak of fire within the three realms. This is divided into four parts; first, there is...
Twenty-two verses clarify the matters of the ground, which is a metaphor for the arising of fire in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Next, three and a half verses clarify the matters within the cave, which is a metaphor for the arising of fire in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Third, two and a half lines of verse clarify the matters in the air, which is a metaphor for the arising of fire in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Fourth, there is one verse that summarizes the three realms; the various hardships are not of one kind, and as for the desire [realm]...

The arising of the fire in the realms is further divided into four parts. First, seventeen and a half verses clarify the categories of things being burned, which serve as a metaphor for the ten afflictions (*daśa-ānuśaya*) of sentient beings.
Second, there is one verse that clarifies the cause for the fire’s arising, serving as a metaphor for the origin of the five turbidities (*pañca-kāṣāya*).

Third, there are two lines that directly clarify the momentum of the fire’s arising, serving as a metaphor for the actual onset of the five turbidities. Fourth, there is one and a half lines that clarify... [text continues]
The signs of being burned are analogous to undergoing the eight sufferings and the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). This section consists of seventeen lines and a half, divided into two parts.
The first sixteen lines correctly clarify that which is burned; the final line and a half provides a summary. Within the section on that which is burned, there are again two parts.

The first six lines clarify the burning of birds and beasts, which is analogous to sentient beings with the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nivaraṇa*). The subsequent ten lines clarify the spirits and ghosts.
"Being burned" is a metaphor for sentient beings with the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). The first five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) are divided into two parts.

The first five and a half lines clarify the five dull [fetters], while the second half-line refers to the fetters of the initial stage. This initial stage is further divided into five; the first half-line is a metaphor for the fetter of pride (*māna-kleśa*).

The hawk, the owl, the eagle, the vulture, the crow, the magpie, the pigeon, and the dove—these represent the sentient beings driven by the affliction of pride (*māna*), who exalt themselves and disparage others, possessing the nature of birds that soar high and look down upon those below. These eight birds serve as metaphors for the eight types of pride.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* clarifies the eight forms of arrogance (*mada*); here, they are correlated with the eight birds: the arrogance of physical vigor is like the hawk.

Pride in one's nature is like that of an owl; pride in wealth is like that of a vulture; pride in power is like that of a hawk; pride in longevity is like that of a crow; pride in intelligence is like that of a magpie;

pride in performing good deeds is like that of a pigeon; and pride in physical beauty is like that of a dove. To look down upon others is arrogance (*māna*); to hold oneself in high esteem is conceit (*mada*);
to cherish oneself is greed (*lobha*); to crave another is lust (*kāma*); to be angry with oneself is resentment (*āghāta*); and to be angry at another is hatred (*dveṣa*). As for oneself...
To be deluded is ignorance (*moha*). To delude others is stupidity (*dauṣprajña*). △ Second, the half-verse analogy for the latent tendency of anger (*pratighānuśaya*):
"Vipers, snakes, and vipers; scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes.

There are three types of anger: the viper’s poison is so potent that it can suck [the air] without being touched, which is an analogy for anger arising without rational basis (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). The viper and scorpion, however, bite only when touched...

The "sting" (*śa*) is a metaphor for anger regarding principles. The centipede (*śatapadī*) is a metaphor for anger regarding conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The worldly say that those with red necks are centipedes, while those that are not red are millipedes (*goṣpada*).
△ Third, there are two lines that serve as metaphors for the latent tendency of ignorance (*moha-anuśaya*).
The gecko and the centipede [assemble] and gather upon it.
Ignorance may arise alone or arise in conjunction. The gecko, the centipede, and so forth, remaining motionless, are like "isolated" ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

The weasels, badgers, and mice represent the correspondence [of the latent dispositions]. The passage beginning with "the various evil insects" illustrates how, from the root of ignorance (*moha*), all the fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise.

This clarifies the characteristics of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) as they condition one another; they may pervade the three realms like crisscrossing lines, arising with such speed as that of a galloping horse.
The line beginning with "excrement and urine" clarifies ignorance: the objects to which the mind becomes attached are all impermanent.
It is suffering, non-self, and impure. Due to delusion and failing to understand this, one conceives of it as pure and the like, thereby giving rise to defiled attachment.

Thus it is said: "Dung beetles and various insects gather upon it" (a supplement states: "To be attached to men and women is to be in a place of foul-smelling excrement and urine; to conceive of the impure as pure is like a dung beetle rolling a ball").
△ Section Four: Two lines clarify the latent tendency of greed (*rāgānuśaya*).
From "foxes, wolves, and jackals" to "seeking food everywhere":
there are two kinds of greed. First, that which possesses power; second, that which lacks power. That which possesses power takes [its object] through its majesty and authority, like a fox.
Regarding "wolves and the like" and "those who lack power": these can only beg for coarse and inferior things from others, such as jackals and the like.
"Chewing" below clarifies the grasping for objects; it refers to drawing beings toward oneself through chewing, rather than through reasoning, which is like treading them underfoot.
The greedy mind seizes its objects; it may seize a single city or a single country, taking them with distinct boundaries as if biting and chewing.
It is also said: the greedy mind seizes its objects whether they are useful or useless. Seizing what is useful is like chewing; seizing what is useless is like trampling.
Furthermore, when the objects are few, it is like chewing; when they are many, it is like trampling. [The result is] flesh and bones in a heap.
"Grass" (*jia*) refers to the accumulation of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), being ignorant of contentment.
"Thereupon, a pack of dogs vied with one another to seize and snatch" refers to powerful greed; "seizing and snatching those who are weak" refers to royal authority.

"Hungering, emaciated, and terrified" means that one is constantly insatiable like one who is hungry, seeking but unable to obtain what is desired like one who is emaciated, and searching in various ways like one who is terrified.
Alas! A person of many desires is poor despite being wealthy. Their heart of affection craves, craving the "flesh" of the five sensory objects;
their mind of views craves, craving the "bones" of principles. They pursue knowledge and views until they have come to understand much—this is precisely what constitutes "many bones."
Dogs seeking bones compete to seize them. In the midst of various views, not having yet obtained the food of the True Dharma is called "hunger";
being unable to subdue and sever these views is called "emaciation"; seeking understanding everywhere is called "trepidation.
One interpretation states that this refers to a greedy person, characterized by longing, expectation, and hope. △ Fifth, the half-verse illustrates the latent tendency of doubt.
"Quarreling and seizing," "barking and howling":

hesitation between two sides is called doubt (*vicikitsā*). When one has not yet decided whether something is right or wrong, it is called quarreling; when one intends that it is right, it is called seizing.
Furthermore, it is said that "to seize" (*kāṭa*) means to snap at and bark. To "snap at and bark" refers to speaking words to decide upon the principles of right and wrong (*kāṭa* means to grasp;

it refers to seizing with all five fingers. *Kṣe* means to pull; it is also said to mean to lunge forward or pull backward. "Snap at" (*kāṭa*); the character *kāṭa* is also written as *niè* [nǐè], meaning to part the lips and bare the teeth.
"Bark" (*hào-fèi*) means to let out a loud, roaring sound). The second half-line concludes the discussion on the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*).
That house is terrifying; its manifestations are such as these.
(The first six lines conclude the explanation of the five dull afflictions. △ The second section consists of ten lines, explaining the five sharp afflictions, which is divided into two parts.
The first half-line provides a general explanation of the sharp afflictions.

They exist everywhere. The *chī-mèi* and *wǎng-liǎng* (goblins and imps) employ the sharp faculties (*li-shì*) to universally take the three realms, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the four truths (*catuḥ-satya*) as their objects; therefore, it is said that they exist everywhere.

Now, ghosts and spirits possess both supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom, whereas birds and beasts do not. Thus, the sharp faculties are compared to ghosts and spirits, while the dull faculties (*dùn-shì*) are likened to insects.

"Beasts" (*chīmèi*): these are the essences of things. The *Tōngsúwén* states: "The monsters of mountains and marshes are called *chī*. The *Xījīngfù* says: "The mountain deity with a tiger’s form is called *chī*; the house-deity with a pig’s head and human form is called *mèi*. "Wǎnglǎng":

transformations of wood and stone (the *Yùpiān* identifies them as water deities). △ Second, nine lines and a half: a specific explanation of the five *kleśas* of the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*). The text is divided into five parts.
The first three lines illustrate wrong view.
From "yakṣas and evil spirits" to "extremely terrifying," [it refers to] those with wrong view.
A yakṣa is a swift-moving spirit; this illustrates how wrong view repudiates cause and effect. Humans are virtuous.

[Response: For example, the principle that supramundane cause and effect are not mixed with afflictions—if one denies this principle, it is like eating human flesh or [becoming] venomous insects and the like;
these are evil retributions. Similarly, the principle that mundane cause and effect are mixed with various afflictions—if one denies this principle, [it is likewise an error].
It is like devouring poisonous insects and the like. That which hatches from eggs, nurses its young, or gives birth is a worldly phenomenon;

it arises from causes of its own kind to produce effects of its own kind. "Each conceals and protects itself" means that because the cause has the capacity for the effect, it is called "concealing" (*gūhana*);

because the effect will certainly be attained and not lost, it is called "protecting" (*rakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, human flesh is wholesome, whereas poisonous insects are unwholesome. The mind of false view denies [this].
There are no matters of good or evil causes and effects; it is like eating and drinking, or like the nurturing of eggs and the birth of offspring.
Generally speaking, both good and evil possess the function of causes and effects arising from one another. When one is satiated by eating, it is the manifestation of the accomplishment of the mind.
When an evil mind is rampant, it is the manifestation of the expansion of the mind. The sound of strife and contention is the internal mind being accomplished externally.
He proclaims the teachings and declares the doctrine of neither cause nor effect; this causes those who hear it to fall into the three miserable realms.

Therefore, it is called "fearful. (Regarding the terms *fu* and *ru*: birth as a bird is called *fu*; birth as a beast is called *ru*. As for the phrase "of the same kind," this refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which yields a result of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Because the offspring resembles the father, it is used as a metaphor.)
△ Second, two lines and two phrases illustrate the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The *kumbhāṇḍa* ghost (up to) "frightening dogs while enjoying oneself" refers to the clinging to precepts and rituals.
The *kumbhāṇḍa* is a superior among ghosts; likewise, tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are able to overcome various insects.
Regarding those who squat upon a mound of earth: by practicing the ten virtuous precepts, they are able to be reborn in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

These six heavens are the high places of the desire realm; their nature is like that of a mound of earth. Furthermore, when non-Buddhist practitioners maintain their precepts and cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they first attain the concentration of the desire realm, or perhaps the "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
This "not-yet-arrived" concentration has not yet transcended the desire realm; it is the summit of the desire realm, just like a mound of earth.

It is a mound. Or, those who are separated by one or two feet attain the meditative absorption of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*). For example, with one foot [of separation], one attains the meditative absorption of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu-samādhi*);

with two feet, one attains the ascent to the higher realms as "going" and the falling back down as "returning. This gives rise to the obscuration of views (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*), like being unrestrained and playing at will.
It is like seizing a dog by its two hind legs; one version says it is like seizing the dog's legs while denying the existence of the causes of suffering (*duḥkha-hetu*).
There is no fruit of suffering. It is like placing one's feet upon one's neck. When the cause (*saṃudaya*) is fundamentally attained, the fruit is obtained; it is like the barking of a dog.

To see clearly and refute [the notion of] "no cause" is to eliminate the principle by which suffering is obtained, thereby causing the [dog] to lose its voice. (Regarding *kumbhāṇḍa*: they are fearsome ghosts. *Cun* means to sit hollowly; *ju* means to sit solidly.

Regarding the subsequent mention of "seizing the dog," there is this single interpretation; hence it says, "one version states. Just as the dog's foot is the cause, seizing it is like slandering [the cause]. Seizing the foot and striking it down is like causing the loss of its voice; hence it says, "causing it to lose its voice. Furthermore, with the dog...)

"Foot. This refers to placing [one's] foot upon the neck of a dog; it is like adding insult to injury by denying the cause of suffering and further repudiating the existence of the fruit of suffering (just as placing a foot upon the neck). △ Third, one and a half lines illustrate the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts (up to) who cry out in search of food.

As for the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): vertically, it enters the three periods of time and conceives of the self as "long"; horizontally, it pervades the five aggregates and conceives of the self as "great."
They conceive of a self as sovereign and do not cultivate wholesome dharmas; thus, they lack shame and remorse, and for this reason are said to be "naked.
Because they are adorned with evil, they are said to be "black. Because they lack the provisions of merit, they are said to be "emaciated.

Those who conceive of a self do not transcend the three realms, and therefore it is said that they "permanently dwell therein. Conceiving of a self within the mind, they speak and proclaim the characteristics of a self; therefore, it is said:
They emit a great, evil cry, hoping that by means of this speech they might attain the fruit of the Way; thus it is said that they "shout and beg for food.
△ Fourth, the partial practice analogy illustrates the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose throats are like needles.

When they see those who have taken [the precepts], their throats constrict and their lives are endangered; yet they preserve their own longevity, perceiving impermanence as non-existent and reckoning it to be nirvana.

Therefore it is said that their throats are like needles (this refers to those who hold views of grasping: they do not take the fruit as the fruit; they do not realize that the fruit of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not nirvana, yet they reckon it to be eternal).
△ Fifth, two lines of verse illustrate the view of extremes.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts (up to) who run about crying out.

Regarding "extreme views" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): they speculate on the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. These two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism are like the two horns on a cow's head.

[The thought] "the body is the self" or "the self is the body" arises based on the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), just as there are two horns on a head. One calculates [existence] as either eternal or annihilated.
This fault can sever supramundane goodness, like eating human flesh; it can sever mundane roots of goodness, like occasionally devouring a dog.
At times one calculates [existence] as eternal, and at other times one calculates it as annihilated; these fluctuations back and forth are like disheveled hair.
To calculate [existence] as permanent is to destroy the view of annihilation; to calculate it as annihilated is to destroy the view of permanence.

It is like being cruel and predatory, lacking the wisdom and concentration to sustain oneself with food and drink, and being oppressed by hunger and thirst. (The first sixteen lines clarify that which is burned.
△ Second, one and a half lines provide a summary.

From "yakṣas and pretas" to "immeasurable terrors," this summarizes the characteristics of afflictions within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It also summarizes the characteristics of sentient beings who are either sharp or dull [in faculties].

Because their minds are entirely outflowing (*sāsrava*) and constantly lack the flavor of the Path, they are said to be "hungry and urgent. The phrase "peering through windows and lattices" clarifies that...
They falsely contemplate the principle of emptiness and yearn for the flavor of the Way;

yet, despite their observations, they are largely mired in attachment and fail to realize the true principle—like looking through a window at the sky, they cannot attain unimpeded vision. (The first seventeen and a half lines of verse, illustrating the ten afflictions, are concluded.
△ The second line clarifies the cause from which fire arises, serving as a metaphor for the origin of the five turbidities.
This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person who has recently gone out; not long after his departure, [the father returns].

The triple world is the place where the Buddha manifests his transformative response; since he first resolved to attain enlightenment, he has vowed to deliver all beings, and thus it is said to "belong to one person.
While the elder was in the house, he was able to ensure they were cautious regarding the fire; however, after he had left, the children remained ignorant.

Therefore, the fire was caused to arise within the inner harmony. This was precisely because during the time of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, he constantly transformed these beings, causing them to subdue the five turbidities.
Once the karmic response of the sentient beings was exhausted, the Tathāgata relinquished his manifested response; subsequently, these beings gave rise to the five turbidities once again.
He departs for other lands according to conditions; it is not a permanent departure, hence it is called "going out briefly. Furthermore, it is said:

from the moment one attains non-arising (*anutpāda*), one no longer takes birth within the triple world (*tridhātu*); thus it is called "departure. Because one will return before long, it is called "brief.
The *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* states: "Frequently manifesting nirvāṇa" is precisely the intention behind leaving the house. △ Third, two lines correctly clarify the arising of the fire.

Power (*śakti*). There are two kinds of power: first, the power of domain (*pradeśa-śakti*); second, the power of majesty (*vibhava-śakti*). The power of domain extends as far as the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
the power of majesty incinerates all that it reaches without exception. Now, the two powers within this realm are likewise so.
Thereafter, the house and its walls collapse on all four sides;
this very place is where the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena give rise to the four inversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings—hence it is called "at once.
Their continuity gradually increases until they become a conflagration; the severing of the life-faculty is the explosion, and the dismemberment by the wind-blades is the [collapse].
"Splitting. Furthermore, it is said that the sounds of groaning and lamentation while undergoing suffering are "cracking. The destruction of the sense faculties is "splitting.

The severing of the breath, the separation of the bones, and the snapping of the tendons constitute "breaking and falling. The dissolution of the four great elements constitutes "the collapsing of walls and foundations.
△ The fourth section, consisting of one and a half lines, clarifies the signs of being burned.
The various ghosts and spirits (up to) were unable to emerge on their own.

Some say that "relatives" refers to the ghosts and spirits, and "wailing" refers to raising one's voice. Following the previous analogy, the "sharp-facultied" (tīkṣṇendriya) are likened to the spirits and ghosts.
Those with sharp faculties may calculate either annihilationism or eternalism. If they calculate eternalism, they claim that dharmas are definitively empty. Once [this is realized]...

Existence returns to non-existence; non-existence is eternal. Those who calculate in terms of annihilationism claim that the nature of dharmas is definitively severed, asserting that there is only this single death and no further continuation.
They all proclaim this as a definitive teaching, and since their position has already been made manifest, it is said that they "raise their voices and cry out loudly."
If they are those with dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*) and those who cling to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), they originally did not intend to sever [their fetters].
Now, seeing impermanence, they merely give rise to doubt and fear, not knowing the means of escape; therefore it is said that they are terrified and cannot emerge by themselves.

(The first twenty-two verses conclude the section on the desire realm. △ Second, there are three and a half lines clarifying the matters within the hole, which serves as an analogy for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The fire breaks out. Regarding the interpretation of the meaning by various schools: "hatred pervades the three realms" refers to this very passage. The text consists of four parts;
the first line clarifies the categories of things that are burned.
Malevolent beasts and venomous insects hide within their burrows, and *piśāca* demons likewise dwell therein.
The concentration of the fourth dhyāna is like such a burrow; although it does not reach the open expanse outside the door, one is still able to escape the fierce flames.
Entering into meditative concentration allows one to escape the coarse evils of the desire realm. This is the power of sharp faculties.
Sentient beings also attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and likewise, *piśāca* ghosts also dwell therein. △ The second line consists of one phrase;
this is the cause for the fire’s arising.
Because their merit is meager, and due to their scanty fortune, they encounter suffering by being close to evil. △ The third line clarifies the force with which the fire arises;
they are oppressed by the fire.

Within the hollows, although there is no fierce flame, there is still the affliction of heat. Although the fourth dhyāna lacks the evils of the desire realm, it still possesses the subtle suffering of the relish of craving;
therefore, it is said to be "oppressed by fire. △ Fourth, two lines clarify the characteristics of being burned.
They harm one another (until they fill all four directions).
The clear and the dull contend for superiority, causing all sentient beings to be driven about. Although their attainment of dhyāna is the same, their calculations differ;
because they differ, they mutually condemn one another as wrong, just as they harm one another. Since they give rise to various views within dhyāna, they are unable to [attain liberation].
One gives rise to untainted concentration and wisdom, yet remains attached to silence as if drinking blood, and further attached to the "limbs" (aṅga) as if devouring meat.

The jackal represents the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which has already been severed by the attainment of the *anāgāmin* stage; therefore, it is said that both have already died previously. This is also called "devouring.
The greed for meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is like a great predatory beast, capable of swallowing the greed of the desire realm. [The four] of the desire realm...
The eight inversions and eight sufferings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are like foul smoke;

they likewise pervade body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, as well as the four great elements, skin, flesh, and so forth. Therefore, it is said that "the four directions are filled. (The section on the form realm concludes.
△ Third, two and a half verses clarify the matters within space, using the analogy of fire arising in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is divided into two parts. First:

First: Clarifying the categories of what is burned. (Regarding the matters within "emptiness": previously it was said that hiding in a burrow serves as a metaphor for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); now, emerging from the burrow, it therefore serves as a metaphor for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the term "within emptiness," this does not refer to empty space. Since the interior of the house was already used as a metaphor for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and entering the burrow for the realm of form, the open ground outside the burrow is now taken as "emptiness" to serve as a metaphor for the formless realm.)
Centipedes, millipedes, and species of venomous snakes, scorched by fire, scramble to exit their burrows.

Just as those who are weary of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) emerge toward the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and being weary of coarse objects of form, contemplate formless phenomena (*ārūpyadharma*)—like the species of venomous snakes emerging from their burrows when burned by fire—if this is so, then hatred (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms. △ Next, one and a half lines clarify the object [of abandonment].
The signs of burning:
the kumbhāṇḍa spirits [run about] in confusion, obstructing the perimeter.

If one attains the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti), one must necessarily extinguish the lower objects of perception; therefore it is said that they "take and eat whatever they encounter. The Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is supreme.

Even at the Peak [of Existence], one still cannot escape the various sufferings of inversion; it is like fire burning upon the head. Even in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, there are the fires of the eight sufferings.
The arising of divergent thoughts in the mind is called the suffering of birth. The non-abiding of every thought-moment is called the suffering of aging.

The agitation of mental activity that obstructs meditative concentration is called the suffering of illness. The falling away from concentration is the suffering of death. The failure to attain concentration despite seeking it is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

One experiences suffering. Seeking meditative concentration but failing to attain it, there must be an obstruction; this is the suffering of association with what is disliked. The mind consists of the four aggregates;
this is the suffering of the five burgeoning aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Because one cannot immediately sever the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the head burns as if on fire.
Lacking the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), one is tormented by hunger and thirst; this is still saṃsāra, wandering in exhaustion amidst pervasive obstructions. (The Three Formless Realms)
[End]. △ Fourth paragraph. Summary of the three realms. The various calamities are not one;
such is that house. It is truly terrifying. Poisonous harm and fires—these various calamities are not one.
(The first general analogy concluded). △ Second, there are thirty-two and a half verses. These praise the individual analogies.
There are four individual analogies, but here only three are praised. The first two and a half verses praise the elder seeing the fire.

The second, thirteen verses, praises the abandonment of the small benches and the use of the carts—the analogy of providing large [vehicles] while sleeping on the [small ones] and giving small [vehicles]. The third has seventeen [verses].
Proceeding with the verses that provide the analogy of the great chariot: the first verse concerns seeing the fire, which has three parts—first, the one who sees;
second, that which is seen; and third, the arising of alarm and fear. This is fully expressed in the verses. The first three lines of the verse praise the person who sees.
At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate. He heard someone say, "Upwardly, he sees clearly;
now it is said he hears. This uses "hearing" to substitute for "seeing. Since hearing must necessarily derive from another, the one who hears is the one standing outside the gate.
The verse above states: "Although I am able to emerge safely through the gate of the combustible, I do not abide in the seat of the ultimate emptiness.
This means that while established in the stage of the *dharmakāya*, one constantly harbors great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and desires to save sentient beings;

thus, one does not dwell in the seat of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). (Regarding "not dwelling in the seat of the ultimate emptiness": the ultimate emptiness is the union of wisdom and principle, sharing the same essence as compassion. Here, it is said that one does not abide in a wisdom devoid of compassion, but rather constantly resides in a compassion endowed with wisdom; therefore, it is called "not dwelling. Thus it is said.
Only by knowing this unconditional compassion (which can then be of the same essence as wisdom) may one proceed. △ Second, one line and one phrase: Verses on the fire seen.
"You sons, because you previously came into this house while playing, being young and ignorant, you were joyfully attached to it."

Question: "The Son has originally not yet emerged; how can it be said that he enters by reason of play? Answer: "It may be that he once resolved his mind [to attain liberation], which is called 'emerging from the triple world.
Yet, because he subsequently regressed, this is called 'entering. It is like a person who lifts their foot intending to go out, but turns back upon reaching the side of the gate;
this is both called 'going out' and also called 'returning to enter. Furthermore, the fundamental nature of reality is inherently pure and is not a phenomenon of the triple world.
Because of ignorance (*avidyā*), conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arises, and thus there is birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore it is said: "First, due to play, one enters [into this world].
That great goodness has not yet taken root is called "childhood"; being shrouded by ignorance is called "lack of knowledge.
△ The third two lines versify the aforementioned: "Immediately becoming greatly terrified and giving rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."
Upon hearing this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house.

(The first section, the parable of the elder seeing the fire, concludes. △ The second section consists of thirteen lines, in verse, concerning the abandonment of the small stools and the provision of the carts.

This consists of two parts. The first has five and a half lines. It versifies the preceding section on the failure to save the children. In the preceding allegory (*upamā*), there was both exhortation (*anuśāsana*) and admonition (*codanā*);

in the subsequent application (*upanaya*), there was only the application of the exhortation. Now, however, it only versifies the admonition. The text of the admonition has three sections; the first consists of four and a half stanzas.
In the verse above, I shall explain the fear and the appropriate means of rescue.
"Appropriate means" refers to the application of the Great Teaching.
"Exhortation" means to describe various calamities and difficulties as a way of admonishing and instructing.

The meaning [of "evil spirits, venomous insects," etc., refers to all matters of suffering and hardship, as explained above]. As for those "tormented by hunger and thirst," it is because they lack concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that they suffer from hunger and thirst; this is already terrifying, let alone being further burned by the fires of turbidity.

Just as when one attains the contaminated concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of the upper realms, one lacks uncontaminated concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and is thus already incinerated by minor fires, how much more so when falling into the lower realm of desire and being burned by great fires? This refers to the torment of hunger and thirst as being this very suffering;
therefore, one should seek the Mahāyāna to be forever free from it. [The second and third lines of the verse] praise not accepting admonitions.
The sons were ignorant; although they heard their father’s instruction, they still took pleasure in their attachments and did not accept his admonitions.
Being young and ignorant, although they heard their father’s instruction, they still took pleasure in their attachments.
Having neither great aspirations nor practicing the minor ones, they forgot both the great and the small, and will surely remain attached to the triple world. (Verse 3, line 1: The actual verse.)
Ignorance ceases its transformations;
he sports and plays without end.
By pointing to the single phrase "nothing more than looking at his father," he provides a verse on the meaning of "relinquishing words of suffering" mentioned above. (Third)

One phrase: "He who has truly ceased his teaching" means that because [the disciples'] views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have not yet ceased, he has therefore ceased his great teaching. If their views and afflictions have not ceased, they still possess the capacity for the Great [Vehicle]. At such a time, the Tathāgata is likewise not stingy regarding the Great;

however, because they possess the capacity for the Small, he causes them to emerge from the turbid world for now, first bestowing the Small upon them. (The first five lines and a half conclude the section on "Saving the Sons"). △ Second, seven lines and a half of verse praise the aforementioned "Using the Carts.
The preceding prose has four parts: first, preparing the three carts; second, knowing the sons' original inclinations; third...
He praises the rarity of the three vehicles. Fourth, he accords with the sons' wishes. Now, in this verse, there are only three meanings;
the "knowledge of the sons' prior intentions" is omitted from the verse. Here, the first three lines of the verse correspond to the "expedient means."
