At this time, the elder (up to) "establishes various skillful means.

The first line clarifies the intended purpose; the next line explains the reason for employing the Lesser Vehicle—because of attachment to views and afflictions (*kleśa*), he provides only the Lesser Vehicle.
The subsequent half-line explains the intent behind using the Lesser Vehicle: if he did not employ the Lesser Vehicle, then both the Great and the Small would perish.
Therefore, it is said: "They will be harmed by fire. Because they are harmed, they lose their bodies; because they lose their bodies, they lose their lives. This concludes the second half-verse.
Regarding the correct contemplation of minor [uses], it says: "He then immediately reflects and devises various skillful means. II.

There are three verses praising the rarity of the three vehicles as an exhortation. Above, the three meanings of exhorting, indicating, and realizing were clarified; now, the verses likewise present these three, repeating them.
There are four ways of exhortation to accomplishment. First, one verse exhorts by addressing all you sons:
"I have various kinds of precious playthings and excellent chariots made of wondrous jewels."
△ Second and third lines of the verse show:
"The sheep-cart, the deer-cart, and the great ox-cart are now outside the gate.

(In the commentary on the turning [of the wheel], it says "outside the gate" means that, as in the demonstration of the Four Noble Truths, one is made to know the supramundane. △ Third line of the verse further exhorts.
"Come forth, all of you!
△ Fourth: One verse in praise of the realization.
'I have fashioned these chariots for you; you may play and enjoy yourselves according to your own inclinations.'"
△ Three verses and one half-line. These verses fulfill the wishes of the sons.

Having heard the teaching [up to] "they are freed from all suffering and distress," these now summarize the six lines of the preceding prose regarding the fulfillment of the sons' wishes. "Rushing forth" summarizes the realization of the Truth (darśana-mārga). "Emptiness" [summarizes the preceding].

[This concludes] the section on the Grounds. The above verses praise the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa). (The analogy of abandoning the sedan chair and using the carriage is finished. △ Third, there are seventeen lines of verse.
These verses praise the extended prose passage on the analogy of the equal bestowal of the great chariots. The text has four parts: first, escaping the peril;

second, requesting the chariots; third, the equal bestowal of the great chariots; and fourth, the joy of obtaining the chariots. The present verses also have four parts. The first five lines praise [the first part].

The first five lines praise the joy of the sons being spared from calamity; this section further divides into two parts. The first line praises their escape from the danger. The second three lines praise the request for the carriage. The third seven and a half lines praise the equal bestowal [of gifts].
The fourth one and a half lines praise the joy of obtaining the carriages. Regarding the initial five lines, they praise how the various sons were spared from the disaster;
this again consists of two parts. The first line praises their escape from the danger.
The elder sees his sons; having emerged from the burning house, they stand at the crossroads and sit upon lion thrones.

Joy is the world; the arising of faith is the human condition; the departure of doubt is the remedy; and the clarity of principle is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Subhūti understands emptiness; his life consists of the wisdom of emptiness. This refers to his practice. Among all those with wisdom, the Buddha’s wisdom is foremost.
The Buddha, regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, charged him to transmit its teaching. Because he was commissioned by the One of Supreme Wisdom, he is called "Wisdom-Life" (Prajñājīvaka).
The three disciples received a limited mandate; they did not take emptiness as the core of their practice. This is according to the classification of teachings (*yōkyō*).
"Mahā" is as explained previously. Regarding the cause for attaining joy: it is because they heard from afar the five-part Dharma-exposition on skillful means (*upāya*).

The scribe merely records that they heard this rare Dharma and heard the two kinds of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). Alternatively, one may say they heard the Dharma as described in four sections and saw the predictions.
This is the fifth section. Such hearing and seeing as this has never occurred before; it is the cause for my joy.

Regarding the arousal of a rare and wondrous mind (*āścaryacittotpāda*), I shall now describe the fourfold discourse on recent analogies. Because this rare and wondrous mind has been aroused, and because the mind has thus been stirred:
This is termed "faith. Because of faith, one enters; entering the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is precisely the meaning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhādhimukti-parivarta*).

(Regarding the fourfold parables: both the prose and the verse sections contain general and specific [analyses], and each likewise contains the opening of the parable and its application; hearing these repeatedly gives rise to a sense of rare wonder). △ Next, the external demeanor is described.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and—[as described in the text]—bowed with reverence and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.

As in the case of Śāriputra, he likewise attained understanding through the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind); this may be inferred from what precedes (as detailed in Śāriputra’s recitation of the verses).
△ Second, his address to the Buddha and self-announcement. The text is divided into two parts: first, the prose; second, the verse. The prose section is further divided into two parts; first—

The summary explanation of the realization consists of two parts: the brief explanation of the realization through the Dharma, and the extensive explanation of the realization through analogies. The brief explanation also has two parts: first, the explanation by means of the Dharma; second, the brief citation of analogies.
The explanation by means of the Dharma further has two parts: first, clarifying that because they received three [vehicles] in the past, they did not seek [the One];
second, clarifying that because they now encounter the One, they naturally attain it. Within the section on "not seeking," there is a heading and an explanation; this is the initial heading.
They addressed the Buddha, saying: "We occupy the foremost positions among the Saṃgha... [until] our hearts find no joy.
As for those who first occupied the foremost positions, their Dharma-ordination years (*dharma-varṣa*) were already advanced; the junior students took us as their models.

Yet, suddenly they have changed their path and altered their course, abandoning the small for the great, and are thus resented by those who come after. To protect ourselves and them, we do not seek [the foremost position]. (2)
My worldly years have already advanced. If one were to become a bodhisattva, they should single-mindedly embrace the Great Way to extensively deliver sentient beings;
but now that I am decrepit and old, I am incapable of such a task. Therefore, I do not seek it, for I have already attained the unconditioned, correct state of nirvana.

One cannot give rise to the Great Mind. Just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, once the knowledge of the exhaustion of birth (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are established, there is nothing further to rely upon or seek.
△ Next, the three things not to be sought are explained.
Why is this? The World-Honored One has caused us [to reach this point] such that not even a single thought of longing or delight arose.
First, it was explained that he did not seek *nirvāṇa* because he had already attained it; next, it was explained that he did not seek it because of his advanced age.

Since it was stated that he was "seated," and further remarked that he was "of declining years," it was explained that he did not seek to be the leader of the Saṃgha. II. Clarifying that because the present assembly is one, he naturally attains [the goal]. This is the summary.
It is understood.
We now, before the Buddha, feel profound personal joy at having obtained great and wholesome benefit.
We shall now, before the Buddha, set forth the reasons for our attainment of understanding. This is based on what we have heard from afar regarding the five chapters, both in brief and in detail.
"Opening the three [vehicles] to reveal the reality": this is why there is cause for celebration. "Obtaining great and wholesome benefit" correctly describes the attainment of understanding;
it refers to having recently heard the rare teaching of the four parables and thereby attained enlightenment—the wholesome benefit of such enlightenment.
△ Second, a brief presentation of the parables.
"Immeasurable treasures are obtained without seeking.

This is like how, though not sought in the past, one now spontaneously obtains the rare Dharma-treasure. (Regarding "immeasurable treasures": previously, under the guidance of the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings, one was called a bodhisattva;

who would have imagined that today one would receive this complete and equal bestowal. (The brief explanation of the first Dharma and its reception and understanding is concluded. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the parable and its reception and understanding.
Explanation. There are two parts: first, the opening of the analogy; second, the application of the analogy. Now, for the first part—the opening of the analogy—there are again two sections.
First is the request to speak: "World-Honored One, we now wish to explain this meaning by means of an analogy."
△ Second, the formal establishment of the parables, which consists of five parts: 1. The Parable of Father and Son Losing Sight of Each Other.
This closely corresponds to the general parable of the burning house and, distantly, to the summary verse of the *Upāya-kauśalya* chapter. 2. The Parable of Father and Son Meeting.

This closely corresponds to the section on seeing the fire in the burning house and, distantly, to the passage in the *Upāya-kauśalya* where [the Buddha] says, "I observe with my Buddha-eye. 3. The Parable of Pursuing and Enticing. This closely corresponds to the section on abandoning the small table in the burning house.

1. The analogy of employing carriages: This refers proximately to the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta* (Chapter on Skillful Means), which sets aside the Great [Vehicle] and bestows the Small; and distantly to the *Vaipulya* sūtras, which follow up with reprimands and critiques.

This is the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*’s "turning of the teaching. 2. The analogy of entrusting the family business: This refers proximately to the *Agni-dāha-parivarta* (Chapter on the Burning House) and others, which bestow great carriages;
and distantly to the "Teaching of the Dharma" (*Dharmadeśanā*), which states: "Directly setting aside skillful means, he speaks only of the unsurpassed path. Furthermore, these two are combined.
The fourth and fifth [sections] together constitute one illustrative analogy; their meaning will be further clarified below. Now, following the text and attaching the meaning:
if one explains the "poor son," one takes the *bāzì* (half-syllable) Dharma-gate of the followers of the Two Vehicles to interpret the text;
if one explains the "elder," one takes the *mǎnzì* (full-syllable) Dharma-gate of Vairocana Buddha to interpret the text. Why? Because the elder within the house...
He casts off his jeweled necklace and dons soiled garments; though the clothing and ornaments differ, the person remains one and the same.

This is like Vairocana Buddha, who conceals his immeasurable buddha-virtues and manifests as a sixteen-foot golden radiance. Holding a vessel for filth, he establishes the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

Although there is a distinction between concealment and manifestation, how does this concern a difference in essence? The first analogy, that of the father and son losing sight of each other, is further divided into four parts. First, the son turns away...
1. The father departs. 2. The two fathers seek their son and stop midway. 3. The son encounters his father’s city. 4. The father experiences both sorrow and joy.
Each of these four sections contains two parts. Regarding the first two: the first is "leaving the father and fleeing," which refers to the five hundred people within the comprehensive parable.
In the past, one formed the bond of a Mahāyāna child with the Father, but soon thereafter lost that understanding and wandered through the five realms of existence;
hence it is said that they may be ten, twenty, or even fifty years old. Although they have all been children of the Buddha, because the meaning of "child" has become weak, they are called "infants.

Because they have not yet established a karmic connection within their own realm, they are said to be "long-dwelling in another country. Second, they turn back toward the source; this collectively illustrates the third point.

Tenth: These conditions possess both subtle and manifest meanings; therefore, it is said they have "grown up. Since these conditions have already undergone suffering, they relate to the Buddha’s great compassion; thus, it is said they "chanced upon their native land.

(This does not refer to those who have established a karmic connection within their own realm and so forth. Originally, the great connection was formed with the Land of Quiescent Light as the soil and the realization of the intended mind as the capacity.

Since the Great Vehicle was lost, both the capacity and the soil were entirely forfeited. Wandering through the five paths, one regards the original land as foreign. Even the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder is no longer one's own realm, let alone the Land of Quiescent Light. Now, the impoverished son currently dwells within the five turbidities. And so forth.

Taking one's current dwelling and comparing it to the original state for the sake of others, from that time onward, one has constantly remained within the triple world; thus it is called "dwelling for a long time. As for those whose conditions have reached maturity, their spiritual capacity (*mārga*) is somewhat thickened, so they are provisionally given a name, yet they have not returned to the beginning and are merely said to be "thirty" years old.

Since the conditions are inferior, suffering serves as the catalyst; therefore, we know this still precedes the minor transformation (*hīna-vinaya*). Arriving without recognizing [the father] is called "meeting"; this is because he was seen in the past, hence it is called the "original.

Regarding the two fathers seeking their sons and stopping midway for both: one father seeks his son and does not find him; this refers to the elder son within the comprehensive parable. From... [text ends].
After sentient beings have regressed from the Great [Vehicle], one waits for their great capacity; because the opportunity has not yet been met, it is said that they "do not obtain" it.

Regarding the phrase "stopping at one city among the two," "the house" leads to the overall analogy of the central mansion. "The great wealthy man" leads to the overall analogy of the virtues and deeds of the elder;
it refers to his internal and external wealth and resources. As for the three sons reaching their father’s city, there are two parts: first, one arrives.

Regarding the origin of the city: it refers to the manifestation of suffering arising from fire. After he had withdrawn from the Great [Vehicle], he traveled through various places and underwent manifold hardships.
Second, as for his eventual arrival at his father’s city: because he used suffering as the catalyst to strike upon the Great Compassion, it is said that he "eventually arrived at his father’s city.
Fourth, as for his father’s dual response of sorrow and joy: first, there was the pain of losing his son in an instant; second, [the joy of seeing him].

He reflects upon the joy of having a son. This constitutes one section within the comprehensive analogy. Since the son was still young, his choice of the gate was improper, which moved his father to sorrow;
it was precisely by means of this gate that he was later led to move his father’s joy. At first, the son had turned his back on his father and departed.
There are two [cases]. First, abandoning one’s father and fleeing away.
This is like a person who, being young—whether ten, twenty, or even fifty years old.

The first analogy is like a person; it represents those of the Two Vehicles. The stages and practices of a Bodhisattva are difficult to know; for now, they are equated with what has already been understood.

"Listen. As for 'being young in years,' it means that because ignorance is thick and heavy, it obscures and blocks the mind of understanding; since the mind of understanding lacks power, one is said to be 'young.
When the roots of goodness are perfumed and one gradually begins to develop attachment [to them], this is called 'growing up.

'Leaving one's father and fleeing' means that regressing from the Great Vehicle is 'leaving'; being shrouded by one's own ignorance is 'fleeing'; and heading toward birth and death is 'departing. Question:"
After the Buddha has relinquished his response [to the world], sentient beings give rise to delusions; this is like a father departing from his son, rather than the son abandoning his father. Answer:

Because sentient beings fail to provide the conditions for his presence, the Buddha departs from the world; thus, it still accords with the principle of the son abandoning the father. As for "dwelling long in another land," [it refers to the Buddha's passing].
Nirvana and the Dharma-realm are the Buddha’s own country; birth-and-death and the five desires are other countries.

Having originally sought liberation, one falls back and does not return; hence it is said that one "dwells for a long time. Alternatively, ten [kalpas] are the heavenly realm and twenty are the human realm.
Fifty years constitute the five paths of existence. When applied to a single individual, they encompass the cycling through all these realms. II. Returning toward the Origin:
Having grown old and being further impoverished, he gradually wandered about until he encountered his own native land.

Regarding the aforementioned term "the immature" (*bāla*): there are two meanings to "immature. First, they are small and foolish; second, because they have not yet encountered suffering, they do not know how to return [to the path].

This is like those who, after having established a karmic connection (*karmapratyaya*), lack the intensity of great understanding and thus do not turn back due to their folly, remaining mired in delusion despite still possessing residual merit.
Now, regarding the term "the grown-up": through the subtle permeation (*vāsana*) of habitual practice, they have gained a slight knowledge directed toward the Way.

Encountering suffering and losing happiness, one contemplates seeking the supreme departure [from suffering]. These two constitute the stimulus that strikes the Buddha; this is called "gradually heading toward the father’s kingdom. As the preceding passage states:
"If a person encounters suffering, for their sake I preach nirvāṇa. If one relies merely on the two virtues of humans and devas, these do not constitute the conditions for perceiving the Buddha.
Remaining within the three realms, one does not see the Buddha-father and fails to obtain the method for ultimate departure; this is what is meant by being "at one's wits' end."
Because they are scorched by the fires of the eight sufferings, they are in distress.

Those who rush about in the four directions in search of food and clothing—since the Buddha has not yet appeared—these ordinary worldlings give rise to the four views regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.

Among these, they seek the Right Path as if seeking food, and they seek the Aiding Path as if seeking clothing. Their weariness with suffering and their quest for principle serve as the conditions for being converted by the Buddha.
The meaning is this: when he first set out, all the non-Buddhists were the first to attain deliverance. This is precisely what is intended.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "carefully observing the four directions" is a metaphor for the Four Noble Truths; according to this, the meaning can be understood.

As for the passage, "Gradually traveling on, he encountered his way back to his native land," this clarifies that although he was weary of suffering and sought liberation by seeking it through heterodox means—thus not following his original intention—he nevertheless encountered the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that he "encounters" [them]. His native country is as described above. The following passage clarifies the city and the house. How are they distinguished?

The *nirvāṇa* of severed defilements (*prahāṇa-dharma*), which wards off what is improper and resists evil, is the city; the house is even more intimate—the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the same essence (*tathatā-svabhāva*) is the house.
△ Second, regarding the cessation of seeking a son, there are two parts: first, seeking a son but not obtaining one.
His father had previously come seeking his son but could not find him.
From the time he first withdrew from the Great Vehicle onward, he sought the capacity [of the son] but did not encounter it; because he did not encounter it, he was said to "not have found" him.
△ Second, they halted at a single city.
He stopped at a certain city where his family was very wealthy; (up to: there were also a great many merchants, appraisers, and guests.
"Stopping at a certain city" means that one does not abandon one's household affairs for the sake of a single son;

it is like how the Buddha does not abandon the propagation of his teachings in other regions simply because there is no spiritual capacity in one place. Now, he takes the land of *upāya-śeṣa* as his kingdom, remaining in this same state.

Dwelling between the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*) constitutes the center. The *nirvāṇa* with remainder serves as the city; abiding in this *nirvāṇa* is called "stopping," and residing therein is the "home.

From this state, two types of responsive manifestations—superior and inferior—are produced: the inferior response corresponds to the *śrāvakas*, while the superior response corresponds to the *bodhisattvas*.
The five who had severed the pervasive afflictions were reborn together in that land, all becoming bodhisattvas.

The Buddha responded to them with his supreme emanation body, training them exclusively in the family business of the Mahāyāna. They remained there, awaiting the opportunity to guide their co-resident sons;
not only was the meaning of "intermediate" (zhōng) appropriate, but the kingdom, city, and family business were all clearly manifest. Thus, they were truly great and wealthy.
The realm of true reality (*dharmatā*) is his home. Being endowed with ten thousand virtues is called wealth.
The merit of the five perfections is called property; Prajñā-wisdom is called treasure. Guiding all toward the Mahāyāna is called immeasurable.
Gold, silver, pearls, and so forth, refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) of the Mahāyāna. This summarizes the aforementioned "great wealth" of the elder.
This is the meaning. As for "the storehouses being full and overflowing": to be full within is "full," while to overflow outside is "overflowing. A granary stores rice; a warehouse stores goods.

The granary is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because meditation gives rise to the one hundred and eight samādhis. The warehouse is a metaphor for the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Because it can give rise to the wisdom of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, it fills itself from within and overflows outwardly; this conveys the meaning of possessing many fields and houses mentioned above.
As for "servants," it refers to the perfection of skillful means and the knowledge-and-vision, all of which are fully complete.
These are adapted flexibly according to circumstances, corresponding to both phenomena and principle. This refers to the fact that [the Buddha] has many attendants;

speaking in terms of their respective positions, those of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) are all like servants. Those of the Separate Teaching (Biejiao) at the stage of the thirty minds are likewise like servants.

In the Separate and Perfect Teachings (Yuanjiao), the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are like ministers, the ten directions (*daśadik*) are like aides, the ten practices (*caryā*) are like officials, and the ten abidings (*vihāra*) are like commoners. Entering for the first time...

Within the realm of the Buddha, throughout the borders of the land, there are none who are not the King’s subjects. Although they have attained the status of subjects, compared to the officials and assistants, they are still distant.
In the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), one separately cultivates various dharmas and is driven about in various ways like an official.

In the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the matters and principles become somewhat deeper; their office is near the King’s side like an assistant. In the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), one assists the Buddha in transforming and teaching others, descending [to aid sentient beings].

The subduing of Māra is like a minister. Thus, the single-mind threefold contemplation (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*) is like an elephant, conveying the Mahāyāna of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). The sequential threefold contemplation (*cidi san guan*) is like a horse, conveying the Mahāyāna of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

The contemplation of emptiness through immediate realization (*jiekong guan*) and the contemplation of emptiness through analytical dissection (*xikong guan*) are like water buffaloes, conveying the Mahāyāna of the two teachings (*liangjiao*).

The contemplation of the analytical dissection of phenomena (*xifa guan*) for one's own practice is like deer, sheep, and so forth, conveying the dharmas of the Two Vehicles (*ersheng*). There is none [superior].
Regarding "number": all provisional and ultimate dharmas are called "vehicles. Provisional and ultimate wisdom-observations are called "elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
It is not only that the teachings are exceedingly numerous; the wisdom-observations are likewise infinite.

Regarding "entering and exiting": duality within non-duality is entering; non-duality within duality is exiting. Furthermore, non-duality within duality is entering; duality within non-duality is exiting.
The second is emergence (*niṣkramaṇa*). That the immeasurable returns to the one is entry (*praveśa*). That within the one there is the immeasurable is emergence.

Using [the power] for the benefit of others is emergence; using it for one’s own practice is entry. Benefiting sentient beings through the dharma of emergence is tranquility (*śānti*); returning the merit of transformation to oneself is benefit (*hita*).
"Traveling throughout other lands" means traveling throughout the three lands; to practice what is not the Way and yet penetrate the Buddha-way—this is its meaning.
Only the Dharma-nature is one's own land. "The merchants and traders are also very numerous" means that the various bodhisattvas are the merchants;
furthermore, because they enter all three lands to seek the benefits of the Dharma, they are said to be numerous. This...
Earth-stage bodhisattvas travel to other realms to hear the Dharma, while Great Beings from other realms come here to hear the sutras; thus they go and return to gather benefit.

Furthermore, the two bodies of response and transformation are like merchants who take the true Dharma and enter the three lands everywhere, benefiting sentient beings through transformation before returning to the Dharma-body;
therefore, it is said that they are "very many. This is like worldly people causing others to seize wealth and prosper.
"Born" means that he himself has also come into existence. △ Third, the son arrives at his father’s city: first, seeking food and clothing.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities.
Initially, having internally regressed from the Mahāyāna, he encountered various sufferings. Deeply aroused by weariness and aversion, he sought liberation;

yet, his grasp of the principle was off-center, leading him to heterodoxy. Because this distorted wisdom had permeated his mind, it was easy for him to enter the correct path and seek transcendence from the world, thereby serving as the cause for his encounter with the Buddha.
He observed the five aggregates (*skandha*) as a village and the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as a town.
The eighteen realms constitute the kingdom; to traverse these in search of principle is called seeking food and clothing. △ Second, arriving at his father’s city:
he eventually reached the city where his father resided.
This refers to one who is heading directly toward the city where his father resides. Taking the realm of suffering as the catalyst, he evokes the Great Compassion of the Buddha;

this is termed "reaching the city. The city is *nirvāṇa*. Since *nirvāṇa* encompasses both the partial (*hīnayāna*) and the full (*mahāyāna*), and sentient beings possess the habitual understanding that allows for the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, it is said that they "reach the city.
△ Fourth, regarding the father’s sorrow and joy, there are two parts. First:
Reflecting on the suffering of having lost his son, the father constantly thinks of him; thus, he remembers his son with earnest diligence.
Since ancient times until now, the Tathāgata has always contemplated his son’s great capacity; therefore, it is said that he "constantly remembers" him for more than fifty years.

"Those" refers to the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*). Since the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) subsumes the asuras, it is referred to as "the remainder. Regarding "never having spoken [of this]":
never before has he spoken of the karmic conditions for such a son to the ministers, assistants, and officials within the *upāya-śeṣa* (convenient remaining) lands.
Furthermore, since his appearance in the world, from the time of the ancient *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies, he has never [spoken of this] to the great... [bodhisattvas].
The Master said: "These śrāvakas were originally children of the Mahāyāna. Since they are not [true] sons of the Buddha, they do not understand the Buddha-dharma;
some are like the deaf or mute, some are preoccupied with their seats and prostrations, and some cast aside their alms bowls in bewilderment—thus they fail in various ways."
Those who harbor regret feel remorse for not having diligently instructed them in the past, resulting in their lack of training and their flight.

They resent that the sons did not contemplate kindness and righteousness, distancing themselves from me and clinging to others. Internally, they resemble the Tathāgata’s own regret for not being earnest enough to lead them into the inner stage of ordinary beings, whereby they have subsequently fallen away from their original understanding.
They resent that the sons lacked resolve and were unable to cultivate diligence and firm intent, fleeing instead into delusion.

He returned; hence, it is said he felt regret and resentment. When he thought of his own aging, he realized that his time for transformation was drawing to a close, yet there was no one to whom he could entrust the Great Dharma—like an old man who has no son.
Question: The various bodhisattvas transformed by the Dharmakāya are all capable of succeeding to the position [of Buddhahood].
Why does he suddenly feel such anxiety? Answer: That which is transformed by the Dharmakāya is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Who, then, speaks of "aging"?

This is not what is being discussed here. Now, to clarify the retinue of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are two types. First, the great beings of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-mahāsattva*) who mutually influence one another;
though their traces appear as disciples, they may fundamentally have been teachers. Furthermore, this does not refer to [the Buddha] thinking of himself as aged and decrepit based on such [traces].

Second, the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who dwell together [with him], beginning with those who first gave rise to the mind of the Way (*bodhicitta*) under the transformation Buddha. These are called...
This is the son; the son succeeds to his father’s vocation so that the lineage may not be severed.

If Śāriputra receives the prediction of enlightenment and becomes the Buddha Padmaprabha, then the seed of the Buddhas in this direction will continue without interruption, and the family estate of the Mahāyāna will be transmitted from one to another in succession.
If Śāriputra lacked the karmic capacity to be transformed, then the wealth of the Mahāyāna teachings would currently have no one to whom it could be entrusted for the future.
The coming of sentient beings is where the seed of the Buddha is entrusted. It is precisely for this reason that I, in my old age, give rise to such sighs. 2.

Reflecting on the joy of having a son, he further thinks: "If I were to have a son, I could entrust my wealth and possessions to him; I would then be at ease and happy, free from any further anxiety."
Those with the capacity for deliverance are called "attaining sons. Bestowing upon them the Buddha’s prediction is called "entrusting the Dharma-treasure.
When this accords with their original aspiration, they further speak of joy. (The first parable of the father and son losing sight of each other ends.

△ Second, the parable of the father and son meeting. This is divided into two parts. First, the son sees the father: the impoverished son works as a hired laborer and recognizes the fire he previously observed within the burning house.
In the "Teaching by Dharma" (dharmaparyāya), the five turbidities seen [by the Buddha] are explained; in the parable, the father seeing his son is illustrated by the elder of the burning house.

In the "Teaching by Dharma," it is seen with the Buddha-eye; in both the "Teaching by Dharma" and the parable, it clarifies that the father sees the son before [he is found]. Herein, it clarifies that the son sees the father before [he is recognized].

From the perspective of the Buddha, his numinous wisdom knows beforehand; as the capacity [of sentient beings] is perfected, he responds accordingly. Thus it is said that "the father sees the son first.
If we speak in terms of sentient beings, there must first be an invocation before there is a response; thus it is said that "the son sees the father first.

The interplay of capacity and response is inconceivable; it is neither subsequent nor prior. Therefore, "prior" and "subsequent" are mentioned alternately. Within the text: first, the son sees the father; second, the father...
Regarding the two sections on "seeing the son," each is further divided into four parts. First, the four points concerning the son seeing his father:
(1) the cause for seeing his father, which is seeking food and clothing; (2) the location where he sees his father, being at the side of the gate;
(3) the appearance of the father, sitting upon a lion throne; and (4) the arising of fear and avoidance, regretting having come here. Now, the first point.
World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son wandered from place to place seeking employment until he happened upon his father’s house.

Having seen his father, he grew weary of suffering and took delight in happiness; by investigating the flavor of principle and gradually accumulating practice, he eventually perfected supramundane roots of goodness.
Therefore it is said that he wandered from place to place seeking employment. By means of these roots of goodness, he was able to strike upon the Buddha’s compassion.

Therefore, it is said that he encountered his father’s house. The father is a metaphor for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) attained after the Path; the house is a metaphor for unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*).
Both the great and small capacities strike upon this house simultaneously. Because there is the capacity of the Great [Vehicle], it is said that he saw his father from afar;

because there is the capacity of the Small [Vehicle], he remained by the side of the gate. If there were only the small capacity and no great, then one would not see the body of sublime marks (*vairocana-kāya*).
The father should not say, "I have now entrusted my wealth and storehouses to you.
If there were only the great and no small, he should not stand by the side of the gate. The son should not say, "This is not a place where I can obtain goods through hired labor.
△ Second, seeing his father's dwelling.
Standing by the side of the gate, he saw his father from afar.
The place where he saw his father was precisely the side of the gate; thus, the two perspectives serve as the means, corresponding to the two sides of the gate.

The capacity for the "round" [teaching] is to see directly through the gate, whereas the Two Vehicles perceive only partial truth, and are therefore said to be at the "side of the gate. This refers merely to the samādhi of emptiness.

The eye of wisdom that perceives partial truth can only glance sideways at the Dharma-body. To "see one's father from afar" refers to two kinds of correct vision: first, near vision; second, distant vision.
Here, it is said that while the great capacity has just begun to arise, the act of calling out and responding is still remote;
therefore, it is called "distant. Furthermore, because the capacity is subtle and not yet fit for a direct response, it is termed "distant. △ Third, the appearance of seeing the father.
"Sitting upon the lion throne" (up to) "variously adorned, with majestic virtue especially sublime.
Regarding "sitting upon the lion throne": it refers to the Dharmakāya of perfect retribution, which dwells securely in the principle of emptiness.

Because there are no further fears of the two types of delusion—general and specific—nor the eight māras, it is said that he sits upon the lion throne. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). 4.
The absence of fear serves as the bed. As for the precious footstool supporting the feet: meditative concentration and wisdom are the feet, and the true reality (*satya*) is the stool.
Unarisen concentration and wisdom rely upon the realm of *tathatā*. "Brāhmaṇa" was formerly translated as "noble and eminent lineage";

this refers to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward. "Kṣatriya" refers to those from the seventh stage downward. "Gṛhapati" (householder) refers to those such as the ordinary beings within the stages of cultivation. Now...

The "Manifestation of the Victorious Response" (ming sheng ying) refers to the response-body of the Bodhisattva, which is the *vairocana* (*rúshuān*) body of exceptional majesty; it is that which is perceived by those of superior faculties.

The "Inferior Manifestation of the Response" (liè ying) corresponds to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); it consists of the six-foot-tall body in tattered robes and is that which is perceived by those of inferior faculties.

This present sutra clarifies the eternally abiding *amṛta* (*tíhú*), which is equal to *nirvāṇa*, and the perfect and sudden *dharmakāya*, which is equal to the *Avataṃsaka*. The elder used as a metaphor is [the Buddha].
The majestic power, as well as the retinue of kṣatriyas, brahmins, and others who respectfully surround him, are all pointed out as being the same as the retinue in the *Avataṃsaka*;
there is no difference at all. The characteristics of the Dharma he preaches are also clearly elucidated therein, and likewise there is no distinction.
"Brahmins" refers to those of pure conduct, noble and refined; they are the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) who have become free from defilement.
"Kṣatriyas" refers to the royal caste; they are those from the first bhūmi up to the ninth bhūmi. "Householders" are wealthy but not noble;
they are the [Bodhisattvas of] the thirty mental states (triṃśac-cittotpāda). "Pearl necklaces" refers to the three: morality (śīla), meditative concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), and dhāraṇī.
[This is] obscure. That which is worth ten million is the adornment of the Dharma-body by means of the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding "officials, commoners, and servants," this is an explanation according to the distinct gates (*nānāmukha*): those who receive the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*) and sever the delusions common to all [vehicles] are called "commoners";
those who receive the distinct teachings (*pratyeka-śāsana*) and sever the delusions common to all are called "officials. If explained according to the same gate (*ekamukha*), it is as follows: [...]
This is the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means). Internally, it is identical to true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); externally, it accords with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

It is analogous to officials and commoners, who possess the principle of internal service and external labor. The white fly-whisk represents the function of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). As for "left and right":

the right refers to the wisdom that enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which uses the whisk to sweep away the dust of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*). The left refers to the wisdom that enters the conventional (*prajñapti*).
Using [the whisk] to sweep away the dust of ignorance—these two constitute the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Middle Way; hence it is said they "stand in attendance.

Covering [it] with a precious canopy represents true compassion (*karuṇā*). Hanging various flowered banners: the flowers are the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the banners are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground signifies the pouring down of the water of the Dharma to moisten the minds of all Bodhisattvas and subdue their delusions.

"Dust" (*rajas*) is also the sprinkling and dispersing of the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon the ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*). "Scattering various named flowers" means to spread the seven flowers of purity (*saptaviśuddhi-puṣpa*), namely:

purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), purity of concentration (*samādhi-viśuddhi*), purity of wisdom (*prajñā-viśuddhi*), purity of the elimination of doubt (*kāṅkṣā-prativinaya-viśuddhi*), purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path (*mārgāmārga-jñāna-viśuddhi*), purity of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana-viśuddhi*), and purity of the final knowledge (*kṣayajñāna-viśuddhi*). Regarding "ethical discipline": [text continues]

The three types of precepts, such as the restraint of moral discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), are [the first]. "Concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the *Śūraṅgama* and other samādhis. "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to true wisdom.
"Elimination of doubt" means having transcended doubts regarding the two truths. "Purity of the path and non-path" means practicing non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-way.
"Purity of knowledge and vision" means that the virtue of wisdom is perfected and one clearly perceives the Buddha.
This is its nature. "Pure through the knowledge of abandonment" means the perfection of the virtue of abandonment, wherein ignorance is forever extinguished.

"Arranging precious objects" refers to the arrangement of the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*). "Entering and exiting as previously explained" means that its majestic power is exceptionally sublime;
its radiance is boundless, its physical forms are boundless, and its ocean of marks is towering and magnificent—this is the Flower Treasury Palace (*Kusumatalagarbha-vimāna*).
How could one fail to recognize that Honored One who shines with universal radiance, yet offer some other interpretation?
△ Fourth, seeing his father and fleeing in fear:
When the impoverished son saw that his father possessed such great power and majesty (up to the point where he) had formed this thought, he fled away in haste.

The impoverished son sees that his father possesses great power and majesty: he is called "Great Power" because his wisdom is vast, and "Great Majesty" because his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are vast;
this is like the meaning of having strength in one's hands and body as described above. "Terrified" means that his faculties are small and weak, and he is cowed by the Great Way (*mahāyāna*).
"Regretting having come here" means that the Buddha originally intended to present the Great Dharma to him, yet [the son] should not have [fled].
It accords with their capacities. Because they possess the intention to regress from the Great Vehicle, it is said that they have come here out of regret.

"Privately harboring such thoughts" means that within their mental capacities there is a hidden, subtle, and latent occurrence; it does not refer to manifestly facing the *sambhogakāya* (the Body of Beatific Response).
"Or perhaps kings, ministers, and so forth" refers to Pāpīyas as the king and his followers as the ministers. Those of inferior capacity have their seeds extinguished and are beyond words.
He said: "To speak of it, it is beyond all forms and appearances.

Having seen this image of the supreme response-body, which is not within the reach of gods or humans, and having heard the characteristics of the Dharma taught, which are utterly different from those of the two vehicles—never before seen or heard by those of meager virtue and small wisdom—one might immediately claim it is Māra, or that it is what Māra has spoken.
Briefly opening the three to reveal the one, Śāriputra fell into doubt, thinking: 'Could this not be Māra acting as a Buddha to disturb and confuse us?'"
It is my own thought. If one were to apply the Great [Vehicle] to the Small [Vehicle] from the outset, one would suspect the Buddha of being a demon;

such a fault existed even before today. Furthermore, the "Victorious Response" (Sambhogakāya) is likened to a householder; the householder represents the Reward-body Buddha (Sambhogakāya-buddha). Therefore, these are the Kings and so forth.
The Dharma-body is the Teacher of the Reward-body; the Teacher is like the King. Many sutras refer to this sutra as the "King of Sutras. When wisdom accords with the Dharma, it is—

This wisdom is equal to the Dharma; therefore, the Reward Buddha (Sambhogakāya) is called "Equal. This is the fruition of the Mahāyāna Dharma, not a place where one gains benefit through the Hīnayāna.
Thus, it may be like a king or those of royal status; it is not a place where I can obtain goods by selling my labor.
This is because those of small capacity cannot receive the Great Transformation. It is not as if one goes to a poor neighborhood, and so forth.
Regarding "food and clothing are easily obtained": the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that one can use the dharma obtained through poverty to deliver those who are inferior.
However, the principle of mere emptiness does not encompass the myriad virtues; it is not the *tathāgatagarbha*. Therefore, it is called a "poor neighborhood.

Because partial emptiness is suited to those of small intelligence, it is said to be a place where one can exert effort. As for "food and clothing are easily obtained," it means being able to attain the state of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Nirvana is the outflow-free (anāsrava) clothing and food. If I were to dwell here for a long time, I might be subjected to coercion and forced to act;
thus, I would have to practice the Mahayana path for immeasurable kalpas, which is why it is called "dwelling for a long time. Originally, I was weary of and terrified of birth and death.
If one cultivates the Mahāyāna, one must necessarily enter the cycle of birth and death and extensively study the myriad practices; therefore, it is said to be "oppressive.
Originally I delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, yet now you compel me to give rise to the Mahāyāna bodhicitta; this is to force me against my will to abandon the Great and take up the Small.
Therefore, it is said that he ran swiftly. △ Second, the parable of the father seeing his son. This also has four parts: first, the place where the father sees his son;
second, the recognition of the son upon seeing him; third, the joy felt by the father upon seeing his son; fourth, the fulfillment of the father's wish upon seeing his son. Now, the first part.
At that time, the wealthy elder saw his son upon the lion seat—that is, the lion throne.

The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata dwells in the realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and fearlessness, clearly illuminating the capacities of sentient beings. △ Second, seeing the son, he immediately recognizes him.
"Upon seeing his son, he recognized him.
"Upon seeing his son, he recognized him" means he knew this was a sentient being with whom he had formed a karmic connection in the past. △ Third, "seeing his son, he rejoiced":
his heart was filled with great joy.
Regarding "the mind is greatly filled with joy": the Buddha constantly observes his son’s capacity; now that this capacity has arisen in accordance with compassion, he is therefore joyful.

This is precisely the realization of the teaching of the Dharma and the arousal of great compassion. [Seeing] the burning house, he is greatly alarmed and terrified; that [realization] clarifies the extraction from suffering.
Therefore, it is said that he was struck with terror; this clarifies the bestowal of happiness. Therefore, it is said that he rejoiced.
△ Fourth, seeing that his son’s wish had been fulfilled, he immediately thought: (up to) "Although I am advanced in years, I still cherish [him] with greed."
He then had this thought: "That there is now someone to whom the treasury may be entrusted is precisely what my son desired.

In the past, I saw sentient beings who had regressed from the Great Vehicle to take up the Lesser Vehicle, seeking food in impoverished neighborhoods and struggling to sustain their lives. I constantly wished to give them wealth, but finding no opportunity, I could not do so.
Today that opportunity has arrived, coinciding with my heart of great compassion; therefore, I say, 'The treasury now has one to whom it may be entrusted. My...

"Constantly mindful" means that it is clear he is not only poor and lacking great wealth, but is also oppressed by the manifold sufferings of wandering through birth and death, and is thus pained by Great Compassion;

therefore, it is said that he is "constantly mindful" of him. Although he wishes to rescue and deliver him, there is no opportunity for salvation, which is why it is said, "there is no way to see him.
Now, since there is a being with the capacity for liberation, it is said, "and suddenly [he appears] of his own accord."

"Come! Because you invoke the mind of great compassion, I say: 'It is most agreeable to my wishes. As for my saying, 'Though I am old in years, I still cherish [this Dharma],' this explains the reason why it accords with my wishes.
I am called 'old' because my period of transformation in this world has come to an end; yet, as I have not yet encountered those of great capacity, the Dharma has not been entrusted to another.
From whom shall future disciples attain liberation? It is for the sake of seeking those who may be saved that I speak thus."

As for the expression "greed and stinginess," now that the capacity [of the children] comes of its own accord, there is no such cause for anxiety; therefore, I say it is "most perfectly suited to my wishes.
(The second analogy, the meeting of father and son, concludes. △ Third, the analogy of pursuing and enticing.

This refers proximately to the abandonment of the low stools and the provision of carts within the burning house, and distantly to the teaching of the Dharma where the Great Vehicle is set aside and the Small Vehicle is bestowed. This text is divided into two parts. First, the dispatching of the attendants.
The person pursued them. Next, he sent two others to lure him forward. The pursuers were physically strong and skillful, yet they did not employ their strength.
Again, three times [he tried], but one used the gate of exhortation; though the method was appropriate, there was no responsive capacity.
He immediately dispatched his attendants to pursue and bring him back [saying], "I have committed no offense against you; why do you seize me?

These four subsequent lines concerning the dispatching of attendants represent the "Gate of Exhortation" (*kuan-men*), which serves as a provisional application (*ni-yi*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which dispatches, while the teaching (*śāsana*) is that which is dispatched.

The meaning of principle (*li-yi*) is primary, whereas the meaning of the teaching (*jiao-yi*) is secondary. From the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna scriptures; this constitutes the provisional application.
Sentient beings who lack the capacity do not receive [the teaching]; toward them, it is like milk. Therefore, it is said that "attendants are sent away.
Furthermore, "attendants" refers to ministers, aides, and the like; this means that Dharma-body Bodhisattvas are dispatched to preach the Mahāyāna.

As in the *Avataṃsaka*, four Bodhisattvas are made to explain the forty stages (*bhūmi*): the Bodhisattva Dharmamati explains the ten abodes (*vihāra*), and the Bodhisattva Guṇākara... [explains the ten practices].
The Bodhisattva Vana expounded the Ten Practices; the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja expounded the Ten Dedications; and the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha expounded the Ten Stages.
These constitute the dispatching of the attendants. "Running swiftly to seize" refers to the clear meaning of the Mahāyāna.

It reveals what is upright and direct. By employing this, one responds to the capacities of beings and swiftly proceeds toward Bodhi. Thus, it is said in the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*: "Its speed is like the wind.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses his own supernatural powers and is also empowered by the Buddha;

thus, he is able to cause others to enter Bodhi swiftly. Regarding the four lines following the phrase "the impoverished son was startled": these refer to the gate of exhortation when there is no receptive capacity. Since it is manifested that there is no receptive capacity, even if...

In the past, I once made such a vow, but having long since abandoned it, I no longer remembered it. Upon suddenly hearing this Great Teaching, I was startled because it contradicted my mind, and I was struck with awe because I did not recognize it.
As for those who cry out in grievance and lamentation: in the Hīnayāna, afflictions are regarded as enemies and birth-and-death as suffering.

If one were to exhort them that afflictions are themselves bodhi, they would cry out in grievance, claiming it is an injustice; if they hear that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, they would [cry out] in great...
To call this "suffering" is to fail to receive the teaching through the gate of exhortation (*kangen*). "I shall not offend you" means "I shall not importune you.

"Why do you use such great transformation to instruct me?"—this encompasses two meanings regarding the gate of exhortation. △ Second, the application of the gate of admonition (*keimon*) to simulate what is not received.
The messengers seize him ever more urgently (until he) becomes increasingly terrified, faints, and falls prostrate on the ground.
The two lines, "The messengers seize him ever more urgently" and "forcibly drag him back," serve as a warning regarding the gate;

whereas the preceding explanation of exhorting toward goodness was still leisurely, this—stating, "I shall now speak of matters of fear"—is urgent and forceful. "Forcibly drag" [indicates the intensity].

As he was about to return, [the father] admonished him with harsh words, intending to make him distance himself from evil. Since the son had no internal receptivity, yet was externally constrained by the Great Transformation, this was like forcibly dragging him back.
At that time, the "poor son" reflects upon himself with the six phrases beginning with "I am myself without fault," which represents the gate of not accepting the admonition.
Because sentient beings commit offenses, they enter the prison of birth and death; because the Bodhisattva possesses compassion, he likewise shares in their offense.
They enter prison. Those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) lack great compassion; this is termed being "without fault.

To cause them to enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is precisely to have them imprisoned despite being without fault. Lacking the great skillful means (*upāya*), they enter birth and death and will inevitably and forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles;
therefore, it is said they "will surely die. Reflecting on such matters, it is said that they become even more terrified. [The text continues: forcibly...
The Mahāyāna is not understood by those of small wisdom; therefore, it is said they become "faint. They immediately give rise to slander and will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms;
therefore, it is said they "fall to the ground," which is likewise a state of delusion and distress, drowning in the ground of ignorance.

△ Third, the exhortation to relinquish [the teaching]: ceasing the transformation through the Mahāyāna. This is divided into four parts: first, reflecting on the cessation of the transformation; second, explaining the cessation of the transformation; third, the actual cessation of the transformation.
The fourth [section] concerns the transformation through breathing according to what is appropriate.
Now, for the first [part]: The father saw him from afar and said to his messenger: (until) "do not speak with him again. Initially, there were two considerations:

first, he knew that those of great resolve have weak [external] power; second, he knew that those of small resolve have strong [external] power. Regarding those of great resolve having weak [external] power: the father...
Because one sees from afar that the small has moved far away from the large, it is called "afar. Because this is a child with whom a karmic connection has been formed, it is said that "one sees.

Regarding the phrase "speaking to the messenger": if "messenger" is understood according to the teaching, it means that while wisdom fundamentally expounds the teaching, when wisdom perceives there is no receptive capacity (*indriya*), wisdom ceases and thus the teaching ceases.
If "messenger" is understood in terms of persons, it refers to speaking to the various bodhisattvas, saying: "There is no need to manifest your honored and wondrous [body]."

Regarding the body: it is made visible to those of the Two Vehicles. In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, [Mañjuśrī] contained Vimalakīrti’s bodily fragrance so that those sentient beings would not give rise to delusion or attachment;
likewise, when Samantabhadra entered this Sahā world, he contracted his body to make it small—all of these carry the same meaning.

As for the phrase "do not force them to come": since they lack the great capacity [for the Dharma], there is fear that their roots of goodness might be harmed; therefore, it says "do not force. (Private note)
This means that for those who do not require this person, one should contemplate the "gate of ceasing through exhortation" (*sī-mén*) as the appropriate course;

for those whom one must not forcibly bring [to the path], one should contemplate the "gate of ceasing through admonition" (*jì-mén*) as the appropriate course. Regarding the three phrases about sprinkling cold water on the face: it signifies knowing that [the person] has small aspirations;

thus, one should employ the principle of "cutting off with ash" to sever the water [of craving]. This removes the heat of the afflictions of views and mental formations (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) from the face. To loathe birth and death is called "turning one's back," while turning toward Nirvana is called "facing."
"Like a face" refers to awakening. To speak of "awakening" means to open the small gates for those of limited capacity so that they may be freed from vexation and realize the Four Noble Truths.
"Do not speak with them again" means that one must certainly cease the teaching of the Mahāyāna. △ Second, the explanation of the intention behind ceasing the transformation [of beings].
Why is this so? It is because the father knows his son [and so forth], yet does not speak to others, saying, "This is my son.

As for the cessation of the Buddha’s transformative activity (*śāsana*), it was because [the disciples] were weary of suffering and delighted in emptiness, yet remained intimate with the inferior and lacked a mind of great compassion;

thus they feared and found the Great Dharma difficult. Consequently, he allowed them to follow their lesser inclinations, which suppressed the Buddha’s original intent; this is why he ceased his transformative activity. This is the thorough examination.
He knew that at the abodes of twenty thousand *koṭi* Buddhas, [the beings] had once resolved their minds on the Way; it was not that they entirely lacked the great capacity [for enlightenment].
For the time being, he suspended his great transformation, for the Buddha’s intention was not yet finished, and he waited for a later period.

As for not speaking to others: within the former teachings of the *Hīnayāna*, he spoke according to the intentions of others, using skillful means to provide protection by calling them "śrāvakas," rather than speaking according to his own intention.
"It is said that this is a Bodhisattva. △ Third, the actual cessation of transformation.
The messenger says to him: "I now release you; go wherever you please.
I now release you" means he knows that the great capacity [of the being] is weak. "Go wherever you please" means he knows that there is only small goodness.
Strong. For these two reasons, he therefore ceased his great transformation. △ Fourth, the cessation of the transformation was appropriate:
the impoverished son rejoiced, having attained what he had never experienced before; rising from the ground, he went to the poor district to seek food and clothing.

The transformation of his teaching was adjusted to suit their capacities; they were not compelled by the Great Teaching. For this reason, they rejoiced and incurred no great sin of slander, thereby escaping the three miserable realms;
hence it is said they "rose from the ground. Because a small amount of goodness had arisen within them, it is said they "arose.

Furthermore, previously they were intended for the Great Dharma but, being bewildered and unable to understand, lay upon the ground of ignorance; now that he has accommodated them with the Small [Vehicle], they are able to attain awakening. Thus...

It is said that he rose from the ground. Among the Four Noble Truths, because he sought the Dharma of the Path, it is said that he went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing (the first dispatch of attendants to pursue him is concluded).
△ Second, the secret dispatch of two men to entice and lead [the children] back. This consists of two parts:
first, the immediate teaching, which leads near by means of the three carts to save the children; second, the distant teaching, which leads [them] to Vārāṇasī to bestow [the Dharma].
Regarding the provisional [teachings]: furthermore, from the passage "on another day" (*itaḥ punar anyadā*) onwards, the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) is to encompass the stage of the Dharmakāya.

Having long illuminated through skillful means (*upāya*), it was not at the Bodhi tree that he first realized the utility of the provisional; having early on discerned sentient beings, he thus concealed the *vairocana-kāya* (the exalted body) and personally associated with those in soiled robes.
This is a retrospective summary of what preceded, used to establish the present understanding. Question: For what reason were the four great disciples able to know the Dharmakāya?

Jiuzhao replied: "By examining what is near, one knows what is far. If, at the beginning at the Bodhi tree, he had known there were no great-capacity beings, he would not have descended from Tuṣita to take birth by means of Right Wisdom.
Furthermore, [he displayed] the presence of afflictions, taking a consort and fathering a son, and the severance of fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind in his final existence.
By these evidences, we know that after casting off the subtle and wondrous necklace of the ocean of marks of the Great and Small Vehicles, he further donned the coarse [garments]."
These worn robes of six feet and their grime have been with me for a long time. For now, I shall first explain the summary of the teaching on the *sīmā* (boundary).

The text of the "Parable" chapter consists of four parts: first, employing skillful means (*upāya*) to provide appropriate guidance; second, knowing the prior inclinations of the mind; third, praising the three vehicles;
and fourth, enabling them to escape the burning house according to their respective wishes. The "Expedient Means" chapter is also like this. Now, first, I shall summarize the preceding section.
"Proposed plan.
At that time, when the elder was about to entice his son [to come], [he said: "We two shall also work together with you.
Regarding "when he was about to entice": since the great transformation [of teaching] has ceased, it would not be right to abandon him alone; wishing to establish skillful means, he spoke thus.
Regarding the phrase "intending to secretly dispatch two people": the four disciples were divided equally among them, and since Bodhisattvas were not involved, it says "two people.

In terms of the Dharma, this refers to the Four Noble Truths of Dependent Origination; in terms of principle, it refers to the conditioned and the true-conventional; in terms of persons, it refers to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
At the outset, when modeled after the Mahāyāna, it is said that "he immediately dispatched attendants," which symbolizes the One True Truth (ekayānasatya). First.

Regarding the Mahāyāna teaching: first, for a bodhisattva, "secret" (*mi*) refers to concealing the ultimate reality as a skillful means (*upāya*), while "expedient" (*shen*) refers to pointing toward the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*) as that which is to be discarded.

In terms of the teachings, "secret" refers to concealing the *pūrṇākṣara* (the full syllable), while "expedient" refers to pointing toward the *ardhākṣara* (the half syllable) as that which is to be discarded.

In terms of persons, it is called "secret" because they internally conceal their bodhisattva practice, and it is called "expedient" because they externally manifest as śrāvakas. As for "form and color," within the teachings of the two vehicles:
Not cultivating the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), but merely preaching suffering, impermanence, and impurity—this is what is meant by having a haggard appearance.
In terms of persons, it refers to those bodhisattvas who conceal their true nature and manifest only their provisional traces; this is not the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).

To lack the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) is called "lacking majestic power. When you say, "You may go to them," it means you should approach them with the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
The Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is for those of lesser capacity. The Great Teaching clarifies principles that are direct and substantial; thus it says, "run swiftly to seize [it].

The Small Teaching clarifies principles that are circuitous and obscure; thus it speaks of "speaking slowly. Regarding the phrase "the place of action," this refers to the two paths of seeing and cultivation, which are the locus for severing delusions.

"I will give you double the price" refers to the five precepts and ten wholesome actions, which merely prevent one from falling into the three miserable realms; whereas now, through the Four Truths and the Ten... [the path leads to liberation].
There are two causes and conditions that can bring about transcendence from birth and death; this constitutes the first "doubling.

Furthermore, while the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress afflictions, now, by cultivating the Four Noble Truths to sever afflictions, one attains Nirvana; this constitutes the second "doubling.

If the impoverished son consents—consent being the presence of the capacity [for teaching]—then the teaching is established. If he does not consent—non-consent being the absence of the capacity—then the teaching is not established. What else would you wish for?

Regarding "that which is to be done": the followers of the Two Vehicles (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) seek only to eliminate afflictions and realize [nirvāṇa], without concern for purifying Buddha-lands or bringing sentient beings to maturity.
This is why it is said, "I hired you to remove the filth; we two shall also work together.

Those of dull faculties among the Two Vehicles must rely on the teachings to practice their conduct before they can cultivate their tasks. In terms of principle, this refers to the mutual support between wisdom and the [Four] Truths.
Regarding the person: this refers to the practice undertaken by both those of provisional capacity and those of ultimate reality together. △ Second, receiving the aforementioned prior intention:
at that time, the two messengers sought the impoverished son and, having already found him—

He immediately sought out the impoverished son; having ascertained that the son possessed the capacity [for enlightenment], he said, "I have already obtained it. This acknowledges the aforementioned understanding of the son's prior intention.
△ Third, acknowledging the aforementioned praise of the three vehicles.

He fully recounted the aforementioned matters, explaining how he had been hired for labor; he took the price of the three carts above and removed the filth of suffering and its origin to obtain the value of the Path and Cessation.
△ Fourth, he received the fulfillment of his original wish and vied with others to escape the burning house.
At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately began clearing away the filth. When the father saw his son, he felt both pity and wonder.

"First taking his wages" refers to those who, having attained their initial aspiration, strive to emerge from the burning house; it represents the Two Vehicles who, longing for the fruit, practice the causes.
This is why they were taken first. When the father saw his sons, he felt pity for them yet marveled at them;
he marveled because they did not seek the Buddha-way, and he pitied them because by taking the path of Arhatship, what they lost was great while what they gained was meager—hence the word "marvel.

This concludes the summary of the meaning within the parable. As for the text that follows: in the teaching through Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), there is only the provisional application of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); in the teaching through parable (*aupamya-deśanā*), there is only the equal distribution of gifts. The two intermediate sections are omitted.

(Taste). (The simultaneous instruction and reception are concluded). △ Second, Reception by Grasping the Meaning. Spiritual wisdom first illuminates; expedient means have been established for a long time.
Wandering along difficult paths, not merely beneath the tree, one finally perceives the causes and conditions, as already explained above.
This text consists of four parts: First, leading with provisional wisdom, having long desired to provide an appropriate model; second, having long known the skillful means, this is...

Regarding his playthings: he has long known the three [vehicles], and must sigh over the three carts. Fourth, he personally instructs his son; the son’s wishes are fulfilled as he receives and practices them.
This is the first instance.
Furthermore, on another day, from within a window, he saw his son’s body from afar.

Furthermore, "again" (*yòu*) is a term used for emphasis. It indicates that, wishing to grasp the essential meaning and lead [beings] to the ground of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), [the author], who has long known the capacities of both the great and the small, reiterates the Buddha’s intention by means of the teachings of "one" and "three. Thus, the chapter is headed with the word "again. As for "another day":
The Two Vehicles consider themselves to be the "expedient means" and regard the non-Two Vehicle teachings as being for others;

this refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Day" (*jì*) signifies time, and it also signifies wisdom (*prajñā*). Relying on the time of the Dharma-body, one employs wisdom to illuminate the capacities [of beings]; hence, it is called "another day.
According to this principle, true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) illuminating reality is "self," while expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminating expedients is "other. This is consistent.

Regarding the instruction on "comprehending": comprehending the activities of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is designated as "self," while activities that are not those of the transformation body are designated as "other.

If one considers the Tathāgata’s own wisdom of provisional and ultimate truth, these are all termed "self. If one considers the Tathāgata’s illumination of provisional and ultimate truth for the sake of transforming others, these are all termed "other.

Within the Tathāgata’s own and other-directed illumination of provisional and ultimate truth, that which illuminates the ultimate is "self," and that which illuminates... [the provisional is "other"].
This refers to the time of investigating and realizing the Dharma-body through the provisional means (*upāya*) for transforming others.

One employs the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) for transforming others to illumine the provisional capacities of beings—whether they exist or not—and to illumine the application of provisional matters—whether they are appropriate or not. All of these are what is illumined by provisional wisdom; therefore, it is called "the other day" (*tadanya-dina*).

From this perspective, one realizes the provisional matters for transforming others in accordance with the teachings. Thus, it is said: "From this principle, one realizes the provisional matters for transforming others in accord with the teachings."
The Two Vehicles describe their own affairs. Regarding "exploring and receiving" (*tanting*): they receive the provisional [manifestations] of the Dharmakāya for themselves and others.

This provisional [aspect] is not the affair of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is termed "other. Although there are these two meanings, both will eventually be realized. For now, we rely on what is received by the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, following the phrasing of the subsequent day, we explore the meaning of "receiving" (*ling*). "Receiving" refers to the Dharma-body’s illumination of sentient capacities. "Windows and doors" signify that partial views are limited;
this represents the expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminating those partial capacities. "Distant" means that the small is far removed from the great, and is thus called "distant.
"Seeing the child" means that because [the being] previously planted the seeds for the Great [Vehicle], they are called a "child"; they are addressed as such by being modeled after the Great.

It is said that this is for the sake of vision; as the windows and doors are narrow and constricted, it is not yet suitable for a great transformation. Therefore, he ceases the grand and applies the small.
△ Second, understanding the skillful means: these are objects of play and enjoyment.
Emaciated and haggard; defiled by excrement, soil, and dust; filthy and impure. Regarding "emaciated" and so forth:
having little power from the cause of cultivation is "emaciated"; having little power from the cause of merit is "haggard. Internally fearing impermanence is "haggard";
externally encountering the eight sufferings is "worn out. The four abodes are "excrement and soil"; ignorance is...
"Dust" means defilement. △ Third, regarding the knowledge that the three vehicles must be praised:
he immediately removes his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments (up to) having an appearance of fear.

"Immediately casting off the exquisite robes" is a metaphor for concealing the immeasurable merits of the *saṃbhogakāya*—the necklaces of the forty-two stages, precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇīs*, as well as the fine, soft, superior garments of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*), and the ornaments of the major and minor marks and the ocean of signs.
If these attire and ornaments were displayed in full splendor, the sons would be startled and terrified; the followers of the two vehicles are not fit to behold such physical marks and excellence.

For this reason, he removes them and puts on coarse and tattered garments. His manifestation in a body sixteen feet tall is "coarse," while his cultivation of the patience of birth and the patience of the Dharma is "tattered.
That dust covers his body signifies that he currently possesses afflictions, being conditioned and subject to outflows (*āsrava*).
The passage beginning with "holding a dustpan" refers solely to the treatment of the outflowing dharmas of views and thought; it does not concern the pure wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

The left hand symbolizes reality (*tattva*), and the right hand symbolizes expedient means (*upāya*). Expedient means are easy to employ; by means of this very method, one severs the fetters and attains Buddhahood. Furthermore, one employs this to transform others:
appearing as if possessed of something to fear, it demonstrates that one shares the same dread of birth and death.

Moreover, there is the retribution of the cold wind and the horse-barley; (regarding "there is also the cold wind" and so forth: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, the Buddha had ten afflictions, namely: the six years of ascetic practice, the slander by Sundarī, the golden staff, and the horse-barley).

1. The barley; 2. Vimalakīrti’s killing of the Śākyas; 3. Begging for alms with an empty bowl; 4. The slander by Ciñcā-mānavikā; 5. Devadatta’s hurling of the mountain; 6. Seeking clothing against the cold wind; 7. Suffering back pain under the twin trees—these constitute the ten [incidents]. 4. The deeds performed as the biological son:

Having attained his wish and undertaken its practice, this refers to the seven categories of the Dharma-gate within the *bodhipākṣika-dharmas* (factors conducive to enlightenment), which manifest the manner of "removing filth.
