World-Honored One, it is as if there were a man who, having traveled for a hundred years through a vast wilderness, suddenly saw a great city adorned with various precious jewels, with towers, gates, and walls all complete. He thought to himself: 'I have now seen this great city, but I lack the means to enter it. At that time, another person appeared and said to him: 'Good man, do not fear. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa... [up to] "...it is truly as you have said. Regarding the two instances of "Excellent":
the first "Excellent" describes his realization of the reality (*tattva*) in both places; the second "Excellent" describes his realization of the skillful means (*upāya*) in both places.
"Well-spoken is the true merit of the Tathāgata": "true" describes the reality, and "merit" refers to...

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* expounds the provisional (*upāya*). Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* anticipates the realization of the ultimate (*tattva*); the Tripiṭaka provides the guidance for the provisional;

the *Vaipulya* (Buddhāvataṃsaka) inspires faith, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* guides one through the teachings—both of these encompass both the provisional and the ultimate. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*’s entrustment of the treasure exclusively discusses the ultimate.

Because its phrasing is subtle and skillful, it is said to be "well-spoken" (*svākhyāta*); because it is entirely the Buddha-dharma, it is said to be... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
"Truly. It is exactly as you have said. This is a term used to confirm [the truth]. (Regarding the "dual narration of both": there are two locations, namely the skillful means and the burning house.

Since in the section on faith and understanding one simultaneously leads from both locations, here too one narrates the two locations that were led from. If it were not so, what benefit would there be in merely narrating them? △ Second, leading [them] regarding what was not yet reached.
The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits that cannot be fully described.

That which exceeds the reach of comprehension refers to those who fall back, those who advance, those who move horizontally, those who move vertically, those who move both horizontally and vertically, and those who move neither horizontally nor vertically—all of whom are beyond his reach.
Why is this? Because the great cloud covers all universally, bestowing pervasive coolness; the great rain moistens everything simultaneously.
There is none who does not receive its grace, causing all in the world to realize and perceive this unprecedented Dharma.

Why then do you uniformly teach only to lead those of the Two Vehicles to obtain benefit, while failing to mention the "small grasses" of humans and devas? This constitutes a retreat that falls short of others.

The Bodhisattva is called "superior grass," and is also called "small trees" and "great trees. They flourish and grow luxuriantly, benefiting both themselves and others, yet they do not claim ownership of these benefits;
this is what is meant by "advancing beyond the reach of others. Furthermore, the ten dharma-realms are all equally perfected as the Buddha-dharma realm.
Furthermore, it suddenly encompasses the two vehicles; yet the remaining eight dharma-realms are not mentioned at all—this is what is meant by "not reaching [them] horizontally.

Moreover, from the shallow to the deep, the seven stages of expedient means all enter into reality; yet the other five expedient means are never mentioned—this is what is meant by "not reaching [them] vertically.
Furthermore, its benefit to the three periods of time has never been suspended for even a moment—this is...

"Neither horizontal nor vertical can reach it. (The phrase "Nahu Xia" [那忽下] criticizes the leveling of the teachings. "Tongguan Zhujou" [通貫諸句] means they penetrate all sentences. "Budao Xia" [不道下] correctly describes the failure to reach it.

Regarding "retreat and advance," from the perspective of the two vehicles' stages, looking upward constitutes "advance" and looking downward constitutes "retreat. Since each of the ten realms possesses its own cause and effect independently of sequential order, it is called "horizontal. Yet, as a single person gradually progresses through them, it also constitutes "vertical. Furthermore, regarding the term "both horizontal and vertical" applied to the three periods of time:

since each period pervades the ten directions and the ten realms, it is also called "horizontal. Such categories have all been matured through the eight teachings following the various flavors [of the Lotus Sutra]. Only today, together with Kāśyapa and others, do we realize whether we are the same or different.)

This is called "vertical. Because they had not yet heard that [the earth] universally sustains all things, the Buddha demonstrated it to them. Now, mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys are collectively termed "one earth. This one earth is capable of producing [all things].
Without ever making distinctions, it takes from that and gives to this. The seeds of grasses and trees all rely upon the earth; they have no other support.
When a single cloud gathers, its density is uniform everywhere; when there is a single rain of a single flavor, it makes no distinction between the withered and the flourishing.
Since the universal moistening is the same, all things universally attain growth. The Tathāgata’s equanimity is inconceivable; truly, he does not first bestow [the sudden] and later [the gradual].
The gradual [path]: the first three and the last one are like a dragon raising auspicious clouds, raining universally upon all.
The body and mind do not receive the rain; it removes heat and attains coolness. These constitute the five vehicles and the seven expedient means.

Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, they are equal, vast, profound, extensive, and far-reaching, inconceivable, and without distinction. This is neither horizontal nor vertical.

"Vertical. This refers to that which is beyond the reach of [the categories of] horizontal and vertical (it is neither horizontal nor vertical, as in the various passages below where "difference" and "non-difference" are joined: non-difference is difference, and difference is non-difference; now, following non-difference, it is called "neither horizontal nor vertical";
yet from the perspective of difference, it is as previously stated regarding the horizontal and so forth). The meaning of being "beyond reach" does not mean a total and sudden negation;

rather, it is because when one looks from the initial mind toward the subsequent mind, one has not yet reached the ultimate stage, and thus it is said to be "inexhaustible. Furthermore, the initial realization of the first letter *A* also contains all that follows.

Regarding the merit of tea: this has merely exhausted the scope of the provisional teachings; there has not yet been leisure to advance toward a comprehensive mastery that encompasses both the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Furthermore, it is appropriate for a Bodhisattva of expedient practice to act in this manner. (The first part, the brief exposition, is concluded. △ Second, the detailed exposition, in two parts.

The prose and the verse. The prose is further divided into two parts: first, the exposition establishing the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one; second, the concluding praise. The first part contains the teaching, the analogy, and the application.
Within the teaching, there are again two sections: first, citing the Dharma King to encourage faith; second, the actual exposition of the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one.
This is the first [section].
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false.
Just as a human king has nothing to fear from without and no duplicity within, how much more so the Dharma King, whose manifold evils have been utterly exhausted?
All his myriad virtues are perfected; whatever he speaks is true and not false. Although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the ultimate.
Outside of the provisional and the ultimate, there is no other dharma. As for the claim that there are "immeasurable" teachings, this meaning is difficult to believe.
Therefore, the Dharma King is cited to encourage faith. Furthermore, this serves as the basis for the subsequent analogy of the great cloud. II.

The actual exposition of the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one has two parts: 1. Explaining the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real by way of the teachings; 2. Explaining the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real by way of wisdom.
Through the two teachings, the two wisdoms are revealed; through the two wisdoms, the two teachings are expounded. Thus, wisdom and teaching mutually accomplish one another.
First: "Regarding all dharmas" (up to) "all have reached the stage of omniscience.

"All dharmas" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*); this is the horizontal dimension. In contrast to the single reality (*eka-tattva*), it constitutes the vertical dimension. If one says [otherwise], it is not so.
It is so. For what reason did you first resolve upon the Great Mind in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, yet in the interim take up the Lesser Vehicle and wander through the five destinies?

Furthermore, even a single person possesses all ten realms of existence; how much more so for those on the seven stages of preparation (*saptavyavasthāna*)? Although these phenomena are numerous, [they are all contained within this].
The *upāya-pāramitā* illuminates them all without exception. It speaks to them according to their respective capacities through various sounds, never failing to meet them where they are.
For humans and devas, it teaches the precepts and wholesome deeds; for those of the two vehicles, it teaches the Truths and Dependent Origination;

for those of the Tripiṭaka, it teaches phenomena and the perfections (*pāramitās*); for those of the Shared Teaching, it teaches non-arising; and for those of the Distinct Teaching, it teaches the gradual stages, thereby revealing the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is...

The title describes its opening of the three [vehicles]. From the passage "according to the Dharma he preached" onwards, it describes the revelation of the reality (śūnyatā) according to the teachings.
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is ultimately non-dual, and thus called "one. Its nature is vast and expansive, and thus called "universal" (*sarva*).
It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, and thus called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). As the foundation of non-abiding, it establishes all dharmas; therefore—
This is named "the Ground. This is the definitive teaching of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Whatever is taught therein is intended to lead all sentient beings to this ground of wisdom.
The texts that reveal the reality are as radiant as the sun; how can one remain in ignorance and slumber, offering alternative interpretations?

Following the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it extensively enumerates all phenomena as being the Mahāyāna. "Yāna" (衍) is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), and "Vehicle" (乘) is the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Reality—
The characteristic is identical to the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). The preceding passage states, "Only this one fact is real," which refers to this stage.

"The other two are not true" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*). This explains the revelation of the provisional and the manifestation of the real according to both the gradual and sudden teachings.
△ Second, the revelation of the provisional and the manifestation of the real by way of wisdom.
The Tathāgata contemplates and knows the ultimate destination of all dharmas, which is all-encompassing wisdom.
Regarding the opening of the provisional to reveal the real through wisdom:

the two phrases "the Tathāgata contemplates and knows all dharmas" up to "penetrating them without obstruction" are able to illuminate the provisional. Furthermore, regarding "thoroughly exhausting and clearly understanding all dharmas" up to... [text continues]
The two phrases concerning wisdom refer to the ability to illumine reality. The two types of wisdom illumine both the partial and the perfect realms;
because they penetrate these without obstruction, one is able to expound the two teachings of the provisional and the real. This passage explains the teachings by means of wisdom.

Within the opening of the provisional, knowing where [beings] ultimately turn toward is the "knowledge of the medicine," while that which is practiced with a deep mind is the "knowledge of the illness. Both the illness and the medicine are provisional dharmas.

Provisional dharmas each have their respective destinations. Precepts, wholesome deeds, and the like, lead proximately to the realms of humans and devas; yet if they serve as the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), even such acts as bowing the head or raising the hands lead distantly to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and so forth, lead proximately to *nirvāṇa*; yet if they serve as the actualizing cause (*karaṇa-hetu*), [they likewise lead to the ultimate fruit].
The path you practice is the bodhisattva way, which leads far toward the place of treasure.

Even so, from the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and their specific and general dharmas, to those toward which one near and far returns, the various routes are likewise different. Furthermore, the precepts and wholesome deeds are the medicine for humans and devas;
the truths, conditions, and perfections are the medicine for those of the three vehicles; and even the general and specific dharma-gates are both general and specific.

The Bodhisattva’s medicine. Furthermore, there are two kinds of conduct arising from the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*): first, attachment to the primary and secondary supports (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*);
second, attachment to the dharmas that are grasped. Attachment to the primary and secondary supports gives rise to the ten grave evil deeds, which obstruct the vehicle of humans and devas.
Attachment to the grasped dharmas gives rise to the four inversions, the three poisons, the six obscurations, the four abodes, the five abodes, and so forth, which obstruct all [virtuous qualities].

Regarding the Holy Vehicle, one should know that the profound mind perceives that the manifestations of illness differ; through expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it illuminates them, attaining unimpeded penetration.

Within the revelation of the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*), furthermore, "thoroughly exhausting and clearly understanding all phenomena" refers to what is illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Since all provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*) enter into the ultimate reality without exception, they are said to be "thoroughly exhausted. Because this is what is known by true wisdom, it is said to be "clearly understood. This is the domain of the Buddha-eye.

Because it sees, it is called "clarity. If this wisdom illuminates this medicine and this illness, but does not illuminate that medicine and that illness—whereas that other wisdom illuminates the latter but cannot illuminate the former—and these various types are distinct from one another, this is the illumination of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

When a single wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses, this is the illumination of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). It is able to show sentient beings such a perfect realm (*pariniṣpanna-viṣaya*).
Wisdom. Therefore, it is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (the first explanation of the Dharma is concluded). △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the analogies; second, the summary of the teachings. The analogies consist of both opening and closing sections. Opening them, there are two:

first, the analogy of differentiation, which illustrates the aforementioned provisional teachings and provisional wisdom; second, the analogy of non-differentiation, which illustrates the aforementioned ultimate teachings and ultimate [wisdom].

This is wisdom (*jñāna*). The three types of grass and two types of trees differ in their fineness and density; therefore, they are said to be "differentiated. Yet, as for the single earth and the single rain, which universally cause them to grow and universally moisten them, there is no differentiation.
If one observes their branches and shoots, one says they are each distinct; yet if one investigates their roots and vitality, none are not the result of the earth and the rain.

Internally, this corresponds to the illumination of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), wherein the seven [realms] and five [skandhas] appear distinct; however, as for the true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*)...
The preceding illumination ultimately returns to the single reality (*eka-tattva*). The single reality is sevenfold and fivefold; the sevenfold and fivefold are the single reality.
This is the non-differentiation within differentiation, and the differentiation within non-differentiation. There are six analogies for this single differentiation:
first, the soil; second, the plants and trees; third, the dense clouds; fourth, the falling rain; fifth, the receiving of moisture; and sixth, the growth. Now, first is the analogy of the soil.

Kāśyapa, it is like this: for example, the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, with its mountains, rivers, valleys, and the great earth—this great thousandfold world system is a metaphor for the world of sentient beings;
the mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands are metaphors for the world of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
There is no separate entity apart from the world that is composed of mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands; likewise, there is no separate entity apart from sentient beings.

Dharmas are composed of the five aggregates. [Supplementary Note: Mountains, rivers, valleys, land, and so forth are assigned to the five aggregates merely for the sake of their numerical correspondence; it is not necessary to fix each one definitively as "this is form" or "this is sensation," and so on.

Even if they can be assigned with great similarity, what of the difference between the sentient and the insentient? As stated below: "Though mountains are high and steep, they also possess the five characteristics such as depressions and elevations; even though land is level, it also possesses the five characteristics such as mounds and ponds.

It is evident that one takes only the numerical correspondence without the need for detailed fixation on each, for the value lies solely in grasping the underlying meaning. For example, although grasses and trees depend upon...
Regarding "the land and so forth": the land and such are not identical to the grasses and trees; yet the substance and trunk of the grasses and trees are merely designated as "grasses and trees.

As for the seeds of the grasses and trees, they have no other name; one simply takes their capacity to produce as the "seed," and that which is produced—the substance and trunk—is called "grass and tree.
All of these take root in the earth, and thus the earth is the foundation. This internally corresponds to the causes and fruits of habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*).
Although they depend upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the five aggregates themselves are not identical to cause and effect.
It is by depending upon the aggregates that there exists a causal condition for cultivation (*vāsanā-hetu*); its growth and fulfillment is termed the "fruit of cultivation" (*vāsanā-phala*).

This fruit and its cause arise in dependence upon the aggregates, just as the seeds of grasses and trees receive moisture and grow, depending upon mountains, rivers, valleys, and the soil to reach fruition. To provide another analogy: although a mountain may be high and steep...
There are also five characteristics, such as depressions and elevations; even though the land may be level, there are still five characteristics such as mounds and ponds.

These correspond to the five vehicles and the five aggregates (*skandhas*): the high mountains represent the five aggregates of a Bodhisattva, the rivers represent those of a Pratyekabuddha, the mountain torrents represent those of a Śrāvaka, the level ground represents those of a Deva, and the low valleys represent those of a human. Each of these five aggregates possesses habitual causes (*vāsanā-hetu*).
The basis for the fruition of cultivation is like mountains, rivers, valleys, and the earth, which all serve as the support for seeds, roots, trunks, and so forth.
Furthermore, the three-thousandfold world system is used as an analogy for the principle of the direct cause, serving as the universal support for all things.
Mountains, rivers, valleys, and the earth are analogies for the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and the resultant form (*rūpa*) of sentient beings.
This is the mind. Grasses, trees, and thickets are likened to the habitual causes of sentient beings. These three dharmas are inseparable from one another.

Habitual tendencies rely upon the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas), yet these aggregates and sense bases do not transcend the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). It is like grasses and trees relying on mountains and rivers, and mountains and rivers relying on the great trichiliocosm.
△ Second, the analogy of the plants and trees that grow [therein].
The various species of plants, forests, and medicinal herbs that grow there differ in their types and vary in their names and forms.
"Herb" (*śāka*) is a general term for grasses; "wood" (*vṛkṣa*) is a collective designation for trees. A multitude of grasses form a thicket (*gaṇa*), and a multitude of trees form a forest (*vana*).
Those possessing superior power to cure diseases are called "medicines" (*oṣadhi*). Just as within the wholesome dharmas, all are capable of curing evil, so it is here.

The untainted wholesome [dharmas] excel in their capacity to counteract delusions. Within the category of inferior plants and trees, those with trunks and branches provide the most extensive shade and yield the greatest utility;

therefore, they serve as metaphors for the two types of bodhisattvas. Regarding "various kinds": this refers to the seeds of cause and effect within the five vehicles and seven wholesome [paths], hence the term "various.
These are precisely the categories. Each has its own designation, which constitutes its name. Each has its own...
The essence and characteristics are precisely form (*rūpa*). △ Third, the analogy of dense clouds:
Dense clouds spread everywhere, completely covering the trichiliocosm.

The clouds possess both form and color, providing cover and shade. As the subsequent text mentions the distant thundering of lightning, the cover and shade serve as an analogy for the Buddha’s compassion.
The physical form and color are like the Buddha appearing in the world; the sound of thunder is like the Buddha’s teaching; and the dense clouds represent the three mysteries (*triguhyāni*).

Compassion is the mystery of mind (*manomayaguhyam*); the physical form and color are the mystery of body (*kāyamayaguhyam*); and the sound of thunder is the mystery of speech (*vāṅmayaguhyam*). "Pervasive" (*mibù*) means to spread everywhere;

because they are both secret and all-pervading, it is said they are "pervasively spread. Through the permeation of compassion, the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) preaches the Dharma, pervading the ten [directions].
The Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said to be "pervasively spread. △ Fourth, the analogy of pouring rain:
"At once, etc., showering down" illustrates the application of the secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*).
Through the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one proclaims and pours down the rain of the Dharma, benefiting and nourishing sentient beings. △ Fifth, soaking...
The analogy of moisture:
its pervasive soaking extends to the great branches and large leaves.
The Dharma-treasure rains universally upon the ground of the hearts of the seven classes of sentient beings; all seeds of habitual causes immediately sprout through hearing.

As for my previous praise of your rarity: ordinary worldlings are prone to backsliding, yet even they can gain benefit upon hearing [the Dharma]. For Bodhisattvas, however, this is their own primary concern."

The explanation is not particularly extraordinary. It is truly rare that those of the Two Vehicles enter the unconditioned state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and are further able to relinquish their realization to enter into reality.
To say they "can know" refers to their ability to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
to say they "can receive and accept" describes how they comprehend and manifest the One Vehicle. △ Second, resolving doubts.
Why is this so? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
Although the Buddha speaks of three vehicles within the One Vehicle—a profound mystery that is hard to comprehend—you are nonetheless able to believe it.
I privately remark that while the preceding passage states, "The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable merits, which you cannot fully describe," the subsequent passage says:
That you are so exceedingly rare and marvelous is because the Buddha’s grace universally covers all, just as clouds and rain provide moisture to everything they reach;
the Buddha’s grace universally sustains all, just as the great earth brings all things to life and growth. How could it be limited to a single individual or a single region?
Therefore, it is said that you cannot fully describe it. Although the Buddha’s grace is universal, sentient beings do not realize it in their daily lives.
They realize it for themselves. It is like the three types of grass and two types of trees that take root in the earth and receive moisture from the rain, yet are unable to know [it].
That you are able to know it is truly rare. (The first long prose section ends. II. Verse Recitation. There are fifty-four and a half lines.

△ Subsequently, two verses concern the two types of wisdom (*dvividhajñāna*). First, one verse explains provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*).
Those with wisdom, upon hearing this, will be able to believe and understand it; those without wisdom will harbor doubt and regret, thereby losing [the Dharma] forever. (Supplementary note:

The Tathāgata has long remained silent and did not speak, yet today, for the sake of Śāriputra and the four great disciples, he employs the analogy of rain to preach the Dharma. He describes how Kāśyapa and others are able to hear, believe, and understand, praising them as having wisdom.

Such is their loss.)
It is exceedingly great). △ Next, one verse explains true wisdom:
"Therefore, Kāśyapa, I teach according to their capacity; by means of various conditions, I cause them to attain right view."
According to various conditions, various teachings are expounded, all for the purpose of causing one to attain the correct view of the Mahāyāna.

This verse expresses the intent of the Tathāgata’s four *siddhāntas*: "Destroying the existence of dharmas" is the *prātipakṣika-siddhānta* (the therapeutic intent); "according to the desires of sentient beings" is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly intent);

"wisdom, hearing, faith, and understanding, whereby doubt and regret are forever lost" constitutes the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the personal intent); and "causing one to attain the correct view" is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate intent).

The meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and the three *siddhāntas* are explained here through the verse on "expounding by means of wisdom and skillful means" so that one may attain right view.
This concludes the first verse, which explains the teaching through the Dharma and reaches the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
△ Second, fifty and a half lines of verse explain the preceding parables. Of these, the first ten and a half lines explain the opening of the parable, while the subsequent forty lines explain...

This is the synthesis of the metaphors. Above, two metaphors were presented: one for the differentiated and one for the non-differentiated. Now, the first nine and a half verses summarize the metaphor of differentiation;
the subsequent single line summarizes the metaphor of non-differentiation. Previously, there were six aspects of differentiation; now, these six are likewise summarized.
The first three lines of the verse use the metaphor of clouds.
Kāśyapa, you should know that [the passage] up to "like something graspable" uses the cloud as a metaphor for the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Because the *saṃbhogakāya* accords with the movement of wisdom, it is called the "Wisdom Cloud. It is able to fully possess the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

Because the Dharma contains moisture, it is said that [the clouds] contain moisture. If the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) were not to preach the Dharma—as in the case of the Buddha Susīma and others—then these clouds would not contain moisture.
The body emits great radiance like a flash of lightning, and the mouth vibrates with the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) like the sound of thunder.
Since the ninety-five kinds of heterodox radiance do not appear, it is said that they are "obscured. This removes the ninety-eight kinds [of afflictions].
It is like the coolness upon the earth when one is afflicted by heat;

it is like something that can be grasped, for the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) descends into the world, appearing as if identical to the three realms of existence so that one might have the intention to seize it, yet in reality it cannot be obtained. △ Second, one verse of gāthā with commentary on the analogy of rain above.
That rain falls equally upon all, descending simultaneously from the four directions, flowing in immeasurable torrents to saturate the entire land.
Likewise, the eightfold voice and the four analytical powers proclaim and pour down the rain of Dharma, descending simultaneously from the four directions so that it is heard by all at once;
this is also called the "fourfold equality. All who possess a mind receive its benefit and nourishment; therefore, it is said that the entire land is saturated. This, then—

This completes the preceding section. Furthermore, it completes the analogy of the mountains and rivers. △ Third, one line: this verse summarizes the preceding analogy of the land, terrain, mountains, and rivers.

This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings at the stage of the seven expedient means (*sapta-vidhā upāya*).

Now, having received the rain of the Dharma, their bodies and speech become supple and soft, just as the soil receives moisture. △ Four lines; this verse praises the preceding analogy of the herbs and trees.
"Those things produced from the deep recesses.

The shrubs, trees, medicinal herbs, and grasses produced from the deep recesses are like the habitual causes planted by sentient beings over a long period of time, hidden within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas);
therefore, they are called "the deep recesses. Now, having received the rain of Dharma, they all attain development and blossoming; therefore, they are called "produced. △ Five.
Two lines and three phrases. These verses praise the preceding analogy of receiving nourishment.
From "the various trees, large and small" up to "receiving nourishment according to their respective capacities," the term "hundred grains" is used broadly;
here it takes the five grains as an analogy for the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), which can produce the hundred kinds of goodness. [The remaining examples include] sugarcane and grapes.
The concentration and wisdom are like a dry land being universally moistened; this illustrates causing those who have not yet attained faith to believe. The remainder is as explained in the text.
△ Sixth, two lines: a verse summarizing the preceding analogy of growth.
All the trees (up to) attain a fresh luster.

According to their essential nature and characteristics, although the extent of their capacities may be great or small, that which moistens them is one and the same, yet each flourishes accordingly.

The first two lines consist of two characters each, praising both that which is produced and that which is moistened; the subsequent single character consists of two characters, praising that which moistens.
This constitutes the praise of non-differentiation. "Yet each flourishes accordingly" praises differentiation, while "not knowing by itself" praises the lack of self-awareness. (One verse)
The analogy has concluded). △ Second, the forty lines. There are two parts to the verses on the synthesis of the analogy:

the first thirty-five stanzas synthesize the distinctions; the next five lines, beginning with "Thus, Kāśyapa," synthesize the absence of distinction. Regarding the synthesis of the analogies for distinctions:
the former provides the direct synthesis, while the latter cites the analogy as a corroboration. Now, in these verses as well, there is first the synthesis, followed by the citation [of the analogy].
The Analogy Section. The first line combines the verse with the analogy of the clouds. The first two phrases equate the body with the clouds;
the latter two phrases present the analogy and apply it to the subject.
The Buddha is also like this. His appearance in the world is like a great cloud that universally covers all.
(Part Two consists of eight lines and a half, praising the aforementioned analogy of rain. The first three lines briefly praise the Ten Epithets.)
"Having emerged into the world... like a great cloud.
These three lines of verse concerning the Ten Epithets are concise in wording yet rich in meaning. "Emerging into the world" refers to the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*) and the Buddha.

He is the One Who Teaches; that is, the Fully Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). He is the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*), the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*)—these are the tenth titles.

Among gods and humans, he is the Tamer of Men (*puruṣadamyasārathi*) and the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). He is the Tathāgata—this is the first title. He is one who has come well and departed well.
Furthermore, he is the Well-Gone One (Sugata) and has emerged from the world; that is, the Knower of the World. △ Within the second section of six topical headings, only two headings are versified.
The first one and a half lines are a verse on the Four Great Vows.
To saturate and nourish all [beings] up to the bliss of nirvāṇa.
As for the four great vows: "to saturate and nourish sentient beings" is the first great vow; "to cause them all to be free from suffering" is the second vow.
This is because they cause all beings to be free from the suffering of cause and effect, thereby attaining peaceful and secure happiness; this is the third vow.
Furthermore, it causes them to attain the bliss of nirvana, which is the fourth vow. The five vehicles all possess worldly happiness, yet [the Buddha] causes them all to attain the supreme happiness.
II. Four Verses Exhorting to Listen and Accept. Within these, the first two verses first praise the Buddha. Next...
For the sake of the great assembly, the following two lines are presented: because the person who can preach is honored, the Dharma he preaches is sublime.

Since the seven types of goodness all ultimately converge in the One Vehicle, he exhorts them to listen and accept it. This cites the absence of differentiation to explain away the notion of differentiation.
The assembly of devas and humans... [down to] "thereby creating causes and conditions.

I observe that all things—from [the aforementioned] up to—being universally moistened like rain.

Mountains and rivers are likened to sentient beings who possess the seven kinds of five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Just as rain falls without discriminating between ravines and valleys, the Buddha’s teaching is impartial;

thus, there is no distinction between "this" and "that. Those with the capacity for awakening are "this," while those lacking such capacity are "that. Planting roots of goodness is "affection," whereas acting in opposition is...

To regard [the Buddha's] work as one's own and the work of Māra as that of another is a form of aversion. [The Buddha’s presence] comes through the resonance of conditions and departs when those conditions are exhausted.
To enter into the ultimate reality is "sitting"; to emerge in provisional means is "standing. The Buddha observes sentient beings in this manner;

this is precisely the intent of the equal rain falling upon mountains and rivers. This verse praises the countless billions of kinds of sentient beings who come to the Buddha’s dwelling to hear the Dharma.

From the noble and the humble, the high and the low (up to) being without indolence or weariness;

from the noble and the humble, even down to those of sharp and dull faculties—these are explained through the successive transmission of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). (The noble and humble/high and low refer to rank;

From the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to [the bodhisattvas], each attains increase.
Regarding "dwelling in their final body," there are two interpretations. One says: the followers of the two vehicles have already severed the pervasive afflictions and dwell in their final body.
If one does not encounter a Buddha or hear the Dharma, and instead attains realization by extinguishing one's lifespan, then the principle of "increase" (vṛddhi) is not established.

Second, it is said that when those of the Two Vehicles attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and abide in their final bodies, they are ripened by the five flavors of the Buddha’s teaching and enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Hearing the Mahāyāna and attaining understanding therein is precisely what constitutes "increase. △ The third section, consisting of one and a half lines, pertains to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*).
It increases.
If all bodhisattvas [from this point] attain increase and firmness, this is the wisdom of the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā-prajñā*).

In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), there is further growth; moreover, there is growth attained while abiding in dhyāna.
Question: Is the "single cloud and single rain" the same as or different from the "single sound"? Answer: On the lower stages, the single sound causes others to hear.

There is one Dharma. The Buddha, with a single voice, is understood differently by each according to their kind. Now, this "single cloud and single rain" is precisely that single voice adapted to each type.
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "The Buddha preaches the Four Truths with a single voice;
the five [monks] hear it as human speech, the eighty thousand devas hear it as celestial speech, and the beings in hell and the yakṣas each hear it in their own language. Thus he proclaims.

Reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven, this constitutes the Brahma-voice (*brahmasvara*). It is also the most wondrous, pure sound obtained as a karmic reward of the Buddha, which is designated as the "Brahma-voice.
If it were merely a Brahma-voice obtained as a karmic reward, then people would not hear it; even if they heard it, they would not understand it.
(The first verse concludes the analogy of differentiation mentioned above. △ The second five lines constitute the verse on the analogy of non-differentiation. Furthermore:
This consists of two parts. The first one and a half verses explain the distinctions within non-distinction.
Thus, from "Kāśyapa, [it is] like a great cloud" up to "each attains its own true fruit," these verses correspond to the aforementioned non-distinction of the single-flavored rain.
"Nourishing people like flowers so that each attains its fruit" is the verse summarizing the aforementioned distinctions.
(The next) two and a half lines summarize both distinction and non-distinction.
"Kāśyapa, you should know" (up to) "all shall attain Buddhahood.
Next, "Kāśyapa, you should know that by means of various causes and conditions," and so forth, clarifies the provisional (*upāya*). The provisional is differentiation;
it corresponds to what has been produced above. Now, "for your sakes," clarifies the real (*tattva*). The real is non-differentiation; it corresponds to [the ultimate].
This refers to the preceding stage. One who has not attained extinction (nirvāṇa) has not yet crossed over the transformation-death (pariṇāmi-śarīra).

The reason for speaking specifically of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) is that their commitment to their respective goals is firm. Humans and devas do not regard their fruits as nirvāṇa, and Bodhisattvas do not take realization midway.
As for this "Bodhisattva path," when a Bodhisattva practices the path, they must also sever the pervasive afflictions (āsrava). You have already severed them.

Exhaustion (*kṣaya*) is itself the Bodhisattva path. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that although one may regress after having generated the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), the wholesome roots previously cultivated are not destroyed;
thus, one attains the same fruit as later on. Regarding the statement that "the wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) of the two vehicles is the Bodhisattva path":

because the followers of the two vehicles cling to their own fruits, [the text] dismissively refers to it as "the Bodhisattva path. Here, "path" (*mārga*) refers to the cause (*hetu*). Question: Do Bodhisattvas not also have fruits?
The *Xinyi* (Commentary on Faith) states: "Attaining the Way is the attainment of the fruit. The *Dapin* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra) states: "Existence of dharmas is the Bodhisattva’s Way;

non-existence of dharmas is the Bodhisattva’s fruit. Why, then, does it not say that this [non-existence] is the Bodhisattva’s fruit? Answer: This meaning should also be understood as applicable here.

What is now stated—whether it be the Way or the fruit—is all a cause for Buddhahood. A cause is precisely the Way. (In some versions, following this passage, there are further prose sections and verses.)

This section was translated by Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty and is titled the *Extended Version of the Lotus Sutra*. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā*) and the "Chapter on Exhortation to Resolve" (*Anuparīndanā*) have been moved to the end; the remainder remains as before, with no alterations. (The "Simile of the Herbs" chapter concludes.)
△ First, the presentation of the chapter titles; second, the explanation of the scriptural text. Now, for the first:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Six, "The Bestowal of Prophecies" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*).

Regarding the term *vyākaraṇa* in the Sanskrit original, this is translated here as "bestowal of prophecy. In various sutras, it is categorized under the section on "Bestowal of Prophecy. [End of] Pure [Exposition].

It is called "Cloud. One receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa) from the arising of Suchness; one receives the prediction from the cessation of Suchness. Since Suchness is without arising or cessation, one knows there is no prediction. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* (*Siyi jing*) says:

"I vow not to hear the name of 'prediction'. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Dapin jing*) says: "Receiving a prediction is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). How is it then in this present sutra? Answer:
If one perceives a prediction or a person who is predicted, this perception must be shattered. The Bodhisattva’s vow for prediction—this is the prediction.

One must grant [predictions]. They are recorded from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet they do not exist from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The four *siddhāntas* (the four ways of teaching) adapt to the occasion, as explained below.

If it is a general prediction, it is like that at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter. If it is a specific prediction, it is as explained after the three weeks. If it is a prediction based on the direct cause (*hetu*), it is like that of Sadāparibhūta.
If it is a prediction based on the contributing cause (*pratyaya*), it is like the ten kinds of offerings in the "Dharma Master" chapter. If...

The Prediction Based on the Conditioned Cause (*pratyaya-hetu-vyākaraṇa*). This is like the prediction given to those endowed with the three roots. If it is a prediction based on the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*), it is extensive; if it is a prediction based on the conditioned cause, it is limited.
It may be a prediction that is delayed, or one that is swift, or one given by a Buddha—as in this text—or a prediction given by a Bodhisattva, as in the case of Sadāparibhūta.

Although there is no fixed determination regarding the kalpa or the land, such a prediction may still be obtained. Furthermore, there is the "prediction in advance" (*pūrva-vyākaraṇa*), as in the *Pūrva-nirmita-ratha-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Phantom City).
The one who has come is this disciple (who may be slow, like a *śrāvaka*, or swift, like the Dragon Girl). Other sutras record only bodhisattvas and not those of the two vehicles;
they record only the good and not the evil; they record only males and not females; they record only humans and devas and not animals. This present sutra records all of these.
If there are four kinds of records regarding the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, this sutra possesses them all. [This has not yet been] initiated.
The bestowal of predictions upon the mind is as described in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging": the prediction of the three turnings regarding the manifestation of the mind of non-arising.

(Furthermore, while other sutras generally bestow predictions of the ultimate fruit of the Dharma-body for the sake of Bodhisattvas, in this chapter, only the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] are predicted, as explained previously and subsequently.
Originally, all Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the great causal event, to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Now, the Great...
The matter has been made manifest; the Buddha’s teaching is complete. Sentient beings have entered [the path], fulfilling the Buddha’s original intent and satisfying their own vows.

It is now appropriate to bestow the prediction (vyākaraṇa), just as a father who encounters his son would surely entrust him with his wealth. Furthermore, the manifestation of non-arising must arise from genuine understanding;
thus, the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is unmistakable. Moreover, because they have clearly realized the Buddha-nature, the prediction is granted. [This applies] to the Śrāvakas.
Entering into reality. Because they are certain to become Buddhas, they receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). It is also called "receiving the decision" (*jue*) or "receiving the prophecy" (*bie*).

"To bestow" (*shou*) has the meaning of giving; "to receive" (*shou*) has the meaning of obtaining; "prediction" (*ji*) refers to recording the event; "decision" (*jue*) means certainty; and "prophecy" (*bie*) means a clear explanation.

When those of middle capacity hear the Dharma and the parable for the second time, the three are opened up to reveal the one, and they fully comprehend and understand it. The Tathāgata then confirms their realization. Although...
He knows within himself that he will become a Buddha, yet the details of the matter remain uncertain.

If he were to receive the Buddha’s sincere word, being granted the prediction of his future fruition, with the kalpa and the land determined and the timing of his realization—whether near or far—clearly prophesied, he would experience great joy.

Because he now receives this from the Buddha and thereby attains his name, it is called the "Chapter on the Prediction" (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta). This passage is the fourth section of the allegorical exposition; the preceding three sections all employed metaphors.

This is explained therein. Within this, the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is also recorded by means of parables; there is no fifth section, as it merely refers back to what precedes or follows and is not discussed in detail.
Furthermore, in the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, it is clarified that all [beings] receive nourishment and each attains growth.

first, the formal bestowing of predictions upon those of medium capacity; second, the granting of permission for the account of past lives for those of inferior capacity.

The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma, Chapter Seven: The Parable of the Phantom City.
An explanation of the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter: "Phantom" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to that which is produced by supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).

Because of supernormal power, that which did not exist suddenly comes into being; this is called "phantom. It serves to prevent wrongdoing and ward off enemies, and is thus termed a "city. Internally, it corresponds to the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
This is the work of skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). By the power of skillful means and wisdom, that which does not exist is spoken of as existing;

this teaching is employed for the sake of transformation, to restrain thoughts and ward off views, and is termed "Nirvāṇa. It provides a temporary respite, leading one into the place of jewels; though it is not ultimate, it is called "extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*).

Because it is a provisional and expedient arrangement, it is called a "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*). This is analogous to what was previously explained (i.e., shaking a tree to produce wind, or raising a fan to create a breeze).

"Like the moon," etc., is an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*). Regarding the classification of teachings: if one follows the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, they conceive of Nirvāṇa as a state of security and give rise to the thought of final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*).
For the Two Vehicles of the Shared Teaching, it is the same as in the Tripiṭaka. The Bodhisattvas, however, are not so.

The *Śāstra* states: When a Bodhisattva passes through a perilous place, one foot enters the city while the other remains outside the gate. Out of mindfulness for sentient beings, he returns from the city to the peril;
he vows to sustain his residual habits (*vāsanā*) and enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), rather than taking emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as a final realization.

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not say that the city is like an illusion; it uses the city to defend against dangers and takes the city as a skillful means (upāya) for passing through its gates.
It does not claim that this [attainment] is the ultimate. The Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) knows there are no thieves or illness, and thus a city is unnecessary.
Since this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching, the title designates the "illusory city" as the very place of treasure (ratnasthāna). This chapter...
Regarding the explanation of the causal circumstances (*nidāna*), those of inferior faculties attain awakening; thus, it should be titled the "Chapter on Past Lives. Answer:

At the beginning of this chapter, the causal circumstances are explained in detail, while at the end, the parable of the conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) is concluded. If one follows the former, it should be called "Past Lives"; however, since the sutra follows the latter, it speaks of the "conjured city.
Furthermore, for those of superior faculties whose doubts are thin, it suffices to take the seven days of contemplation under the Bodhi tree to clarify the karmic conditions (*ālambana*).
Those of middling faculties have a dense doubt; [the Buddha] probes and takes up the unsurpassed path taught by twenty trillion Buddhas as the karmic conditions for them.

Those of inferior faculties have even thicker doubt; thus, he clarifies that their karmic conditions were established long ago in past lives. If one traces back from the beginning of those past lives...

It clarifies the causes and conditions of the distant past; it speaks of the interim period; it refers to the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*) to clarify the provisional stage, and it refers to the "jeweled destination" (*ratna-sthāna*) to clarify the ultimate goal.
The compiler of the sutra designates this chapter from a central position so as to encompass both the beginning and the end.

Following this logical convenience, it is called the "Chapter on the Transformed City. Question: The transformed city is provisional, while the jeweled destination is real. For what reason is the real abandoned in favor of the provisional? Answer: Because...
Knowing that the city is a transformation, one then knows that the place of jewels is real; thus, by designating the transformation, the reality is not lost. △ Next, the scriptural text is explained.

△ The Threefold Enlightenment is Perfectly Accomplished.

As for the fact that the Buddha-dharma does not manifest before them: it is because the realm of sentient beings has not yet been emptied, and by the power of their vows, they cause the Buddha-dharma not to manifest. After ten minor kalpas have passed, the teachings of all Buddhas will then manifest before them, and they will attain perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).

When merit is perfected and the Way is manifested, one naturally becomes a Buddha; this was not the original vow of the Buddha. An ancient analogy compares it to a fire-stirring stick: the intent is to stir the fire, yet after stirring for a long time, the stick spontaneously ignites, though it was originally not intended to burn.

Stirring the fire symbolizes wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*); the burning of the stick symbolizes cessation-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). When wisdom and cessation are complete, they are accomplished without being sought. Nevertheless, although Buddhahood is attained, the vow to deliver sentient beings remains unfulfilled; thus, even after fruition, one continues to practice the causes until the end of the future, without ever reaching an end.
