The twelve aspects of the teaching and the twelve aspects of practice. Regarding the twelve aspects of the teaching, these refer to the demonstration, the exhortation, and the realization.

Regarding the twelve aspects of practice, in each of the three turnings, there arise vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Furthermore, the twelve aspects of the teaching function as the means of turning, while the twelve aspects of practice function as that which is turned.
The twelve aspects (*ākāra*) constitute the wheel; the twelve teachings do not. (Regarding the distinction between what is the wheel and what is not: "wheel" has the meaning of crushing and grinding.
Since only the teachings constitute the practice, how could they crush delusion? If they do not crush delusion, they cannot even bear the name of a "wheel.

If one establishes the meaning of two wheels, then regarding the eyes, knowledge, clarity, and awakening—these four mental states applied to the forty-eight factors across the four noble truths of the higher and lower realms—they constitute sixteen moments of mind. That is to say, [the four] regarding suffering...

Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) is the eye; Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is wisdom (*jñāna*); subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) is clarity (*vidyā*); and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is awakening (*buddhi*).
Patience is the cause and knowledge is the fruit. The same applies to the remaining three truths (*satya*). Thus, sixteen moments of mind (*citta*) are established.

Since individuals with the three faculties each attain these sixteen moments of mind, forty-eight mental applications (*ākāra*) are established. The twelve truths (comprising four truths for each of the three turnings) constitute the teaching (*deśanā-dharma*).
The Wheel: These twelve practices constitute the wheel of practice (*caryā-cakra*). As for the wheel of teaching (*deśanā-cakra*), it is that which is able to turn;

it is solely the power of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) that turns it, and what is turned thereby consists of the twelve teachings. If it is the wheel of practice, there are twelve teachings that can turn it, and the practices being turned are likewise twelve.
These may apply to three types of persons or be restricted to a single person; here, we proceed according to the three [stages] of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).

A person of sharp faculties, upon hearing this teaching and turning toward it, immediately gives rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Because these three types of people together constitute the full expression, it is called the "twelvefold aspect.
As for that which śramaṇas and others cannot turn: since they have not even heard it, they are unable to know it.
How much less could they turn it? Although the Brahmins heard its name, they did not understand its principle; the same was true for Māra and Brahmā.
As for "turning," it means to turn this Dharma-measure into the minds of others, causing them to attain awakening and shatter the sixty-two views.
This is what is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. Because it lacks this quality, it cannot be turned by Māra, Brahmā, or others.

The Four Truths of the Hīnayāna take arising and ceasing as their essence, whereas the Mahāyāna takes non-arising as its essence. As for the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, they are merely specific aspects;

upon close observation, they are simply the Four Truths. When considered in terms of Suffering and its Accumulation, they consist of ignorance through old age and death; when considered in terms of the Path...
With cessation, there is the cessation of ignorance, and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, those who contemplate them with inferior wisdom attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; those who contemplate them with middling wisdom attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
those who contemplate them with superior wisdom attain the enlightenment of a bodhisattva; and those who contemplate them with the highest of superior wisdom attain the enlightenment of a Buddha."△
Second, attaining the Way by hearing the Dharma.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans (at the first assembly when the Truths and Dependent Origination were taught), six hundred trillion nayutas of people, because they did not grasp at any dharmas, attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*). They all attained [it].

Profound and wondrous meditative concentration, the three insights and six supernormal powers, and the possession of the eight liberations. The second [is the Vaipulya Mahāyāna]; the third [is Prajñā].

The fourth [period] (that is, when he later preached the Lotus Sūtra): while he was preaching the Dharma, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and nayutas in measure, likewise attained liberation of mind from the outflows by virtue of not grasping at any dharmas. From that time onward, [it continued].
The assembly of śrāvakas was immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation. [Supplementary Note:

Because they do not accept any phenomena, their minds are liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). For acceptance is itself suffering; by not accepting, the mind is liberated from all outflows. This is indeed the natural principle. The Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated here as "right reception" (*shèngshòu*). Not receiving any sensations is called "right reception. Question:

The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses of sentient beings arise and perish in every moment, and the three types of sensation (*vedanā*) are fiercely active. How can one not receive them? Answer: The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Seeing and that which is seen..."

The conditions, as well as the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally, they do not exist. This seeing and these conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. If a practitioner can, regarding this, believe and understand it as it truly is, and deeply investigate it within themselves to awaken to and clarify the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), then there will be no sensation.

There being no sensation, there is no "one who feels," nor even the non-experience of such non-feeling. This is called the non-acceptance of all dharmas. Thus, the mind attains liberation from all outflows (*āsrava*) and awakens to and clarifies the true mark.

Furthermore, as for why the *Sūtra* does not mention the *Avataṃsaka* when enumerating the four periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], it is simply a textual omission; in principle, it must certainly be included. From this point onward, the phrase "immeasurable and incalculable śrāvakas" clarifies that those who heard the Dharma and attained the Way were so numerous that they could not be measured or counted. One must...

Know that these śrāvakas are all great śrāvakas who were the peers of the sixteen princes; they have fully practiced the five samādhis and will later hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* together with us. That is to say, we of today are truly śrāvakas who, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, cause all to hear;

we are not śrāvakas of the limited teachings. (The first turning of the half-character wheel of Dharma is concluded). △ Second, the second prince’s renewed request for the turning of the full-character wheel of Dharma, in two parts:
First, the seven sections beginning with "leaving home"; Second, the formal establishment of karmic affinity. The first [part] has seven [sections].
Within this section, there are seven parts: first, the renunciation; second, the request for the Dharma; third, those being led also renounce; fourth, the Buddha accepts the request;
fifth, among the assembly at that time, some understand while others do not; sixth, the preaching of the Dharma; seventh, having finished speaking, he enters meditative concentration. Now, the first.
At that time, the sixteen princes... [up to] sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"The various faculties" refers to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Because the six faculties are pure, they are said to be "penetrating and sharp. Furthermore, because the six faculties function interchangeably, they are said to be "penetrating";
because they enter the realm of the Buddha, they are said to be "sharp. "Wisdom is clear and lucid" means opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
This is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. △ Second, the request for the Dharma. They all addressed the Buddha, saying...
[up to] "...that which is contemplated by their profound resolve, the Buddha himself knows and witnesses.
That Buddha first preached the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]. All the merits of the Great Vehicle for his children were fully complete. Out of compassion for those in other directions...

This constitutes a second request for the Buddha to reveal the provisional and manifest the real. The phrase "the śrāvakas have all already attained accomplishment" clarifies that their obstacles have been removed and their spiritual faculties have been activated;

it is for this reason that they make the request. The statement "our aspiration is for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision" indicates that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* exclusively elucidates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
To be intent solely upon this is precisely to request the fulfillment of the "full letters" (the Mahāyāna), thereby setting aside the "half-letters" (the Hīnayāna).
The text is as clear as this. △ Third, those who were to be led forth also renounced the household life.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (until) the King immediately granted his permission.
△ Fourth, the Four Buddhas Accept the Invitation.
At that time, those Buddhas accepted the invitation of the śrāmaṇera (up to) "they all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered [it].

Regarding the phrase "after twenty thousand kalpas," since the previous bestowal has already been long established, it cannot be that there was nothing occurring in the interim; this is in anticipation of the subsequent text.
[The Buddha] thought: "Within twenty thousand kalpas, he will certainly preach the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
The text says: "He preaches the six pāramitās and various matters of supernatural powers (abhijñā). Prajñā is the practice; supernatural powers are the phenomena.
Most Vaipulya sūtras clarify inconceivable phenomena, which are the practices. Furthermore, the verse states: "Discriminating the true Dharma" refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
This clarifies the meaning of the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). △ At that time, among the assembly, some understood while others did not.
When this sutra was being preached (until the point where it says), "millions of billions of kinds [of beings] all gave rise to doubt."
The sixteen śrāmaṇeras, those of the two vehicles, and those who attained faith and understanding immediately were exceptions;
the remaining ten million all gave rise to doubt and confusion. This group of the unenlightened was precisely the one that established the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* connection with the sixteen sons.
△ Sixth: Preaching the Dharma for Eight Thousand Kalpas.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting.
△ Seven: After finishing the preaching, he entered meditative concentration.
Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in dhyāna-concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
Having finished expounding the Dharma, he entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This was precisely the proximate cause for establishing a karmic connection.

Because the Buddha had entered absorption and did not emerge, the assembly filled with doubt and hesitation had no one to consult. Later, on the sixteenth day, he preached the sutra again for those who still did not understand.
In the text, the location where he entered absorption is clarified as being a quiet chamber; "entering absorption" refers specifically to abiding therein.

Regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*): the duration of entering into concentration is precisely eighty-four thousand *kalpas* (the repetition "云云" [yún yún] indicates that the meaning of the duration is fully explained herein).

How could the Buddhas ever not be in union with concentration? It is simply because the capacities of sentient beings reside within the sixteen periods; the limits for establishing the karmic connection (*kalyāṇa-mitra-bandhana*) require such a length of time.

This concludes the seven sections beginning with the request for the Dharma by the renunciant, as described in the subsequent text. △ Second, the actual establishment of the karmic connection. This consists of two parts.
First is the formation of a karmic connection through the discourse on the Dharma; second is the formation of a karmic connection through the discourse by way of analogy.

Regarding the discourse on the Dharma, there are three parts: first, clarifying the formation of a karmic connection together in the past; second, clarifying their mutual encounters during the intervening period;

third, clarifying that he now returns to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Regarding the first [of these three], there are four points: first, knowing that the Buddha has entered meditative concentration; second, the prince’s secret lecture; third...
First, the multitude attained benefit. Second, the Buddha arose from his meditative absorption. Third, he praised the sixteen bodhisattvas;

it was because the Buddha had entered absorption that they were able to speak. Fourth, the Buddha knew that his work of transformation was nearing completion and would no longer bring these individuals to spiritual maturity.
Therefore, he caused the prince to form a karmic connection with them.
Furthermore, knowing that these beings would surely attain ultimate liberation through the prince, he entered meditative absorption and did not emerge for a long time. This is the first instance.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration, [proceeded as follows].
II. The Prince’s Re-exposition:
Each ascended the Dharma seat (up to) extensively expounding and analyzing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
△ Third, the benefit of preaching the Dharma.
Each and every one [of them] was led across to the mind of *samyaksambodhi*.

Because they all gave rise to the bodhicitta, it is said that they were "led across. When they first gave rise to this mind, they made the vow: "I shall become a Buddha. Thus, [they have already] done so.
Having completed the deliverance [of beings], he did not employ the single Buddha-vehicle by teaching it as three.
△ Fourth, the Buddha arises from samādhi, praising and exhorting faith. This section further contains two parts: first, the formal praise of the sixteen bodhisattvas.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū (up to: reveals and instructs sentient beings so that they may enter therein.
△ Second, exhorting others to draw near:
"You all should repeatedly draw near... [to] the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s *samyaksambodhi*."
(I. The conclusion of the formation of karmic connections in the past. △ Second, explaining the constant meeting and encountering throughout the intermediate period.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... until "to this day, it is not exhausted."
There are three types of encounters. First, those who encounter [the teaching] and constantly receive the Mahāyāna;

these individuals have already achieved realization during the interim and have not reached the present [state]. Second, those who encounter [the teaching] but, having encountered a regression from the Mahāyāna, are instead received with the Hīnayāna;

these individuals have not yet fully exhausted [their karmic conditions] during the interim, and now they are able to hear the Mahāyāna teachings once again. Third, those who merely encounter [the teaching].
Small. Regardless of encountering the Great, if one has not yet crossed over in the interim, then even now it is not exhausted;
only when one begins to receive the Great, up until attaining the Way after extinction, is this the case. Question:

If it takes as much time as the number of atoms described above to finally attain Arhatship, one should know that the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) must be extremely difficult to reach. Answer: One explanation says that the Great Sage—
Skillful means. Relying on the four *siddhāntas*, he speaks in this way: sometimes he says the Buddha-way is long and distant, and sometimes he says the Buddha-way is easily accomplished.
To those who feel weary of its length, he speaks of it as short; to those who conceive the thought that it is easy, he speaks of it as long.

Sometimes it is to arouse past roots of goodness, sometimes to accord with worldly desires, and sometimes so that by hearing these explanations of length and brevity, they may immediately enter the [first] stage.

One meaning: it should be understood that all these are expedient practices of the four *siddhāntas*, intended merely to lead those of true practice into the Way (the section on "constantly meeting one another in the interim" concludes here).
△ Third, clarifying that today he returns to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*. This passage further has two parts: first, reconciling the ancient with the present;
second, clarifying the return to preaching the *Lotus Sūtra*. Regarding the reconciliation of the ancient with the present, there are further two parts: the first...
The Master’s [teaching] across the ancient and modern eras; second, the disciples’ [practice] across the ancient and modern eras. First:
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you... until you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The sixteen *śrāmaṇeras* represent the past; those who become Buddhas in the eight directions represent the present.
△ Next, the assembly of disciples consists of two parts concerning the ancient and the modern. First, the assembly of present disciples.
"O bhikṣus, those of us who were śrāmaṇeras [at that time] are these present śrāvaka disciples.
Furthermore, there are four [categories] in the present: first, those who do not regress, who abide in *sambodhi*; second, these sentient beings who have regressed, who now abide as śrāvakas;
third, 'For what reason? and so forth, which explains the meaning of gradual entry; fourth, 'At that time...'"

The section "At that time, those who were transformed" below correctly concludes the ancient and modern [accounts]. These four sections are as they appear in the text; there is no need for further analytical explanation.
△ Second, the assembly of disciples after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples [who,] up to the point of excluding those who have heard the Tathāgatas’ skillful means in preaching the Dharma, will harbor doubts, saying:
"Those of the present age have been able to hear the Buddha preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter the One Vehicle;

they can thus be included among those with whom a karmic connection has been established. But as for those of the future, they will not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before entering parinirvāṇa—how could such people ever abandon [their attachments]?"
"Small [vehicle practitioners] shall attain entry into the One Vehicle. The commentary explains: "Although it is said they have attained extinction (nirvāṇa), in the end they will all gather to hear:
'I am a Buddha in another land,' and thus they shall hear this sutra. Regarding "another land," this refers to the remaining lands within the general teachings of the Three Vehicles.
"Except for those who speak through the skillful means of the Tathāgatas" serves to sever doubts; these three are spoken of as skillful means, for in reality there are no three.
(Concluding the comparison of past and present). △ Second, explaining that the Dharma Flower is now being preached again.

This also has three parts: first, the purity of the assembly; second, the actual preaching of the Lotus Sutra; third, the explanation of the previous intention for bestowing the three vehicles. Now, the first.
If the Tathāgata, O bhikṣus, knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, he enters into profound meditative concentration.
When the time for parinirvāṇa arrives—that is, when the Buddhas have appeared in the world and the teaching of the path is nearing its completion—he then preaches this sūtra.

Just as Kāśyapa Buddha, Candrasūryapradīpa, and others, entered *nirvāṇa* immediately after finishing the preaching of this sutra, so too did Śākyamuni, having finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, announce his imminent extinction.
Those whose assembly was pure obtained the benefit of the Tripiṭaka teachings and were spared from calamity.
Those with firm faith and understanding attained mutual trust in their hearts regarding the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) teachings. They thoroughly realized emptiness.

Regarding the Dharma: having heard the teaching of Prajñā, one attains thorough realization within the dharma of emptiness; this refers to the intention behind the turning of the wheel of the teaching.
△ Second, the formal exposition of the Lotus Sūtra.
He then assembled the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas (until the point where it says) "only through the single Buddha-vehicle can one attain extinction.

Regarding the assembly of bodhisattvas: this refers to the gathering of kinsmen and others for whom this sutra is preached. The preceding section explained "kinsmen" as referring to the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body who serve as the retinue of influence and response.
Verifying its meaning through this passage, the significance becomes clear. [Thus it is said: "He assembled the various bodhisattvas."
This assembly of kinsmen and the host of śrāvakas is his calling upon his son. △ Third, explaining the three intentions behind the gift:
"Bhikṣus, you should know" (up to) "if such a person hears this, they will immediately believe and accept it."
Question: If there are no followers of the Two Vehicles who attain extinction (nirvāṇa), for what reason did the Tathāgata previously preach the provisional teachings?
It is said that the Tathāgata knew that sentient beings possessed inferior dispositions and desires, were attached to the five sensory objects, and were afflicted by the five turbidities;

therefore, he first preached the three [vehicles] to cause them to break through their afflictions and escape from calamity, and later preached the One [Vehicle]. Once the teaching of the One Dharma was completed—[Note: This parable of the "transformed city" and the "jeweled destination" in this sutra is intended for the Two Vehicles...]

It is taught that the *Avataṃsaka* also contains this meaning; it was spoken for the sake of the eighth stage, the Immovable Bodhisattva. One should contemplate these two sutras together, for only then will one understand the gates of provisional and ultimate cultivation and realization, and not become stranded halfway.

△ Second, the parable of establishing a connection through teaching. This consists of both opening and closing sections. The opening parable is divided into two parts. First is the Parable of the Guide.
The first analogy is like the initial assembly for a lecture, where a great connection is established together. The second analogy, that of the guide, is like meeting midway;
this refers to the current preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

If they had met midway and heard the Dharma from me, all would have attained *sambodhi*, and thus no analogy would have been provided for such persons. However, if they met midway but now remain as śrāvakas, [the analogy applies].
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the metaphor established specifically for these people. Regarding the first metaphor of the guide, there are five textual sections.

First is the metaphor of the "five hundred *yojanas*," which illustrates the aforementioned multitude who have not yet crossed over and who take pleasure in and are attached to the various realms of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
2. The analogy of the perilous and evil paths illustrates the aforementioned multitudes who have not yet crossed over;
their afflictions and defilements are heavy, making it difficult for them to believe in or understand the Tathāgata’s wisdom. 3.

The analogy of the many multitudes precisely illustrates the hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings who all give rise to doubt and fail to understand. 4. The desire to pass beyond this path and reach the precious treasure.

The analogy of the location illustrates the assembly that heard and subsequently preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* mentioned above; their Mahāyāna faculties have been awakened, and they desire to reach the place of treasure.
Fifth is the analogy of the single guide, which illustrates the sixteenth prince mentioned above. First, there is the analogy of the five hundred *yojanas*.
For example, there are five hundred *yojanas*. Regarding these five hundred *yojanas*:
the realms of retribution within the triple world constitute three hundred; the remaining lands constitute four hundred;
and the realm of true retribution constitutes five hundred. The subsequent passage provides a summary analogy, stating: "Knowing all births and deaths, [and yet] births and deaths..."

This clarifies that there are five hundred locations. However, the Buddha’s intent is difficult to comprehend and requires further extensive explanation. The delusions of vision (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) constitute one hundred;

the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*)—namely, the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), and anger (*pratigha*)—constitute two hundred; and the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) constitute three hundred.
(Elation, pride, ignorance, attachment to the realm of form, and attachment to the formless realm)—the "dust-sands" constitute four hundred, and ignorance constitutes five hundred.

The subsequent text combines these with metaphors, stating that "afflictions," "perils," and "evil realms" support one another in their meaning. Entering the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) enables one to pass through three hundred;

entering the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) enables one to pass through four hundred; entering the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*) enables one to pass through five hundred. The subsequent combined text states: "Skillfully knowing..."
The characteristics of the perilous path being either passable or obstructed correspond to the mutual support of the two meanings of the five hundred [teachings] regarding both cause and effect.
△ Second, the analogy of the perilous and evil paths.
"A perilous and evil path, a desolate and uninhabited place of fear.

Regarding "perilous and evil path," it is a metaphor for the causes and effects of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The distinction between fragmented and transformative [rebirth] constitutes the perilous nature of the effect.
The five abodes of views and thoughts constitute the perilous nature of the cause. Because of these causes and effects, it is called an "evil path."

Furthermore, regarding "no person": there are two kinds of paths. First, that which is vast and desolate, yet has a person upon whom one can rely; second, that which is vast and desolate, and has no person upon whom one can rely.
This is like having nirvana within saṃsāra, or bodhi within affliction (*kleśa*); although it is vast and desolate, there is still a person upon whom one can rely.
If, however, within saṃsāra and affliction there were neither nirvana nor bodhi—just as there is no disease within medicine—then [it would be like] disease...
There is no medicine within; this is utterly desolate, with no one upon whom one can rely. △ Third, the analogy of the great multitude.
"If there were a great multitude"—this refers to the multitude of beings being transformed by the prince who have not yet been delivered. △ Fourth, the desire to cross the perilous pass.
The analogy of the path:

wishing to traverse this road to reach a place of rare treasures represents the arousal of the capacity for the Mahāyāna, desiring to pass through this perilous path to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that one reaches a place of rare treasures.
△ Fifth, the analogy of the single guide:
There was a single guide, wise, intelligent, and far-sighted, who well understood the characteristics of the dangers and the passages, the obstructions and the openings, of the perilous path.
This "guide" is none other than the original teacher Śākyamuni, the sixteenth prince. His eyes and ears were pure, as it says:

"Cleverness" (*cóng*) refers to the purity of the mental faculty (*manas*), which is termed "sharpness" (*lì*). In summary, this is the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). "Wisdom" (*zhì*) refers to the threefold wisdom within the single mind.

"Clarity" (*míng*) refers to being fully endowed with the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*). (Supplementary note: One who well knows the characteristics of the dangers of the path—whether it is passable or obstructed—is "clear.

To see no danger where there is danger is "passable"; to see danger where there is no danger is "obstructed. The Guide knows all such characteristics regarding delusion and awakening, passability and obstruction. (The first analogy of the Guide is concluded). △ Second, the Guide... [text continues]
The analogy of the guide consists of three parts: first, the analogy of the multitude being led, which illustrates those who originally formed karmic connections but have not yet attained liberation;

though their original conditions were lost, they are now led by the guide. Second, the analogy of weariness and retreat along the way, which illustrates those who encountered [the Buddha] midway, regressed from the Great Vehicle to embrace the Lesser, and found rest at the illusory city.
Third, the analogy of destroying the transformation and leading them to the place of treasure.
This is analogous to how, upon returning from above, [the father] preached the Lotus Sūtra and bestowed great chariots equally upon those in the burning house;
the meaning is the same as how, within the skillful means, he spoke only of the unsurpassed path. This is now the analogy for the multitude of people first brought along.
He leads the multitude with the intention of crossing over this peril.
As for the people he leads, they are generally a group of those with whom he has established karmic connections (*saṃbandha*). To discuss them specifically:

those who have already received great benefit in the past have finished being led; those who have not yet received great benefit are precisely the ones currently being led. If one calculates by the number of five hundred people, three...

"The ten sons" refers to those who have not yet attained awakening. △ Second, the parable of slackening and retreating midway. The text is divided into two parts: first, retreating from the Great [Vehicle];

second, being led toward the Small [Vehicle]. Retreating from the Great corresponds to the first part of the above [parable], while being led toward the Small corresponds to the third part of the above [parable].
The main section on regression is divided into three parts: First, regressing due to weariness midway: this corresponds to the aforementioned lack of great capacity for the higher path.
Second, speaking to the Guide: this corresponds to the aforementioned refusal of exhortation and admonition. "We are utterly exhausted" refers to the door of refusing exhortation;
"and yet we are terrified" refers to the door of refusing admonition. Third, being unable to proceed further: this corresponds to the aforementioned cessation of the transformative teaching.
Furthermore, those who now falter and retreat on the initial path—this multitude of people whom they lead faltering and retreating midway—what is meant by "midway"?
It does not mean halfway through the journey; rather, it refers to the point from the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up until reaching Buddhahood.
End. Because the intention to turn back arises between these two pillars, it is called the "Middle Way. △ Second, addressing the Guide:
He addresses the Guide, saying, "We are utterly exhausted and furthermore filled with fear."
Regarding "addressing the Guide," there is the universal guide of compassion, as the text says:
"There was a guide who led a great multitude of people. There is the guide with whom one forms a karmic connection, as the text says:
"The multitude of people being led addressed the guide. There is the guide of skillful wisdom, as the text says: "The guide [was many]..."
These are the various skillful means (*upāya*). There is inherently the Guide of True Wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), as the text says: "The Guide knows these people.
Now, when it says "informing the Guide," it specifically refers to informing the Guide who establishes karmic connections (*karmabandha*).

For by retreating from the Great [Vehicle], one undergoes extinction in the Great; by being received into the Small [Vehicle], one is born in the Small. This cycle of one birth and one extinction moves the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This is called "speaking white. The prince knew that he was retreating from the Great [Vehicle]. This refers to hearing what he spoke:
because his roots of goodness were feeble and obscured by ignorance, he said he was "exhausted," meaning he was weary of birth and death; this is termed "fear.
△ Third, being unable to advance further.
They cannot advance further. The path ahead is still long; now they wish to retreat. "Cannot advance further;
the path ahead is still long" means that the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the dust-like [afflictions] (*rajas*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are difficult to sever abruptly.

Nevertheless, by employing the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to receive them, they are not allowed to retreat to the realms of humans or devas; there is also the sense of advancing [in this way]. (1. Retreat)

[End of the first section]. △ Second, using the small [vehicle] to lead toward the three [vehicles]. First, lamenting the loss of the jewel: knowing there is the small [vehicle] but not the great, [the text says]:
"The Guide possesses many skillful means... why would he abandon the great, precious jewel and wish to turn back?"
△ Second, the analogy of creating a city by transformation. There are two parts to the actual application of the skillful means.
First, the actual creation: having formed this thought... [up to] he created a city.
The analogy of boarding the carriage says: "I have created these carriages for you all; since this city exists, it was necessary to first construct them.
△ Second, the teaching of the transformation.
He addressed the multitude, saying: "If you can proceed forward to the place of treasure, you may also go there.
This explains the parable of the conjured city, intended to encourage those above by pointing toward the realization of the goal. He said: "Do not be afraid; do not turn back."
"Exhorting to turn" means causing one to advance and enter the city. "Now, this great city...

up to 'acting according to one's will'" is "showing to turn," which indicates that the city is fit for dwelling. "If one enters this city, one will swiftly attain peace and security" is "turning through realization."
This praises the peace and security of the city. Although one may reach the place of jewels and proceed there, such words cannot be spoken openly before the present Buddha has revealed [the truth].
If one were to speak of past lives, such words would indeed be appropriate. Why?
Because once the intention to retreat was known, the Prince taught them, saying: "If you all fear birth and death, for now..."
First attain the news of nirvana, and only then proceed further upon the Great Path; this may also be done according to one’s own inclination.
It is also like people today who wish to study the Mahāyāna but fear and dread birth and death, and thus feel a desire to retreat.
If someone encourages them, saying, "You should first sever the afflictions and realize the stage of an Arhat, and only then seek the Great Path again," this can also be achieved. △ Third, Entering.
The analogy of the city illustrates the entry into awakening through the Three Vehicles.
At that time, the exhausted multitude conceives the thought of peace and security and experiences great joy;

this is the stage of hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). That which has never occurred before is the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Being freed from the evil realms is the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). This is a state of sublime bliss.

"Safety" refers to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). "Entering the city first" refers to the stage of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*). "Having already crossed over the perception [of fire]" refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

This is identical to the sons' desire for the burning house and their courageous and energetic pushing themselves out of it; they have already given rise to the perception that they have crossed over.

Just as one who has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) possesses the perception of peace; and just as one who has attained the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is further endowed with the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*).

Just as one who has already crossed over realizes the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*), which is like peace. (The second part, "receding from the Great Vehicle and connecting to the Small Vehicle" by creating the illusory city, is concluded.

△ Third: The Parable of Extinguishing the Illusion and Leading to the Place of Jewels. Regarding the "place of jewels," there are three passages in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: first, reaching Bodhi; [the others follow].

The mind [proceeds] in three stages: first, to the bodhicitta; second, to bodhi; and third, to the gate of great nirvāṇa. If one reaches the bodhicitta, one will necessarily reach both bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Regarding the citation of these three passages: reaching the bodhicitta refers to reaching the cause, while bodhi and nirvāṇa refer to reaching the fruit.
Within the fruit, there are wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); bodhi is wisdom, and nirvāṇa is abandonment. This is explained in full.

From beginning to end, it fully explains wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); therefore, it is said to consist of three sections. Furthermore, there are three meanings to "exceeding five hundred [leagues]":
first, escaping the evil realms; second, obtaining a good path; and third, reaching the place of treasure. Bodhicitta is what delivers one from the evil realms;
bodhisattva practice is like a level road; and the third is attaining the Buddha-way, which is like arriving at the place of treasure. As the subsequent text says: "Now, for..."
"What you have said is true; what you have attained is not cessation. This is the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the five hundred evil paths.
For the sake of the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), you should exert great diligence; this refers to practicing the excellent path of bodhi. You shall realize omniscience."
The ten powers and other Buddha-dharmas refer to attaining the path of the Buddha.
Why is it necessary that five hundred are saved by the Two Vehicles, three hundred by the Bodhisattvas, and five hundred by the Buddha Vehicle? Within this there are two [points].
First, knowing that [the breath] has ceased.
At that time, the guide knew that this multitude had attained rest and was no longer weary.
That they had attained rest and were no longer weary is analogous to the arrival of the time for supreme *nirvāṇa* and the subsequent purification of the assembly.
They are spared from calamity; this is the arousal of the great capacity. △ Second, proceeding toward the place of treasure:
[The Buddha] immediately extinguishes the conjured city and says to the multitude: "...it was merely for the purpose of providing rest."
He immediately extinguishes the conjured city and leads them toward the place of treasure. This is analogous to the aforementioned correct preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, which reveals the true aspect.
There are two meanings to the "place of treasure. If one takes the ultimate sense, then the supreme fruit is the place of treasure. As the preceding text states:
"Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true aspect of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). If one divides it according to stages of entry, then from the initial generation of the mind...
The mind abiding [in suchness] is the locus of the treasure. Therefore, the preceding text states: "The unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained spontaneously without seeking.
It further states: "One has obtained one's share of the Buddha-dharma; all that which a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been attained.

The locus of the treasure is near—the great city you previously saw was created by me as a provisional manifestation. This immediately employs the parable of the discarded authority to clarify the parable of the revealed reality. Above.
It is said: "The wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. These people should enter the Buddha-wisdom gradually by means of this Dharma. Question:
Both the chariot and the city are metaphors for the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Why is there no chariot [in the parable of the elder], while the city exists?

Furthermore, why is the chariot threefold while the city is one? And why is the chariot moving while the city is stationary? Answer: Outside the gate of the elder’s house, there is a chariot; because there is a partition [between it and the interior].
The sons do not see it, yet one may provisionally assume there are carts outside the gate; however, the carts themselves are actually non-existent.

A city situated in a remote place cannot be provisionally assumed [in the same way], and therefore the city is existent. Regarding the application of principle and teaching: one adheres to the three teachings to grasp the underlying principle.

Thus, all three teachings attain the principle; this is the "meaning" (the *artha*), which is like a city. When one takes the principle to interpret the teaching, since the principle is singular, these [distinct] teachings cease to exist;
they are like the chariots. Question: What is the difference between the transformation into the three chariots and the transformation into the city?
Answer: The three carts serve as metaphors for the Wheel of the Dharma (dharmacakra); the conjured city serves as a metaphor for the Wheel of Supernatural Powers (ṛddhicakra).

Furthermore, the carts are used as metaphors for sound, which the sons hear but do not see; the city is used as a metaphor for form (rūpa), and thus the sons enter the city and conceive the thought of peace and security.
(The second section on the analogy of leading and guiding is concluded.)

Question: Regarding the five locations where the three are opened up to reveal the one, what is the difference between them? Answer: Generally speaking, there is no difference; specifically speaking, there are distinctions.

First, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, the three are opened up to reveal the one from the perspective of the teaching (*śāsana*). The text says: "The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle;
there is neither a second nor a third. Second, in the "Burning House" chapter, it is from the perspective of practice (*pratipatti*).
The three [vehicles] are opened to reveal the one. "Vehicle" (*yāna*) carries the sense of transport; transport is a metaphor for practice. The text says:

"Each riding upon a great vehicle, they roam in the four directions, sporting and enjoying happiness. Within the third stage of faith and understanding, with respect to persons, the three are opened to reveal the one.
It concludes by identifying those who were hired laborers as being none other than the sons of the elder. We ourselves have from of old truly been the sons of the Buddha.

Furthermore, in the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, the provisional and the real are clarified through the distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation, without the need for rejection or selection.
It merely clarifies that sentient beings do not know [this], and thus the Buddha causes them to know it. If one understands the seven kinds of differentiation, one knows the provisional;

if one understands that they are equally based on a single principle without differentiation, one knows the real. Differentiation and non-differentiation are such that, while there is non-differentiation, there is differentiation.
This is distinct; it is merely intended to make this meaning known. It never says that "non-existence becomes existence.
This is spoken according to the Buddha’s own intention regarding the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate within his own practice; therefore, while the Buddha can know it, sentient beings do not.

This also serves to clarify the provisional and the ultimate through both what precedes and what follows (regarding "what precedes and what follows": it generally clarifies the four preceding chapters as well as the subsequent "City of Transformation"). It clarifies the knowledge and ignorance regarding the provisional and the ultimate.
This is the meaning of "not knowing. Fifth, the present "Transformation City" (pariṇāmika-nagara) primarily concerns the principle (*li*) of opening the three [vehicles] to reveal the one.

Both the "Jewel Place" (*ratnasthāna*) and the "Transformation City" refer to the two principles of the Small and Great [Vehicles]. By subverting the transformative principles of the Two Vehicles, it reveals the true, singular principle of the Jewel Place.
Below, in the fifth chapter on "Understanding through Realization," the raising of the jewel as a parable likewise concerns the principle. (End of preceding section on Opening)

The analogy concludes). △ Second, the application of the analogy. First, the formal application; second, the citation of the scriptural passage for application. Regarding the first two [points], the first is the application to the Guide:
"O Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is also like this... those who should go and should be delivered."
The Tathāgata corresponds to the analogy of the Guide. "You all" corresponds to the analogy of the multitude of people.

Knowing the dangers and perils of the various births, deaths, afflictions, and evil paths corresponds to the analogy of the treacherous and evil road. The two characters "long" and "distant" correspond to the analogy of the five hundred *yojanas*.
Those who "should go" and "should be delivered" correspond to those who are wise, intelligent, and capable of traversing the perilous path.

The analogy of reaching the place of the most precious treasure. △ Second, the combined analogy of leading and guiding has three parts. First, the combination regarding the lack of capacity for the Great [Vehicle]:
"If sentient beings were to hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle... they would have to undergo diligent suffering for a long time before they could achieve success."
The three characters "if sentient beings" correspond to the analogy of the multitude of people being led along.

"Hearing only the Single Buddha Vehicle, yet not desiring to see the Buddha, and so forth, undergoing arduous suffering for a long time before finally achieving success" corresponds to the analogy of becoming weary and retreating midway.

The preceding analogy concerned those who originally possessed the Great [Vehicle] but regressed to connect with the Small; now I shall apply it to the present context. Regarding the three points concerning regression from the Great [Vehicle] mentioned above:

"merely hearing of the One Buddha Vehicle" corresponds to the regression due to weariness midway, representing the sense of lacking the capacity (*anabhavyatā*). "Not wishing to see the Buddha" [corresponds to the other two].
"Unwilling to hear the Dharma" means that he addressed the Teacher above, refusing his exhortations and advice;

"he then formed this thought" means that he was unable to proceed further above, having ceased his intention to transform others. △ Second, the above describes the regression from the Great [Vehicle] and the reception of the Small [Vehicle].
The Buddha knows that these minds are timid and inferior, and thus speaks of two types of nirvāṇa.
"The Buddha knows these minds" corresponds to the phrase above regarding the Great Guide’s many skillful means; it refers to his intentional adaptation to their capacities.

"Timid and inferior" corresponds to the phrase above "these [beings] are to be pitied," indicating that he perceives they possess limited faculties. Consequently, he causes them to find rest within the Middle Way.
The "ancient one" refers to the manifestation of the conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*), which serves as a metaphor for the multitude entering the city.

To speak of two types of *nirvāṇa* midway through the journey means that while the delusions of the triple world (*tridhātu*) have been exhausted, the *avidyā* (ignorance) as vast as the sands of the Ganges has not yet been shattered; between these two poles, one distinguishes between *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
These are also the *nirvāṇas* of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. Furthermore, once the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) is exhausted, [the transformation...]

The *Yì* has not yet eliminated [the defilements]. Between the two deaths, they are distinguished as having remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) or being without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). Therefore, it is called the "Middle Way.

(1. The first section, the formal correspondence, is concluded. △ Second, the citation of the parable and its application. This cites and connects the parable of regression to correspond with the bestowal of the three vehicles.

(The first prose section ends). △ Second, the verse commentary. It consists of forty-nine and a half lines of verse, divided into two parts.
The first twenty-two and a half lines eulogize the causes for establishing the connection (*saṃbandha*). The subsequent twenty-seven lines eulogize the second part:

the actual establishment of the connection. Within the former, there are remote and proximate causes; the first eulogizes the remote causes, and the next eulogizes the proximate causes. [The remote causes...]

There are two parts. The first verse praises the Great Attainment of Enlightenment; the subsequent verses praise the arrival of the Brahmās from the ten directions requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Now, the first three lines praise the events preceding the attainment of enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... (down to) again rained down fresh and exquisite [flowers].
II. One verse-line correctly describes his attainment of the Way.

The sixteen sons of that Buddha (up to) shall fulfill me and all others.

The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; appearing but once in the course of a long eon, he awakens all living beings and causes all things to tremble.
[Section Two: Five Stanzas] These stanzas praise the Brahmās of the ten directions who come seeking the light.

In the various worlds of the eastern direction... (up to) turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

"The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom accepted the invitation of those people.

He proclaims various teachings (up to: "You all should know this.

"When this Dharma is proclaimed (up to: one cannot reach its limit."
(The first five lines, concerning the turning of the Small [Vehicle], are concluded). △ Second, five and a half lines: the Prince’s renewed request for the turning of the Great [Vehicle].

△ Five lines. This verse praises his entry into meditative concentration after finishing the preaching of the sutra.

After that Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a quiet chamber, sitting with single-minded focus in one place for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.

(The above concludes the verses on the occasion for establishing the connection. △ The second section consists of twenty-seven lines. The verses on the actual establishment of the connection are divided into two parts:
the first eight lines are verses on the Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), and the subsequent nineteen lines are verses on the parable-exposition (*upamādeśanā*). The above is the Dharma-exposition.

There are three [sections]. The first three lines of verse summarize the first [part]: the causal conditions established in the past. The next line summarizes the second [part]: their meeting in the interim. The final four lines summarize the third [part]: returning today to preach the Lotus Sūtra. Now, the first [section]: The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats, free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge had gained liberation of mind. Among them were the elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākapphiṇa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Revata, Kaphiṇa, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāmpati, Bhadrika, Pilindavatsa, Vakula, Bakkula, Svāgata, and others such as these—twelve thousand bhikṣus in all. There were also five thousand bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats, free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge had gained liberation of mind. Among them were the bhikṣuṇī Aśokadattā, Dhanadattā, Śrīdattā, Padmavati, Yaśodattā, Sugandhamukhā, and others such as these—five thousand bhikṣuṇīs in all. There were also ten thousand upāsakas, all of whom were arhats, free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge had gained liberation of mind. Among them were the upāsaka Citta, Uttara, Gaṅgika, Vatsa, Bhadra, Subhadra, and others such as these—ten thousand upāsakas in all. There were also twenty thousand upāsikās, all of whom were arhats, free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge had gained liberation of mind. Among them were the upāsikā Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā, Uttarā, Guptā, Yasovatī, Bhadrā, Subhadrā, and others such as these—twenty thousand upāsikās in all. At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by this great assembly, which was vast, sublime, and worthy of offerings. Having entered this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance from the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
