The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher.

Regarding the explanation of this chapter on the Dharma-preacher: there are five types of Dharma-preachers herein—first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; and fifth, transcribing.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies six types of Dharma-preachers: one receives [the teaching] through the power of faith and upholds it through the power of mindfulness.

To look at the text is "reading" (*pāṭha*). To not forget it is "reciting" (*svādhyāya*). To proclaim and explain it is "expounding" (*deśanā*). Since the scriptures of the sages are difficult to understand, they require interpretation;
thus, there are six kinds of Dharma-preachers (*dharmabhāṇaka*). Now, in this sutra, these are combined: upholding and reciting are made into one, and explaining and expounding are made into one.

Expounding and reciting constitute two; adding writing makes five. This is the specific analysis. Four persons are for one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*); one person is for transforming others (*para-vinaya*).
From a general perspective, if one follows the five dharmas oneself, one is a Dharma-master of self-practice; if one teaches the five dharmas to others, one is a Dharma-master of transforming others.
Because of following [the precepts] oneself, they are collectively called "disciples" (*śiṣya*); because of transforming others, they are collectively... [called "teachers"].

It is called the "Dharma Master" chapter; following this general sense, it is thus named the Dharma Master Chapter. If these are condensed into three [categories], then upholding [the teaching] is mental action (*manas-karman*);
reading, reciting, and explaining it is vocal action (*vāk-karman*); and writing it down is physical action (*kāya-karman*).

To discuss them individually, vocal action is for the sake of transforming others, while physical and mental actions pertain to one's own practice. From a comprehensive perspective, these three types of action constitute one’s own standard of conduct, which is precisely the method of one's own practice.
The Master [teaches] through the instruction of the three karmas; this is the Dharma-master who transforms others, hence it is called the "Dharma-master Chapter. Furthermore, there are three gates:

practicing these five dharmas for one's own cultivation constitutes the gate of merit and virtue; proclaiming and disseminating the five dharmas to extensively benefit all beings constitutes the gate of transforming others;
and cultivating oneself while benefiting others in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings constitutes the gate of repaying kindness. Moreover—
These are the three dharmas. Reciting, chanting, copying, and transcribing are the external practice; this is the Tathāgata’s robe. Upholding and maintaining [the teachings] is the internal practice;
this is the Tathāgata’s seat. Expounding and benefiting others is the Tathāgata’s chamber. Regarding the Tathāgata’s chamber, it is specifically the cultivation of others.
Regarding the robe and the seat, they are specifically the cultivation of oneself. Generally speaking, however, this is not so: compassion covers all things, and wisdom and benefit return to oneself.
To call it a "room" is to block out evil from others and shield one's own flaws. To call it "clothing" is because only by settling the mind in emptiness can one bring peace to others;
bringing peace to others is simultaneously bringing peace to oneself. To call this a "seat" refers to these three dharmas of self-discipline, which also qualify one as a Dharma Master.
Furthermore, in benefiting sentient beings, one must take compassion as the primary entry into the room, and employ patience when engaging with the realm of existence.

This serves as the foundation. To save others, taking the extinction of the self as the fundamental principle, and being able to practice these three dharmas so that the Great Teaching is proclaimed and spread—such a person is the reliance of the world and is therefore called a Dharma Master.
Furthermore, in compassion, he surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; in gentleness, he surpasses all ordinary beings and non-Buddhists;
and in the seat of emptiness, he surpasses bodhisattvas who engage in analytical reduction of substance or partial views. Thus, Vimalakīrti...
It is said: For example, one may only be considered brave after having conquered an enemy. Furthermore, compassion destroys the celestial Māra; gentleness destroys the skandha-māra;
and emptiness destroys the affliction-māra and the death-māra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"To transform all sentient beings and contemplate all things as empty, so that Māra finds no opportunity. A sūtra says: "All wholesome dharmas have compassion as their root; patience is supreme."
The Way is signless and supreme. Were one to discuss its perfect practice, it could not be fully described. Regarding the title "Dharma Master" (Fashi): "Dharma" (fa) refers to the rules and norms;
"Master" (shi) refers to a teacher or craftsman. Although the Dharma provides the standard, its essence does not propagate itself; its transmission depends upon persons.
One who masters the five methods of scriptural interpretation may all be called a "Master. By upholding the Dharma, they perfect their own practice, taking the wondrous Dharma as their teacher.

The Master has personally accomplished the wondrous Dharma; therefore, he is called a "Dharma Master" (*dharmabhāṇaka*). Furthermore, there are five types of persons who are able to instruct and mold others through the wondrous Dharma;
thus, the term "Dharma" is used to designate the "Master. Consequently, it is titled the "Chapter on the Dharma Master.

If one is a Dharma Master by virtue of following the Dharma oneself, or a Dharma Master by virtue of molding others through the Dharma—both being termed "Dharma Master"—this is an explanation of the chapter based on its causal conditions (*nidāna*). There are many such varieties.
[Commentary: All [these sections] explain the chapters according to the teaching methods of the Perfect Dharma (*yuanjiao*).

The first three weeks constitute the formal exposition of the Trace Gate (*jimén zhèngshuō*). Having completed the sections on realization, understanding, and receiving predictions, the five chapters below constitute the propagation of the Trace Gate (*jimén liútōng*).
This is not merely to provide benefit and protection for the contemporary era; it is further intended to ferry and nourish future generations. Therefore, there are these five chapters.
The *Circulation* chapter and the two chapters on the "Dharma Master" and the "Jeweled Stūpa" clarify that the merit of propagating the sūtra is profound and its blessings weighty.
The *Dharmodgata* chapter cites past instances of propagating the sūtra, wherein both self and others were benefited, thereby proving the depth and gravity of such merit.

In the *Dharani* chapter, those among the eighty thousand great beings who have perfected the power of patience propagate the sūtra in this land, while those who have newly attained the stage of "recollection" propagate it in other lands.
The first chapter, "Peaceful Conduct" (Anle-xing). Formerly referred to as "Receiving the Regressive and Circulating [the Teaching]," it is intended for those of the outer stage who are beginners;

they rejoice in this supreme merit and vow to propagate the sutra during the Final Dharma age. They observe that the Śrāvakas are intimidated and hear that the Bodhisattvas are subjected to banishment and humiliation. (Supplementary note:

Regarding the "intimidation of the Śrāvakas," it refers to instances such as Vimalakīrti’s refutation and the dismissal of the flower-offering and prostration at the seat. Thus, when the Buddha ordered them to inquire after his illness, they all replied, "That superior man is difficult to engage in dialogue with. This is the sense of being intimidated. Regarding the "banishment and humiliation of the Bodhisattvas," it is found in the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra*...)

The "common" [teaching] refers to Bodhisattvas; the "distinct" teaching refers to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) outside the Perfect Teaching. These are enumerated as the seven expedient means (*upāya*). Because they cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom, this carries the sense of being cast aside and humiliated.

Seeing that their own strength is weak and that they benefit neither themselves nor others, they give rise to despondency and retreat. For such people, the Buddha preached the "Peaceful Practices" (*anurakṣaṇācaryā*); by relying upon them, one propagates the Dharma without fearing danger or suffering.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the World-Honored One himself speaks of the merit and blessings of propagating the sutra and commands its circulation.

The "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa. The Many Treasures Buddha and his emanations both bear witness to and assist [the teaching], exhorting its seeking and circulation. (Regarding the phrase "from the external stages of the ordinary person to those who do not worry about danger and suffering":

there are five grades of external ordinary persons who rejoice in the merit of widely propagating the teaching. Yet they see the Śrāvakas as objects of dread; they observe that the Mahāsattvas have been ostracized by the multitude; and they reflect that their own power of contemplation is not yet deep, fearing they will lose the path of the two benefits.

For those whose minds thus wish to retreat, the Buddha preaches the four practices of peaceful dwelling so that such afflictions shall not occur. To distance themselves from the ten vexations, it is said "they do not worry. As for "both bearing witness and assisting": the Jeweled Stupa comes to bear witness to the sutra, while the emanations gather to assist in its opening. Through this witnessing and assistance, the invitation for circulation [is fulfilled].)
[General Explanation].
△ Next, the explanation of the scriptural text. In the "Dharma-Teacher" chapter, the initial prose and verse praise the five kinds of dharma-teachers who are able to uphold the Dharma;
the subsequent prose and verse praise the Dharma that is upheld and further demonstrate the mastery of the sutra.
The Rectification of the Path. First, there are two [categories]. First, regarding the disciples who have received the Way, their merit is profound and their blessings are heavy.

Second, regarding the teachers who transmit the Way, their merit is profound and their blessings are heavy. Within the category of disciples, there are again two: first, disciples during the Buddha’s lifetime; second, disciples after his parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the initial reference to the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas] as told by Bhaiṣajyarāja, "cause" (yin) means to rely upon or entrust. It signifies the desire to rely upon the Sublime Dharma.

Entrusting it to Medicine King, he causes him to receive and uphold it; he addresses the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas] so that they may all circulate it. Regarding the question "Do you see? directed at the person:
this specifically indicates the person who attains merit by upholding the sutra. There are two types of disciples during the Buddha’s lifetime: first, those distinguished from the general multitude;
second, those distinguished as having the conditions for receiving the prediction [of enlightenment]. This is the first.

At that time, the World-Honored One, because of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and others of this kind—those who attained wondrous awakening according to their capacities in the presence of the Buddha—were those of great learning and profound understanding, namely the two thousand five hundred [bhikṣus].
All of them have already been granted both general and specific predictions in person. Those now being selected as a class may belong to one of the eight assemblies (aṣṭau parṣadaḥ).
...and so forth. Or they may belong to the categories of the fourfold assembly or the three vehicles. As for those who merely "hang" at the seat of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* [Note:

"Hang" (絓) is an archaic form of "guà," meaning they temporarily occupy the seat of the *Lotus Sūtra*, yet are not the primary audience; however, this cannot be definitively determined]. △ Second, distinguishing those who receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
"All before the Buddha" (up to "shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi"):
"All before the Buddha" clarifies the timing—that they encountered the Buddha while he was seated. "A single phrase or a single verse": [refers to the teaching].

To have heard the Dharma for even a very short time—even for a single thought-moment—is the shortest possible duration. Yet all such individuals are granted the prediction that they shall attain Bodhi;
this clarifies that even with extremely little hearing and an extremely brief duration, through the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one ultimately attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
How much more so for those who hear it in full, maintain it throughout their lives, propagate it in five ways, and make offerings with the three karmas of body, speech, and mind!

(Regarding the phrase "even for a single thought-moment," etc.: it clarifies that by relying on this single thought, one will certainly attain Bodhi; the remote cause does not perish, and it is through this that [enlightenment] is triggered. This is not like other forms of merit, and for this reason, it is singled out. To investigate thoroughly, one must fully practice all the dharmas of the Buddhas.

Even after the Two Vehicles have received their prediction, they still pass through kalpas; yet, how does understanding the purport of these sutras differ from being fully endowed [with them]? It is merely a matter of whether one practices for oneself and transforms others from beginning to end.

As for those who hear a single phrase or a single verse—referring to those of little learning and shallow understanding—they are all now granted a prediction. If even those with so little are predicted, how much more so those with much?
"Profound! By means of the few, one may infer the many. If it is thus universally vast, then as it is so for the lower realms, it is likewise for the middle and upper realms;

this can be known through inference and need not be explained further. In the *Jian-shi-sanmei-jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seeing Reality), there is a separate record concerning the Four Heavenly Kings, all named Huochi (Fire-Holding).
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, they are all named Indraketu (Indra-Banner). King Vaideha (Wang Juyi) is named Wuzhuo (Non-Attachment)."

In the Yāma Heaven, they are all named Pure Wisdom (Vimalajñāna); in Tuṣita, they are all named Śakra Dharma King. For the two higher heavens as well, the predictions are given collectively without specifying individual names.
In the Brahmā Heaven, they are named Great Intellectual Power (Mahājñānabala); these belong to the class of those who have heard much and understand the profound.
What I have now recorded is merely the meager understanding of one of shallow capacity. Regarding "a single verse or a single line," the *Ekottarāgama-saṃgraha* states:
"It refers to taking essential verses from within the sūtras, such as those concerning the Four Noble Truths. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: [as follows].
"Contemptuous disdain is called 'aversion' (*nibbidā*). Not seeking is called 'desirelessness' (*virāga*). A mind free from defilement is called 'liberation' (*vimutti*).

Casting off the burden is called 'Nirvana' (*nibbāna*). Contemptuous disdain refers to the origin (*samudaya*); not seeking refers to suffering (*dukkha*); freedom from defilement is the path (*magga*); casting off the burden is cessation (*nirodha*). It is also said:

The Buddha said to Pūrṇa: "I have four phrases, namely the Four Noble Truths; these include the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and so forth. If one takes the essential phrases from the Gate of Traces, they are:
revealing, instructing, awakening, and entering; riding this precious vehicle to travel through the four directions;

the four practices of peaceful dwelling; and exhorting the arousal of the four intentions. As for the 'exhortation to arouse the four intentions,' they are: first, being protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; second, planting the roots of all virtues; third, entering the correct [path]..."

The Determinate Assembly (niyata-rāśi). Fourth, they give rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings. In the sub-commentary below, these four dharmas are also correlated with opening, showing, awakening, and entering. Although this is essential for the provisional traces (jia), once the fundamental reality (ben) is revealed, it becomes essential for the fundamental reality itself, as will be fully demonstrated below.
Regarding "one who rejoices for a single thought-moment": even if one has not yet personally practiced, but merely rejoices in the Dharma and in others, the merit and reward are still vast;
how much more so when one reaches the stage of actual practice? There are two aspects to the mind of rejoicing:

if, upon hearing the revelation of the provisional to manifest the ultimate, one immediately, within a single thought-moment, deeply understands the principle that is neither provisional nor ultimate, and believes in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, while being able to simultaneously understand the provisional as well.
In reality, phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused; thus, although one possesses the nature of afflictions, one is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.

This is "congratulatory joy" (anumodanā) discussed in terms of the vertical dimension. Although one has not yet attained the true mind of congratulatory joy, being able to understand it in this way—since the Dharma is thus, so too are persons—is "congratulatory joy" discussed in terms of the horizontal dimension.
Thus, it is both horizontal and vertical, and both vertical and horizontal.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "It would be better to hear little but understand much of the meaning and flavor. This is precisely that intent. This shall be explained further below.
Second, clarifying the disciples after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa: first, regarding the classes of disciples who appear earliest, I have briefly cited individuals;
by this example, the rest may be understood. Next, it says, "I also grant them a prediction [of enlightenment]"; the merit and retribution are to be understood as previously explained.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja... (up to) "I also bestow upon him the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
(The section on the first disciple-disciple is concluded. △ Second, the section on the teacher-disciples. This consists of prose and verse. The prose section has two parts.

First there is the specific, followed by the general. Regarding the specific: "persons" refers to those of superior and inferior status; "time" refers to the present and the future. Regarding the general:

it disregards whether one is superior or inferior, or present or future, universally clarifying that one incurs offense by acting contrary [to the teacher] and gains merit by acting in accordance with them. Within the specific, there are again two parts:
first, clarifying the present life; second, clarifying the period after death. Within the present life, there are again two parts: first, clarifying the teacher of inferior quality.

Next, the superior grade of teacher is clarified. The inferior grade of teacher is divided into two parts: first, the characteristics of the teacher are clarified; second, the merit and retribution of the teacher are clarified.
Now, for the first part:
"If there be another person who receives, maintains, reads, and recites [this sutra], up to and including joining their palms in reverent worship."
Regarding the "characteristics of the teacher," these refer to the five kinds of Dharma-preachers and the ten kinds of offerings (the ten kinds of offerings are: first, flowers; second, incense;

third, necklaces; fourth, powdered incense; fifth, unguents; sixth, burning incense; seventh, banners and canopies; eighth, robes; ninth, music and performance; tenth, joining the palms). Next, the merit and retribution of the lower grade are explained.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know" (up to) "extensively expounding and analyzing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

That those who have made offerings [to him] possess profound causes from the past; that he has been born into this human world out of compassion for sentient beings demonstrates the greatness of his manifest merit.
The passage beginning with "If there should be someone who asks... clarifies the gravity of his future retribution. △ Second, the clarification of the superior grade of teacher.
This also has two parts: first, to illustrate the characteristics of a superior teacher; second, to clarify the superior merit and retribution [of such a teacher].
How much more so for one who is able to fully receive and uphold [the sūtra], make various offerings, and extensively expound this scripture?

(The masters regarding the present life are concluded. △ Second, clarifying the masters regarding [the state] after death. These also have superior and inferior grades. Within the inferior grade, there are likewise two types.
First, to identify those of the inferior grade: these are those who merely grasp the general meaning vertically.

If such sons or daughters of good family [from the beginning] down to even a single phrase possess wisdom but lack extensive learning, they are only capable of speaking in private; they are not yet fit to be among the assembly. Therefore, they are teachers of the lowest grade.
Even if they understand a single phrase by speaking it in secret to one person, because they have neither heard extensively nor studied much, [they cannot be considered true teachers].
Divergent views must not be discussed within the assembly. If any inquiry or challenge remains unresolved, it will prevent the True Principle from being widely proclaimed.
As clarified in the *Śāstra*, one who possesses wisdom but lacks learning is like a light rain without thunder.
If one wishes to elaborate upon this single phrase, it must be said that these are merely spoken in private. II. Explaining the Merit and Retribution:
One should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, sent by the Tathāgata, and performs the work of the Tathāgata.

This sutra is that which was spoken by the wisdom of suchness; it speaks of the principle of suchness. Today, the practitioner who upholds this teaching of suchness and proclaims the principle of suchness is one sent by the Tathāgata.
One who performs the work of the Tathāgata takes the illumination of the principle of suchness by the wisdom of suchness as their task.
Today, the practitioner who relies on the teaching of suchness and practices according to the principle of suchness is performing the work of the Tathāgata.
It is thus: Suchness as wisdom and suchness as principle constitute the activity of transforming sentient beings.

If a practitioner today possesses great compassion and expounds the principle of True Suchness from this sutra for the sake of others, thereby causing them to benefit and be born [in the Pure Land], this is also called performing the work of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the "Contemplation of the Mind" (Kuan-hsin): the messenger of the Tathāgata uses the mind of wisdom to contemplate objects; these objects are themselves True Suchness.

As for this: when an object arises and triggers wisdom, that wisdom is employed by the *tathatā* (suchness). That which is dispatched by the *Tathāgata* refers to the wisdom of contemplation arising from within *tathatā*.
To perform the deeds of a *Tathāgata* means to traverse all phenomena, finding none that are not *tathatā*;
*tathatā* itself is the work of the Buddha. Second, to clarify those of the superior grade: the calculation of their merit and retribution is omitted here; this intention may be [inferred].
One knows this.
How much more so when one extensively expounds it for others amidst the great assembly.

(The first specific explanation is concluded. △ Second, the general explanation of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers: those who act contrary [to the teaching] incur offense; those who act in accordance [with it]...
One obtains merit.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there should be an evil person... [up to] ...the sake of *sambodhi*.

In this context, the gravity of the offense or merit is not discussed in terms of whether the field of merit is fertile or barren; rather, it is clarified according to the initial and final states of mind to demonstrate their relative lightness or heaviness.
A beginner practitioner, already possessing afflictions (*kleśa*), will have their studies abandoned if obstacles are added;

therefore, they incur much demerit. The Buddha, however, is impartial; evil cannot oppress him, so how could he be obstructed? Therefore, it is said that his transgressions are light. The same applies to offerings:
such a person has needs, and if they receive offerings, the task of their cultivation will be accomplished; thus, merit is bestowed upon the donor.

Superior. The Buddha, however, has no further needs; all matters are already fulfilled. Thus, although offerings are presented, they provide no benefit to the Buddha, and for this reason it is said that the reward is inferior.
It is like a prince in distress: providing him with his necessities brings great merit, yet if one brings dishonor upon the royal lineage, the offense incurred is not slight;
thus both the merit and the transgression are grave. If one were to offer food and clothing to a Great King for the sake of an urgent matter...

"Subtle! Though you wish to assail and humiliate them, you cannot cause them harm; therefore, both their offenses and merits are slight. 'The King of Medicine' and below clarify recitation and chanting.
To be adorned as the Buddha is to accord with him and thereby obtain merit. The Buddha is adorned by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);
this person is able to cultivate concentration and wisdom. One who 'shoulders the burden for the Tathāgata'—to carry on the back is 'to bear,' while to carry on the shoulder is..."
To carry refers to the essence of the Dharma-body, which is neither provisional nor real; this is what constitutes the Tathāgata’s bearing.

To be able to employ both the provisional and the real is the function of the two wisdoms; this is what constitutes the Tathāgata’s carrying. One should pay homage toward whichever direction one is facing.
The preceding section clarified taking the Dharma as one's teacher; this section clarifies being capable of serving as a teacher for sentient beings.

This person’s orientation is entirely in accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*); they are all worthy of reverence and compliance. Compliance is precisely "orientation" (*xiàng*), and reverence is precisely "etiquette" (*lǐ*). To revere and comply with them is the practice.
[This concludes] the two general explanations, including the offerings and so forth. △ Second, the verses in praise consist of sixteen lines divided into three parts.
The first two verses do not repeat the prose; they separately exhort and encourage one's own practice and the benefiting of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way... and also make offerings to those who uphold it.
Next, thirteen lines praise the specific and general aspects of the Teacher's gate; the final line praises the sutra, summarizing both the specific and the general.

Within this, there are again two parts: first, seven lines of verse that treat the subject specifically; second, six lines of verse that treat it generally. In the preceding section on specific categories, there were both present and future [masters].

Now, of these, the first four lines of verse concern the present, while the latter three lines concern the future. Regarding these two types of masters—present and future—each has its own superior and inferior levels.
Now, for the first verse: the first half-line reveals the Dharma Master, and the second half-line reveals the karmic reward.
"If there be one who can receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, know that such a person is sent by the Buddha to have compassion for all sentient beings."
△ Next, three lines. These verses praise the superior teacher of the present. The first half-line identifies the superior teacher;
the following two and a half lines praise his meritorious retribution.
"Those who are able to receive and uphold [the Dharma], up to those who make offerings to the teacher of the Dharma.
△ The final three lines of verse concern the future; the first two lines are an anticipatory (or *krama*) verse. They surpass even the superior grade of teachers.
Among these, the first half-line concerns the Dharma-master. In the prose (*gadya*), the karmic reward was originally omitted, but it is now present in this verse. Second.
One line and a half clarify the karmic retribution for merit.
From "After my parinirvāṇa, in the evil age" (up to) "I hope to hear it for even a brief moment.
△ Next, one line concludes the verse on the teacher of the lower grade. The first half of the line praises the person; the second half of the line praises [the teaching].
This is the retribution for merit.
If there are those who, in future ages, receive and uphold this sutra, I shall dispatch them among human beings to perform the work of the Tathāgata.
(The first individual verse concludes. △ The second section consists of six lines; it praises the aforementioned general gate, which also has two parts. The first two lines praise...
Those who oppose it incur sin. The two verses on the four practices follow this by showing that one obtains merit;
if, within a single eon... (up to) "I have now obtained great benefit."
△ Third section, one line: Praising the supreme excellence of the sutra.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: Of all the various sutras I have preached, among them, the Lotus Sutra is the foremost.
(End of the prose and verse praise for the five kinds of Dharma-preachers). △ Second, the praise of the Dharma upheld and the method for propagating the sutra.
The Dharma upheld is the method for self-discipline; the method for propagating the sutra is the method for guiding others.
There are both prose and verse sections. In the prose, there is first a praise of the Dharma of the sutra, followed by a praise of its method. The praise of the Dharma is fivefold:

first, praise regarding the Dharma itself, which includes both descriptive praise and comparative evaluation; second, praise regarding the person; third, praise regarding the location; fourth, praise regarding the cause;

and fifth, praise regarding the fruit. Because the Dharma is sublime, the person is noble; because the person is noble, the location is honored; and because the location is honored, the cause is perfected.
This refers to the perfection of causes and the culmination of fruits. First, regarding the praise based on the Dharma:
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Bhaisajyarāja, saying: "...[omitted]... there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy; how much more so after my parinirvāṇa."

First, regarding the praise of the Dharma, it shall now be explained. This sutra is the most supreme. "Already" (*yi*) refers to the gradual and sudden teachings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Dapin jing*) upwards.
"Now" (*jin*) refers to being in the same assembly, namely the *Anantamukha-saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*). "Shall" (*dang*) refers to...
This refers to *nirvāṇa*. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other texts, both gradual and sudden approaches are accompanied by skillful means (*upāya*), making it easier to gain faith.
Now, in the *Anantamukha-nirdeśa*, the one gives rise to the infinite, yet the infinite has not yet returned to the one; this is also easy to believe.

Now, in the *Dharmapada* (Lotus Sūtra), regarding the Dharma, all distinctions are harmonized and integrated back into the single Dharma. Regarding the persons [involved], both teacher and disciple, as well as their original and manifested forms, are likewise [unified].
It has been for a long time. These two gates are both the opposite of what came before; they are difficult to believe and difficult to understand. They are matters that are hard to confront head-on.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already been preached, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* follows later, and thus it is easier to believe. (Regarding "confronting head-on": the *Lotus Sūtra* comes first, like a great battle-hardened army that is difficult to break;

the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* comes later, like a remaining faction that is not so difficult. To face the vanguard first is what makes it "not easy. As for the "treasury of secret essentials," it is called "secret" because it was hidden and not spoken; it summarizes all into one.

This is of the utmost importance. The True Suchness and the Reality-mark (dharmatā) are contained within as a treasury; they cannot be distributed. Because the Dharma is subtle and difficult to believe, it may be transmitted only to those of profound wisdom.
To those without wisdom, it would only increase their transgressions; therefore, it must not be spoken of recklessly. From ancient times until now...

Regarding that which has never been explicitly taught: within the Tripiṭaka, it is not stated that those of the Two Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor is the fundamental and manifested status of teacher and disciple clarified.

Although the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras speak of the treasury of the true mark (dharmatā), they likewise do not state that those of the Five Vehicles attain Buddhahood, nor do they reveal the manifested to disclose the fundamental.
Since the various sūtras of the Sudden and Gradual teachings have not yet been harmonized, it is termed "secret."
This sutra fully expounds the secret teachings of the past; it is the opening of the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), and it is itself the secret treasury.
Such a secret treasury has never been revealed before. Even while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were many who harbored resentment and jealousy;
for over forty years, he could not speak of it immediately. Now, although he wishes to speak of it, five thousand [disciples] immediately withdraw from their seats. The Buddha—
If it is so even in the present world, how much more so will it be in the future, when the principle is difficult to transform? △ Second, the praise by way of persons:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know... [up to] ...then the Tathāgata will stroke their heads with his hand."

When this Dharma resides in a person, that person becomes noble and honored. That which is "covered by the Tathāgata’s robe" refers to taking the cultivation and study of great patience (*mahākṣānti*) as one's garment.
As the previous passage stated, it is the "adornment of the Tathāgata. Regarding "being protected by the Buddha," true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the Buddha.
True wisdom is the child; honoring the true mark (dharmatā) gives rise to true wisdom, and one is then protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
The fourfold faith constitutes the power of faith; the four great vows constitute the power of aspiration; and great wisdom constitutes the power of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Faith is faith in principle; principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Aspiration is the establishment of practice; practice is liberation. These are the roots of goodness. The root—
It is indeed difficult to move; this is precisely Prajñā. One should know that these three powers are the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
When the beginner dwells herein, they are no different from a Buddha; therefore, it is called "dwelling together with the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, through the power of faith, one cultivates the Tathāgata’s wisdom of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); the Tathāgata takes ultimate emptiness as his dwelling, and this person’s power of faith likewise does so.
They also study ultimate emptiness; therefore, they dwell together with the Tathāgata. Regarding "the hand rubbing the head":

this person, through the power of their vows and the power of goodness, employs their own practice of the provisional and the real as a stimulus-response (*gangan*). "Stimulus-response" is termed the "head. The Tathāgata, by means of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others, is termed the "hand.
This hand opens and develops the "head"—the provisional and real of the former's own practice—thereby effecting a resonance between stimulus and response.
Their paths intersect; therefore, it is called *mudhā*. *Mudhā* means "bestowal of prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*).
△ Third, praising by way of location: "Wherever the Medicine King [is], he is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Wherever this Dharma resides, that place is noble. Indeed, those places where the Buddha was born, attained the Way, turned the wheel of the Dharma, and entered *nirvāṇa*—the sites where the Dharma King traveled—all should have stupas erected.

This sutra is the birthplace of the Dharma-body, the field for attaining the Way, the true essence of the wheel of the Dharma, and the cave of Great *Nirvāṇa*. Wherever this sutra is located, it must be honored with a stupa. It is not...

Regarding the further enshrining of śarīra: the *Śāstra* (Shèlùn) states that "fragmented bone" is the śarīra of the physical body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while "sūtra scrolls" are the śarīra of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This sūtra is the śarīra of the Dharma-body; it is unnecessary to further enshrine the śarīra of the physical body.

Both the physical and Dharma-bodies have their own "whole" and "fragmented" forms, all of which can be explained as follows... (The citation from the *Śāstra* to prove that both the physical and Dharma-bodies each possess whole and fragmented forms is as stated above).

Now, the four characteristics will be explained. [The case of] Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna is that the physical body (*janmakāya*) remains whole; this is the "whole" aspect. Regarding the two aspects of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): the various provisional teachings represent the "fragmented" Dharma-body, whereas the single reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* represents the "whole" Dharma-body.

This can be seen through a detailed examination of the four teachings and five periods. Thus we know that in all other sutras, the whole and fragmented aspects are mixed; only in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Dharma-body whole. There is no other dharma, for one immediately enters into reality. (Supplementary Note: Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna sitting together in a single stupa is the physical body remaining whole.
The relics (*śarīra*) of the Buddhas after cremation, which serve as a field of merit for sentient beings, are the physical body being fragmented. △ Fourth, praising by citing the cause.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, whether lay or ordained, who can thus skillfully practice the bodhisattva path.

Those who have not yet skillfully practiced follow the three preceding teachings; these are like fragmented śarīra relics of the Dharma-body, as they have not yet been able to deliver others through skillful means.
If one enters the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), this is like a whole-body śarīra relic, for it constitutes skillful delivery and is therefore the true skillful practice.

△ Fifth, praising by citing the fruits. The text consists of five parts: first, clarifying the proximate fruit; second, providing an analogy; third, applying the analogy; fourth, explaining the proximate fruit;
and fifth, distinguishing what is not [the fruit]. Now, the first part.

If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way (up to) those who attain proximity to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should know that those who will certainly attain proximity to the fruit of *saṃbodhi* are called "those in the proximate stage" (*upaniṣad*) within the *Anurakṣita-pratipatti* (Practice of Peaceful Conduct).
This fruit of *bodhi* has as its essence the sphere of the Buddha’s eye and the Buddha’s wisdom for knowing and seeing; it is of two kinds. The first is the initial...
The Bodhi of the Mind. Second is the Bodhi of the Subsequent Mind. What is here called "near" refers specifically to being close to the Bodhi of the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
Furthermore, when one cultivates the perfect cause in anticipation of the perfect fruit and attains a semblance of understanding, it is termed "near.

The preceding section praised the cultivation of both common and specific causes based on the perspective of the cause; this refers to the stage where one is not yet proficient and remains distant from the perfect fruit. If, however, one cultivates the perfect cause, then...

This is wholesome conduct; it is close to the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*). Now, taking the perfect, suchness-as-it-is wisdom (*tathatā-yathābhūta-jñāna*) as the cause, it is itself taken as the fruit.
Suchness prior to the Path is the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); suchness during the Path is the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), also called the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*);
and suchness after the Path is the perfect fruit. Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* says: "The Mahāyāna cause is..."
This is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true mark. The *Śāstra* states: "The initial contemplation of the true mark is called the cause;

the completion of that contemplation is called the fruit. Discussing this from the perspective of principle, True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the true mark are fundamentally without cause and effect, nor do they possess sequence.
However, in relation to the cultivation of sentient beings, there exist both sequence and cause and effect. △
Second, the opening of the analogy:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is as if there were a person who, being parched with thirst, required water... up to "...his mind becomes resolved, knowing that water must be near.

This analogy has two interpretations: the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and the gate of teaching (*deśanā*). Regarding the gate of contemplation: the minds of sentient beings are endowed with all afflictions...
Afflictions are called the high plateau; the cultivation of contemplative wisdom is called digging through it, whereby one finally realizes the flavor of principle, like obtaining clear water.

Based on general contemplation, the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi) is like dry soil, the stage of Nature (gotra-bhūmi) is like damp soil and mud, and the realization of the Truths (satyadarśana) is like obtaining clear water.
Regarding specific contemplation, entering from the conventional into emptiness, one sees only emptiness and does not see non-emptiness, thereby severing the four abidings, as follows:
When one digs into dry soil, it is still far from water; thus, emerging from the provisional through the empty, one first realizes it is not provisional, and now realizes it is not empty.
By means of these two contemplations, one enters the Middle Way and is able to subdue ignorance. When one turns to see moist soil, it is close to water.
Thus, the perfect contemplation of the Middle Way—neither empty nor provisional, yet illuminating both the empty and the provisional—is like gradually reaching moist mud.

The four abidings (*catur-vihāra*) are already exhausted and ignorance (*avidyā*) is already subdued; one has attained a semblance of the perfect understanding of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Therefore, it is said to be "like mud. If one enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the true understanding of the Middle Way is awakened, whereby ignorance is shattered, just as mud becomes clear.
One then perceives the Middle Way, like seeing clear water. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "The Buddha-nature is water. One should know that this refers to the successive stages in order.

Regarding the "teaching gates": the earth is a metaphor for the scriptural teachings, and the water is a metaphor for the Middle Way. The teachings expound the Middle Way, just as soil contains water.
The teaching gate of the Tripiṭaka has not yet expounded the Middle Way; it is like dry soil.

The Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings incorporate expedient means to explain the meaning of the Middle Way, like seeing moist soil. The Lotus Sūtra teaching is direct and manifest, explaining the Unsurpassed [Way].

The Way is like seeing mud. By means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teaching, one generates the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, thereby immediately awakening to the Middle Way and truly perceiving Buddha-nature.
The true wisdom thus produced no longer relies on the literal text, just as once pure water is obtained, the appearance of soil no longer remains.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "When a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, they immediately attain Bodhi and know all dharmas. This is because...
The self-nature of the mind achieves the body of wisdom; it is not realized through another. △ Third, the combined analogy:
"The Bodhisattva is also like this" (up to) "one must know that they have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, to obtain hearing, contemplation, and cultivation is precisely the perfect observation of the three wisdoms; only then can one approach the fruit.
This is not the hearing, contemplation, and cultivation found within the "dry" or "moist" teachings. △ Fourth, the explanation of the meaning of "attaining proximity."
Why is this? (Up to: "He brings all Bodhisattvas to fulfillment and reveals it to them.
"All Bodhisattvas" clarifies the various provisional causes; "triple awakening" (*tri-bodhi*) clarifies all provisional fruits.
Both provisional causes and provisional fruits are subsumed within this sutra, just as dry and moist soil alike depend upon water.
Therefore, it is said that they are "subsumed. Regarding the opening of the gate of expedient means and the revealing of the true aspect: what was not previously taught is now all taught.
Previously, when one spoke of all worldly affairs, livelihoods, and productive enterprises, how could these ever have been anything other than expedient means?

Now all of these are opened; they are the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and do not contradict one another. Previously, the provisional means (*upāya*) of the Hīnayāna and the fruits of the Hīnayāna were taught.
Since even the fruits of the Hīnayāna are not yet the gate of true reality, how much less so the minor provisional means?
Yet, by opening them all, they become the true reality. What you all practice is the Bodhisattva path; this is the definitive understanding.
The Dharma of the Śrāvakas is the king of all sutras. That which was previously taught as two expedient gates is now fully opened;
this is itself the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa). How could it still be merely a gate? It causes all sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Whether a single form or a single fragrance, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. Whether it be a gate or not a gate, all are opened.
This reveals the true mark and manifests the water of the Buddha-nature. Had it not been opened, it would have remained deep, firm, dark, and remote, such that no one could reach it;
now that it has been opened, one immediately perceives the water, with no dry earth remaining. Furthermore, this may be explained by means of the three types of wisdom.

All [these] belong to this sutra; that is, the perfect *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing). This sutra opens up the provisional means; that is, the perfect *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection).
To reveal the true aspect is the perfect *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation). These three are profound and remote;
now that the Buddha has opened them up and revealed them, one immediately attains the vision of the Truth. △ Five: Distinguishing the Non-True.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas [up to] you should know that they are those of overweening pride (adhimāna).

They are all like dry earth; they are not even moist earth, let alone having seen water. (This concludes the praise of the Dharma upheld. △ Second.
A brief indication of the method for propagating this sutra consists of two parts: first, showing the method; second, clarifying the benefits. Now, for the first:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there be sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, desire to preach this [sutra] for the fourfold assembly..."
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, how should it be preached? (This is the question posed to introduce the topic.

Good sons and good daughters, having entered the Tathāgata’s chamber, donned the Tathāgata’s robe, and sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat, they should then extensively preach this sūtra for the fourfold assembly (this indicates the three dharmas).
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s robe is gentleness...
The seat of the Tathāgata is the mind of patience and forbearance; it is the emptiness of all phenomena (explaining the three dharmas).

Abiding therein, one then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expounds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly (exhorting the practice of the three dharmas).
Cultivating the Tathāgata’s dwelling is great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*). If considered from the perspective of its being of one substance (*samatā*), it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
if it provides shelter for sentient beings, it is liberation (*vimukti*); and its ability to cause sentient beings to realize their identity with that same substance is wisdom (*prajñā*).

Cultivating the Tathāgata’s robe is gentleness and patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). If considered from the perspective of what is covered by it, it is the Dharma-body; if it is able to cover [sentient beings], [it is compassion].
This is precisely the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*). If one harmonizes with the light to benefit all beings, this is liberation (*vimukti*).

Cultivating the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). As for the act of sitting upon it, this is wisdom (*prajñā*). As for that which is sat upon, this is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). When body and seat are in silent accord, this is liberation.
Furthermore, great compassion that brings peace and happiness is the practice of the supportive and consummating stages (*sambhara-marga*); gentleness that subdues anger is...
The practice of contemplative observation is the practice of true nature (*dharmatā*). Within the "Peaceful Practices" (*sukhavihāra*), these three dharmas are further elaborated.
As for the "Tathāgata’s adornment" mentioned in the preceding text, this refers to the robe. That which is "borne upon the Tathāgata’s shoulder" refers to this seat.
"Carrying" means to carry and transport; this is the act of entering the chamber. △ Second, raising five benefits as an exhortation.
Circulation.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble for them a congregation to hear the Dharma (the first being the dispatching of emanated persons), and I shall also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to their preaching of the Dharma. These emanated persons, having heard...
They will faithfully accept the Dharma, following it without opposition (2. dispatching emanations of the fourfold assembly).

If there is a teacher of the Dharma in a secluded place, I shall at that time extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth, to listen to their preaching of the Dharma (3. dispatching emanations of the eight classes of beings).
Although I am in another land, from time to time I shall cause those who preach this Dharma to behold my body (the fourth: seeing the Buddha’s body).
If they should forget or lose any phrases or clauses of this sutra, I shall speak them for them again so that they may attain completeness (the fifth: bestowing dhāraṇī).
If one’s initial resolve is not yet pure, one may only dispatch emanated persons; it is not yet appropriate to dispatch emanations of the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings.
If one were to see devas and nāgas, one might rely on this to become arrogant, which would obstruct and damage one’s path; therefore, they should not be allowed to be seen.
If the mind is free from attachment and reliance, then one is capable of seeing the Buddha, let alone devas and nāgas, for one has attained *dhāraṇī* and personally realized the benefit.

△ First, the chapter title is presented; next, the scriptural text is explained. Now, the first:
The Lotus Sutra of the Marvelous Dharma, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
In the "Chapter on the Seeing of the Jeweled Stūpa," the term *stūpa* (Sanskrit) is translated here as "square mound" (*fāng fén*). It is also called a "spiritual temple" (*líng miào*) or a *caitya*.
A *caitya* refers to a site that does not contain a physical body. Since this stūpa contains the entire body without it being dispersed, it is not termed a *caitya*.

The Āgamas clarify four types of *caityas* (here rendered as *zhīwēi*, i.e., *caitya*): namely, the place of birth, the place where enlightenment was attained, the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and the place of final nirvāṇa.
Stūpas were erected at four locations. The present Jewel Stūpa is the sacred shrine where the former Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
As the Sūtra says: "The three bodies of the Buddhas are produced from this sūtra. It is here that all Buddhas sit upon the site of enlightenment;
it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma; and it is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa. This Lotus Sūtra alone is [the source of] the three periods of time."
Regarding the four *caityas* of all Buddhas: those of past Buddhas have already resided there, those of present Buddhas sit together there, and those of future Buddhas shall likewise do so.
This stūpa has emerged to manifest this matter clearly for all four assemblies to behold; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jewel Stūpa. In the *Śrī-kaṇṭha-sūtra*, Subhūti asks:
"Are the merits of the birth-body, the whole-body [relic], and the pulverized-body equal? The Buddha says: "They are not equal. The birth..."
Teaching through body and speech, he trained the three karmas until they were fully purified. Sentient beings thereby attained the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
His relics were entirely fragmented, yet his majestic spiritual power and radiance allowed those who made offerings to them to obtain merit; for this reason, they are not equal. Again, it was asked:
"The Tathāgata Śikhin taught the Dharma and transformed beings for twelve nayuta kalpas (i.e., nayutas), and his relics were likewise so."
"It must be so. The Buddha said, "All of these are produced by the supernatural power of Tathāgata Śikhin. In that sutra, the wooden case was completely shattered and the śarīras were all present;
this was due to the power of the *jāti-kāya* (birth-body) Buddha. In the present sutra, the wooden case remains intact while the *jāti-kāya* śarīras are completely shattered;

the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) śarīras are universally pervasive and perfect, and they all emerge from within the sutra. This reveals the merit of this sutra and the greatness of its power for vast upholding."

It surged forth from the earth to bear witness to this matter, and the fourfold assembly all beheld it; hence it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa. The masters of the Northern Land say:
"When the Buddha was preaching the sūtra for Śāriputra, the jeweled stūpa had already appeared to serve as a witness.

If [it were to appear] after the preaching of the sūtra was finished, what would it come to witness? It was the compiler of the sūtra who established the sequence, placing it after the three cycles [of teaching]. This is...

Human sentiments are not to be trusted. Now, according to the *Sārvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra* (i.e., the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), when the Buddha was preaching the *Lotus Sūtra* with innumerable verses, a stupa made of the seven treasures emerged from the earth.
Within it was a golden throne, and upon the throne was a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna (in Sanskrit; in Chinese, "Great Treasure," i.e., *Prabhūtaratna*). He praised [the teaching].
The Venerable One said: "I have come specifically to make offerings. I pray that you will sit upon my golden couch and further expound for me the *Sārvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra*.
Based on the testimony of this sutra, it is clear that after the three cycles of teachings, he was requested again regarding his lifespan;

the Sage’s explicit words are there, yet you are unwilling to accept them. How can one rely on such human-fabricated interpretations? This stupa is precisely intended to serve as proof of what preceded."

At the request [of Śākyamuni], it surged forth from the earth, and the fourfold assembly all beheld it; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa. To represent the three bodies (*trikāya*):

the Many-Treasures Buddha (*Prabhūtaratna*) represents the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya*); Śākyamuni represents the Reward-body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*); and the manifested bodies represent the Response-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Although these three Buddhas are three, they are neither identical nor distinct. One should speak thus, and such is the faith and understanding. The stūpa emerged in two parts.
A single utterance serves to authenticate what precedes and to initiate what follows. To authenticate what precedes is to verify that the three cycles of teaching were all entirely true.
If "truth" is stated briefly, it means they are all in accord with the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena).
If "truth" is stated extensively, it means they are free from the four propositions and transcend the hundred negations. If explained according to the middle way, it refers to the eight negations.
It is called "Reality. The stupa emerging from the earth demonstrates non-extinction; sharing a seat and sitting together demonstrates non-arising;
entering the stupa demonstrates non-permanence; manifesting the stupa demonstrates non-interruption; the division of the body demonstrates non-identity; the whole body demonstrates non-difference;
the many jewels yielding their seats demonstrates non-coming; and Śākyamuni sitting upon half the seat demonstrates non-going. Thus, the eight negations are made manifest. Therefore...

This is the truth. Furthermore, regarding the propagation of the section on the realization of the traces (*yùnmò*), the merit of upholding this sutra is profound and the power of its wide dissemination is great;
all of these are true. As for "equal great wisdom" (*píngděng dàhuì*), how does it relate to *prajñā*? The *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 79, states:
"Prajñā is the wondrous Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, like a city gate through which all four directions may enter. One should know that Prajñā..."

If [one speaks of] the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is also called the "Wondrous Dharma" (*miao-fa*). This sutra is called the "Great Wisdom of Equality" (*pingdeng da-hui*). These two titles refer to one another;

their intended meaning can thus be understood. Regarding the subsequent section: if one wishes to open the stupa, it is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), clarify the profound entrustment (*parindanā*), and let the sound reach the lower realms.

One then summons the original disciples to discuss the measure of the Buddha’s lifespan. (As for the mention of "Mingxuan" and others, this briefly cites the title of the sutra; since "Xuan" encompasses the entire work, it says: "The Buddha wished to use this Wondrous...")

The Dharma is equal [to all]. The stupa of remote antiquity surges forth from the earth, opening the power of sovereign supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) to manifest the benefit of beings in past ages.
It emits a great sound, opening the power of the lion’s majestic stride to manifest throughout the ten directions.
It reveals the provisional to disclose the ultimate, for it possesses a great vow: that if any future Buddhas shall preach this sutra...

My jeweled stūpas shall all arrive at those places to serve as witnesses, manifesting the great, powerful, and majestic force, and revealing that which is eternally abiding and indestructible in the future.
Furthermore, when the stūpa is in the air, it likewise testifies to what preceded and what follows;

for those of the seven stages of expedient means, the principle remains hidden and obscured by ignorance, just as when the stūpa is on the ground. Upon hearing the three turnings of the wheel, they are revealed.
Third, the manifestation of reality: opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to reveal the Dharmakāya, like a stupa surging into the sky. This verifies what preceded:
that the Dharmakāya attained through cultivation has long been manifest, like a stupa already in the sky, which no one was able to open.

This signifies that the original ground has long been accomplished, yet remains unrecognized by the multitude. If one reveals the traces to manifest the fundamental, one will attain thorough understanding without doubt; this initiates what follows.

Furthermore, regarding those who attain liberation through contemplation of the mind: by practicing contemplation in accordance with the sutras, they become in resonance with the Dharma-body, and object and wisdom necessarily converge, just as the stupa came to bear witness to the sutra.
Since object and wisdom have converged, the great retribution is perfected, just as Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna sat together upon a single seat.
Because the great retribution is perfected, he manifests responses according to the capacities of beings, just as the emanated bodies all assemble. Due to...
Because Prabhūtaratna appears, the three Buddhas are made manifest; because one upholds this sutra, one is endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).

This is precisely the meaning of the "Universal Worthy Contemplation Cloud," which states that the three kinds of Buddha-bodies arise from the Vaipulya [sūtras]. △ Next, the text of the sūtra is explained.
This chapter consists of prose and verse. The prose section has three parts: first, the manifestation of the Prabhūtaratna Stūpa;
second, the distant gathering of the emanated bodies; and third, Śākyamuni’s proclamation of the invitation. The first part contains six sections, the first of which is the appearance of the stūpa.
1. The devas make offerings; 2. Prabhūtaratna praises him; 3. The assembly is struck with wonder and doubt;
4. Mahāsusvarā asks a question; 5. The Tathāgata answers. Now, the first [section].
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures, reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
That the stupa is made of the seven treasures clarifies the ground of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

By means of the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven noble riches of its inherent virtue, the "stupa" represents the realm of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), which is the locus upon which the Dharma-body relies. Its height of five hundred *yojanas* signifies...
The two myriads of *li* vertically clarify the ten thousand practices within the cause and the ten thousand virtues within the fruit.

The breadth of two hundred and fifty *yojanas* is precisely ten thousand *li*, representing the adornment with ten thousand wholesome deeds. As for "ground," it is the ground of the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*).
By having nothing to destroy, one destroys ignorance; by having nothing to dwell upon, one dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The various precious objects represent the manifold adornments of meditative concentration and wisdom. The railings are the dhāraṇīs.
The thousands of myriads of grottoes and chambers are the abodes of immeasurable compassion, as well as the dwellings of immeasurable emptiness. The banners and streamers—

This is the supreme mark of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). As for the hanging jeweled necklaces: they represent the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*), which adorn the Dharma-body above while reaching down to cover sentient beings.
The ten billion jeweled bells represent the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The fragrance emanating from the four sides represents the wind of the Path of the Four Truths blowing forth the fragrance of the four virtues. Reaching as high as the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings signifies—
This exhausts the principle of the Four Noble Truths. △ Second, the offerings of the devas:
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down *mandārava* flowers (extending to) reverently honoring, respecting, and praising [the Buddha].
The explanation based on the facts can be understood as before. To further explain it according to principle: the thirty minds constitute thirty stages;

the ten grounds constitute one; Equal Enlightenment constitutes one; and Sublime Enlightenment constitutes one. Combined, these make thirty-three, all of which equally rely upon the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
As for "raining down *māndārava* flowers," the initial mind also possesses the merits of the forty-two stages, and the final mind is likewise so.
All these are flowers of the causes belonging to the forty stages that turn toward the Dharma-body.

The various devas, nāgas, and others mentioned below—namely, those of the inner and outer stages of ordinary beings—likewise rely upon the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) to practice the causes directed toward the fruit. △ Third, the praise of Prabhūtaratna:
This serves as the formal proof that the previous revelation of the provisional and manifestation of the real was not in vain.
At that time, a great sound issued forth from within the jeweled stupa... [up to] "that which has been spoken is all true reality.
As for "equal great wisdom," this is the wisdom of all Buddhas; it is like the aforementioned meaning of walking with even steps and upright justice.

There are two kinds of equality: first, the equality of dharmas, which is the principle of the Middle Way; second, the equality of sentient beings, meaning that all sentient beings equally attain the Buddha-wisdom.
"Great" refers to the previously explained sense of being lofty and vast. Regarding the contemplation of the mind: the contemplation of emptiness is vertical equality;

the contemplation of the provisional is horizontal equality; and the contemplation of the Middle is both horizontal and vertical equality. To simultaneously illumine these two equalities is itself equality.
"O Mahāmati! 'Thus, thus' means: first, it is according to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); second, it is according to the nature of the faculties (*indriya*).

Both are the ultimate reality. (Supplementary note: "First, according to the true nature of phenomena" refers to the *bhūtatathatā* of all dharmas. "Second, according to the nature of the faculties" refers to the threefold teaching given according to the three grades of faculties—superior, middling, and inferior.)
All of this is true. Therefore, it is said that they are as they are according to the nature of dharmas (which is like their root-nature). △ Fourth, the assembly was struck with wonder and doubt.
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the great jeweled stupa dwelling in mid-air (until) it withdrew to stand to one side.
△ Inquiry arising from doubt regarding the causes for the proclamation of the five great joys. According to the intent of the subsequent response, there should be three questions:
first, asking by what cause this stūpa exists; second, asking why the stūpa emerges from the earth;
and third, asking why it emits such sounds.
At that time, there were Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas (up to) who uttered these sounds.

in order to testify to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they have emerged from the earth.
At that time, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa (up to) “I shall bear witness for you” and praised him, saying, “Excellent!
△ Second, answering the first question in retrospect: it was by the command of that Buddha that he was ordered to construct this stūpa.
After that Buddha attained enlightenment... (up to) "one great stūpa should be erected.
△ Third, the answer to the third [question]: this sound was uttered for the purpose of providing testimony.
That Buddha, by the power of his supernatural faculties and vows... [up to] praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
The *Śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was unable to preach the Dharma before entering parinirvāṇa. The Master’s interpretation is not so; that Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus" refers precisely to those who were to be transformed [by the teaching]. How can it be said that he did not preach? It must be as follows:
Much Treasure (Prabhūtaratna) likewise attains the opening of the three [vehicles], yet he cannot manifest the reality. Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: "He cannot preach the Dharma.
For this reason, although he has entered parinirvāṇa, wherever the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is preached, he immediately rejoices and provides witness.

(Regarding the address to the bhikṣus and others: this verifies that all four assemblies were present; it is not that the Dharma was not being preached. It must have been Prabhūtaratna. Question: Is there not even a single Buddha in the worlds of the ten directions who cannot open [the Dharma]?

Regarding the manifestation [of the stupa]: as for those who do not manifest, they all ought to make a vow; why should it be only Prabhūtaratna? If one does not make a vow, their path to Buddhahood would differ [from others]. If one makes a vow, all are fit to hear the sutra. Furthermore, the transformations of all Buddhas are preceded by their foreknowledge of the capacities [of beings].

How could it be that after attaining Buddhahood, they were unable to manifest [the stupa], only beginning to make a vow at this point? Answer: Whether they are the same or different, whether they manifest or do not manifest, and whether they have a vow or no vow—all these are according to conditions (*pratyaya*). If it is appropriate for them to have a vow, they will all come without exception; why worry that they will not assemble? That they make the vow later is also a matter of discerning the objects [of their response].
[Supplementary Note by Zhen: According to the Sūtra, when the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna was practicing the bodhisattva path in his previous lives, he made this great vow:

"If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, there should be a place in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, may my stūpa emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, acting as a witness and praising it, saying, 'Excellent! This appears not to be what the *Śāstra* says—that Prabhūtaratna cannot preach the Dharma and has already entered extinction—nor is it what the Great Master’s commentary states.

It seems rather that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna is able to open [the provisional] but cannot manifest the Real; therefore, the *Śāstra* says only that he cannot preach the Dharma. Furthermore, this is not what Jingxi says regarding "sameness and difference" or "opening and not opening," nor about "having a vow and not having one."]

The vows are all [fulfilled]. Regarding the passage beginning with "discerning objects according to conditions" and so forth, as explained in the three preceding sections, it appears not to accord with the intent of the great vow made by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna when he was practicing the bodhisattva path.

As for that intent, the verse in the "Expedient Means" chapter says: "The appearance of Buddhas in the world is rare; To encounter them is exceedingly difficult. Even if they appear in the world, To hear this Dharma is even more difficult. Throughout immeasurable and countless kalpas, To hear this Dharma is likewise difficult.

Those who are able to listen to this Dharma— Such people are also difficult to find. It is like the udumbara flower: All love and delight in it; A rarity for gods and humans, Appearing only once in a long while. To hear the Dharma with joy and praise, Or even to utter a single word, Is to have already made offerings To all those of the three periods of time."

"Buddha! Such a person is most rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower. This verse consists of four and a half lines; the first two lines contain four difficulties: first, the difficulty of encountering a Buddha; second, the difficulty of this Dharma being preached; third, the difficulty of hearing this Dharma; and fourth, the difficulty of finding one who is able to listen.

Because of these four difficulties, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna made a vow while on the bodhisattva path that when he cultivated this wondrous Dharma and attained Buddhahood, he would proclaim this wondrous Dharma. After his parinirvāṇa, wherever in the ten directions any Buddha preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha’s stupa shall surge forth from the earth to bear witness and praise its excellence.

Because it is so difficult to encounter, one rejoices at having met it, honoring it without ever abandoning it. The latter two and a half lines of verse begin with the first line, which cites the metaphor of the udumbara flower (*utpala*) to illustrate that it appears only once in a great while.

The subsequent one and a half lines explain this specifically in terms of the Dharma: it refers to one who hears the Dharma with joy and offers a single word of praise. The merit such a person obtains is equal to making offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time; such a person is rare and even rarer than the udumbara flower. "Exceeding" (the flower).

"Oudumbara! This is the realization of the sutra after the passing of all Buddhas. Among the Buddhas of the ten directions, there is not a single Buddha who is the equal of Prabhūtaratna Buddha. Furthermore, since his parinirvāṇa countless kalpas ago, there has not been a single Buddha among those of the ten directions who has not preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Their stupas all emerge and manifest; hearing the Dharma, they bear witness, and they utter voices praising it as excellent. How inconceivable this is!

Moreover, this witnessing and praise is also because, after the parinirvāṇa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, he used his entire physical body as a jeweled stupa to manifest before the great assembly, opening the two doors to reveal the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, the Dharmadhātu-body clouds of Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna appear everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions."

They become Buddhas and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma; and their stupas likewise emerge before them in the lands of the ten directions—those places where all Buddhas preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—hearing the Dharma and praising its excellence, appearing simultaneously without priority or sequence.

This is because Prabhūtaratna Buddha, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions, shares the same single suchness (*tathatā*) in attaining supreme perfect enlightenment. Throughout the three periods of time, they exist simultaneously; throughout the ten directions, they occupy a single place.

They revere the wondrous Dharma and witness the sutras everywhere, never for a moment departing from it. It is equal to empty space and identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is inexhaustible, inexhaustible, and inconceivable. (The first section, on the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna, is concluded.
