At that time, each of the Buddhas was beneath a jeweled tree... [and so on] until it was likewise for all.

The Buddhas collectively granted their consent (*kṣānti*) to open the stūpa, just as the formal procedure for granting consent is performed within the *saṃgha*. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies that numerous Buddhas grant their consent;
the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* also states that numerous Buddhas from the ten directions together preach the *Avataṃsaka*. The Great [Assembly]... [text continues].
The chapter also states: "The thousand Buddhas together preach the Prajñā; none of them are said to be emanations (vibhakta-kāya) of Śākyamuni.
According to the present sutra, they should indeed be emanations. Because that [other] scripture includes skillful means (*upāya*), it does not explicitly state this during its discourse.

The present sutra not only lists many [Buddhas], but also directly identifies them as emanations, all of whom have come to give their consent (*chanda*). (This is like giving consent within the Saṃgha; it is not necessarily...)

It is entirely identical to the ritual procedures within the monastic community; hence it is said, "as if [hearing] them. By the power of the Vow of Prabhūtaratna, all Buddhas were required to assemble. Furthermore, so that the assembly at that time would know that the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) were numerous, these Buddhas gathered to open the stupa.

Yet, even though they assembled, they did not arrive [in person]; instead, they dispatched their attendants to convey greetings and inquiries, much like the formal transmission of a *chanda* (consent). Therefore, the various attendants merely extended their greetings and offered no words of *chanda*. As for the many Buddhas who granted their *chanda* to this Great Assembly, they did so from within the great empty pavilion in the two realms of desire and form.

He extensively gathered all the Buddhas of the ten directions as twenty-one clouds. In the southern direction there was a Buddha named Suvarṇagarbha (Golden Treasury). When those bodhisattvas saw the light, they questioned that Buddha, and that Buddha replied: "In the world-system of the northern direction..."

There is a Buddha named Śākyamuni who wishes to preach the Dharma for the great assembly in order to shatter their great arrogance. He has sent an envoy to me requesting a portion [of my merit]; I now grant it to him. It is the same in other directions; he has dispatched one Great Bodhisattva from each, accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, to come here.

There is no difference in the verses of praise or the words of the request. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was likewise spoken by a thousand Buddhas. Now that the provisional means (*upāya*) have been revealed, he next wishes to manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Because he desires to show that the paths of all Buddhas are identical, he has caused all the Buddhas to grant their consent.

Someone asked: "Since the assembly is all together in the void, for what reason do the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya) still remain upon the earth? Now, in response: the assembly has already heard from the Trace Gate (jīmen) that the provisional was opened; they have now entered the Land of Quiescent Light (jiguang). Therefore, their abiding in the void represents this.

The emanated bodies manifest traces, each with its own land of those to be transformed; thus, their remaining on the earth represents this. Furthermore, as Śākyamuni will soon manifest his fundamental nature (mūlakāya), he likewise first abides in the void to represent it. Each has its own significance; there is no need for doubt. △ Second, Śākyamuni opens the stupa.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—[from "until"]—is like removing the bolts and opening the great city gate.
"Opening the stūpa" refers to the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*). "Beholding the Buddha" refers to the manifestation of the ultimate (*tattva*).

This also serves as a verification of what preceded [the *Jikimon* (Trace Gate) revelation of the provisional and manifestation of the ultimate], and further prepares for what follows [the *Honmon* (Root Gate) revelation of the trace and manifestation of the root]. "Like removing the bolts" means removing the obstacles so that the capacity for awakening may be activated.

(2. The gathering of the divided bodies from afar is concluded). △ Third, Śākyamuni proclaims the call for the circulation [of the teaching].
With a great voice, he universally addresses the fourfold assembly... until: "The entrustment has its place."
This passage contains three points: first, the loud proclamation of the call; second, the arrival of the time for entrustment; and third, that there is a specific recipient for the entrustment.

Regarding "having a recipient": if the Buddha were still in the world, he would benefit sentient beings according to their capacities by preaching the True Dharma himself, without depending on others.
Now, as the Buddha’s conditions for transformation have reached their end, he wishes to ensure that this Dharma will bring benefit without limit; therefore, it must be entrusted for circulation.

Regarding those to whom it is entrusted, there are two intentions: first, to ensure its presence in the near term by entrusting it to eighty-two thousand long-resident bodhisattvas to propagate and proclaim it in this land;
second, to ensure its presence in the distant future by entrusting it to his original disciples.
[He causes] the atoms of the thousand worlds below to circulate wherever they touch. Furthermore, he initiates [the discourse on] the lifespan (the figures of eighty thousand and twenty thousand:

the eighty thousand appear at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter; the twenty thousand appear at the head of the "Upholding" chapter). △ Second, the verse recitation consists of forty-eight lines, praising the three aforementioned points.
The first three and a half lines praise the parinirvāṇa of Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One... [omitted] ...constantly for the sake of hearing the Dharma. [Section Two: Eight and a half lines.

This verse praises the gathering of the emanated bodies (of the Buddhas). Regarding the gathering of the emanated Buddhas, there were seven points in the preceding text; here, the verse is extremely concise and does not follow the original order.]

Yun: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been translated four times; two versions were preserved while two were lost.

Dharmarakṣa—whose name means "Dharma-protector"—translated it in Chang’an during the Western Jin dynasty, titled the *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka). Dharmarakṣa further expounded upon it, and this is the version inherited by Daoan and Tandi.
Kumārajīva—translated as "Child Longevity"—was a native of Kucha. During the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty...

Sengrui divided it into nine sections (*kheṭa*). At that time, there were twenty-eight chapters; the palace ladies of Chang’an requested that this particular chapter be delayed [in its recitation].

In the interior [lands], as transmitted in Jiangdong, there are only twenty-seven chapters. During the Liang dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Man, who lectured on the sutra one hundred times and then immolated his body at Changsha Commandery;
he subsequently placed this chapter before the "Anzhichi" (Anuparīndanā) chapter.

This was his personal arrangement and had not yet been heard of throughout the world. During the Chen dynasty, there was the Chan Master of Nanyue, who placed this chapter next to the "Bao ta" (Ratnakoṭi) chapter.

Thereafter, in the evening, I compared it with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and found them to be in great agreement. Now that the four rivers have become conflated, I have consulted the old edition from Chang’an;

Regarding the four practices for peace and happiness: they consist of śamatha and vipaśyanā, compassion and loving-kindness, the guidance of the three karmas, and the vow.

Because there is śamatha in the bodily karma, one is detached from coarse physical actions; because there is vipaśyanā, one does not apprehend the body, does not apprehend bodily karma, and does not apprehend that which is capable of detachment.
Because there is nothing to be attained, one does not fall among ordinary beings. Because there is compassion, one diligently cultivates physical karma to extensively benefit all.
Because one does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles, one possesses the practice of *śamatha*. Wearing the robe of patience, one possesses the practice of *vipaśyanā*.

Sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat, one possesses compassion and thus enters the Tathāgata’s chamber. Through the practice of *śamatha* that abandons faults, one immediately accomplishes the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Contemplating practice without attachment immediately constitutes the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). Compassion that benefits others immediately constitutes the virtue of beneficence (*anugraha-guṇa*).

The virtue of beneficence supports and perfects the virtue of wisdom; the virtue of wisdom supports and perfects the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). This is called the "peaceful and blissful practice of bodily action.

(○ [Supplement by the Editor]: Question: The body, mind, and the vessel-world before us—all phenomena—are vividly undergoing birth and cessation. Why do you say that one should contemplate all phenomena as empty, as their true marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth?

Answer: All phenomena exist merely through causes and conditions. That which arises from conditions has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); its very substance is quiescent extinction, which is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Because they fail to penetrate the lack of intrinsic nature in dependent origination, they take them to be real phenomena and give rise to the two views of self and dharmas, like seeing a snake upon a rope. In eighty years, I have never once given rise to thoughts of desire, nor have I even once given rise to a single thought of pride. I have never accepted a robe from a householder, nor a robe made of cut patches, nor have I ever requested another to make a robe for me."

He once mended his robes with a needle; he never accepted invitations; he never begged for food from householders; he never leaned against a wall; he never looked upon the face of a woman; he never entered a nunnery; he never exchanged greetings with a nun, nor even spoke to them on the road. This pearl, so difficult to believe in, has long remained within [the Buddha’s] topknot, never recklessly given to others; now it is bestowed upon you. This pearl possesses two meanings: "luminous" (*ming*) and "perfectly round" (*yuan*).
"Luminous" is a metaphor for the wisdom of the Middle Way; "perfectly round" is a metaphor for the Eternal. Its presence "upon the crown" signifies that which is venerated as the ultimate fruit;
its location "within the topknot" signifies that it was truly concealed by provisional means. To "untie the topknot" is to reveal the provisional; to "bestow the pearl" is to...
Revealing the Reality. △ Next, the synthesis also has two parts. First, synthesizing with the Tathāgata Dharma-King:
seeing that the army of noble sages has achieved great merit, his heart is filled with great joy.
The Tathāgata is also like this... (up to) at that time the Tathāgata was also greatly rejoiced. (Regarding the phrase "seeing the worthy sages and so forth" in the *Zhongjing* [Combined Sūtra]:

the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: "Knowing suffering destroys the skandha-māra; severing accumulation leaves one free from the kleśa-māra; realizing cessation leaves one free from the mṛtyu-māra; practicing the path destroys the devaputra-māra.

The reason the *devaputra-māra* is not mentioned here is that while followers of the Hīnayāna mostly sever the first three māras, they have not yet destroyed the *devaputra-māra*. Nevertheless, there is the sense of "destruction" [in the latter]. Regarding the phrase "possessing greatness" in the Sūtra: when the Tathāgata sees these worthy sages of the Hīnayāna who have already eliminated the causes and effects within the realms, he names them [as having overcome] the skandhas.)

The battle reaches its conclusion after the Prajñāpāramitā; this is called the Great Meritorious Achievement. Therefore, the three poisons and the like are for the time being contained within the "Small" [Vehicle]. Thereafter, as time passes, it is generally termed "Joy" (prāmodya).
△ Second, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Dharma that the Tathāgata had not previously taught, is now finally expounded.

"Knowledge" is the name for the fruit; this is the first [aspect of] the unity of practice. The "first teaching" is the unity of instruction;

The two verses consist of fourteen and a half lines. They eulogize the aforementioned practice of the Dharma and the praise of the sutra, divided into two parts. The first four lines eulogize the practice of the Dharma;
the second, consisting of ten and a half lines, eulogizes the aforementioned praise of the difficulty of hearing this sutra. The former part is further divided into two:
the first line is a transposed verse summarizing the accomplishment of the practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all beings, one is then able to expound the sutras praised by the Buddha."

The preceding section provided a general clarification of the accomplishment of practice; now, the verse specifically reveals it. "Constantly practicing patience" refers to the accomplishment of practice while wearing robes;

"compassionately pitying all beings" refers to the accomplishment of practice while entering the chamber; "thereby being able to expound [the Dharma]" refers to the accomplishment of practice while sitting on the seat.
Next, three lines of verse describe the method of cultivation.
In the future age of the final dharma (until: causing them to dwell therein).

For example, as [the text] from "one of great strength" up to "joyfully bestows it.

Suppose there is a brave and capable man who is able to perform difficult tasks; the king unties the bright pearl from within his topknot and grants it to him.

Having known the sentient beings... [it was] for your sake that I have preached it.
(The four vows and the practice of peaceful conduct are concluded. (The second, the separate explanation of the four dharmas, is concluded. △ Third, the long [section].
This section provides a general summary of the practice, describing the signs of accomplishment and response to encourage cultivation.
It consists of twenty-three lines of verse in three parts. First, one and a half lines exhort the cultivation of four dharmas.
"After my parinirvāṇa... [up to] these four dharmas.
△ Next, twenty and a half lines cite the three retributions to provide exhortation; this is also called the "Purification of the Three Obstructions.
The final line is the summary. When the three obstructions are purified, the evil karma of the present life and future lives is exhausted, and one immediately attains the present life.

Regarding the superior retribution in future lives: the first line states that there will be no sorrow, affliction, illness, or pain; this refers to the transformation of karmic obstacles into present-life retribution.
Those who read this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, as well as free from illness, and their complexions will be bright and pure.
△ Second, half of the practice prevents being born into poverty, low status, or ugliness. This is the transformation of karmic obstacles; it is the transformation of the retribution of birth.
One will not be born into poverty, low status, or ugliness.
△ Section Three consists of nineteen lines. It clarifies the transformation of subsequent retribution. The transformation of the afflictive hindrances of the three poisons is divided into two parts.
The first three lines specifically clarify the transformation of the three afflictive hindrances; the subsequent sixteen lines generally clarify the transformation of all hindrances.
This is the first part.
"Sentient beings delight in seeing [him], like the shining of the sun.

This passage has three parts. First, one line clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of greed. Those with excessive desire are treated with contempt by others, and it further obstructs rebirth in the Brahma Heaven.
Because the obstacle of desire is transformed, he is someone whom people delight to see, and celestial youths serve him. Next, one line clarifies... [text continues]
The obstacle of hatred is transformed. By abandoning hatred, one removes the internal swords and arrows; thus, when entering battle, one is not wounded by external blades.

The subsequent line clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of delusion: fearless like a lion king, one wanders with sovereign ease; wisdom is like the sun, universally illuminating the four continents.
△ The second section consists of sixteen lines, which collectively clarify all obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

This transformation is also a transformation of future retribution (*paścātpākaja*). That the present manifestation of these signs occurs while upholding the sutra should be understood as having been accomplished long ago in the past;
it merely arises now by virtue of conditions. Furthermore, the various signs such as the causes and fruits of attaining Buddhahood are likewise all transformations of future retribution.
Therefore, within a dream, one sees the signs of future retribution across hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas;

all these events manifest within a single thought-moment of dreaming to represent the wondrous Dharma, which is inconceivable. Within the one is the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable is the one;

these signs appear beforehand so that the fruit shall later be realized. (Since peace and happiness are the practice of the Tathāgata, those who propagate the sutra prefigure the attainment of its fruition. Thus we know that the power of the merit of propagation is not small.)

Question: Why does he arrive at this point and immediately praise the teaching? Answer: This occurs at the end of the section on the propagation of the traces (the *jibun ryūtsū*). Previously, it was clarified that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the merit of propagating the sutra is profound. Ancient Buddhas have testified to the sutra, and now the present Buddha has attained enlightenment;

the benefits of its proclamation and dissemination across two hundred and eighty million worlds in this land and other directions are immeasurable. That people obtain such wondrous merit is truly due to the reality of the Dharma. Therefore, at the end of the propagation, he again distinguishes that which is propagated. What is it that is propagated? It is the revelation through the three turnings of the wheel.

Thus, he cites the majestic subduing of the Wheel-Turning King and how his military hosts obtained merit. Since there are degrees of merit—great and small—the rewards bestowed are not the same. Following these four lines, he again provides a summary to manifest that the merit of these four practices is perfected. One who can practice these deeds also possesses the power to propagate the sutra, thereby transforming others.

The merit returns to oneself; thus, the signs of fruition manifest first, enabling the Great Being to experience in a single moment a dream spanning more than a billion lifetimes, thereby demonstrating that the merit of propagating the teaching throughout one lifetime surpasses that of many kalpas. Furthermore, there are six [aspects]:

from the initial stage of faith up to the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight phases of manifestation in wondrous enlightenment, all are adorned by the Tathāgata’s adornments as his own adornment—this is the retribution for patience.
Regarding the first three practices, he dreams of entering the ten stages of faith. Furthermore, there are two [aspects]; in the first two and a half practices, he manifests compassion.
[The text] says:
"If, in a dream... [up to] reverently joining the palms.
△ Next half-line: the retribution for right view and freedom from delusion.
He sees his own body and [the Buddhas] preach the Dharma for him.
△ Second, six lines and a half: Dreaming of entering the Ten Abodes;
furthermore, he sees the various Buddhas (up to) joining his palms to listen to the Dharma.

Since it is said that one who realizes non-retrogressive wisdom is immediately conferred the prediction [of enlightenment], one should know that this refers to attaining the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) where one receives the prediction through the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
△ Third, three phrases: dreaming of practicing the ten practices (*daśa-pratipatti*).
Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests practicing wholesome dharmas;
again, seeing oneself in mountain forests, one knows this to be the practice of wholesome dharmas through the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). (Section Four, One Sentence:
Dream-Realization of the Ten Dedications.)
Realizing all true marks. Realizing all true marks.
Know that these are the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); they constitute the position of correctly contemplating the Middle Way. △ Five [verses], two lines each:
Entering the ten stages in a dream.
He enters deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Entering deeply into meditative concentration, he attains the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*) within the tenth stage (*daśama-bhūmi*).

He then enters the adamantine concentration (*vajra-samādhi*), whereupon all Buddhas appear before him, touching his head with their hands to confer upon him the office of a Buddha. (Regarding the term "stainless," this has already been attained from the first dwelling [stage]. If one speaks of entering the adamantine concentration, the meaning corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment [*samyak-sambodhi*], which properly belongs within the tenth stage.)
△ Sixth, the discourse on the five elements being entrusted to the Wondrous Enlightenment:
"The bodies of all Buddhas are golden-colored" (up to) "like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has vanished.

One dreams of the Buddha manifesting the eight phases [of enlightenment] and thereby realizes the Wondrous Enlightenment. This stage may correspond to the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), wherein one is able to attain Buddhahood through the eight phases.

This is the characteristic [of the dream]. It remains within the preceding stages and is merely discussed as a metaphor for ultimate awakening. As for "the dreamer," from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha*, all possess dreams;
only the Buddha does not dream. Because he is free from doubt and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he does not dream.
Dreams arise due to five causes, as stated in the verse: "Through a doubting mind, through discrimination, through learning, through present circumstances, and by the arrival of non-human beings."

They spoke to one another: "Because of these five matters in a dream, and furthermore because of what has been experienced through hearing and seeing, as well as various afflictions—making seven matters in total—dreams occur.
If even the present mental consciousness does not perceive visible forms, how could the mental faculty perceive visible forms within a dream?"
Answer: These are all merely perceptions based on what has been previously seen or heard; they are simply signs of auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
Within a dream, there is no supernormal power (*abhijñā*) nor knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*); how, then, could one see future events? Answer:

This is not the domain of the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), but rather a form of inference (*anumāna*). People have had such dreams in the past and experienced such results; now, by means of this comparison...

[The Buddha] said, "I know. He asked, "Who sleeps? He replied, "Those in the five realms of existence and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) all sleep. Even those in the womb whose sense faculties (*indriya*) are complete are sleeping;
even the Buddha sleeps. He asked, "Sleep is delusion (*moha*) and an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*). How is this [statement] to be reconciled with that?"

Answer: The Buddha, having given rise to the desire to manifest before [beings], sleeps for the sake of regulating his body; this is not the sleep of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) nor the sleep of delusion (*moha*).
(The preceding twenty and a half lines conclude by citing the three retributions to provide exhortation. △ The final line summarizes the completion of the practice.
If, in the evil ages of the future, one should preach this foremost Dharma, that person shall obtain great benefit, including all the aforementioned merits.
(The third summary on the signs of the accomplishment of practice and the resulting auspicious omens is concluded. (The "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" is concluded.)
△ First, the table of contents is presented; next, the scriptural text is explained. Now, for the first part:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Fifteen, "The Emergence from the Earth. To explain this chapter on the emergence:
the Teacher is august and the Way is venerable; one bows with reverent devotion. At a single command from the Tathāgata, they rush forth from the four quarters.

[The Buddha] emerged from the earth; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (the world). Throughout the three periods of time, he guides and transforms beings, his beneficence and benefit being boundless.
As a single moon casts ten thousand reflections, who could fathom this? He summons the past to manifest [the truth], and propagates the Sūtra to benefit the present.

Hence it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (for the sake of men). Space is serene and still, without beginning or end; yet those who are deluded cling to outward traces and remain in darkness.
Its fundamental principle is to summon the past to reveal the present and to shatter the near to manifest the distant; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth.

(The analogy of space and so forth serves as the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* [the standpoint of therapeutic remedy], referring to what is symbolized. Space is the principle (*li*); the fundamental and the derivative are phenomena (*shi*). While phenomena possess the fundamental and the derivative, the principle has no such sequence of early or late. Those who are deluded confuse the principle and remain in darkness regarding the fundamental and the derivative; thus, they cling to the near derivative and lose sight of the distant fundamental.)

The fundamental and the manifested remain obscure; how much more so regarding the inconceivable oneness! Thus, the disciple of the fundamental [state] dwells in the lower void, while the teacher of the fundamental state has long dwelt in the void. The present teacher and disciple dwell in the present void. The long-term void and the present void, as well as the lower void, are one in essence.

Although they are one in essence, the fundamental disciple originally knew the near-trace, whereas the present disciple still remains deluded regarding the distant fundamental. To shatter the attachment to the near, the past is summoned to reveal the present. Because the present disciple brings forth a request through doubt, only upon hearing the teaching is it shattered.

To destroy the evil of clinging to the near, it is called "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*). The young father at the site of enlightenment and the old child in the land of tranquil light manifest the power of their medicine, causing all to...

This is understood; therefore, it is said that they "emerge from the earth. Regarding the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint): why is Śākyamuni at the site of enlightenment (*śīta-vana*) depicted as having newly attained [Buddhahood], while the Bodhisattva of Peaceful Light (*Śāntaprabha*) is depicted as having long practiced?

Why is the father young and the son old? According to the meaning of the subsequent analogy of the father and son: the father has long ago taken the medicine of "rejuvenation" that restores the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowing wisdom);

thus, though he is old, he appears young. The son has also long received the formula for the eternal and deathless; thus, though he is young, he appears old. Although each possesses the merit of taking this medicine, the father and son have long been established in these four *siddhāntas*. While this provides a general explanation for the present text, the underlying intent encompasses all of them.

Regarding the subsequent chapters: however, the first *Siddhi* has its text in this present chapter; the second *Siddhi* incorporates the subsequent chapters; and the third and fourth *Siddhis* draw upon the subsequent chapters. All of these serve to assist the latter [chapters] in order to achieve manifest clarity and distance. This is because they give rise to the good and destroy the evil by means of seeing the root.

Thus we know that the world is the basis for the three *siddhāntas*. Therefore, in the "Emergence from the Earth" chapter, the focus is specifically on the world. The text says: "From where do they come? By what causes and conditions have they gathered?
Now, by explaining this chapter through various meanings, I shall clarify the understanding of the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*;
hence it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth. Next, the explanation of the scriptural text: From here below begins the second major section, the Opening of the Root Gate.
The traces manifest the fundamental source. This reveals the proximate traces of the Master’s school and manifests the remote foundation of the Buddha-ground.
The text is divided into three parts: first, from here below until "you yourselves shall hear it through this," which constitutes the introductory section;
second, from "At that time, Śākyamuni addressed Maitreya" below, until the nineteen lines spoken by Maitreya in the *Bhadrakalpika-parivarta* (Chapter on the Distinction of Merit).
The verse marks the section on the formal exposition. The eleven chapters and a half following the verses constitute the section on the dissemination [of the teaching].
The introductory text is divided into two parts: first, the introduction of the miraculous emergence; second, the introduction of the inquiry. The emergence is further divided into three parts:
first, the bodhisattvas from other directions requesting the propagation of the sutra; second, the Tathāgata’s refusal; third, the miraculous emergence from below. This is the first part.

At that time, bodhisattvas from other lands—[from the phrase "lands of other directions" to] "should expound it widely in this land"—having heard that the merit of transmitting the sutra is great, all desired to make a vow to dwell here and propagate it;
thus they requested [the Buddha] to do so. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s refusal.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas (up to the point where he) was about to preach this sūtra extensively.
The Tathāgata stopped him for three reasons. First, each of you has your own specific responsibility;
if you remain in this land, it would neglect the benefit of others. Second, although one may wish to proclaim the matters for establishing karmic connections between other regions and this land...
First, bestowing [the teachings] may be beneficial or obstructive. Second, if one were to permit it, one would be unable to summon those from the lower realms;

if they did not come, the traces [of the teaching] could not be destroyed and the ultimate truth could not be revealed—this constitutes the third point. Thus, the Tathāgata prohibited it. There are likewise three reasons for summoning those from the lower realms:
they are long-standing disciples; they are summoned to propagate the wondrous Dharma; and because their conditions are profound and vast, they are capable [of this task].
It benefits this land universally; it benefits the lands of the manifested bodies universally; it benefits the lands of other directions universally.
Furthermore, it reveals the near to open up the distant; therefore, they stop there and summon those below. The third section, "The Emergence from Below," is divided into two parts:

first, the narrative by the sutra compiler describing the phenomena; second, the inquiry after their well-being. Each of these two sections contains five items. Regarding the first five: first, the emergence.
When the Buddha spoke these words, [the beings of] the Sahā world [emerged] simultaneously from the earth.
II. Physical Characteristics:
The bodies of all these bodhisattvas were golden in color, possessed the thirty-two marks, and emitted immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, the dwelling place.
Initially, it was entirely beneath this Sahā world, abiding in the void of this realm.

As for the dwelling place, it is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*). "Constant" refers to the quality of permanence; "quiescent" refers to the quality of bliss; "light" refers to purity.
I am this secret treasury of the four virtues; it is my dwelling place. By means of the dharma of non-abiding, I abide within this secret treasury.
"The lower direction" refers to the abyssal depths of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the ultimate ground of the profound mystery; therefore, it is called the lower direction.
That which is below does not belong to this; that which is within emptiness does not belong to that. Neither this nor that is precisely the Middle Way.
To emerge from this without being above, without being below this, neither above nor below, but dwelling within emptiness—this too is the Middle Way.
△ Fourth, coming because of having heard the command.
These bodhisattvas, having heard the sounds spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, have come from below.
As for the reasons for their coming: they have come because they heard the summons; they have come to propagate the Dharma; they have come to shatter attachments;
they have come to reveal the fundamental source—all as described above. △ Five: The Retinue.

Each and every bodhisattva—from those [numbering] as many as cannot be known even by calculation or analogy—has a retinue that, if judged by human sentiment, would be considered large for one leading sixty thousand, fifty thousand, or a *gaṅgā-saṃkhyeya* of followers, and small for one leading three, two, or one;
while one who is alone would be considered solitary. However, if one seeks this according to the text:
Sixty thousand or fifty thousand are few; those who are solitary are many. The text says: "Those who dwell alone and solitary, their number exceeds even the above.
If one relies on the Dharma-gate, every single one is the virtue of the Teacher, capable of leading the multitude to the place of treasure.
One should know that the solitary individual is not alone, and sixty thousand are not many; the one is indeed the one.
The Path is pure. Two refers to concentration and wisdom. Three refers to precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Four refers to the Four Noble Truths. Five refers to the five eyes.
Six refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Each perfection encompasses the ten dharma-realms; each realm has ten [aspects], making one hundred.
One hundred possesses one thousand; one thousand realms possess ten thousand. Thus, one perfection encompasses ten thousand, and the six perfections [encompass sixty thousand].
Sixty thousand Dharma-gates: many are not considered many; one is not considered few. It is neither many nor few, yet it is both many and few.
(The first section, the narrative by the sūtra-reciter, consisting of five parts, concludes. △ Second, the inquiry after his well-being, which is divided into five parts:
1. Offerings of the three karmas; 2. The words of the inquiry; 3. The Buddha’s response regarding his peace and well-being; 4. Verses of rejoicing; 5. [The conclusion].
The Tathāgata praised this; it is now first [described].
These bodhisattvas filled the empty space of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.
Regarding their initial offering of the three karmas, it lasted for fifty minor kalpas, yet was perceived as being like half a day by the fourfold assembly, who saw them everywhere.
This is to conceal the long and manifest the short; by borrowing his supernatural power, he causes the narrow to appear as vast.
Both are inconceivable. To prostrate and circumambulate is with the body; to praise the Dharma is with the mouth; to gaze up in reverence is with the mind.
That fifty minor eons are perceived as half a day—this is the inconceivability of time. It is not that the Tathāgata’s vision does not [perceive the full duration].
Second, regarding the two aspects: the Bodhisattvas below constantly face [the Buddha] and offer praise, while the Tathāgata remains silent and constantly accepts their eulogies.
To those who understand, what is short is made long—meaning fifty small kalpas; to those who are deluded, what is long is made short—meaning it is like half a day.
This serves as an introductory lead-in for the fundamental and the manifested. Before the Tathāgata has spoken, those in darkness abandon the fundamental and cling to the manifested. The Buddha...
If one reveals and clarifies this, one realizes what is near and reaches what is far; thus one also knows that the inconceivable is one.

That the fourfold assembly sees the Bodhisattva everywhere is likewise inconceivable. Indeed, what is seen by the fleshly eye and the divine eye does not extend far, yet what is now beheld fills all of empty space.
Seeing the intensity of the rain, one knows the dragon is great; seeing the abundance of the flowers, one knows the pond is deep.
Seeing the Bodhisattvas filling the void, one knows that the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm).
△ Second, the expression of greetings:
Among this assembly of Bodhisattvas, there were four leaders who spoke in verse, saying:
"Is the World-Honored One at ease? (Up to: Has he become weary? This section has three parts:
first, the designation of the four guides; second, the presentation of the inquiry; and third, the repetition of the verse.

As for mentioning only these four individuals, it is intended to illustrate the forty stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, just as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions only Dharmamati and Guṇakara.
The Golden Banner and the Golden Treasury explain the forty stages. △ Third, the Buddha’s Answer Regarding Peace and Bliss:
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas... [until] they enter the Buddha-wisdom.

The Tathāgata answered fully regarding the two matters of peace and ease of deliverance. These two things are mutually supportive: ease of deliverance leads to peace, and peace leads to ease of deliverance.
Ease of deliverance consists of two aspects: first, those with sharp faculties and thick merit who, throughout successive lifetimes, have constantly received the Great Transformation;
upon first seeing my body, they immediately receive the *Avataṃsaka* and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is like fruit that is ripe and easily falls; such is this assembly.
They are easy to deliver. Yet, because their faculties are dull and their merit is meager, they have not received the Great Transformation throughout successive lifetimes.
For the sake of such people, it was necessary to open up the sudden teaching and explain the gradual; thus, they were tamed through the Tripitaka, the Vaipulya, and the Prajñāpāramitā.

Now, by hearing the Lotus Sutra, these same individuals enter the Buddha-wisdom. Although this is more difficult than [entering] the previous [Avataṃsaka], for the Buddha it is exceedingly easy. The Buddha—

One must recognize what is appropriate and employ skillful means to find the right course. "Thinly applying ointment and using warm compresses" is like an infant who, for the sake of illness, must temporarily be weaned from milk; one uses poison as a temporary measure to coat the nipple.

Once the potency of the medicine has subsided, the breast is washed clean so the child may drink again. The nature of the milk before and after is no different; it is only for the sake of the illness that the temporary measures of administering or withholding are established.

It is also like a carbuncle: when the heat is at its peak, one must apply cold compresses. When the heat subsides and the inflammation ceases, the body before and after is not different. One applies the compress temporarily for the heat; once the heat has receded, it returns to its original state. Entering here and entering there—the two states are not different. It is only because the faculties are dull.

[This refers to] those whose time of entry has not yet arrived; they are like an abscess or an infant that still requires the application of ointments and compresses, being temporarily brought to maturity by the three substances such as curd, and are thus said to be "thin" (i.e., immature). △ Fourth, the recitation of verses in sympathetic joy.
At that time, the great Bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent... (up to)... we rejoice.
Those who understand and rejoice in the questioner are none other than the four great beings from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the [Bodhisattva] Body from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The son requested three times; all [these requests] were capable inquiries. That which was inquired about was precisely the inquiry into the Buddha’s wisdom.

An explanation of the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata. As for "Tathāgata," it is the general designation for the two Buddhas and three Buddhas—the Fundamental Buddha and the Traces-Buddha—of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. "Lifespan" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) means measurement;

This is because it explains two or three aspects of the Buddha’s merit; hence, it is called the "Chapter on the Life Span of the Tathāgata. The meaning of "Tathāgata" is manifold;

for now, we shall clarify two or three types of Tathāgatas, and the rest may be understood by analogy. As for the two types of Tathāgatas: first is the *dharmakāya* (True Body), and second is the *nirmāṇakāya* (Response Body).

Regarding the True Body, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "Because he has come (*āgata*) to achieve perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) by means of the path of reality (*tathatā-mārga*), he is called the Tathāgata. "By means of" refers to...

The Dharma is suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*). Reality is the object of suchness. The Path (*mārga*) is the cause; awakening (*bodhi*) is the fruit. If one discusses the vehicle (*yāna*) alone, there is nothing known;
if one clarifies reality alone, there is no one who knows. When object and wisdom are in union, there is cause and fruit:

when the illumination of the object is not yet exhaustive, it is called the cause; when the source is fully exhausted, it is the fruit. Thus the meanings of the Path and Awakening are established, which is precisely "riding upon suchness" (*tathatā-yāna*).
The Realized Way (Bhūtārtha-mārga). Coming to achieve perfect enlightenment—this is the True Body Tathāgata (Dharmakāya-tathāgata). Second, the Response Body (Nirmāṇakāya):

by means of wisdom as it truly is (yathābhūta-jñāna), riding upon the path as it truly is, coming to take birth within the three realms of existence (trai-dhātuka) and manifesting the achievement of perfect enlightenment—this is the Response Body Tathāgata.

Third, the Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says: "To understand according to the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), and according to the characteristics of phenomena..."
It is called the Tathāgata. The two phrases of the treatise [refer to] the fulfillment of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

"Understanding according to the dharma-characteristic" (*yathādharma-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the fulfillment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). "Explaining according to the dharma-characteristic" (*yathādharma-lakṣaṇa-vyākhyāna*) refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Regarding the first phrase, "according to the dharma-characteristic":
"suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to the realm of the true mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is neither cause nor fruit, and whose nature remains constant whether a Buddha appears or not.
The characteristics are thus constant; to pervade all places without variation is "Thusness" (tathatā). To arrive without moving is "Coming" (āgata).
This is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata. Regarding the subsequent explanation: it refers to the wisdom of the suchness of phenomena (dharmatathatājñāna).

Riding upon the true path of suchness, one comes to achieve wondrous enlightenment. Wisdom accords with suchness; from the perspective of principle, it is called "Suchness," and from the perspective of wisdom, it is called "Coming."
This is precisely the Sambhogakāya Tathāgata. Therefore, the Treatise states: "To understand according to the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) is called 'Tathāgata' (Thus-Come-One).

To teach according to the characteristics of phenomena is because the object and wisdom of Suchness (tathatā) are united; thus, one is able to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment in every place.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "As mercury mixed with pure gold can coat all manner of forms, so the merit combined with the Dharmakāya responds to beings in every place."
Manifestly dwelling, accomplishing the path through the eight phases, and turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma—this is the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body) Tathāgata. Therefore, the treatise states:
"One who speaks in accordance with the characteristics of phenomena is called a Tathāgata. The Dharmakāya (Dharma Body) Tathāgata is named Vairocana, which translates as "pervading all places.
The Saṃbhogakāya (Reward Body) Tathāgata is named Rocana, which translates as "pure and full. The Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata...

He is named Śākyamuni, which translates as "The One Who Crosses Over the *Vajrākṣa* Stone" (*Wòjiāo*). Regarding the *Vajrākṣa*: in the "Chapter on Names and Titles" of the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, it is listed that there is a stone in the great ocean called *Jiāo* (the Scorched).

When the myriad streams pour over it, they are all exhausted upon reaching the stone; for this reason, the waters of the great ocean do not increase. The transmigration of sentient beings is like this scorched stone:

though the five desires pour over it, they never reach satiety. Only a Buddha can deliver them—this is why he is so called. These three Tathāgatas cannot be taken individually. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:

The Dharma-body is not [a separate entity], Prajñā is not [a separate entity], and Liberation is not [a separate entity]. When these three dharmas are fully integrated, it is called the Secret Treasury;
this is named Great Nirvāṇa. It is like the three dots of the letter *i*: they cannot be said to be one or different, nor can they be arranged vertically, horizontally, or separately.

To contemplate these three dharmas as a perfect whole is what is designated by the provisional name "Tathāgata. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* concludes the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, forming the lotus pedestal.

The root is the basis, while the flowers and leaves are the branches; these are distinguished as separate conditions. Although it is explained in this way, the root and the branches cannot be separated from one another.

Synthesizing the intent of all the sūtras, one should know that it is clear that the three Buddhas are neither identical nor different.

Question: This chapter does not mention the names of the three Buddhas; why then do you provide this explanation? Answer: Although their names are not explicitly stated, their meaning is fully present.
The text says: "Neither identical nor different; not as the triple world is, yet seeing the triple world. This is not a partial identity.
To manifest the suchness of perfection is precisely the meaning of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is said:

"The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are. This is the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna), which accords with the realm of suchness. Omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is this knowing.

The Buddha-eye is seeing; this is the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is said that sometimes one manifests one's own body and one's own affairs, or manifests another's body and another's affairs;
this is the meaning of the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata. If there are only the three Tathāgatas of intrinsic virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), they are horizontal;
if there are only the three Tathāgatas of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), they are vertical. First is the Dharma-body, followed by the Reward-body.
The "subsequent response" is also sequential. This present sutra, however, speaks of the perfect [teaching], wherein the three Tathāgatas are neither sequential nor horizontal.
Since even the sequential and horizontal Tathāgatas do not accord with the meaning of this [present] teaching, how much less so the Tathāgatas of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings?

Furthermore, those instances prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that clarify the perfect Tathāgata are all merely teachings spoken within the provisional traces (*traces*). [This is] the third [point]: revealing the origin by manifesting the fundamental.
The Tathāgata is forever distinct from all other sūtras. The treatise states: "Because he manifests the attainment of unexcelled great bodhi, there are three kinds of bodhi:
first, the bodhi of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), which appears according to what is appropriate, as in the sūtra: 'He departed from the palace of the Śākyas';
second, the bodhi of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), wherein the ten stages are fulfilled and eternal nirvāṇa is attained, as in the sūtra: 'I have indeed attained [it]...'"
The Buddha has already come after immeasurable and boundless kalpas. The three dharmas of the Buddha’s bodhi are the Tathāgatagarbha, the intrinsically pure nirvāṇa, and the unchanging.
As the sūtra says: "Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are.

The sūtra provides the meaning, while the śāstra reveals the names. If one does not provide the above interpretation, how could it accord with the sūtra and the śāstra? Next, the lifespan is explained.

"Measure" (*pramāṇa*) means the sense of "experiencing" (*vedanā*). Because *tathatā* is not separated from all phenomena, it is called "experiencing. Furthermore, because the object and the wisdom are in correspondence, it is called "experiencing.
Moreover, because it is obtained as retribution throughout a single lifetime and continues without interruption for a hundred years, it is called "experiencing. As for "measure":

This is an exposition. Regarding the Tathāgata of the Dharma (*dharmatathāgata*), he takes the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) as his life. Regarding the Tathāgata of Retribution (*vipākatathāgata*), he takes wisdom (*prajñā*) as his life.

Regarding the Tathāgata of Response (*nirmāṇatathāgata*), he takes the shared engagement with the principle as his life. As for the Tathāgata of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāyatathāgata*), the one whose life is the principle of suchness, whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the nature and characteristics remain eternally as they are;
this does not depend on whether there is correspondence (*saṃprayoga*) or non-continuity (correspondence refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*, while continuity refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*).
There is neither measure nor immeasurability. The text states: "Neither identical nor different; neither empty nor real.
This is indeed the designation of the Dharma-body according to the principle. As for the designation of the Reward-body Tathāgata, it is by means of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*).
The seal accords with the realm of suchness (*tathatā*). The realm gives rise to wisdom as its retribution; wisdom merging with the realm constitutes reception.
Since the realm is immeasurable and boundless, eternally abiding and indestructible, wisdom is likewise so. As the container is large, the lid is large. The text says:

"Such is the power of my wisdom, obtained through long-cultivated practice. The light of my insight illuminates the immeasurable, and my lifespan spans countless eons. This is the definitive expression.
This measures the wisdom-life of the *sambhogakāya* Tathāgata. Regarding the measurement of the *nirmāṇakāya*:

the *nirmāṇakāya* shares the same conditions; when the conditions are long, it is long; when the conditions are short, it is short, and so forth. From its own perspective, what does this matter to me? A text states:
"It repeatedly manifests birth and repeatedly manifests extinction; or again, it speaks of itself with different names and varying ages. This...

This is the definitive measurement of the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya), which shares the same objective conditions as the Buddha’s life. Furthermore, the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) is neither measurable nor immeasurable.

The Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) is measurable prior to the vajra-like samādhi and immeasurable thereafter. The Responsive Body is measurable according to conditions, yet immeasurable in its uninterrupted application of activity.
Regarding the general measurement, three phrases pertain to the sages, while one phrase belongs to ordinary beings. That is to say:

That which is finite and impermanent is entirely contrary to the meaning of the Buddha. (Supplementary note: To say it is finite and impermanent is because ordinary beings remain in delusion; the Dharmakāya, following conditions, transmigrates through the five paths.)

This is finite, not infinite; it is impermanent, not truly eternal. Therefore, it is said that none of these constitute the meaning of the Buddha. Although they do not constitute the meaning of the Buddha, the nature of the Dharmakāya is pure and cannot be defiled by afflictions; it is identical in essence to the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata and serves as the basis for the Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya.

Thus, it can be considered a single phrase, forming a set of four phrases. When the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive the Buddha’s lifespan, it is like winter sunlight; what the Bodhisattvas perceive is like spring sunlight;
only when a Buddha perceives a Buddha is the lifespan immeasurable, like summer sunlight. This is because ordinary beings—

Now, this vast world is shrouded in obscurity and dimness. Although the practitioners of the two vehicles—the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*—have severed the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), they do not perceive the Middle Way.

Even if they cast off the body of segmented birth (*pariccheda-śarīra*) and receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), as long as they have not shattered ignorance (*avidyā*), that which is venerated in that land remains but a superior response-body (*vairocana-nirmāṇakāya*).
Therefore, those of the two vehicles see only the winter sun. As for the bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), what they perceive is likewise limited.
The same as before. If one breaks through ignorance and attains even a portion of the *dharmakāya*, this is spoken of in terms of "giving.

To say that one attains the vision of the *saṃbhogakāya* and its lifespan is spoken of in terms of "taking away"; yet this is still merely the *prabhāsvarakāya* (the superior response-body). It has not yet exhausted the source of the *saṃbhogakāya*, nor reached the ultimate limit of the *dharmatā*.
The Buddha-lifespan perceived at this stage is like the spring sun; only between Buddha and Buddha can the nature be fully exhausted.
The source [of this teaching] is the vision of the Dharma-body’s lifespan, which is like the summer sun. The Great Sūtra employs three analogies to illustrate it:
among all that is eternal, space is foremost; among all lifespans, the Tathāgata is foremost. This illustrates the lifespan of the Dharma-body.
It is without beginning and without end; its nature and characteristics are concentrated and serene, unlike those of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) or *vipākakāya* (retribution body).

Second, it is like the four rivers, all of which flow back to the great ocean; this illustrates that the myriad virtues cultivated by the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) all evoke the ocean of longevity within the city of the Buddha.
Third, from Lake Anavatapta flow the four great rivers; this illustrates that the longevity of the *nirmāṇakāya* proceeds from the *dharmakāya* (truth body) and the *saṃbhogakāya*.
[The Buddha] emerged. This is to measure and compare with others’ strengths and weaknesses. This chapter’s exposition comprehensively clarifies the three bodies (*trikāya*).

If understood from a specific perspective, it primarily concerns the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Why? Because the meaning facilitates the coherence of the text. Regarding "the meaning facilitates": the wisdom of the reward body is in sublime accord with the ultimate and in harmonious resonance with the mundane;
thus, the three bodies are perfectly complete. Therefore, it is said that the meaning facilitates. Regarding "the coherence of the text": since my attaining Buddhahood, it has been very...

Because it is immensely remote, it is able to benefit sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. That which is accomplished is the *dharmakāya*; that which accomplishes is the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Because the *dharma* and *saṃbhoga* bodies are unified, they are able to benefit all things; thus it is said that the words coincide.
Inferring from this, the primary intent is to discuss the merits of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha. Furthermore, such various merits of the three bodies are all...
That which was first accomplished long ago beneath the Bodhi tree at this site is called the "Original" (hon).

That which was accomplished today at the site of the Path of Quiescence in the interim is called the "Trace" (shaku). These are what are referred to as the "Original and the Trace" in the various sutras.

That is to say, the Dharma-body and its retribution (dharmabhāṣa) accomplished at the site of the tranquil extinction of the Path constitute the "Root. The two types of responsive bodies (nirmāṇakāya), superior and inferior, arising from that Root constitute the "Traces.
As clarified in the present sutra, taking the three bodies accomplished at the site of tranquil extinction and those accomplished during the intermediate period, all are designated as "Traces.
Taking the three bodies obtained at the original site of the Path in the past, they are designated as the "Root. Therefore, in relation to the various sutras...

They are distinct. It is not without the fundamental that the traces are manifested; it is not without the traces that the fundamental is revealed. Although the fundamental and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

Question: If that which is accomplished nearby is the provisional means (upāya) and that which is accomplished afar is the ultimate reality (bhūtatathatā), then [how does this relate to] the Great [Flower Garland Sutra’s] Place of the Tranquil Extinction?

It has already transcended the previous nine kalpas, all of which were established as skillful means (*upāya*). If that is so, since the Lotus Sūtra of the Buddha’s original teaching has long since been opened, why is the case of Sadāparibhūta considered more recent?
The answer is: one should know that after the Lotus Sūtra, there are further skillful means; for it opens up the three [vehicles] to manifest the one.
The Way of all Buddhas is the same. Opening up the near to reveal the far is likewise the same for all Buddhas.
Thus we know that by relying on the fundamental reality accomplished from time immemorial, it is truly without beginning or end and cannot be measured or compared.
That which has a beginning and an end, or a near and a far, refers only to its manifested traces (having thus concluded the preliminary exposition of the chapter titles).

△ Next, the scriptural text is explained. In the preceding chapter, the near was briefly opened and the far revealed; this stirred attachments and gave rise to doubt. In this chapter, the near is extensively opened and the far revealed;
this severs doubt and engenders faith. The text is divided into two parts: first, an exhortation to believe; second, the formal response. Regarding the exhortation to believe:

the Buddha’s intent constitutes the exhortation, and the assembly’s reception thereof constitutes belief. This section contains three exhortations and three requests, with repeated requests following repeated exhortations.

Admonition. In the Trace Gate (Ji-men), there are three requests and one admonition; here, there are four requests and four admonitions. Taken together from beginning to end, there are five admonitions and seven requests.

These concern a most extraordinary and momentous matter, expressed with great earnestness and gravity. Now, regarding the first admonition on faith, there are four parts, of which the first three are admonitions.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas (up to): "You all should believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of sincerity and truth.
These three admonitions are earnest exhortations. *Cheng* (sincerity) means loyalty; *di* (truth) means thorough reality. It does not deceive others.
When one speaks, it reaches the truth. Formerly, during the seven stages of expedient means, speech was according to the intentions of others and was not a declaration of sincere reality.
Now, speech is according to one's own intention, revealing the essentials; therefore, the words are called "sincere and true. △ Second and third: The Request.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, [proceeded] thus three times until they had made this request.
△ This was the third entreaty.
They spoke again, saying: "We only pray that you will explain it; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words."
△ The Fourfold Admonition.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas would not cease their threefold request, addressed them, saying: "Listen attentively" (having first completed the admonition regarding faith).
△ Second, the formal response, which consists of prose and verse. The prose is divided into two parts: 1. [The first part...]
This section refutes the near to reveal the far, benefiting sentient beings across the three periods of time. It further consists of two parts: first, exposing the sentiments that cling to the near;
second, formally refuting the near to reveal the far. This is the first part.
"By the power of the Tathāgata’s secret supernatural penetrations" (up to) "attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This scriptural passage consists of three sections. First, the phrase "the power of the Tathāgata’s secret supernatural penetrations" identifies the dharma that was previously misunderstood;
it is the very foundation upon which the Tathāgata attained enlightenment long ago. That one body is itself the three bodies is what is termed "secret. That the three bodies are...
The single body is called "mysterious" (*mi*). Furthermore, that which was not previously taught is called "secret" (*bi*). That which is known only by the Buddha himself is called "mysterious.
As for the power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), it is the function of the three bodies. "Spiritual" (*shen*) refers to the principle of natural immovability.
This is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmakāya*). Penetrating wisdom that is unobstructed and inconceivable is the Reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Power, which is sovereign functional efficacy, is the Response body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Next, the phrase "all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras" refers to those beings who are subject to delusion.
All three [bodies] are said to manifest from Śākyamuni’s departure from the palace of the Śākyas toward Gayā.

The city is not far away. Sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he attains perfect awakening (samyak-saṃbodhi). This is a sentiment regarding the distance of delusion. In this original exposition, there is no further mention of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha);
it addresses only the bodhisattvas. Bodhisattvas are included within the three wholesome realms of existence: devas, humans, and asuras. There are three types of bodhisattvas:
those from the lower regions, those from other directions, and those who have long resided [there]. "Those from the lower regions" refers to the original inhabitants.
Because they are transformed by the Sun (the Buddha), there is no attachment to what is called "nearness. Regarding those who have long resided in other directions, there are two types:

first, those who arise from the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). These were already previously attained to the non-arising [of birth] in past lives, or had already previously heard of the manifestation of their origins and the revelation of their fundamental nature.

Even if one has not yet heard it, upon the exhaustion of retribution, one will receive the Dharma-nature body; within the stage of the Dharma-body, one should naturally be able to hear this teaching of the long duration.
Therefore, one should give rise to the thought that Bodhisattvas mostly lack attachment to what is near.

This applies to both those who have now for the first time attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and those who have not yet attained it. △ Second, the actual refutation of "nearness."
To manifest the remote, one shatters the delusion of clinging to the near in order to reveal the primordial source that has existed for a long time.

The three successive instances in the preceding text where the Tathāgata earnestly exhorted and cautioned you, saying, "You should all believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth," refer precisely to this.
The text consists of two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the distant [time]. Second, the establishment of analogies for comparison.
Now, the first part: "Furthermore, son of good family... for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas."

(An interpolated supplement states: "However" refers to the intention of allowing [the Buddha] to provisionally accept [the request]. From the words "Good son" onwards, he immediately revokes it, saying that it is not only [since the time of] Gayā; in truth, since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed.
This is what the Tathāgata speaks according to reality; therefore, he says "in truth"). △ Second, setting forth a parable for comparison, in three parts:
1. Presenting the parable and asking a question; 2. The answer; 3. The application. Now, the first part.
"For example, if there were five hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* [beings]—[up to that point]—would one be able to know their number?
△ Second, in the answer, it is shown that three people do not know.
Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others all addressed the Buddha, saying: [omitted] "In this way, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless.
△ Third, the combined analogy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas: [omitted] "for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
The realm touched by even a single falling atom is already ineffable; how much more so the realm untouched by falling atoms?
Since the realms of both falling and non-falling atoms cannot be described, how could the atoms themselves—both falling and non-falling—be described?
How much less, then, can that which transcends these be described?

Supplementary Note: Regarding the analogy of wiping away dust from within the sutras, it serves to measure the vast and remote origin of the lifespan of our original teacher, Śākyamuni, since his attainment of Buddhahood.
As for the name of that original Buddha, there has been no definitive identification of which Buddha it refers to throughout ancient or modern times.

Some take the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) to be the fundamental basis for remote accomplishment; yet the Dharma-body has neither duration nor proximity, nor does it possess either accomplishment or non-accomplishment.
The Great Master directly points out that this is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). It accords with the supreme above and responds to those below, such that the three bodies are perfectly complete.
Such merits were all fully cultivated and accomplished long ago beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment; thus it is named [the Reward-body].
This is the essence; all else is merely its trace. "Buddha" is the name of this essence. Allow me, with my limited perspective, to venture a discussion upon it.
Looking back through the vast expanse of antiquity, there was no Buddha until the very first, Vipaśyin Tathāgata (King of Majestic Sound).

Through the power of the internal permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the power of the instruction of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), he attained self-awakening and self-cultivation through untaught wisdom and spontaneous wisdom, thereby reaching [enlightenment] on his own.

The attainment of Buddhahood through these causal conditions is recorded in certain sutras; however, fearing that this sutra might not yet have reached those of wisdom at the time, it was never specifically pointed out.
Only the various patriarchs of the Chan school frequently cited the events prior to King Ābhāsvara to enable people to realize their fundamental nature.
This is found throughout the Chan scriptures. The *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma Jewel* states:
"Before the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, one may attain it; after the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, to awaken by oneself without a teacher is to be a natural outsider.
Formerly, Huangbo served as the head seat under Nanquan. One day, while carrying his alms bowl through the hall, he sat upon Nanquan’s seat. Nanquan said:
"Venerable sir, for how many years have you practiced the Way? Huangbo replied, "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja. Nanquan said, "He is still but a grandson of Old Master Wang.
Huangbo then passed beyond his station. National Teacher Shenyuan of Gushan often asked students, "What is the teacher of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha?
Caoshan also said, "Even King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja had not yet awakened. Mī...

How could Leqier be conscious? Although the causal conditions of the Vīrya-ghoṣa (Wei-yin) Buddha have not yet been verified in the sūtras, there are the words of the various patriarchs of the Chan school who have proclaimed them;
these may also be relied upon to clarify that the Ancient Buddha Vīrya-ghoṣa is the fundamental source from which my own teacher was distantly formed.
This is also consistent with the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging" in the present sūtra, which speaks of the primordial Vīrya-ghoṣa-rāja Tathāgata.

Come! There is a profound and silent accord with this. As the Sūtra says: "In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King of Awesome Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja).
He dwelt in the world preaching the Dharma, his lifespan lasting for four hundred trillion nayutas of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
After that Buddha had extensively benefited sentient beings, he then entered parinirvāṇa."
In this very land, there were furthermore twenty trillion Buddhas who appeared in the world, all bearing the same name: King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja).

These were the disciples taught during a single lifetime by that original Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound, over the course of forty trillion nayuta *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas. Among them was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Constantly...
Not disparaging others, he left the household life within the Buddha’s Dharma. This bhikṣu did not specialize in reading or reciting the sūtras, but practiced only prostrations.

He bestowed predictions of enlightenment upon the fourfold assembly. Even as his time of death approached, he heard in the void of space the entire Lotus Sūtra, consisting of twenty quadrillion verses, as previously preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; he was able to receive them all.
He maintained it and immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the six sense faculties. His lifespan was further increased by two million billion nayutas of years.
He extensively proclaimed this Lotus Sūtra for the fourfold assembly. Regarding the question raised previously within the explanation of the title of the chapter:
That which is accomplished in the near term is the skillful means (*upāya*); that which is accomplished in the distant term is the ultimate truth (*bhūtatathatā*).

In the *Avataṃsaka*, at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Great Sūtra transcends nine kalpas; all of these constitute skillful means. If this is so, then since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has already opened the path for the distant goal, why does Sadāparibhūta still act as if it were near?
Answer: One should know that even after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there are further skillful means. Based on this explicit text, [the practice of] Sadāparibhūta...
This is precisely the trace of practicing the cause after attaining the fruit under Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.

Now, when we weigh the remote origins of our own Master Śākyamuni’s attainment of enlightenment, we find that he is none other than Sadāparibhūta, who is himself Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja; thus they are one and the same person.

Although there is a distinction between the fundamental and the manifested, their essence is fundamentally no different. The words of the Buddhas and the teachings of the patriarchs mutually corroborate one another, making this point clear and manifest.

It is as clear as pointing at one's own palm; what further doubt could there be? Why is this? The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is beginningless, and the initial attainment of the Way by the Tathāgata King of Majestic Voice (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja*) is likewise beginningless.

Although the Bhikṣu Never-Despising (*Sadāparibhūta*) attained the Way after leaving home during the era of the Buddha-Image Dharma, which might seem to have a beginning, in reality it borders upon the beginningless. This is because the lifespan of the Bhikṣu Never-Despising is also...
It cannot be measured; how much less so for King Majestic Voice (Vaiśvānara-rāja)!

Therefore, regarding his beginningless lifespan, even if one were to take five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms and grind them into fine dust, [it would not suffice].
Passing through five hundred thousand million billion worlds to the east, one places a single mote of dust.

Proceeding thus to the east until all these motes of dust have been exhausted—the world-systems beneath those deposited motes are already unspeakable; how much more so the world-systems beneath those where no dust was deposited?
Since the world-systems beneath the deposited and non-deposited motes are already unspeakable, how much more so the world-systems beneath both the deposited and non-deposited motes?
How could it be described? How much less so for that which exceeds this? How could it ever be expressed?

Although the Tathāgata has established such inconceivable and vast parables to make known that his own Teacher attained the Way from time immemorial and is fundamentally remote—like a single hair compared to the great void—not even one ten-thousandth part can be measured by them. Why is this?
This is because his lifespan is beginningless; how could it be measured? Yet, since the fundamental reality (*ben*) is thus, how could its manifestations (*ji*) not be so? Why is this?

From the fundamental reality descending as manifestations, the fundamental reality is itself the manifestation. By opening the manifestations to reveal the fundamental reality, the manifestation is itself the fundamental reality.

Essence and function are as one; past and present share a single boundary. How inconceivable are the Tathāgata’s meritorious virtues in benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time!
Question: The principle by which King Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara) attained self-awakening without a teacher is difficult for the world to clarify; many harbor doubts regarding it.

Please further resolve this doubt. He replied: "Although from the time of Vīradhvaja onwards there has been a succession of teachers transmitting the teachings to one another, ultimate awakening and clarity arise from the power of the internal permeation of True Suchness within each individual—the spontaneous wisdom that requires no teacher."
The teacher’s instruction serves merely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). It is like a grain seed that, by relying on the power of soil and water, sprouts and bears fruit;
yet it ultimately emerges from the grain itself, which is what is called the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Since it does not emerge from the soil or water, why should there be any doubt regarding this dominant condition? Furthermore, he asked: "How is the 'Chapter on the Differentiation of Merits' [to be understood]?"

Within this assembly, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, upon hearing the lifespan of the Tathāgata, immediately attained realization and entered the stages of abiding, practice, and direction, up to the stage of being "born only once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
They increased their path and diminished their births, receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the Dharma-body.
Answer: These are indeed great Bodhisattvas who have practiced for many kalpas; let us set them aside for now.
Even in this present age of the Final Dharma, there are practitioners who have newly resolved their minds to study and cultivate the perfect Dharma of the One Vehicle.

If they can, according to reality, believe in and understand the merits of the original and manifested traces of Venerable Wei-yin (Vimalakīrti), as being equal and non-dual with my own original and manifested traces, they too shall attain the reduction of births and receive a prediction of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because Bhīṣmagarjitasvarakalpa, the Buddhas, the sages of the Three Vehicles, and all ordinary beings share the same True Suchness (*tathatā*).
