Its substance pervades the Dharma-realm; it begins with the beginningless and extends to the end of the future. If one turns the faculty of mind for even a single thought-moment, one immediately returns to what was originally attained.
What difference could there possibly be? (This concludes the first section: "Refuting the Proximate to Reveal the Distant and Primordial Basis.")

Second, the clarification of benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. (Supplementary note: "Benefiting beings throughout the three periods" refers to the function of manifesting traces from the fundamental after Vīra-ghoṣa attained the Way.

Within each manifestation of a trace, there are three periods: viewed from the preceding, it is the past; viewed from the succeeding, it is the future; the intermediate period is self-evident. These manifestations of both the trace and the fundamental, and the mutual appearance of the fundamental and the trace, are inexhaustible—just as in the cases of Dīpaṃkara, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, and the sixteenth prince, who established karmic conditions on that day and attained Buddhahood today.

This is what is meant by "in every place he speaks of himself with different names and varying ages, and likewise manifests entry into nirvana"; all these are the merits of benefiting beings throughout the three periods within the traces of Vīra-ghoṣa, which never come to an end.)

The text consists of two parts: first, the explanation by way of dharma; second, the explanation by way of analogy. The first part further has two sections: first, clarifying how [the Buddha] benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time;

second, summarizing that this is not in vain. The first of these further has three sections: first, clarifying how he benefits beings in the past; second, clarifying how he benefits beings in the present.
The three insights clarify the future benefit of sentient beings. Regarding the first [of the past], there are also three: first, the locus of benefiting beings;
second, clearing away traces of doubt regarding the intermediate period; and third, correctly clarifying the benefit of beings. This is the first.
From that time until now, in guiding and benefiting sentient beings, there are those who must manifest in various places.
Since the preceding metaphors have been cited for a very long duration, one might ask where he has resided throughout that time; therefore, it is said that he "constantly dwells in this land."

And he performs Buddha-work in other lands. [Supplementary note: From that time until now, my constant presence here in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings allows us to see that the beings of Sahā share a great affinity with my Original Teacher.

Beginning from the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja up to the present day as Śākyamuni, he has never abandoned us throughout successive lives, constantly following and transforming us. How could we ever repay such kindness and virtue?

Only by obtaining even a single phrase or a single verse from within this sutra, taking it to heart, generating deep faith and understanding, and practicing according to the teaching—thereby benefiting both oneself and others—might one hope to repay him even in the slightest degree. If one merely plows the field in vain...]

To speak of emptiness while abandoning practice is to deceive oneself and others; the harm is no small matter. It not only contravenes the Buddha’s intent, but also betrays one's own spiritual nature. △ Second, clearing away traces of intermediate doubt.
"O sons of good family" (up to) "thus all are distinguished through skillful means.
Within this interval, he brushes away doubts concerning the traces of retribution from below upward—doubts regarding cause and doubt regarding effect.

In the teachings of the past, it was said that causes were practiced in various places and predictions were received in various places; now he brushes away these doubts and points to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara as [the source].
To sweep away doubts regarding the cause, I further speak of his entry into nirvana, thereby sweeping away doubts regarding the result.
Such matters of cause and effect are not of a single strand; they are all my skillful means and are not literal teachings.

Supplementary Note: The scripture clears away intermediate doubts regarding the traces [of the Buddha's manifestations]. When it says, "I speak of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others," it mentions only the single Buddha Dīpaṃkara;

however, among the assemblies of all Buddhas, the matters of his manifesting traces and practicing the causes [for enlightenment] are immeasurable and boundless, such that they cannot be fully enumerated.
Therefore, the word "and others" (等, *ādi*) is used to include them. Since the names of all these Buddhas cannot...

Investigation: It has already been clarified above that the Bodhisattva Constantly-Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta) within this very sutra is the trace of the practice of causes after attaining fruition by the Buddha King of Majestic Sound (Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja). Furthermore, the sixteenth prince of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū is Śākyamuni;
therein lies the vast scale of the remote origin of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, wherein one trichiliocosm of lands—
Grinding earth into ink, one travels eastward across a thousand lands and drops a single dot.
Continuing in this manner until all the earth has been used up for ink, every land traversed—whether marked by a dot or not—is entirely rubbed into dust. One speck of dust represents one kalpa;
since that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, more time has elapsed than even this number. It may truly be called a vast distance. If [one were to]...

If one were to grind those five hundred thousand ten-thousand million nayutas of trichiliocosms of the Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras Tathāgata into fine dust and use these particles as a measure to calculate time, then days and kalpas would increase exponentially; how could they ever be compared?
Thus we know that Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was also a skillful means of Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras, just like Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others—not only the sixteen princes.
This refers to the fact that in various places he spoke of his own name differently and his age as being either great or small;

citing one instance to illustrate the rest is intended merely to allow one to recognize the general outline. △ Third, the actual clarification of benefiting sentient beings has two parts: first, the response of the faculties;
second, the manifestation of transformation. Now, the first:
"Good sons (up to) 'according to their capacity for deliverance,' those who come to my presence are none other than sentient beings of the past;
their gradual and sudden faculties silently strike against the Dharma-body."
Regarding "observing with the Buddha-eye": this refers to one who has long since attained Buddhahood. Using the Buddha-eye to discern and illuminate, there is nothing overlooked or omitted.
When intending to manifest the two types of responses—the inferior and the superior—to benefit beings, there are generally two powers of the wholesome faculty:
first, to elicit the magnificent retributions of humans and devas; second, to elicit the fruit-retribution of the Buddha-way. If one observes with the Dharma-eye, one knows the myriad virtues.

Regarding the gravity or lightness [of karmic retribution], each receives a corresponding "flower-reward" (hua-bao), yet one cannot ultimately know that they will eventually attain the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*).

If one employs the Buddha-eye to perfectly illumine all wholesome deeds, one knows their beginning and end. This sutra exclusively clarifies how the Buddha-eye contemplates and knows the myriad wholesome deeds of sentient beings;
this is the ultimate, primary intention for which the Buddha appears in the world. Faith.

The "various faculties" (*indriya*) refer to the five faculties. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the cause of realization (*vyañjanahetu*), while the remaining faculties are the causes of conditions (*pratyayahetu*).

These two types of wholesome faculties each possess degrees of sharpness or dullness, encompassing both sudden and gradual capacities for enlightenment. Sharpness or dullness within the sudden capacity refers to the faculties of the Perfect (*yuan*) and Distinct (*bie*) vehicles;

sharpness or dullness within the gradual capacity refers to the faculties and conditions of the Tripitaka (*zang*) and Shared (*tong*) vehicles. Furthermore, the faculties of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) are termed "dull."
The roots of the Mahāyāna are called "sharp," while the roots of the Hīnayāna are called "moderate. Those of the human and celestial vehicles are called "dull.

The sharp or dull faculties of all sentient beings within the ten dharma realms constitute their "capacity" (*mūka*). Evil dharmas are not employed, as evil dharmas are that which is to be remedied and are not the two causes of conditions or completion.
The Tathāgata fully illuminates the good capacities of the ten realms and delivers them according to what is appropriate for each.

And he manifests both form and voice to provide dual benefit. △ Second, the transformation through giving is divided into two parts: first, the benefit of form and voice; second, the joy derived from that benefit.
Within the benefit of form and voice, there are two sections; first, the benefit of form: clarifying that what is not born appears as born, and what is not extinguished appears as extinguished.
In various places, he speaks of his own names as being different; he also manifests by saying that he will enter nirvana at different ages, whether young or old.

Regarding his speaking of different names: sentient beings have varying capacities, and their physical forms have degrees of excellence or inferiority. Since these forms are already diverse, [he adapts accordingly].
The names are different. As for the difference in age—whether great or small—this refers to the superiority or inferiority of their physical forms.

The superior one is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (Response Body), and the inferior one is the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (Transformation Body). Regarding the difference in names, this refers to the two Buddhas manifesting lifespans that are either limited or limitless.
Regarding "in every place": if discussed vertically, it refers to the lands where one practiced causes in the past; if discussed horizontally, it refers to the lands of the ten directions.

Although the names differ, even with respect to vertical locations, there are differences in the names of the dharmas produced, such as the present *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) in relation to the past Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others. This also applies to horizontal lands.

There are names for dharmas that arise, just as the present [Buddha] manifests divided bodies. This is also like the various different names of Śākyamuni listed among the titles in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
As for the differences in age, this clarifies the length of his lifespan according to the manifested response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) appearing in each instance;
at times it is said he has a lifespan of twenty thousand years, as was the case during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, or...

The lifespan is eighty thousand years, as it was during the time of Maitreya Buddha. By comparing these periods, one can understand their relative magnitude in both vertical and horizontal dimensions.

Regarding the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body, the size of their lifespans is entirely according to what is necessary to deliver sentient beings; they merely manifest themselves and the length of their lives accordingly.
Furthermore, they may manifest by saying, "I shall enter nirvana," for those who are to be delivered through the attainment of extinction. That is to say—
He manifests his parinirvāṇa so that beings may, through longing and veneration, attain liberation. This meaning will be illustrated in the following section on analogies.
Next, regarding the benefit of sound:
he further employs various skillful means to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Having small bodies and short lifespans refers to the teaching of gradual instruction; therefore, it is said that there are "various skillful means.
Having large bodies and long lifespans refers to the teaching of sudden instruction; therefore, it is said that he "preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma. △ Second, the joy of attaining benefit.
It enables sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy;
although it begins gradually, it ultimately causes them to enter the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, it is said that it causes all to attain joy, and based upon this very joy—

This refers to bestowing transformation and benefiting others. The Buddha, relying on the four *siddhāntas*, bestows both physical and vocal benefits. Sentient beings thereby obtain these four advantages;

when these accord with their capacities, they rejoice. As the subsequent text states: "All is real and not false"—this is precisely that meaning. (The first section, on benefiting beings in the past, is concluded.
△ Second, clarifying the benefit of beings in the present. It is not that those who are not born manifest birth; this is...
The Tathāgata’s Lion-Sprint Samādhi possesses ten meritorious qualities:

first, knowing whether the faculties of sentient beings are mature or immature, and whether they are pure or impure; second, using the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma to teach those not yet liberated so that they all enter the Law and Discipline;
third, his great vows pervade the ten directions, and his voice is likewise—whether as a single sound...

Pervading hundreds of thousands of millions of sounds, each sound extends throughout the Dharma-realm, universally teaching all classes of beings by turning the unsurpassed wheel four times, transforming sentient beings so that they all attain extinction (nirvāṇa).
Fifth, he is able to manifest leaving the household life, shaving his head, and upholding the pure precepts.
Sixth, his nature and conduct accord with emptiness. Seventh, he emits light to manifest extinction; he may appear or disappear, manifesting the primary and secondary marks or remaining hidden.

[He possesses] the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Eighth, he subdues the four māras. Ninth, he causes others to enter the essential point and increases their *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Tenth, he is fully endowed with the basis of the ten wholesome paths of action—the three of body and four of speech, etc. (This tenth merit consists simply of the three karmas proceeding according to wisdom, as well as the three secrets;

on the stage of Buddhahood, by means of the Lion Samādhi, he shakes off the dust and defilements of others; this is true for every Buddha). The text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the responsive resonance of the capacity (*indriya*); second, clarifying the response.
Transformation. First:

"O sons of good family, when the Tathāgata sees sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*), whose merit is meager and whose defilements are heavy—'the Tathāgata sees' means that he illuminates them with the Buddha-eye. As for those sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings, what they perceive..."
It is a matter of [teaching] capacity. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Although the great assembly is pure, there are others who delight in the Lesser Dharma;

they may give rise to doubt and regret, leading to long-term decline and affliction. Out of compassion for them, he remains silent. A verse says: "The others have not practiced for long; their wisdom is not yet clear.
Relying on consciousness rather than on gnosis, they feel anxiety and regret upon hearing this. Fearing they will fall into evil realms, he reflects upon this."

Therefore, it was not mentioned. Upon examining that sutra, there are no śrāvakas or followers of the two vehicles; rather, it merely refers to those who have not practiced for long as "persons who delight in the small dharma.
The Master said: "Those who delight in the small" are not people of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), but rather those who take pleasure in what is near at hand, and thus are called "small.
Now, this shall be explained comprehensively: that which is called craving for the twenty-five states of existence is precisely [the nature of] man.
Those whose faculties are those of the heavens come to me; this is called "delighting in the Lesser Dharma.

Those who crave the bliss of nirvana and seek their own individual liberation—namely, those whose faculties are those of the two vehicles—also come to me; they too are said to "delight in the Lesser Dharma," for they take pleasure in gradual progression.
The Buddha-way is circuitous. Thus, the three types of bodhisattvas—those of the *zang*, *tong*, and *bie* capacities—come to me; this is also called "delighting in the lesser Dharma.
Those of "meager virtue" have weak and inferior functional power regarding the two virtues of the conditions (*yuán*) and the realization (*liǎo*). As the text below states: "The sons are young.

Those with "heavy defilements" have not yet eliminated the afflictions of views (*jiàn*) and thought (*sī*). Question: Is it not the case that he manifests birth within non-birth, fully employing both the sudden and the gradual?

Regarding the second point on transformation: those such as the seven stages of expedient means are for those who delight in the Small Dharma; the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] accords with those who should delight in the Great Dharma.
Why, then, is it collectively judged that they delight in the Small Dharma? Answer: The meaning was briefly indicated previously; now it shall be explained in detail.

There are four general points. First, regarding the past: although they may have resolved upon the Great Mind, they were unable to practice with single-minded diligence and remained largely attached [to worldly things].
Corrupt desires prevent one from transcending the world; thus, corrupt desire is termed the "lesser Dharma. Second, regarding the present:

as when the Buddha has not yet appeared in the world, although various devas and humans possess great spiritual capacity (*mahā-indriya*), their minds are defiled by worldly pleasures and they cling to false views;
therefore, they are said to delight in the lesser Dharma. These two meanings are identical in intent to the subsequent analogy of "rolling about on the ground."

Third, regarding practice: although one does not delight in the base desires and minor dharmas of the triple world, one may still delight in the extinction through ash-like cessation (*pāṃśukula-nirvāṇa*) of the three vehicles;

this is also called a "minor dharma. Although one does not delight in the proximate fruits of the three vehicles, one may delight in practicing the One Vehicle through gradual and distinct stages, unable to practice it universally and instantaneously within a single mind; therefore, this is called "delighting in the minor. These three points are based on...
The "gate of causes" clarifies the delight in the Lesser Dharma. Fourth is the "gate of results":

they take pleasure in hearing about the minor [attainment] achieved through near completion—leaving the palace of the Śākyas and first attaining bodhi—and do not desire to hear with joy the long-distant, great, and enduring path; hence it is said they "delight in the small.
Such a narrow-mindedness is not something that begins only today. If they had previously delighted in the Great [Vehicle], the Buddha would not have spoken of his initial attainment of completion.

Regarding the statement that [the Buddha] has only recently attained enlightenment: this is solely for the sake of those who delight in the Lesser Dharma. Second, the clarification of the manifested transformation (nirmāṇa-kāya).

This involves manifesting birth where there is no actual birth. This has two parts: first, manifesting birth; second, benefiting others. Manifesting birth further has two aspects: first, manifesting birth; second, non-birth.
Regarding "manifesting birth," it means the traces appear as being born. Regarding "non-birth," it means that he was not born at the very beginning. Now, the first [of these].
Manifesting in this life, he speaks for the sake of such people, saying: "I left home at a young age and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For the sake of these people, he says: "I have only now attained *bodhi*. Previously, it was explained that those of two types of capacities—the sharp and the dull—come to evoke the *dharmakāya*.

Now, there are manifested two types of response-bodies: the inferior and the superior. The inferior response-body responds to those of dull faculties, while the superior response-body responds to those of sharp faculties.
Both of these response-bodies possess both the birth-body and the dharma-body. Regarding the production of the two bodies of the inferior response-body: it enters the womb by means of correct wisdom.
Regarding his birth, he took seven steps, as described by Kātyāyanīputra, until his return after six years of ascetic practice;

this is called the "birth of the physical body" (*janmakāya*). As for the "birth of the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*), it refers to the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅgika-dharmakāya*) attained when the fetters and habitual tendencies are completely severed through the thirty-four moments of mind.
Regarding the "superior response-body" (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇakāya*), it is as in the *Avataṃsaka*...
As stated in the sūtras and other texts: dwelling within the womb of Māyā together with the bodhisattvas, he constantly expounds the Mahāyāna;
when he emerges and takes seven steps in each of the ten directions, this is called "birth as the birth-body" (*janma-kāya*). As for "birth as the dharma-body" (*dharma-kāya*):

at the site of the terrace of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), at the final moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), he exhausts ignorance, attains the wisdom corresponding to wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), and thoroughly illuminates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) with its myriad virtues.
The knowledge of all modes is perfectly luminous and universally complete; this is called the birth of the Dharma-body. As for those who have left the household life:

the inferior response-body leaves the house of *pariccheda-vedanīya-karma* (segmented existence), while the superior response-body leaves the house of the two deaths (*dvimaraṇa*). As for those who have attained *bodhi*:

the inferior response-body attains the untainted knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) produced by the four noble truths with outflows; this is termed *bodhi*. The superior response-body, however, directly illuminates the three truths as one reality.
The Way of all-knowledge is bodhi. II. Not born (meaning not newly arisen from the beginning).
Yet, in reality, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been for as long as this; [up to] making such a statement.
However, I have indeed realized the ultimate; it clarifies that the fundamental reality is originally unarisen.
It is only gods, humans, and asuras who perceive these two kinds of arising dharmas and these two bodies, claiming they have newly arisen.
This is not so; for I have long since attained these two bodies of the dharma of arising. Today’s birth is not a real birth; therefore it is said, "For such a long time, for such a long time."

"Such as" refers to the aforementioned analogy of long duration. From "But by means of skillful means" onwards, it clarifies that since there is no actual birth, for what reason does he manifest birth?
It is for the sake of benefiting and bringing joy to those who follow the Dharma of the Small Vehicle—those of meager virtue and heavy defilements—so that they may attain the Buddha-way;
therefore it says, "But by means of skillful means, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, making such statements. This is not a real birth, yet he manifests birth.

Therefore, it is said that he speaks in this manner. Other sutras refute the arising and non-arising of the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), yet they do not refute the arising and non-arising of the inferior response-dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This present sutra, however, directly refutes the arising and non-arising of the superior response-dharma-body.

Why is this? Since my actual attainment of Buddhahood has been for as long as this, it is known that the claims today regarding the arising of both the inferior and superior *dharmakāyas* are all refuted;
thus, "arising" is non-arising, which is forever distinct from other sutras.

(Although the text speaks of two types of *nirmāṇakāya*, each having both an arising-body and a *dharmakāya*, the fivefold *dharmakāya* within the inferior *nirmāṇakāya* is identical in meaning to the arising-body, while that within the superior *nirmāṇakāya*, though called the arising-body, is identical in meaning to the *dharmakāya*). △ Second, the clarification.
The benefit is twofold. First, the forms and sounds are explained; second, their non-falsity is explained. Now, for the first:
"O sons of good family" (up to) "or manifesting things to others.
"Speaking" refers to the teaching of sound; "manifesting" refers to the appearance of form. These forms and sounds do not arise from either self or other. If one speaks of the Dharma-body, it is...

To speak of one's own body; if one speaks of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), this is to speak of another's body. To say "I encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha" is to speak of one's own body; to say "Dīpaṃkara was my teacher" is to speak of another's body.
To manifest the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) is to manifest one's own affairs; to manifest the secondary environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) is to manifest another's affairs.
Speech that accords with the intentions of others is to speak of another's body; speech that accords with one's own intentions is to speak of [one's own body].
The same applies to showing one's own self or matters concerning oneself and others. △ Next, clarifying that [the teaching] is not in vain, which has two parts:
first, specifically clarifying that the benefit of the voice is not in vain; second, the explanation, which explains both aspects of being not in vain. Now, the first part.
All that has been spoken is true and not false. Regarding "not false from the beginning":
the two types of capacities—gradual and sudden—receiving these two kinds of forms and sounds all receive benefit that is not in vain.

In the preceding chapter on the past, it was clarified that all were filled with joy, which resembles worldly benefit; here, it is clarified that all are not in vain, distinguishing between superior and inferior [capacities].
Form and sound linger within the two capacities, and the benefits of the four *siddhāntas* are obtained;
none of these are in vain. △ Second, the dual explanation of how the two benefits are not in vain. This has two parts: first, revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to manifest the two benefits;

second, responding to capacities and applying transformation to manifest the two benefits. Now, for the first [of these] (herein there are six phrases: first, "the Tathāgata has departed"; second, "nor does he remain in the world"; third, "neither real nor unreal").
Fourth, it is neither like nor different. Fifth, it departs unlike the three realms. Sixth, it departs in this manner.
Why is this? [From here until: The Tathāgata perceives clearly and without error.
Why is this so? This is a question regarding how it is that the Tathāgata’s two benefits are not in vain. Therefore, the explanation states:

"The Tathāgata knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are; there is no birth-and-death, and so forth. To know and see as they truly are is precisely real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
It is to illuminate the reality of the triple world according to the principle of suchness (*yathābhūtam*). Since reality is thus, there are no [inherently existent] triple worlds.

The "causal characteristics" (the three delusions are the causes). "There is no birth-and-death" means there are no resultant characteristics of the two types of death (i.e., *pariccheda* and *pariṇāma*). "Whether falling back or emerging":
the arising of the accumulation [of karma] is called "falling back" (accumulation refers to *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, meaning the accumulation of causes and the accumulation of results;

it is the falling back and descending into the triple world). The manifestation of impermanent results is called "emerging" (Śrāvakas enter the Path from suffering; contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are the causes, while realizing Arhatship and exiting beyond the triple world is the result. These are termed "impermanent results").
This follows from the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya) and its designation. There is neither one who remains in the world nor one who has attained parinirvāṇa;

nor is there one remaining in the world of saṃsāra, nor one who has entered the extinction of nirvāṇa. Since both of these are extinguished, it is said that "there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has attained parinirvāṇa.
As for "neither real nor unreal": it is not real in terms of parinirvāṇa, nor is it unreal in terms of saṃsāra; therefore, it is said to be "not real."
It is not false. "Neither identical nor different" means it is not different from the mundane world, nor is it identical to the supramundane *tathatā* (suchness).
Therefore, it is said to be "neither identical nor different. This clarifies the Middle Way.
"Not as the three realms see the three realms" means it is not like the characteristics of the three realms as perceived by sentient beings within the two kinds of triple-world systems.

Regarding the two kinds of the three realms (*traidhātuka*): the name "three realms" applies both to within and beyond the realms. As for the three realms beyond [the world], they are established by analogy with those within. Because the Middle Way principle has not yet been fully exhausted, the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) throughout the transformation lands are collectively termed the "three realms," and the sublime six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are collectively termed the "delusions of thought" (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

These characteristics were explained in detail in the ancient *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra*. Only the Buddha alone, as it truly is, exhaustively illuminates the reality of the three realms; he internally possesses the function of true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).
This is also a statement according to his own intention (*svābhiprāyika-vacana*), or it is a statement concerning himself.
This concerns the matter of the body. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no conceptual differentiation.
Furthermore, through the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), he perceives the characteristics of the three realms according to their measure;

yet, within the state of non-dual death, he manifests the bodies of the two deaths in accordance with the intentions of others, teaching that there are two deaths. While there is actually neither falling back nor emerging, he teaches that there is falling back in accordance with the intentions of others.

There is an emergence, yet there is neither one who remains in the world nor one who passes into extinction. Rather, in accordance with the inclinations of others, he manifests birth in the world and manifests entry into nirvana;
he speaks of those remaining in the world and those who have attained extinction. Though these are not real, he speaks of the reality of nirvana.
Without there being any reality, he speaks of the emptiness of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Without there being any distinction between the three times, he speaks of their distinctions.
Without there being suchness (*tathatā*) in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he speaks of suchness.

Being identical with the triple world and perceiving the triple world—all these are expressions according to the intentions of others, termed "speaking of the affairs of another's body" or "demonstrating the affairs of another's body. Such matters are [taught] by the Tathāgata.
The two wisdoms clearly and precisely discern the Two Truths without error; thus, both verbal expression and physical manifestation provide dual benefit, all of which is real and not false.
[I venture to supplement:
In the "Expedient Means" chapter of the Trace Gate, the Tathāgata revealed the provisional to manifest the real, in order to lead sentient beings...
The passage "producing [the state of] revealing, awakening, entering, and realizing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" merely sets forth the headings without providing an explanatory text.
The Great Master [Chih-i] explained each of these through four meanings; thus, there is no principle left unexplored and no matter left uncomprehended.

Indeed, the Great Master’s exposition is identical to the Buddha’s teaching—there is no duality and no distinction between them. Now, within the "Life Span" chapter of the Essential Gate (Honmon), the provisional traces are revealed.
To reveal the source: for kalpas long ago, [the Buddha] knew by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and saw by means of the Buddha-eye.

He has opened up and revealed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for the sake of all sentient beings. There are six points of meaning which the Buddha himself explains, so that those who are ready may awaken to them and enter them by themselves.
That is to say: the Tathāgata knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are; there is no...
There is birth and death, whether in decline or emergence; yet one knows and sees them as they truly are, such that there is neither one abiding in the world nor one who has entered extinction.
One knows and sees them as they truly are, neither real nor unreal. One knows and sees them as they truly are, neither identical nor different.
One knows and sees them as they truly are: not as the triple world perceives the triple world. One knows and sees that such matters do not exist.

This is an error. It is because the dharmas of the ten realms—the distinctions between the causes and effects, and the defilement and purity, of both sages and ordinary beings—are all the true mark of *tathatā*, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All dharmas exist without exception."
All enter into that which is suchness and devoid of intrinsic nature. Therefore, each is negated by means of a double negation, returning to the Middle Way of the Dharmakāya.
Since beginningless kalpas, the trace and the source, and the source and the trace, have manifested to one another without limit:

the source-source is the trace, and the trace-trace is the source. If the practitioner can thus ultimately awaken to this as it truly is and realize it through ultimate entry, [they shall attain liberation].
"O stepmother, today the Tathāgata reveals his traces to manifest his fundamental nature for the sake of all sentient beings; he opens up and demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
△ Second, the manifestation of transformation according to capacities to reveal the two benefits. This has two parts. First, clarifying the resonance of capacity.
Because sentient beings possess various natures (up to) various modes of recollection and discrimination, their gradual and sudden faculties and natures each vary in many ways;
this requires the use of the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint established for individuals). This is the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta*.

This is precisely for the purpose of generating all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). These roots of goodness are themselves natures (*prakṛti*); through the cultivation of desire, they become nature.

Why, then, does [the text] first mention nature and subsequently desire? The explanation states: because there exists the nature of the original-day faculties (*mūladivasendriya-prakṛti*), one is able to give rise to the desires and pleasures of the present day.

It is like how, due to the afflictions (*kleśa*), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arise; and again, due to the five aggregates, further afflictions arise. There is neither priority nor posteriority between them.

Sexual desire is likewise so. It must arise from the habituation of desire in order to become an innate disposition (*prakṛti*). (To provide an illustration for this: as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:

"Good son, the bodies of all sentient beings and their afflictions (*kleśa*) are simultaneous; there is no priority or posteriority between them. Although there is no priority or posteriority, one must rely upon afflictions to obtain a body; one never obtains afflictions by relying on the body. Sexual desire is also like this.

Although there is no priority or posteriority, it is only through the habituation of desire that it finally becomes an innate disposition. The point of the analogy is this: although in the present context disposition comes first and desire comes later, in the ultimate sense, the principle of desire must occupy the prior position; hence it is said that "habituation of desire forms the disposition"). As for "desire," there are two types: gradual and sudden.
Regarding "faculties" (*indriya*): since various desires and inclinations differ, this requires the use of the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint). Regarding "practices":

since practitioners perform their activities according to their inclinations and cultivate various practices accordingly, this requires the use of the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of the person).

Regarding "obstacles": since attachment within practice leads to hindrances, this requires the use of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of counteraction). As for "recollection," it is wisdom.
This is precisely "similar understanding. Through the practice of cultivation, one is able to give rise to this understanding; this is the skillful means (*upāya*).

Yet, as it has not yet accorded with ultimate principle, it remains a contemplation based on mental recollection and conceptualization (*saṃjñā-vipaśyanā*). Whether gradualist or suddenist practitioners, while residing in the stages of the outer or inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they possess various roots of goodness and a yearning aspiration.
Because of this aspiration, they engage in cultivation; because of their cultivation, they attain similar understanding. This must employ the [second]...

Regarding the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth): because it arises from the three [other] *siddhāntas*, it is also termed "ultimate" throughout all stages of both internal and external ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). However, the designation of "conceptual wisdom" (*saṃjñā-prajñā*) must pertain to the stage of the cause;

for example, when one practices the five repentances prior to the five ranks (*pañca-varga*), even the initial entry into sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) may still be termed "ultimate. How much more so upon entering the stage of the internal ordinary being? Furthermore, prior to sympathetic joy, if one attains even a slight degree of meditative concentration (*samādhi-citta*), that too may be termed "entry into the ultimate," let alone upon entering the first rank.
According to the conceptual understanding attained by each, he further preaches the Dharma for them, whereby they immediately achieve clear awakening.

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*): even when one desires to practice the second stage (*bhūmi*) while on the first stage, one still employs mental recollection and conceptualization regarding the realm of the second stage.
Once genuine understanding of the second stage arises, such recollection, thought, and contemplation are eliminated, and the phenomena of language cease.

This continues until the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), where one finally attains ultimate liberation from recollection and conceptualization, obtaining eternal, quiescent illumination. △ Next, the correspondence.
Applying transformations according to the capacities [of beings],
he desires to cause them to produce various roots of goodness (up to the point where they are never for a moment abandoned).
Directly facing these capacities, he applies the benefit of his own and others' voices to various gradual and sudden faculties, causing them to produce various [realizations].

Because of these roots of goodness, he manifests various matters concerning his own and others' bodies, various sounds and teachings for himself and others, and various causes, conditions, and parables.
If he addresses those with gradual capacity, he employs the various causes, conditions, and parables from the four gates within the Tripitaka.
Within each individual gate, there are further variations. For example, for those who are indolent, one teaches the patience regarding suffering;
for those with pride, one teaches the patience regarding impermanence, and so forth. This applies equally to the four gates of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa*).

If addressing those of sudden capacity, such as in the Distinct and Complete Teachings (*bipākya* and *vaipulya*), there are likewise four gates for each, with various distinctions just as when the thirty-two bodhisattvas each spoke their own teachings.
Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality: The various types of practices and characteristics within the *Avataṃsaka* are all for the sake of various capacities;
they employ numerous metaphors and verbal expressions to preach the Dharma. That the Buddha-works performed have never been suspended for even a moment is, in summary, not in vain.
As described above, these various forms and sounds—whether pertaining to oneself or others—all cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way.
This refers to knowledge and vision. Because it is not for the sake of the minor matters of humans, devas, or the two vehicles, it is called "the Buddha-work performed.
If only one person were to attain extinction while others did not, the Buddha-work performed would be rendered deficient.
Such deficiency would cause the multitude to fail to obtain true benefit. How could it then be said that all is real and not false? How is it all real? In the past—
It is said: "I sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and did not attain a single dharma as real. The seven expedient means (upāya) are all not ultimate cessation.
The two types of nirvāṇa are but empty fists of expedient means; thus one knows they are merely provisional and have not yet seen that all are real.

If the seven provisional [teachings] previously bestowed had ultimately failed to lead one into the one reality, they could be called 'empty. But since they draw one forth [to realization], there is no emptiness in them."
That which emerges and does not re-enter is truly real; thus we know that what was previously empty is now made real.

That all are real and not empty, such that the Buddha’s work is never abandoned—this is precisely the meaning [of this passage]. (2. Presently benefiting beings is not the manifestation of birth; the section on the present manifestation of birth is concluded.
△ Third, benefiting beings in the future is not the extinction of the present. There are two parts: first, clarifying that it is not the extinction of the present; second, clarifying...

The benefit of manifesting extinction. This section also has two parts: first, clarifying that the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction; second, clarifying the proclamation of extinction within the provisional traces.
The first part also has two sub-sections: first, clarifying the permanence of the fruit—that the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction.
"In this way, since I attained Buddhahood, [I have remained] for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, eternally abiding and never perishing.

Regarding "eternally abiding and never perishing," these four characters are employed to clarify that his future power and majesty are formidable, and that he will eternally abide to benefit sentient beings until the end of the future.
Next, the cause is cited by way of analogy with the fruit to clarify eternal abiding.
"O sons of good family... [up to] it is even double that number.
To illustrate the result by means of the cause: when the Buddha cultivated the perfect cause and ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*), he had already attained eternal life;

since this eternal life is inexhaustible, it is already double the aforementioned number—how much more so, then, the result itself? It is like the case of a crown prince: even during his time as a prince, his emoluments were already beyond measure.
How much more so when one has ascended to the supreme pinnacle—how could the bestowal of his emoluments ever be exhausted? △ Second, the proclamation of extinction within the traces:
yet this is not an actual parinirvāṇa; nevertheless, he proclaims that he shall enter parinirvāṇa.

All three bodies possess the sense of being non-extinguished while proclaiming extinction. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Dharma is fundamentally unborn; now it is without extinction.
This refers to the fact that the Dharmakāya is non-extinguished. Furthermore, it says: "This is the meaning of quiescent extinction," which is the proclamation of extinction.
Why is this? If one has already fully realized [the truth], one does not proclaim "quiescence"; it is for those who have not yet realized it that one proclaims it.
If one says "illumination-quiescence," this is proclaiming cessation; if one says "quiescence-illumination," this is proclaiming arising.
Now, as for the Dharmakāya, although it is neither arising nor ceasing, it also possesses arising and ceasing. If the deluded mind clings to it, then afflictions arise and wisdom [is obscured].
Cessation. If one understands that the mind is without defilement, wisdom arises and afflictions cease. The cessation of delusion and the arising of understanding—this is cessation as impermanence.

If understanding arises and delusion ceases, this is quiescent cessation (*śānta-nirodha*). These instances of arising and cessation are all distinguished in relation to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
If the two conditions of delusion and understanding were absent, then one would not proclaim the existence of such arising and cessation. Thus it is said.

The body is not extinguished, yet one proclaims its extinction. Who possesses wisdom? Who possesses afflictions? To say that wisdom can destroy afflictions [is a misconception]. Wisdom and ignorance are fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
this is because the essence of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is itself without arising or ceasing. This means that light and darkness do not exclude one another;

this is precisely the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya* being non-extinguishable. Light is wisdom; darkness is ignorance (*avidyā*). Since their essential nature is entirely identical, they cannot exclude each other. Since there is no mutual exclusion, there is no extinction. Sentient beings have not yet...
Having heard this, he claimed that this [teacher] was himself the Buddha and became arrogant and self-indulgent, no longer practicing the Way.
Therefore, he further proclaimed: "The Way can extinguish delusions. When afflictions exist, there is no wisdom; when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions.
Is it not the case, then, that wisdom can extinguish afflictions? This refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) which, though not itself extinguished, proclaims extinction.

This must be the function of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Since their essence is without cessation, how could their function ever be exhausted? Thus, the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is indeed imperishable;
however, for the sake of sentient beings, if they were to see the Buddha constantly, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence.

Therefore, [the Buddha] proclaims: "Tonight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, the Dharma-body is inherently luminous and imperishable; when the Reward-body is said to be imperishable, it must be understood in reference to the Dharma-body.

Regarding the *kāya*: it is said that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) does not undergo extinction. This must be understood in terms of the *dharmakāya* (truth body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).

The *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are eternally so; the application of the *nirmāṇakāya* is uninterrupted. As long as sentient beings are not exhausted, it does not enter extinction. Furthermore, from the perspective of its essential nature, the *dharmakāya* is neither born nor extinguished.

The *saṃbhogakāya*, having fully realized this, is incapable of birth or extinction. The *nirmāṇakāya* continues in succession without birth or extinction. (The first section, concerning how that which is non-extinguishing manifests as extinction, is concluded.)

△ Second, the clarification of manifesting extinction to benefit sentient beings is divided into two parts: first, the harm caused by not manifesting extinction for sentient beings; second, the benefit brought to sentient beings by proclaiming extinction.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the harm caused by not manifesting extinction; second, a detailed explanation of the meaning of not manifesting extinction.
Now, the first [point].
The Tathāgata, by means of these skillful expedients, enters into the net of conceptualization and false views.
As for those who suffer loss—such as the people of former times who delighted in inferior teachings—they see the Buddha as being constantly present, yet they do not plant roots of goodness;

being poor, lowly, and base, they do not give rise to the two kinds of goodness, and thus it is of no benefit to them. Because their views and afflictions are not severed, and because they do not abandon the two evils, this is [the case].

There is harm. One becomes greedily attached to the five desires and enters into discursive thought (*vitarka*). Discursive thought is precisely the delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), while the five desires are the delusion of mental formations (*bhāvanā-āsrava*).
Because the defilements of sentient beings are thus heavy, it is necessary to proclaim extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

If extinction were not proclaimed, the two evils would arise and not be extinguished, and the two virtues would be diminished and not arise. If one relies on the four *siddhāntas*, the manifestation of extinction is as follows:
Second, two evils are extinguished and two virtues arise. To extinguish the two evils, one employs the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as an antidote;
the ultimate truth extinguishes unarisen evil, while the antidote extinguishes arisen evil. For the sake of people, the world gives rise to two virtues:
the world gives rise to unarisen virtue, and for the sake of people, it gives rise to already-arisen virtue. Furthermore, the world extinguishes already-arisen evil, [and] the antidote...
To eliminate and extinguish unarisen evil is like the five aggregates of dhyāna extinguishing the evils of the desire realm; this is the worldly extinction of already arisen evil.
To produce in people already arisen good is the production of unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) good that has not yet arisen, which pertains to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the meaning of non-extinction.

If one perceives the Tathāgata as eternally present and imperishable, [up to] a mind of reverence, yet if one perceives the Buddha as being constantly present, one may instead give rise to a mind of arrogance and self-indulgence; thus there is harm, and one is unable to generate reverence.
Therefore, it is of no benefit. Pride and self-indulgence increase the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); weariness and indolence give rise to the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

If one does not conceive the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, one cannot produce the realization of the Truths (*satyadarśana*). If one lacks reverence, one cannot produce the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

For this reason, it is appropriate that [the Buddha] manifest his parinirvāṇa; for if the three Buddhas did not manifest their passing, there would be the sense of pride and self-indulgence in all cases.
They then claim that the suchness of sentient beings is the suchness of Maitreya; that this single suchness is non-dual suchness, and that equality itself is the truth.
From this, arrogance arises in their hearts, leading them to claim that all afflictions are fundamentally unarisen and, even now, are without cessation.
"What need is there to cultivate the Path? they say, immediately indulging in self-will and negligence, proclaiming that this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, hearing that all sentient beings are themselves the characteristic of *bodhi*, and that the characteristic of *bodhi* is the characteristic of afflictions (*kleśa*), and that light and darkness do not exclude one another yet manifest the *bodhi* of the Buddha, sentient beings hear this and again give rise to arrogance and indulgence, no longer cultivating wholesome virtues.
Out of laziness and negligence, for the sake of such people, it is proclaimed that the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* can extinguish afflictions;

yet the power of ignorance is great, and it is only through the *buddhabodhi*-wisdom that it can be extinguished. The *nirmāṇakāya* does not actually extinguish [afflictions], but its manifestation of extinction is easy to understand.

(First, regarding the Dharma-body: the Dharma-body is fundamentally without the name "quiescent extinction. For those with overweening pride who reckon that suchness is no different [from ordinary phenomena], it is necessary to proclaim "quiescent extinction," as will be explained in detail below.
If one proclaims that "the Dharma is originally unborn and now likewise unextinguished," why must there necessarily be extinction of delusion before there is quiescent extinction? As the Sūtra says:
Wisdom does not extinguish afflictions; rather, when there is light, there is no darkness. You now possess afflictions in full measure—how could you possibly have wisdom?
One should know that wisdom is able to extinguish obstructing delusions.

When sentient beings hear this proclamation of "extinguishing," they immediately conceive the thought that the Three Buddhas are difficult to encounter, and they give rise to a mind of reverence. (1. End of the section on how the existence of afflictions is not extinguished. △ 2.
It is clear that proclaiming extinction is beneficial;
therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful means (upāya), [extending] until he says "nirvāṇa.

He first indicates that the three Buddhas are difficult to encounter. Sentient beings delight in and cling to inferior teachings, and their obstacles of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are heavy. Upon hearing that the Buddha—
"Extinction. This leads them to become arrogant and self-indulgent, and they do not cultivate the Path. The following section provides the explanation.
Among those of meager merit, some may see a Buddha after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, while others may not. If one sees three Buddhas, that person has much goodness and little evil;
for such a person, I do not proclaim extinction. Such a person sees the Buddha as always present on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Or...

They do not see the Buddha because their obstructions are heavy and their roots of goodness are slight. For them, it is taught that the three bodies (trikāya) are difficult to realize. Upon hearing this, sentient beings think:
"Although the three Buddhas are neither born nor extinguished, one must nonetheless give rise to goodness and extinguish delusions in order to attain realization and vision.
This matter is not easy," and thus they say it is "difficult to encounter. Those who harbor such longing and yearn with thirsty admiration—

This clarifies that there is no loss in manifesting [the Buddha’s presence] and passing into extinction (for, by cherishing the Buddha, one is able to extinguish all darkness of ignorance through the light of wisdom; one ultimately awakens to and enters the true reality of all dharmas, not merely severing views and afflictions to exit the twenty-five realms of existence within the triple world.

Therefore, it is said that there is benefit). (1. The section on benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time is concluded. △ 2. Second, the summary of the non-futility [of the Buddha’s appearance].
Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is thus: for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false.
Benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time, this is the case for all Buddhas; they cause beings to obtain real benefit, and therefore it is not false.

(The first explanation by way of the Dharma is concluded. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy. This consists of the introductory analogy and the application of the analogy. The introductory analogy is divided into two parts: first, the skilled physician.

The analogy of the physician’s son illustrates how [the Buddha] benefits sentient beings across the three periods of time. Second, the analogy of the physician’s son’s actual benefit illustrates the summary of the preceding section on non-futility.
This first part also has three sections: first, the analogy of the physician’s long journey, which illustrates benefiting sentient beings in the past; second, the analogy of his return.
This is like the present response-body (nirmāṇakāya). [The text] again employs three similes to illustrate the future response-body. First:
It is, for example, as if a skilled physician, wise and sagacious, [having traveled] far away to another land.
Regarding the first type of skilled physician: there are ten kinds of physicians. The first treats a disease such that it increases and does not diminish, or sometimes even leads to death.
This is like the non-Buddhists who hold the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*); they act wickedly at will, teaching others to give rise to false views and severing their roots of goodness.

Once the Dharma-body has perished, the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) also dies. The second treats a disease such that it neither increases nor diminishes. This is like the non-Buddhists who practice asceticism while holding to the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*).

4. Those who throw themselves from cliffs or enter fire, practicing asceticism and performing good deeds, yet fail to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), experience neither loss nor gain.
They are like those treated by worldly physicians: once cured, the illness returns. This refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cultivate meditative concentration to sever the fetters. 4.
Regarding the treatment of illness: it can cause the patient to recover so that the disease does not recur; yet, what is treated is not universal.

This refers to those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), who treat only one or two types of beings with whom they have a karmic connection, and cannot treat all universally. Fifth, although [the Buddha] is able to treat all universally, [the others] are not.

Yet they lack the skillful means to treat suffering; the *Śāstra* calls this "clumsy perfection" (*duḥkhapāramitā*). This refers to the Bodhisattvas' vast treatment through compassion via the six perfections.
These six are the wondrous arts for treating illness; they can cure those with pain and affliction, yet they cannot cure one who is destined to die.

This is analogous to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*), who realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) but only treat ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) who undergo cycles of rebirth, and not those beyond such cycles.
This treats those of the two vehicles who are like parched seeds. Although the seventh [stage] treats diseases that are difficult to cure, it does not treat all diseases simultaneously;

this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*). As the *Āgama* says: "A skilled physician has four qualities: first, he well knows the symptoms of the disease; second, he knows the origin of the disease; third, he well knows the methods of treatment; fourth, he ensures the disease never recurs.

Yet this physician’s knowledge of disease symptoms does not transcend the internal realms; his knowledge of the origin of the disease does not transcend the dependent and the primary; his methods of treatment do not exceed birth, death, and impermanence; and his prevention of recurrence merely results in abiding in the two types of nirvana.

[The first] five can treat all illnesses at once, yet cannot restore them to their original state; this corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the initial mind of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
The ninth [stage] can treat all illnesses everywhere and can also restore them to their original state, yet cannot cause them to exceed their original state;
this corresponds to the final mind of the Perfect Teaching. The eleventh [stage] treats [illnesses] at all times.
All illnesses can be restored to normalcy; moreover, they are made to exceed their original state, which is precisely what the Tathāgata does. [Supplementary Note:

While those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) can treat and restore to the original state, they cannot cause it to exceed it. The Buddha, however, exceeds the original state. Originally, there was neither illness nor medicine. It is simply because the Tathāgata treats the delusions of sentient beings and causes them all to reach the ground of omniscience that he is called the Ultimate Good Physician.
The first three types of physicians are the "old physicians" mentioned in the Mahāyāna Sūtras, who employ the medicine of milk. The latter six are all "guest" physicians.
A physician without skill merely employs such dharmas as impermanence and suffering, which is like using bitter, pungent, or sour medicines.
When a skilled physician arrives from afar, he instead prescribes milk; he is the ultimate, consummate physician. "Consummate" (liang) means "skillful.
Internally, the three types of penetration and the five eyes constitute the eight skills. Having mastered the nature of the medicine, he is a skillful healer who externally recognizes the illness.

"Source" refers to the ability to employ medicine (the "eight arts" mentioned in the sutras are eight successive instances of using metaphors to treat eight kinds of illnesses; here, we shall merely clarify the number eight).

"Wisdom" refers to the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate, through which one deeply understands the two truths. "Erudition and penetration" refers to the five eyes discerning the capacities of beings, ensuring that sudden and gradual teachings do not deviate from their proper application.
The twelve divisions of the teaching have extremely profound principles and phrasing; they are like clearly refining medicinal formulas, relying upon the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).
*Dāna* (generosity) cures the illnesses of sentient beings, just as one skillfully treats various diseases. The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states:
"The Great Physician, the King of Physicians—being a Great Physician, he is called a 'skilled physician. He has many sons; for instance, ten may be sons of the Śrāvakas."

Twenty refers to the sons of the Pratyekabuddhas (the first "one" refers to the Śrāvakas; since ten are contained within one, it is called "if ten. The second "two" refers to the Pratyekabuddhas; since ten are contained within two, it is called "twenty").
That each possesses ten clarifies the perfect number. A hundred refers to the sons of the Bodhisattvas. Regarding the sons of the Bodhisattvas, there are generally three meanings of "seed."
First, with respect to all sentient beings, they all possess the three kinds of Buddha-nature as inherent qualities; thus, they are all sons of the Buddha. Therefore, it is said:
"The sentient beings therein are all my children. This text states: "There are many children. In terms of the ten mental factors (*citta-dharmas*), there are one hundred children.
The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the direct cause of Buddha-nature (*pratyaya-hetu-buddhatva*); wisdom (*prajñā*) is the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*).
The remaining nine factors support one another; they belong to the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

When one factor arises, the other nine provide assistance. In this way, they constitute a hundred. (Regarding the ten mental factors: although mental factors are extremely numerous, we shall provisionally take ten wholesome factors—namely, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, pliancy, equanimity, awakening, and precept.

These ten factors assist the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), enabling it to abandon evil and turn toward good, to transform the mundane into the sacred, and to understand all dharma-gates. Since each single factor possesses these ten, they thus constitute a hundred. Therefore, the three causes of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) all belong to [this category].
The true cause refers to the Buddha-sons. Second, regarding those who were established as Buddha-sons through past karmic conditions, such as the sixteen princes:

Regarding this analysis: the Buddha’s words are perfect and subtle; one must not use provisional stages to explain the sutra.

Therefore, while the Trace Gate reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the sequence of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, the present Root Gate—where the Path increases and birth is diminished—is explained entirely in terms of the perfect stages.

"As for those who, upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding—they will be able, according to where they have heard it, to [attain liberation]."
Suddenly, one attains clarity and illumination. This means entering in accordance with the words, free from all obstructions.
One believes that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; furthermore, one believes that the Buddha-dharma is not separated from any dharma.

each individual organ possesses one thousand merits. Furthermore, within a single mind, the ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātu*) are complete;
each realm possesses the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), thus forming one hundred. Each sense organ universally apprehends the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), thus there are six [hundred].

One hundred [times] two—the adornments of both concentration and wisdom—equals one thousand two hundred. Each and every faculty is adorned with concentration and wisdom, equally numbering one thousand two hundred.
If one discusses the purity of the six faculties, such purity does not concern whether merit is small or great.
If one speaks of adornment, it can be full, it can be contracted, and it can be equal. This is what is meant by "equal adornment."
Each faculty has six thousand [qualities]. To say "twelve thousand" reveals its capacity for expansion; to say "eight hundred" reveals its capacity for contraction.
To say "pure" means there is neither expansion nor contraction, and no equality, as the six faculties function interchangeably because the faculties are sovereign.
Because it is inconceivable. If one were to judge it unilaterally, one would lose the essential meaning.
Regarding the stage of "semblance": if based on the four wheels, it is the stage of the iron wheel; if based on the fifty-two stages, it is the ten stages of faith;

if based on the *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing), it is the ten great minds of goodness. Now, in contrast to the "Ever-Diligent" (Sadāprarudita), it corresponds to the second of the ten stages of faith.
This refers to the mind. Although the titles in various sutras differ, they all refer to the stage of semblance within the Perfect Teaching.
