△ Next, there is a separate explanation in six chapters, each consisting of both prose and verse. This is now the first: the eye organ.
These sons and daughters of good family (up to) spoke these verses:
"If, in the midst of a great assembly... the power of the fleshly eye is thus.

[This concludes] the Chapter on the Root of Sleep. It clarifies that what is produced by one's parents is called the "fleshly eye," yet that which it perceives surpasses even the divine eye. *Brahma*.

The King replied: "One who has attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) sees throughout the great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) within his own realm. Beyond the great trichiliocosm, there is a wind-wheel (*vāyumaṇḍala*) that acts as an obstruction to the eye;
thus, one cannot see what lies outside. If one is in another realm, one does not see the great trichiliocosm universally, because it is not under one's jurisdiction.

A *śrāvaka* of lesser capacity sees a small trichiliocosm (*sāhasracūḍikālokadhātu*), a *śrāvaka* of greater capacity sees a great trichiliocosm, and a *pratyekabuddha* sees a hundred [small trichiliocosms]."
In the Buddha-world, there is no obstruction by wind-circles, nor is there any separation between one's own realm and others'.

Since the eye of this sutra and treatise can now see both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm, it must be the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). How then can it be called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)?

This is the stage of semblance (*sadrśa-bhūmi*) in the Perfect Teaching; through the power of the sutra, there is the function of superior faculties. However, as true reality has not yet been manifested, it cannot be termed the divine eye. It is still...

This is called the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). For example, it is like the provisional means (*upāya*) of the Hīnayāna: as long as one has not attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one does not yet possess what is termed the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*) or "divine ear" (*divya-śrotra*).
Because it is still a body subject to segmentation (*paricchinna-kāya*), it is called "born of father and mother. Although it is called the fleshly eye, it possesses the functions of the five eyes:

through the function of the fleshly eye, one sees the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm; through the function of the divine eye, one sees all sentient beings and their karmic causes and conditions. The [function of the] Dharma-eye...
The function of the eye (*cakṣus*): its eyes are exceedingly pure. The function of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*): it perceives all at once the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm;
it perceives karma and perceives purity, and furthermore, it perfectly subdues the afflictions above the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The function of the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*):

as the Great Sūtra says, "Though one possesses the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye. Because it is the Buddha-eye, it is called pure. Because it is endowed with the five eyes, it is said to be "adorned" (*vyūha*).
The ability to expand and contract is called the superior function of the faculties; it is called mastery over the faculties.
How could this possibly be understood merely as eight hundred or twelve hundred [yojanas]? △ Second, the faculty of hearing.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence (Sadāprarudita) [from the passage] up to "spoke these verses" says:
"The ears born of one's parents... having already perfected such merit.

This concludes the Chapter on the Ear Faculty. It universally hears the sounds of the ten dharma-realms within and without the trichiliocosm. Hearing the six paths of rebirth refers to the fleshly ear.
There are two kinds of heavenly ears: hearing the Two Vehicles is the ear of wisdom; hearing the Bodhisattvas is the ear of Dharma; hearing the Buddhas is the Buddha-ear.

Furthermore, the fleshly ears born of one's parents that can hear both the internal and external are the heavenly ears; hearing without attachment is the ear of wisdom; hearing without error is the ear of Dharma;
hearing all things simultaneously and reciprocally is the Buddha-ear. By analogy with the ears, the same applies to the eyes.
The eye is also like this: seeing humans and devas is the two eyes; seeing the Two Vehicles is the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*);
seeing bodhisattvas is the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*); seeing the Buddha is the buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*). △ Third, the nose faculty.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence (Sadāparigraha), up to the point where he spoke in verse:
"This person’s nose is pure... first attaining this mark of the nose. The chapter on the faculty of the nose (*ghrāṇendriya*) is also like this.
That which is produced by one's parents is the physical, fleshy nose; that which exists within and without the great trichiliocosm is the celestial nose.
The nose: when it is neither defiled nor attached, it is the nose of wisdom (*prajñā-nāsikā*); when it discerns without error, it is the nose of the Dharma (*dharma-nāsikā*);

when its functions are simultaneously interchanged, it is the nose of the Buddha (*buddha-nāsikā*). This chapter clarifies this interchangeability: when the nose perceives what is good or foul, distinguishes between the noble and the base, or beholds the adornments of celestial palaces and the like, then the nose possesses the function of the eye.
When reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, being able to know through the scent, then the nose possesses the function of the ear.

The nose has the function of smelling the flowers, fruits, and essences of various trees, as well as the fragrance of ghee and oil; it has the function of the tongue, for when entering or emerging from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there are eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*).
Even the playful indulgence in the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) is a matter of touch; thus, the nose has the function of the body.

It also knows those whose minds are defiled by desire, delusion, and anger, as well as those who cultivate goodness; thus, the nose has the function of the mind. The faculty of the nose is sovereign, and its superior function is such that—

Now, as with the five faculties, it is likewise so (because the faculty of the nose is most thoroughly detailed, its mutual functions are further analyzed; by analogy, the other faculties should also be understood in this way, though the text is abbreviated).
△ Four, the faculty of the tongue.
Furthermore, [the Buddha], Constantly Diligent (Sadāparibhūta), spoke in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of this person is pure... [omitted] ...or at times he manifests his body.
The chapter on the tongue-faculty is also like this. That which is born of one's parents is the physical tongue; it is able to produce the ten dharma-realms.
Regarding speech: based on this, the meaning of the five tongues is clarified. That which can produce the speech of the ten dharma realms is the celestial tongue (*divya-jihvā*).

That which is indestructible is the wisdom tongue (*prajñā-jihvā*). That which is unerring is the Dharma tongue (*dharma-jihvā*). That which functions simultaneously and interchangeably is the Buddha tongue (*buddha-jihvā*). Question:
When bitter, astringent, or foul flavors reach the tongue, they all transform into supreme flavors. When various forms reach the eye, why do they not likewise transform into the wondrous?

Regarding form (*rūpa*): it was not previously categorized [in the same way]. Taste has both the capacity to cause harm and to bring benefit; that which causes harm changes, while that which does not cause harm does not change.

Because various forms do not destroy the eye, they were not categorized in the same way. Now, the explanation is not so: all forms are identical to the Buddha’s form, and all sounds are identical to the Buddha’s sound;
as such, they are all equally pure. Thus, there is no impediment to categorizing them. One thoroughly knows all phenomena of form and all phenomena of sound. There is... [no obstruction].
There is no error in this confusion; there is also no hindrance to discernment. How could the faculty of sovereign mastery be interpreted as something dull and obstructive?
△ Five: The Body Faculty.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence (up to) spoke these verses:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra... (up to) all things appear therein.
The Chapter on the Body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also like this: everything that exists in the world appears within the body; this is the function of the physical body.

Manifesting within the body as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the function of the celestial body (*devakāya*). Manifesting within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles is the function of the wisdom body (*jñānakāya*).
Manifesting within the body of a Bodhisattva is the function of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Manifesting within the body of a Buddha is the function of the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).
These manifest simultaneously, function interchangeably at once, are simultaneously without error, and are simultaneously without attachment (the faculty of the body).
The middle [state] is said to be: non-delusion, which is the provisional; non-attachment, which is emptiness; and the simultaneous illumination of both, which is named the Middle.
△ Sixth, the mental faculty. Furthermore, Constant Diligence (up to) spoke these verses:
This person’s mind is pure (up to) because they uphold the Lotus Sūtra.
The chapter on the faculty of mind is also like this. All worldly means of livelihood and production accord with the True Dharma; thus, the person’s mind is pure.
One fully knows all that the mind of heaven performs and all that heaven moves. The purity of the heavenly intention corresponds to the Four Noble Truths; the four months correspond to these truths.
One year consists of twelve months, which are the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. This does not contradict the true nature (*dharmatā*), and thus the wisdom-intention is pure.
One month corresponds to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and the purity of the Bodhisattva’s intention means that whatever they contemplate is entirely the teaching of the former Buddhas.
As stated in the sūtras, this refers to the purity of the Buddha’s mind: at one time it is perfectly luminous; at one time it is perfectly interpenetrating;

at one time it is untainted; and at one time it is unerring. Its faculties and functions are sovereign, capable of expanding and contracting, equalizing and purifying (as described in the "Chapter on Rejoicing").

The initial chapter on "Comparative Measurement" distinguishes the merits by directly clarifying the four levels of faith and the five grades of practitioners. Herein, the "Merit of the Dharma Master" clarifies only the merits of the six sense organs corresponding to those stages.

In the "Chapter on Not Despising," it clarifies the present and future retributions for those who propagate the sutra, including the purification of the six sense organs and the entrustment of supernatural powers; this shows that those who have attained the fruit naturally manifest the power and function of propagating the sutra to encourage its circulation. The chapters on Bhaisajyaraja, Gadgadasvara, and Avalokitesvara clarify the merits of those close to the state of true personhood in propagating the sutra. Therefore, from the "Chapter on Rejoicing" onwards, there is no need for detailed explanation;
I shall merely indicate the textual structure to demonstrate the transmission and propagation, so that the significance of the merit of circulation may be understood of itself.

First, one should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the causal stage is identical to or different from the awakening of the resultant stage.
If one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation while seeking the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither born nor extinguished—there is no such possibility.

(Commentary: These two definitive meanings are both taught for the sake of the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. "Reversing the hearing to return to one's own nature" refers to the first [meaning]: the mind that is neither born nor extinguished. "Following sounds to flow and circulate" refers to the second [meaning]:
acting as a common medium for thieves, robbing oneself of one's own family treasure. As for the second meaning, you should carefully examine the root of afflictions.
Since beginningless time, who has initiated karma and moistened rebirth? Who acts and who receives the retribution? It is your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the six [faculties].
Acting as a mediator for thieves, they plunder the treasures of their own home.

Because of this, sentient beings have been bound by entanglements within the world since beginningless time, and thus cannot transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). What is meant by "sentient-being world"?

"World" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time (the three periods of past, present, and future); "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial direction (east, west, south, and north). These realms and worlds intersect, forming twelve [realms].

Four times three makes twelve—twelve by turning around (meaning that when the three periods of time intersect with the four directions, it is four times three equals twelve; and when the four directions intersect with the three periods of time, it is four times three equals twelve; hence it is said, "twelve by turning around"). The transformations flow through three layers:

one, ten, hundred, and thousand (meaning that through the transformations of the three periods of time, there is the principle of three layers: the first layer multiplies one by twelve; the second layer multiplies ten by twelve to make one hundred and twenty;

the third layer multiplies a hundred by twelve to make one thousand and two; hence it is said, "the transformations flow through three layers: one, ten, hundred, and thousand"). Thus, summarizing from beginning to end, within each of the six sense faculties, there are their respective merits.

There are one thousand two hundred [units of merit]. Among these, you must further determine their relative superiority and inferiority: the faculty of the eye possesses eight hundred merits; the faculty of the ear is complete with one thousand two hundred merits;
the faculty of the nose possesses eight hundred merits; the faculty of the tongue is complete with one thousand two hundred merits;
the faculty of the body possesses eight hundred merits; and the faculty of the mind is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.

Regarding the "One Hundred Merits" (where each of the six sense faculties possesses twelve hundred [qualities], yet there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority): these differences between sharp and dull capacities are merely based on the specific dispositions of those in this region.

Now that the selection has been clarified, one is led to enter the Way through the faculty of hearing, because the auditory faculty is universally penetrating (*avaivartika*) and possesses the three kinds of reality (*tattva*). There are three explanations provided by the Great Master: first, relying on the peaceful conduct of the three karmas to fulfill the ten wholesome paths;

second, relying on the single mind to encompass the ten dharma-realms; and third, relying on the purity of the six faculties to judge the expansion and contraction of merit. The Great Master’s exegesis deeply accords with the intent of the sutra. As the Tathāgata judged in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Three times four makes twelve; these revolve and transform into three layers; from one, ten, hundred, and thousand... Those who read this...

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty: The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging.

Regarding the explanation of the chapter on the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging: inwardly he harbors the realization of "never disparaging," and outwardly he shows reverence toward the objects of "never disparaging."
In body, he stands in the practice of "not disparaging"; in speech, he proclaims the teaching of "not disparaging"; and others take him as the model for "not disparaging.

Regarding the interpretation of "not disparaging," the *Fa-hua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "This bodhisattva knows that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and therefore does not dare to disparage them. There are five kinds of Buddha-nature:

first, the Buddha-nature of the direct cause (*zhengyin foxing*), which pervades both the fundamental and the actual; second, the Buddha-nature of the conditional cause (*yuan yin foxing*) and the Buddha-nature of the consummating cause (*liao yin foxing*), which are the seeds..."
The seeds have existed inherently; they are not something acquired only now. As for the nature of the fruit and the nature of the fruit-of-fruit, one will certainly attain them;

it is by no means in vain. This is called the understanding of "Not Disparaging. Applying this understanding to all people—realizing that they are likewise so—is called the sphere of "Revering Not Disparaging.
Because one reveres this sphere, it is called the practice of "Not Disparaging. Because one proclaims these words, it is called [the teaching of] "Not Disparaging."

Regarding the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*): formerly, those who disparaged [this tradition] used this term to refer to people; now, the compilers of the sutras use it to designate this chapter. (As for "the causal nature pervades both delusion and awakening":

because the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*) pervades both the causes and effects of delusion and awakening, the "conditions" and "understanding" are said to have seeds that are originally present. This refers back to the nature-endowment to clarify the two causes. Because they are contrasted with the newly perfumed [seeds], they constitute the cultivated endowment (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).

These three serve as the cause; when the cause transforms into the fruit, the bodhi and nirvāṇa within that fruit are called the "fruit-nature. Since the nature-endowment is originally present, it is called the "fruit-of-fruit nature"). The *Jian-shi sanmei* (Samādhi of Seeing Reality) states: "The Buddha is the father."
The King said, "Are all beings Buddhas? The King asked, "Are all sentient beings themselves Buddhas?

The Buddha replied, "If one sees sentient beings as they truly are, then for that person, they are indeed Buddhas. Applying this analogy to my own case: if I do not see the Buddha as he truly is, then I am not a Buddha.
It is like a beginner at archery who misses the target most of the time; in such a case, one should take the ground itself as the target. There is no [other way].

In the past, there was no attachment. If one follows false discrimination and perceives a distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas, then one is not a Buddha. If one contemplates according to reality, then there is nothing that is not a Buddha.

The former is the explanation according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda* (Dependent Origination) school; the latter is the explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjiao*). (Regarding "The former is the *Pratītyasamutpāda* school," etc.)

The first part, consisting of five phrases beginning with "internally harboring the understanding of not disparaging," refers to this. The latter part concerning the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is explained according to the teaching method (*jiaoyue*); it begins from the passage on the Samādhi of Seeing Reality (*jian shi sanmei*). △ Next, the scriptural text is interpreted.
This chapter cites people as witnesses to prove that the merits of the five faculties are profound and the retribution for the six sense organs is weighty.

In the past, I expressed sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) and thereby obtained both present and future rewards; this is done to encourage the circulation [of this scripture]. (Regarding "In the past, I expressed sympathetic joy and obtained present and future rewards": this further clarifies the purpose of the coming account. Thus, the subsequent text says:

"When I was about to pass away, I heard in full the *Lotus Sūtra* previously preached by Buddha Prabhūtaratna [Vaiśvānara], whereby I attained purity of the six faculties and my lifespan was further increased—this is the present reward. After my life ended, I again encountered two thousand billion Buddhas, all of whom... )

The title *Sūryapradīpa* (Sun-Moon-Lamp) refers to the retribution received in this very life. By these causes and conditions, he further encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named *Meghasvarendrarāja* (Cloud-Sovereign-Lamp-King); subsequently, he encountered ten million *koṭis* of Buddhas—this refers to future retribution. Within the retribution of the present life, he attained the purification of the six sense faculties;

therefore, his merit in propagating this sutra is not slight. When it was circulated in the past, the three types of retribution were manifest; that it is circulated today is truly not in vain. The text consists of prose and verse. The prose is divided into three parts:
first, a dual reference to the offenses and blessings of the preceding chapter; second, a dual opening regarding faith and slander in the present chapter.

The three pairs of exhortations (exhorting by citing [the favorable] and obstructing [the unfavorable]; exhorting by citing [the upholder] and obstructing [the destroyer]). Regarding the first pair of citations: first, one cites the offenses, as explained in the "Dharma Master" chapter;
next, one cites the merits, as explained in the "Merit" chapter, according to the text. Now, for the first [of these].

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta... [up to] the purity of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (the first pair concludes the preceding discussion on sin and merit).
△ Second pair: opening the gates of faith and slander. This concerns the fundamental reality and its manifestations.

Now, first [regarding the "Root of the Matter" (*vṛttamūla*): *Vṛttamūla* refers to the initial period of Bhīṣmagarjitanirghoṣa; since this is the root of the matter concerning Aśoka, it is called the "Root of the Matter. hence it is called the "Original Matter. Essence and function are non-dual and inconceivable). As for the "Root of the Matter," its time, season, name, eon, land, and preaching of the Dharma are all as stated in the text.

By what causes and conditions does one attain great power? [From here until] "you shall all become Buddhas.

One attains the grand principle of the correct teaching and the wondrous benefit of its circulation. [Supplementary note: "Attaining the grand principle of the correct teaching" refers to the correct exposition of the Trace Gate.]

The threefold exposition of the Dharma reveals the provisional to manifest the real, bestowing upon the disciples the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood. The primary teaching of the "Original Gate" (Honmon) reveals the trace to manifest the origin, enabling the bodhisattvas to increase their path and diminish their births, thereby receiving the prediction of the Dharma-body.

Regarding those who obtain the wondrous benefit of the circulation [of the teaching], there are five chapters in the circulation section of the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon): first, the Chapter on the Dharma Master, who propagates the Dharma by establishing the three guidelines; second, the Chapter on the Ancient Buddhas, in which the jeweled stupa emerges to testify to the sutra;

third, the Chapter on Sadāparibhūta, in which teacher and disciple transmit the wondrous sutra and receive the prediction of attaining the Way; fourth, the Chapter on Encouraging the Retention, in which twenty thousand bodhisattvas and others vow to uphold and expound it in the evil age; and fifth, the Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry, which asks about the method for propagating the sutra in the final age and initiates the "Peaceful Practices. These constitute the circulation of the Trace Gate. As for the circulation of the Original Gate...

The *Tong* (Comprehensive) consists of eleven and a half chapters. One chapter, the "Distinguishing Merit" (*Bianzheng Gongde*), first clarifies the four kinds of faith in the present age, and subsequently clarifies the five grades [of merit] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. The second is the "Rejoicing" (*Suixi*) chapter, which compares and evaluates the merit of the fiftieth person at the very end.

Even those who obtain the benefit of a single phrase or a single verse, though unable to propagate and transform others—being far inferior to those mentioned previously—possess merits so vast and inconceivable that they are difficult to fathom;

how much more so for those who first hear the sutra and then successively teach it to others? How can their merit be measured? 1. The Chapter on the Merits of the Three Dharma-Masters: manifesting the retribution of the purification of the six sense faculties. 2. The Reverent Prostration of Never-Disparaging: the three types of retribution becoming perfectly clear and bright.

3. The Inconceivable Divine Power of the Tathāgata. 4. The Sincere and Repeated Entrustment. 5. Bhaiṣajyarāja’s disregard for his own life and his cherishing of the Dharma. 6. Gadgadasvara, through the Samādhi of Manifesting Forms According to Kind, propagating and transmitting the teachings to all classes of beings. 7. Avalokiteśvara’s universal manifestation through the Universal Gate. 8. Dhāraṇī: assisting the orthodox and crushing the heterodox.

The fundamental narrative of King Śubhavyūha having been clarified, the great vows of Samantabhadra are now exhorted for circulation without end; this constitutes the eleven chapters and a half of the "Expedient Means" (Hōben) section of the Latter Part.

As for the various chapters mentioned above, they were either composed by Great Beings of the Dharma-body or by ancient Buddhas manifesting their forms to assist and promote the Dharma-education. By touching upon every category of being, they circulate universally for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, revealing, instructing, awakening, and leading them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and bestowing upon them the prediction of Buddhahood.

Regarding the circulation of the main exposition, although the full text comprises no fewer than sixty thousand words, the passage from "Not disparaging the Bodhisattva" down to "I deeply respect you all"—a mere twenty-four characters—encompasses it entirely. It contains the thesis, the inquiry, and the explanation; it is truly [the essence].

This means attaining the great purport of the correct teaching and obtaining the wondrous benefit of its circulation. He is named "Ever-Not-Light" (Sadāparibhūta) because he does not slight himself or others.

"This person" refers to the One Principle (Ekayāna). "Whatever is seen" refers to the One Truth (Ekatattva). "All bowing in prostration" refers to the One Practice (Ekacaryā). And "speaking these words" refers to the One Teaching (Ekadeśanā).
These constitute the fourfold "One" that reveals the provisional and manifests the real. From the passage beginning with "Even seeing from afar" onwards...
This is the first unity of Principle; therefore, going to pay homage is the first unity of Practice. To speak thus is the first unity of Teaching;
and the fourfold assembly is the first unity of Persons. These constitute the fourfold unities that reveal the remote by opening up the proximate. The text says:
"Those who do not specialize in reading and reciting the scriptures, but practice only prostrations—these are the rank of those who initially rejoice in accordance [with the teaching]."
I rejoice in all phenomena, for they all possess the nature of peace and bliss; they are all of one true reality. I rejoice in all people, for they all possess the three Buddha-natures:
the recitation of the scriptures is the *nirvedhabhāga* (the nature as the cause of realization); the practice of the Bodhisattva path is the *pratyaya-bhāga* (the nature as the causal condition);
and the fact that one does not dare to treat others with contempt but instead holds them in deep reverence is the *mūla-bhāga* (the fundamental nature). To revere people...
The Dharma is to refrain from contention; this is the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). To not disparage others but to hold them in deep respect is to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat.
To endure being struck or reviled is to don the Tathāgata’s robe. To constantly practice with a heart of compassion without ceasing is to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Furthermore, deep respect is the mental action (*manas-karma*); not disparaging others is the verbal action (*vāk-karma*).

Therefore, going to pay homage is an action of the body (*kāyakarman*). These three, when conjoined with compassion (*maitrī* and *karuṇā*), constitute the vow for the practice of peaceful dwelling (*sukhavihāra*).
If these four [aspects] are thus, how could they not be called the wondrous benefit of the propagation [of the teaching]? What else could they be?
△ Second, clarifying the faults of those who disparage it.
Among the fourfold assembly (up to) he was called "Never-Disparaging.
Those who gave rise to a mind of anger and were impure did not accept even one of the four [teachings]. They reviled him, saying, "You are ignorant. To know wisdom is to understand principle;
since they said he was ignorant, he did not accept even one principle. The bhikṣus and others likewise did not accept even one principle from him. From...
First, regarding "not receiving [the teaching]": what has come? It is the failure to practice it. Second, regarding "not receiving the instruction": it is the bestowing of false predictions.
Third, regarding "those who have been constantly reviled for many years": this refers to not receiving the fourfold [teaching] that opens up the provisional and reveals the real.

Fourth, regarding "fleeing away and reaching [this place] to dwell, proclaiming aloud": this likewise refers to not receiving the fourfold [teaching] that opens up the near and reveals the far, which is the original ground.
First: Because he constantly spoke these words, those who were bound by faith developed deep conviction without ceasing.

As for the fourfold assembly giving him the name "Never-Disparaging," this signifies that those bound by disparagement continued their slanders without stopping. Question: When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he hesitated and did not preach;
yet Never-Disparaging, upon seeing him once, spoke immediately. Why is this? Answer: It is because [Never-Disparaging] already possessed goodness from the very beginning.

Śākyamuni protects them by means of the small [teachings] (ultimately leading them to enter the reality), whereas "Not Disparaging" (Adhimukta) forcefully infuses them with the great [teachings] (planting the seeds of Buddhahood within them).
△ Third, the dual clarification of the retributions for faith and disparagement. First, regarding the retribution for those who have faith, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the retribution of faith; second, correlating the past and present. This is the first.
When this bhikṣu is on the verge of death (until) his merits are fulfilled, he shall attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the believer’s three types of retribution: in the present life, they obtain the purification of the six sense faculties; in the next life, they encounter the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; and thereafter, they encounter two thousand billion buddhas.
The power of supernormal knowledges is the purity of bodily action (*kāyakarman*); the power of eloquence in joyful exposition is the purity of verbal action (*vākkarman*). Good.
The power of tranquility is the purity of mental action. △ Second, the reconciliation of the ancient and the modern, in two parts.
First, the reconciliation: "What do you think, Mahāsthāmaprāpta? ... it was my own body."
△ Next, he exhorts those with faith to comply.
"If I, in past lives... (up to) "...shall quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
△ Second, explaining the retribution for those who disparage [the teaching], which is further divided into two parts. First, explaining the retribution itself.

Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time the fourfold assembly (up to the point of) being taught and transformed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, those who disparage [this teaching] shall obtain both good and evil fruits.
Because of their slander, they fall into the evil realms; yet by hearing the name of the Buddha-nature, through the power of the "poisonous drum," [they are saved].

Obtaining a Wholesome Fruitful Retribution. (Question: If one falls into suffering due to slander, why does the Bodhisattva create the cause for such suffering? Answer: For those who lack wholesome causes, they fall even without slandering; yet falling into evil due to slander must necessarily result in benefit.

It is like a person who has fallen to the ground and rises from that very ground; therefore, by means of "correct slander," one receives those who are about to fall into error. △ Second, correlating the ancient and the modern.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? ... [up to] 'this is one who has attained non-retrogression.
(The two pairs concerning faith and slander have been concluded. △ Third, the pair that raises exhortations: it cites compliance to exclude opposition, and exhorts upholding to exclude slander.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—up to the point of transcribing this sūtra—possesses great power and will ultimately bring about a great fruit.
You must strive diligently in the practice of the five kinds of conduct (the five kinds of practitioners of the Dharma are:

first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; and fifth, transcribing). [This concludes the prose section on the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" and the purification of the six sense faculties, with each section thus titled. (The first long prose section ends.)
△ Second, the verses in praise consist of nineteen and a half lines. The first fifteen and a half lines merely praise the causes and effects of faith and slander;
the final four lines praise the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]. These are evident in the text itself, so they are not detailed here.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"In the past there was a Buddha... (up to) "...clinging to dharmas. As for clinging to dharmas:
these dharmas cannot be pointed out. If one definitively asserts that they exist, that is precisely clinging to dharmas. And so forth...
"Samādhi" refers to that which is neither existent nor non-existent; it is also called "the Dharma of those who have attained realization. The *Buddhapiṭaka* states:
"The sin of a wheel of swords killing the people of Jambudvīpa is still small compared to the sin of one who preaches the Mahāyāna while harboring a mind of attainment."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To contend with existence by means of grasping at non-existence, and even to contend with existence and non-existence by means of grasping at neither existence nor non-existence, is like a leather bag and a dragon-rope;
both fail to avoid suffering. The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "The Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness primarily to transform those who cling to existence.

If there are those who become attached to emptiness, they cannot be transformed by the Buddhas. If one definitively asserts that all phenomena are neither... [existence nor non-existence], [this is likewise a fault].

To claim that "it exists" rather than "it is non-existent" is called the discourse of the deluded. If one loses the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, whether acting for oneself or transforming others, one is in all cases attached to dharmas.
If one attains the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, both self and others are free from attachment.
The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (up to): such a sūtra as this;
after hundreds of billions of kalpas (up to): he will swiftly attain the Buddha-way.
(The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging concludes.)
△ First, the table of contents is presented; next, the scriptural text is explained. Now, for the first [section]:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-one, “The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers” (*Tathāgata-ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa-parivarta*).
Regarding the term “Tathāgata”: this has already been explained above (see the explanation in the *Ayuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta*). “Supernatural power” (*ṛddhi*) means that which cannot be fathomed.

"Power" (*bala*) refers to functional efficacy (*kāritra*). When it is unfathomable, the natural essence (*dharmatā-svabhāva*) is profound; when it manifests as functional efficacy, the power of transformation is great.
Because the profound Dharma is here entrusted [to others] by manifesting ten kinds of great powers, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on Spiritual Powers" (*Ṛddhibala-parivarta*).
Next, the scriptural text is explained. From this chapter downward, there are eight chapters in total concerning the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching]. This present chapter...

The preceding chapter clarified how the Bodhisattvas received their mandate to propagate the sutra; the following chapter concerns the Tathāgata’s conferral of the entrustment by stroking their heads.

The text of the present chapter consists of prose and verse. The prose section is divided into three parts: first, the Bodhisattvas receiving their mandate; second, the Buddha manifesting his supernatural powers; and third, the summary of the essential points and the exhortation to uphold the teaching.
The first part is further divided into two sections: first, the narrator describing the respectful demeanor.
At that time, bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a thousand worlds (up to) gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
△ Second, they made a vow to propagate the sutra and addressed the Buddha, saying (up to): "We shall explain it, copy it, and make offerings to it."
This section consists of three parts: first, the time, which refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; second, the location, which refers to the lands of the various emanations;

and third, the vows made thereafter. (Supplementary note: When the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, all the Buddhas of the ten directions who were his emanations simultaneously entered parinirvāṇa, like the moon falling from the heavens.)

The moon falls upon a thousand rivers at once. Thus, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) emerged and made a vow to propagate the Dharma in the lands where those emanated Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, thereby benefiting both himself and others.
△ Second, the manifestation of the ten supernatural powers is divided into two parts. First, the assembly addressed.
At that time, the World-Honored One [appeared] before the entire assembly.

Regarding the phrase "before Mañjuśrī and the others": these are the members of the assembly manifested through his traces (*vyañjana*). Regarding "those who have long resided here": these are the original members of the assembly from the lower direction. Regarding "all":

these include those who have come from other directions, as well as those who have come from the emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddhas. Question: Why is it that we see only those from the lower direction?
[The questioner] asks: "Why is it that [the Buddha] does not make a vow, as Mañjuśrī and others do? [The answer: It is replied:
As stated in the preceding text, "In my land there are naturally bodhisattvas who can uphold this sutra," this already includes such a vow. △ Second, the actual manifestation of supernatural power.
Manifesting great supernormal powers (up to) as if in a single buddha-field. Regarding the ten supernormal powers:

first, the mark of extending the tongue, as expounded in the present sutra—opening the three to reveal the one, concealing the internal while manifesting the external, setting aside the near to reveal the distant, and clarifying how he benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—all of these are true and not false. This is the person of merit.

His tongue reached his nose; the three marks of a Buddha reached the hairline; now they have reached the Brahma Heaven, transcending both ordinary beings and sages, extending to the summit of the Pure Heavens.
Since these marks are so extraordinary, the teaching is all the more credible. Second, as for the pores of his entire body:
Light radiates from his entire body, illuminating the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not shine brightly; this signifies that the realm of wisdom is exhaustive.
The brilliance first emitted from the ūrṇā-kośa above his brow in the east signified the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*) and the initial perception of the single principle.

Now that the *mūlaparivarta* (Root Chapter) has concluded, he emits all-encompassing light to illuminate all lands, enabling those at the initial stage of causality to reach the ultimate state of Equal Enlightenment (*samantabhadra*).
The Buddha’s wisdom and the various emanations of the Buddhas are likewise thus. The three coughs are the manner of about to speak;
they are also a sign of unobstructed flow. For over forty years, the truth was concealed; now it is finally extended and revealed.
There is no lingering obstruction; this is my great worldly task fully accomplished. For this reason, I cough.
Desiring to entrust this Dharma to the bodhisattvas so that they may guide and benefit sentient beings in future generations, I am about to speak of this matter;
for this reason, I cough. This coughing possesses two meanings: first, coughing to signify that the task is finished; second, coughing to entrust it to others. (4)
A "snap of the fingers" signifies sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). It is sympathetic joy toward the seven stages of expedient means as they collectively enter the Perfect Path;

it is sympathetic joy toward the Perfect Path, which increases wisdom and diminishes birth; it is sympathetic joy toward all Bodhisattvas who uphold the truly pure Great Dharma; and it is sympathetic joy toward future generations who shall obtain the unsurpassed treasure.
This single snap of the fingers penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally across the ten directions—these are the five stages and six kinds [of realization].

"Movement" signifies the movement of ignorance through six stages, from the initial mind to the final mind; it now clarifies that [this movement] further moves the six sense organs of all people, causing them to attain purity.
"The Six Universal Vision Great Assemblies" signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is identical, and from this point forward, it shall likewise be so.
The five thousand [monks] rose and departed; they were moved by three transformations. Thus it was.

Having lost their original mind, they were unable to manifest benefit. It was appropriate that they should not extinguish their present evil, but rather follow the various bodhisattvas, propagate the sutras, and attain the Way, entering the Buddha-wisdom no differently than those in the present assembly. This also demonstrates that there is one and the same potential for the future.

1. The sound of chanting in the seven voids signifies that there will be one who teaches in the future. 2. The eightfold "Namo" (Homage) and taking refuge as a disciple of the Buddha signifies that there will be one person in the future.
3. The ninth, the scattering of various objects from afar and their gathering like clouds, signifies that there will be one who practices in the future.
4. The tenth, the universal unity of the ten directions as being one Buddha, [signifies...]
“Earth” signifies the unity of principle. Question: How is it known that the ten marks express the present meaning and also express the future meaning?
Answer: The text says: “By means of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, because I am entrusting this sutra, even this cannot be exhausted.
Thus, expressing the present and expressing the future—their significance is clear. △ Third, the summary and entrustment. The text consists of four parts.
First, the praise and entrustment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Śikhin and others, [saying] "...yet one could not exhaustively describe it.
Second, the summary and entrustment.
To summarize: [from] "In short" up to "all are proclaimed and clearly expounded in this sutra," there are four summary phrases.
"All dharmas" means that all are Buddha-dharmas; this summarizes the name "All are Sublime.
"All powers" refers to unimpeded penetration and the possession of the eight masteries; this summarizes "Sublime."
"Application. "All secret treasuries" refers to the fact that throughout all places, everything is the true mark (*dharmatā*); this concludes the wondrous essence.
"All profound matters" refers to the fact that cause and effect are profound matters; this concludes the wondrous principle.
"All are proclaimed and clearly expounded in this sutra" summarizes the entire scripture as consisting of only these four [sections], grasping its essential pivot.

The Bestowal (Regarding the four phrases of the essential core: the two gates of the Original and the Traces each have their own fundamental principle and function; yet the substance of these two gates is no different in either place.

These names crown these three and encompass them all. How could the essentials of this entire work exceed this? Therefore, they are gathered together to ensure its circulation. As for the eight kinds of mastery, see the *Zhi guan ji*). △ Third, the Exhortation and Entrustment, as in the text.
Therefore, you all—[up to] "within this"—should all erect stupas and make offerings to them.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the entrustment.
Why is this so? [Up to] "all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa herein."
The Sutra states: "Wherever this scripture is located, a stupa should be erected there. The essential teaching within the Sutra consists of four matters:

"The site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) explains the aforementioned profound matter; "attaining bodhi" explains the aforementioned secret treasury; and "turning the wheel of Dharma" [explains the remaining matter].

The explanation of all dharmas above concludes with the entry into *nirvāṇa*. The explanation of the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) above completes these four essentials, which encompass the entirety of the sūtra’s text;
therefore, stūpas should be erected for each of them. As for what is meant by "essentials": attaining *bodhi* is the *dharmakāya*;
turning the wheel of the Dharma is *prajñā*; entering *nirvāṇa* is *vimukti*. These three dharmas constitute the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), and the Buddha abides therein.
"Middle" (*madhya*) is precisely the meaning of "stūpa. The *Āgama* states: "When a Buddha appears in the world, stūpas are erected at only four places:

the place of birth, the place of attaining the Way, the place of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and the place of entering Nirvāṇa. Sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the place where the Dharma-body is born;
all other matters are as stated in the text. (The first long prose section concludes. II. The Verse Recitation consists of sixteen lines, divided into three parts. First, the initial four lines:

The verse mentions ten supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), yet there are only five; the latter five are omitted. The first five are manifest in the present, and they are retained here for their essential importance.
The two sets of five—the former and the latter—differ only in being present or future. By citing the present as an illustration for the future, the latter set is thus abbreviated.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Buddhas, the saviors of the world... manifest immeasurable supernatural powers.
Next, there are ten and a half lines which summarize the essential points. This section further divides into two parts; the first two lines concern the merits of such a person.
The general summary verse consists of four dharmas, [extending] from "entrusting this sutra" to "its limit cannot be apprehended.
△ Second, eight and a half lines provide a specific summary of the four dharmas, which is further divided into four parts. The first one and a half lines summarize all dharmas.
To uphold the Dharma is to uphold the body of the Buddha.
Those who can uphold this sutra (up to) shall teach and transform all bodhisattvas.
△ Second, two lines of verse on supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). This supernatural power causes the Buddha to rejoice.
Those who can uphold this sutra (up to) shall also cause them to attain joy.
△ Third, the secret essentials of the one-line verse may be explained:
"The secret essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when sitting at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall also attain it before long."
△ Section Four consists of four lines. These verses describe matters of profound depth: preaching the Dharma to shatter darkness and enter the One Vehicle.
This is the profoundly deep matter of the Buddha.
Those who can uphold this sutra (up to) will ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
△ The final one and a half lines constitute the summary verse of the conclusion.
Therefore, the wise person (up to) "will certainly have no doubt" (*tathāgata-prabhāva-parivarta* ends).
△ First, the headings of the chapters are presented; next, the scriptural text is explained. Now, for the first [part]:
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-two, "Entrusting" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*). To explain the title of the chapter:
"entrusting" (*parīndanā*) refers to that which the Buddha has committed to others; "burdening" (*parīndita*) means to trouble you with the task of proclaiming it. This is derived from the Sage...

It is so named because it conveys the essential meaning; thus, it is called "entrustment" (*zhùlèi*). "Entrust" (*zhù*) means to receive what is entrusted with the highest reverence; "cumulative burden" (*lèi*) means to accept it with joy rather than weariness.
This name is derived from the respectful compliance of the Bodhisattva. Thus, it is called "entrustment. "Entrust" refers to that which is entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata;
"cumulative burden" refers to the Bodhisattva’s sincere heart bearing this upon his head. This name is derived from the synthesis of the giving and the receiving. Thus, it is called "entrustment."
This is the chapter. Therefore, the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person, extended his hand to stroke [the disciple's] head, and bestowed upon him the Dharma that is difficult to encounter.

The great assembly bowed their bodies and joined their palms, saying, "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall reverently practice and uphold it," as they earnestly received and transmitted [the teaching].
Therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*). △ Next, the explanation of the scriptural text. The text is divided into two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s entrustment;
second, the joy of the assembly. The first part has three sections: 1. The entrustment; 2. The Bodhisattvas’ acceptance; 3. The conclusion and dispersal.
The first of these also has three sub-sections: 1. The formal entrustment.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [extended his hand] so that all sentient beings might universally hear and know it.

Regarding the "true entrustment": the Buddha, with the skillful hand of his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), rubbed the crowns of the heads of immeasurable great Bodhisattvas who possess true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).
Because the Tathāgata transmits the Way to transform others, it is called the "hand of provisional wisdom. As for the Bodhisattvas' own practice:
Because one receives the Way, it is called the "Crown of Real Wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna-śīrṣa*). Extending the hand to stroke the crown of the head is the entrustment of the body.
The provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) approaching the real wisdom is the entrustment of the mind. To speak these words is the entrustment of the mouth.
These passages contain the fourfold intention of the *siddhāntas*. "I have cultivated this dharma difficult to obtain for immeasurable kalpas"—this [arises from]...
The former Buddhas received and studied [this teaching]; now it is entrusted to you. You shall transmit it to others, so that the lineage continues through the three periods of time;

this is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint). Its single-minded dissemination is the *pudgala-siddhānta* (individual standpoint). Causing it to increase extensively is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (therapeutic standpoint).
That which benefits is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint). △ Second, the explanation of the entrustment.
Why is this so? (Up to: This is called explaining the Buddha’s intent and entrusting [the teaching] to him.
△ Third, the admonition and entrustment:
"In future ages... (up to: ...then one will have repaid the kindness of all Buddhas."
Regarding the entrustment: if [the disciples] have deep roots and sharp wisdom, one should speak directly of the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*).

If they are not yet capable, one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them within other profound dharmas. The Buddha-wisdom is profound but not "other"; the six stages of expedient means (*ṣaḍupāya*) are "other" but not profound;

the sequential teaching of the distinct doctrine (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śikṣā-anupūrva*) is both "other" and profound. You should be able to use these "other" and profound teachings to assist in proclaiming the Buddha-wisdom.

The wise person skillfully repays the Buddha’s kindness; this is called the admonition and entrustment (the six stages of expedient means refer to the two vehicles of the two teachings, the bodhisattvas of the two teachings, and the distinct [teaching’s] faith, abiding, practice, and transference;
the distinct "deep" refers to the first stage of the distinct teaching being equal to the first dwelling of the perfect teaching). △ Second, the Bodhisattva’s acceptance.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [from "up to"] replied, "So be it, World-Honored One;

we pray you have no further concern. They received this with joyful minds; they received it physically by bowing their bodies and lowering their heads; they received it verbally by raising their voices in unison;
and they received it mentally as well. As the World-Honored One has commanded, they received it like a great donor.
"Come, O Assembly! You should practice with full diligence. Receive the intention of the Tathāgata’s robe with no stinginess; may you have no anxieties.

Receive the intention of the Tathāgata’s seat, which is free from fear. The Buddha thus entrusted [the teachings] three times, and the Bodhisattvas received them three times, all exactly as written in the text.
△ Third, the proclamation for dispersal.
At that time, the stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna returned to its original state.

Prabhūtaratna had come to bear witness to the sutra; his emanations had gathered to open the stūpa. Once the task of opening the stūpa was completed, he commanded the emanations to return to their original places.
Thus they departed and were no longer visible. The stūpa remained for the purpose of hearing the sutra. The primary doctrine of the "Original Chapter" is hereby concluded.
The circulation was not yet complete; therefore, the stupa returned to its former state (the Tathāgata’s entrustment concluded). △ Next, the great assembly rejoiced.
When these words were spoken (up to) "having heard what the Buddha taught, they all greatly rejoiced."
The Buddhas rejoice because they have accomplished the task of transforming others; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice.
Furthermore, it is said that one rejoices because of the purity of the person—the Buddha is such a one. One rejoices because of hearing the pure Dharma—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is such a one.
They rejoice because they have heard the Dharma and attained realization; these are those who have benefited from the very beginning in the present.
Because these three conditions are fully met, there is great joy. (The *Parīndanā-parivarta* concludes.)
△ First, the presentation of the chapter titles; second, the explanation of the scriptural text.
Now, for the first: *The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Three: The Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja*.
Regarding the explanation of the Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the *Sūtra of Contemplation* states: "Formerly named Jyotīrasa, from the Venerable Sūrya..."
The King of the Treasures (Ratnarāja), having heard the teaching of the Buddha’s wisdom, offered medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing:
"In the future, may I be able to cure the dual ailments of body and mind for all sentient beings. The entire world rejoiced and called him the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja).
This text clarifies that Sarvasattvapriyadarśana suddenly renounced his own body and further burned both his arms; he regarded his life as light and the Dharma as heavy, even unto death.
The Way exists; by citing the past, the present is illuminated. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Past Deeds" (*Pūrvayoga-parivarta*).

If one infers this meaning, Starlight (*Jyotīrasa*) should follow after Joyful Vision (*Priyadarśana*), for from the time he made his vow upon relinquishing his medicine, he was named Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*).

Next, the scriptural text is explained. The following five chapters all concern the propagation [of the teaching] through transforming others. This present chapter clarifies the teacher who transforms others.
I only pray that the Great Dharma may be widely proclaimed and disseminated, and that all sentient beings may obtain great benefit.
For this reason, I exhaust my supernatural powers and the remainder of my life, with profound and sincere devotion, yet my resolve remains undiminished, hoping thereby to cause my disciples—

The lineage of the Dharma is like that of a teacher: I transmit the illumination to you, and you in turn transmit the illumination; thus illumination continues without end—this is the intent of the teacher.
Therefore, know that this chapter exhorts teachers who propagate the Dharma. The subsequent sections, such as the two chapters on "Wondrous Sound" and "Avalokiteśvara," follow this same principle.
Know that these are Great Beings from other directions who have received the mandate to propagate this sutra. They manifest their physical bodies universally, and their forms have no fixed standard;
they cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can they be fathomed by the intellect of the ordinary person. Wherever you hear of them, do not give rise to thoughts of contempt.
Since light conceptualization does not defile the mind with respect to the Dharma, we know this refers to the lower grade; thus, it is an exhortation for disciples who receive the Dharma.
Some say that while the Buddhas perform Buddha-works in the higher grades, Bodhisattvas perform Buddha-works in this lower grade. This is merely a general observation;
for there are Bodhisattvas in the higher grades as well, and there are Buddhas in this lower grade as well. Now, the three cycles [of teaching] are clarified.
Opening the three to reveal the one; the section on the Perfect Cause is thus concluded. The "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" clarifies the dharma of the vehicle of vehicles (*yānayāna*).

The "Chapter on the Lifespan" clarifies the fruit of the vehicle of vehicles. In the following chapter, it clarifies the person of the vehicle of vehicles. Therefore, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states:
The Mahāyāna is that which is mounted by great beings such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī. Bhaiṣajyarāja mounts the vehicle of ascetic practice;
Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara mount the vehicle of samādhi; Dhāraṇī mounts the vehicle of total retention (dhāraṇī); Suvarṇaprabhāsa mounts the vehicle of vows;
and Samantabhadra mounts the vehicle of supernormal powers (abhijñā). One who understands it in this way, at...

The meaning of the "Conveying to Others" (pariṇāmanā) follows as a natural consequence.
