The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Five: The Universal Gate of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

The commentary on the "Universal Gate" chapter of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Sūtra has both general and specific aspects. The general aspect consists of ten pairs; the specific aspect consists of five pairs. Regarding the ten pairs:
the first is person and dharma, up to the tenth, which is wisdom and abandonment. As for the pair of person and dharma:
"Avalokiteśvara" refers to the person, and "Universal Gate" refers to the dharma. There are many kinds of persons, and there are many kinds of dharmas. The sūtra states...

Second, the question-and-answer section. Based on the preceding questions and answers, this section discusses the person of Avalokiteśvara; based on the subsequent questions and answers, it discusses the *pūrmadvāra* (Universal Gate) Dharma.
Because the person and the Dharma are combined in the title, it is called the "Avalokiteśvara *Pūrmadvāra* Chapter.

Second, regarding compassion: "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the Great Compassion that uproots suffering; through it, those with hundreds of thousands of afflictions all attain liberation. This is the Universal Gate.
As for this, according to the subsequent dialogue, one should preach the Dharma to those who are to be delivered by bestowing great compassion and happiness.
Third, regarding the two adornments: Avalokiteśvara is adorned with wisdom; wisdom can sever delusions, just as there is no darkness when it is bright.
The Universal Gate (Samantamukha) refers to the adornment of merit. Merit can transform one's lifespan, like a jewel raining down treasures. Regarding the four dharmas that correspond:
"Avalokiteśvara" means observing the profound within the objective realm; this is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). "Universal Gate" means manifesting according to what is appropriate;
this is the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya). Regarding the five medicinal jewels: "Avalokiteśvara" is likened to the king of medicinal trees, whose entire body heals all ailments. Universal...

The "Gates" (dvāra) are like the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels (cintāmaṇi-rāja). According to one's wishes, it bestows [whatever is desired] (as described in detail in the fifth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

The six "hidden" (míng) and "manifest" (xiǎn) [gates]: Avalokiteśvara provides benefit through the hidden; there is nothing seen or heard, yet the three poisons and seven calamities are all eliminated, and the two types of seeking and the two types of vows are both fulfilled.
The "Universal Gate" (Pumen): he provides benefit through the manifest; with one's own eyes, one beholds the thirty [transformations].
Third, regarding the three sacred forms: the ear hears the teachings of nineteen honored ones. Seventh, regarding following oneself or others:

"Avalokiteśvara" (Observing the World's Sounds) follows one's own intention and illuminates true wisdom (*jñāna*). "Universal Gateway" (*Samantamukha*) follows the intentions of others and illuminates provisional wisdom (*upāya*).

Eighth, regarding essence and function: "Avalokiteśvara" is the essence, remaining unmoved from the fundamental limit (*dharmadhātu*). "Universal Gateway" is the function, manifesting traces according to the square or the round.
Furthermore, the nine conditions correspond to the two causes. "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the fundamental seed of the *vidyā-hetu* (the cause of awakening);
"Samantamukha" refers to the fundamental seed of the *pratyaya-hetu* (the causal condition). Tenth, regarding wisdom and severance:

"Avalokiteśvara" represents the ultimate virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), like the moon on the fourteenth night, its clear radiance about to reach fullness. "Samantamukha" represents the ultimate severance.
Virtue is like the moon on the twenty-ninth night; its false radiance is about to end. The two question-and-answer passages of the sutra text contain immeasurable meanings.
Briefly employing ten pairs—from "person and dharma" at the beginning to "wisdom and abandonment" at the end—I have explained the general title of this chapter;
such is its meaning. As for the specific discussion of the five sections, they refer to Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate (*Pumen*). First, as for "contemplation" (*guan*): it is contemplation.

There are several types: namely, analytical contemplation (*vibhāga-vipaśyanā*), essential contemplation (*svabhāva-vipaśyanā*), sequential contemplation (*anupūrva-vipaśyanā*), and perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*).

Analytical contemplation is the negation of form to enter into emptiness. Essential contemplation is that form itself is emptiness. Sequential contemplation proceeds from analytical contemplation up to perfect contemplation.
Perfect contemplation is that analytical contemplation itself is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and so on, up to sequential contemplation, which is also the true reality.
This is the characteristic. Now, setting aside the three contemplations, we discuss only the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*). The text speaks of the "Universal Gate" (*pumen*);
if the contemplation were not perfect, the gate would not be called "universal. This is precisely that meaning. Regarding the "two worlds" (*er-shi*), there are many kinds of worlds:

namely, the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), the unconditioned world (*asaṃskṛta-loka*), the world of the two extremes, and the world of the inconceivable (*acintya-loka*). The conditioned world refers to the world of the triple realm (*tridhātu*). The unconditioned...
"Worlds" refers to the two types of nirvāṇa. "The worlds of the two extremes" refers to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"The inconceivable world" refers to the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Having excluded all other worlds, one takes up only the inconceivable world. As for the "three sounds":

It is a matter of capacity (*ki*). Capacities are also of many kinds: the capacity of humans and devas, the capacity of those of the two vehicles, the capacity of bodhisattvas, and the capacity of Buddhas.

Regarding the capacity of humans and devas, it is: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Regarding the capacity of those of the two vehicles, it is: "To feel weary of and fear birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)."
They delight in and esteem the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Those with the capacity of a bodhisattva prioritize others before themselves; they are compassionate, benevolent, and yielding.
Those with the capacity of a Buddha enter into all dharmas by means of universal contemplation;

as those who are entirely unimpeded, they transcend birth and death through the single path. Discarding the capacities for other sounds, he provides his response only by taking the capacity for the Buddha-sound.
Because of these responsive causes and conditions, he is named Avalokiteśvara. Regarding the fourth term, "Universal" (Pu): it means all-pervasive. All dharmas are immeasurable;
if one does not attain universality, then they are partial dharmas. If one attains universality, then they are perfect dharmas.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*) states: "All dharmas are deviant; all dharmas are correct. Briefly summarized, this clarifies universality through ten dharmas.
Having grasped this meaning, one can infer that there are no dharmas that are not universal—namely, the universality of compassion, the universality of the great vows, and so forth.
The universality of practice; the universality of being free from delusion; the universality of entering the Dharma-gates; the universality of spiritual powers; the universality of skillful means;

the universality of preaching the Dharma; the universality of maturing sentient beings; and the universality of making offerings to all Buddhas. Regarding the first, the universality of compassion, it begins with humans and devas.

Ultimately reaching the stage of a Bodhisattva, all possess compassion (*maitrī*). However, there are those that are universal and those that are not. When the objects of compassion consist of both sentient beings (*sattva*) and phenomena (*dharma*), the essence of compassion is partial;
because its engagement with objects is not extensive, it cannot be called universal. Compassion without object (*anālambana*) shares the same essence as the true mark (*dharmatā*);
since its principle is perfect, there is nowhere that compassion does not pervade. It is like a magnet attracting iron: they correspond spontaneously. Such is this compassion.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) permeates all things universally; this is called the universality of compassion. Second, the universality of the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*): "Great" (*mahā*) means vast, and "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means to restrain.
Because one broadly restrains and resolves the mind, it is called a "great vow. This great vow arises in relation to the Four Noble Truths.

If it were restricted to the four truths of conditioned arising, non-arising, or the immeasurable, it would not encompass all phenomena exhaustively and thus could not be called universal. However, if it is based on the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*)...
The Four Truths are called the universality of the great vow. Regarding the universality of the three practices:

for example, before the Buddha encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, whatever he practiced did not accord with the principle; from the time he received the prediction [of enlightenment], every action immediately coincided with the principle.
For one who practices by traversing the methods through wisdom and principle, there is no practice that is not universal. Regarding the universality of severing delusions through the four [wisdoms]:

if one employs the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) to sever the delusions of the four abodes, the dust-like afflictions (*rajas*), and so forth, it is like pruning away branches and twigs.
It is not called "universal severance of delusions. If one uses the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) to sever ignorance, then all five stages (*pañcavihāra*) are exhausted;
like removing the root, this is called the "universality of severing delusions. Regarding the "universality of entering the Dharma-gate":

that which precedes the Path is called "cultivating skillful means," while that which is entered after the Path is called "entering the Dharma-gate. If the followers of the Two Vehicles enter a single concentration with a single mind, [one...]
The mind acts as one; it cannot be manifold. Furthermore, because it is bound by concentration (*samādhi*), it is not called "universal" (*pūrṇa*).

If it traverses the various stages (*bhūmi*) individually according to their shallow or deep gradations, it is likewise not called universal. However, when one enters the King Samādhi, all samādhis are entirely contained within it;

without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one manifests all manner of dignified postures (*īryāpatha*). Therefore, it is called the "Universal Dharma Gate. [The six supernatural powers...]
Regarding "universal penetration": the divine eye of a great arhat illuminates a trichiliocosm; that of a pratyekabuddha illuminates a hundred buddha-worlds;

and that of a bodhisattva illuminates worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In all these cases, because the objects of perception are narrow, the resulting supernormal powers are likewise partial.

However, for one who cultivates based on the true nature (dharmatā), when one power is manifested, all are manifested—just as described above regarding the semblance of supernormal powers. How much more so, then, would this be true for actual supernormal powers?

Puyaya. Regarding "universal" (*puyu*) in the context of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), there are two types: the expedient means prior to the Path, which is subsumed within the practice; and the expedient means subsequent to the Path, which also has two aspects.
The first is the essential nature (*dharmatā*), as explained in the section on entering the Dharma-gate. The second is the transformative function (*nirmāṇa-prayoga*), as discussed here.
To guide sentient beings according to their capacities and accord with the conditions of the Way, one acts with simultaneous and universal perfection.

Although various activities are performed, there is no loss or diminution within the reality-limit (*dharmatā-bhūtakoṭi*) of the Dharma-nature; this is called the universality of skillful means (*upāya*). Eighth, the universality of preaching the Dharma:

one is able to use a single wondrous voice to accord with the capacities of the ten dharma-realms, enabling all to attain liberation according to their respective natures and types, as in the practice of...

The lute and zither; therefore, it is named "Universal in Preaching the Dharma. Ninth, "Universality in Accomplishing Sentient Beings" means that all worldly and world-transcending undertakings are performed by the Bodhisattva.

Whether it be digging wells, constructing boats, Shen Nong tasting medicinal herbs, the shade of clouds, or the light of the sun—these benefit sentient beings, even extending to benefiting all worthies and sages, providing instruction and guidance.
Benefit and gladden them, causing them to enter into *sambodhi*. This is called "accomplishing the maturation of sentient beings. Regarding "universally [engaging in] digging wells and so forth":

as the *Avataṃsaka* states, "If there is a world that has first been formed, whatever requisites for livelihood sentient beings require, the Bodhisattva at that time acts as a craftsman; he never manufactures instruments for killing. Regarding "universally making the ten kinds of offerings to all Buddhas":
if one performs external material offerings, one universally offers them with a single meal, a single flower, or a single incense stick at one time.
All Buddhas, neither preceding nor following one another, are equally honored simultaneously. Within a single atom, various atoms emerge;
it is likewise so. For those who practice internal contemplation, perfect wisdom guides all practices; this perfect wisdom is called the Buddha.
When all practices support the perfect wisdom, this is the offering to the Buddha. If practices support other forms of wisdom, it is not called a universal offering;

when all practices support the perfect wisdom, this is called a universal offering. Regarding the five gates: entering emptiness from the conventional means that emptiness is unobstructed while the conventional is obstructed;
entering the conventional from emptiness means that the conventional is unobstructed while emptiness is obstructed. To be unobstructed in only one direction is not universal; it is obstructed.
Therefore, it is not a [limited] gate. The Middle Way is neither empty nor provisional; it correctly penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*) and simultaneously illuminates the two truths.

Thus, it is called "Universal" (*samanta*). Because it correctly penetrates, it is called a "gate. The Universal Gate is perfectly penetrating; its meanings are immeasurable, but ten are briefly cited here.

By analogy, the rest may be understood. Next, the scriptural text is explained. This chapter still concerns the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*). It is a transformation...
This is its circulation. The text has two parts: first, the prose; second, the verses. The prose section consists of three parts:

first, the question; second, the answer; third, the benefits gained by those who hear this chapter. There are two rounds of questions and answers. Now, for the first round, the question is divided into three sections.
First, the narrator describes the ritual of the request.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to) spoke these words.
"The time" refers to the conclusion of the exposition of the bodhisattvas of the eastern direction; it is now the time to speak of the bodhisattvas of the western direction (*loka-nirukti*).

It refers to the conclusion of the generation of wholesome roots in the east; it is now the time to speak of the generation of wholesome roots in the west (*pudgala-nirukti*). It refers to the severing of doubts regarding the east.
[The section on] the East is concluded. Next, the time of severing doubts in the West is explained (*pratipakṣa-siddhi*).

Having finished explaining the attainment of the Way in the East, next the time of attaining the Way in the West is explained (*paramārtha*). As for "Inexhaustible Intent" (*Akṣayamati*): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that emptiness is inexhaustible;
the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* clarifies the eighty gates of inexhaustibility; and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is inexhaustible is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible. Therefore...

The title is "Inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*). (First, citing emptiness from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the provisional designations from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, and the Middle Way from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: when the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies emptiness, it is inexhaustible; the eighty gates of inexhaustibility in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* involve many different approaches, which constitute the provisional;

as for the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, "that which is inexhaustible has neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion"—because it is the negation of both extremes, it is the Middle. These three sūtras are taken together to explain "inexhaustibility" through the three contemplations and the three wisdoms.
The meaning of "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the subject, and "inexhaustibility" is the object. Wisdom accords with the object; [this refers to] relying solely on...

Regarding the "object" (*viṣaya*), one should say it is inexhaustible. Regarding the "wisdom" (*jñāna*) alone, one should say it pertains to the "mind" (*manas*). When object and wisdom are spoken of together, it is called the "Inexhaustible Mind.
Furthermore, the mind is the foundation of both the mundane and supramundane; moreover, the mind is the Middle Way within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Therefore, it is said that being able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the "Supreme Samādhi. This is an explanation of the names based on the three wisdoms and the three contemplations. △
The second [section] concerns the inquiry regarding the name "Inexhaustible" (*Akṣayamati*) as the causal condition for upholding [the teaching]. It asks:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara named 'Avalokiteśvara'?
Regarding the questioner, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Endowed with the two kinds of adornment, he is able to ask and able to answer. O Akṣayamati, previously [he was characterized] by wisdom...
Adornment. Questioning Avalokiteśvara regarding the adornment of wisdom, the Buddha answered that it is the adornment of wisdom by which Avalokiteśvara is adorned.
△ Third, the Tathāgata answers by explaining how he rescues beings from suffering upon hearing their cries. This is divided into three parts: first, the general answer; second, the specific answer;
third, the answer encouraging the holding of the name. The general answer is further divided into three: first, many people encounter suffering; second, hearing the name...
Regarding the titles: third, the attainment of liberation.
First, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (up to the point where it says) "they undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
As for those who undergo suffering: there are many kinds of suffering; one person may undergo many sufferings, many people may undergo a single suffering, or many people may undergo many sufferings.
"Suffering. One person undergoes one suffering; now, the text speaks of hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of sentient beings—this refers to many people.
They undergo various afflictions—this refers to many sufferings. By citing the many, the few are revealed: if even the many can be saved, how much more so the few?

(Regarding the four phrases beginning with "many sufferings" and "one person," in each phrase, those who suffer are all to be saved, and all may hold the Name. Because there is the universal [benefit] of five individuals and ten pairs, every thought-moment brings benefit to all. This is true for all Perfect Bodhisattvas; they simply act according to conditions.)
△ Second, hearing the name and title:
Hearing of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly calling upon his name.
Encountering suffering is evil; calling upon the name is good. The union of good and evil constitutes the meaning of the "stimulus" (ki). △ Third, attaining liberation.
"Delivered.
Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara immediately observes their voices, and all obtain liberation; all obtain liberation.
This is the 'response' (ying). This is the causal condition of stimulus and resonance, and thus he is named Avalokiteśvara. It is also..."
The causal conditions of persons and dharmas, up to the causal conditions of wisdom and abandonment, are called Avalokiteśvara.

Subsequent instances are named in this manner; there is no need for further elaboration in the text. [Supplementary Note: It is not said that one "hears" his voice, but rather that one "contemplates. This is because the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) of the Bodhisattva are the function inherent in the essence.

Each faculty is perfectly complete; one faculty is all faculties, and all faculties are one faculty. Therefore, it is called the True Contemplation, the Pure Contemplation, the Contemplation of Vast Wisdom, the Contemplation of Compassion, and the Contemplation of Loving-kindness. One should always vow to and constantly gaze upon them. Since the six faculties are thus, the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are likewise so. One...

All dust is one dust; all dust is one dust. Therefore it is said: "Wondrous Sound, Observer of the World’s Sounds; Brahma-sound, Tide-sound; surpassing the sounds of that world. For this reason, one should constantly keep [him] in mind.

This is because the faculties and objects of the Bodhisattva are entirely wondrous form and wondrous mind, the entire substance of which is the true mark (dharmatā), pervading the Dharma-realm. He universally responds to the capacities of all beings, seeking out their voices to rescue them from suffering—not merely through the mutual functioning of the six sense-faculties.

(The general answer is concluded. △ Second, the detailed answer is divided into three parts: I. Response to the vocal capacity; II. Response to the mental capacity; III. Response to the physical capacity. (This is the detailed answer.)

Regarding the three types of karmic capacities: the seven calamities are the capacity of speech, because one invokes the Name; the three poisons are the capacity of mind, because one maintains constant mindfulness;
and the two kinds of seeking are the capacity of body, because one constantly performs prostrations. The capacity of speech is further divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the seven calamities, followed by the conclusion. First, the calamity of fire.
If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara... (up to) "by virtue of the majestic spiritual power of this Bodhisattva," there are four kinds of fire-related calamities.
First, holding the name is good; second, encountering fire is evil; third, the application (*yōng*); fourth, the conclusion (*jié*).
Within each of these calamities, there are three instances by way of analogy: first, the fire of karmic retribution, from the hells upward to the First Dhyāna Heaven.

All discuss the correspondence between capacity and response. Second, the fire of evil karma: from the hells up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), all discuss the correspondence between capacity and response.
Third, the fire of afflictions: from the hells up to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), all discuss the correspondence between capacity and response. Seventh, the seven calamities.
The three poisons and the two cravings are all treated in this manner; they are like the sound in an empty valley, where the response never fails to match the call.
△ Second, the peril of water:
if one is being swept away by a great flood, by invoking his name, one will immediately find shallow ground.
△ Third, the peril of rākṣasas.
If there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings... (up to) for these reasons he is named Avalokiteśvara.
△ Fourth, the peril of kings.
Furthermore, if there should be someone on the verge of being harmed [up to] who attains liberation.
△ Fifth, the calamity of spirits.
If within a trichiliocosm [up to] how much more so regarding further harm?
△ Sixth, the difficulty of shackles and fetters.
Even if there were a person [who... all are completely severed and destroyed, and one immediately attains liberation.
△ Seventh, the difficulty of hostile bandits.
If [in] a trichiliocosm [world-system]... by reciting his name, one is immediately liberated.
△ Next, the conclusion:
"O Akṣayamati, such is the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara."
△ Second, the response to the mental faculties.
If there are sentient beings with much lust (up to) they shall attain freedom from delusion.
△ Next, the conclusion.
Akṣayamati, for this reason, sentient beings should constantly maintain mindfulness in their hearts.
△ Section Three: The Functions of the Three Bodies is divided into two parts. The first two concern seeking.
If there is a woman who wishes to seek a son (up to) being loved and respected by all people.
For those seeking a son, there is a formal vow, followed by the practice of meritorious deeds; for those seeking a daughter, the text briefly mentions the practice of meritorious deeds.

This is because the acts of prostration and making offerings are the same in both cases, and thus they are omitted [from the latter]. Furthermore, since their respective vows differ, they are set forth separately.
△ Next, the conclusion.
The merit of Akṣayamati (up to) "is not in vain.

The summary follows the text (the second part, answering separately regarding the three karmas and their capacities, is concluded). △ Third, the exhortation to uphold, which consists of three parts: first, the exhortation to uphold;
second, the comparative evaluation; third, the concluding praise. Now, the first [part]: the exhortation to uphold.
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Although the aforementioned holy name and wondrous virtues do not distinguish his physical form or substance, if one wishes to take refuge and revere him, it is appropriate to hold his name.
For this reason, he is exhorted to uphold it. △ Second, the comparative evaluation.
Akṣayamati, if there were someone [to describe them], even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas they could not be exhausted.
The *Ru Dacheng Lun* (Treatise on Entering the Mahāyāna) states: "The Dharmakāya is singular; its manifested forms (*nirmāṇakāya*) are manifold. This accounts for sixty-two billion manifestations.
They are equal as one Dharma-body. The Wise One said: "The person of the Perfect Teaching is one; the person of the Partial Teaching is many.
This means that sixty-two billion partial bodhisattvas are equal to one perfect bodhisattva. △ Third, the conclusion and praise.
Akṣayamati (up to) attains such immeasurable and boundless benefit of merit.
(The first round of question and answer concludes. △ The second round of question and answer has two parts: first, Akṣayamati asks while traveling and teaching in the Sahā world.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] ...what is the nature of the power of skillful means?

There are three intentions in this question: first, how he wanders in questioning with the body; second, how he speaks in questioning with the mouth; and third, the intention of questioning through skillful means.
These are the uncalculated powers of the three secrets of this Bodhisattva, which adapt to and accord with the capacities of sentient beings. △ Second, the Tathāgata, by means of universality...
The response by way of a manifestation at the gate also has three parts: first, a specific response; second, a general response; and third, an exhortation to make offerings. Regarding the first:
the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying, "Good son... [and so forth] ...and preached the Dharma for him."

"Those who should be [taught]" refers to the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*). "Manifesting bodies" answers the question regarding his movements; "preaching the Dharma" answers the question regarding his speech.

Altogether there are thirty-three manifestations of body and nineteen instances of preaching the Dharma (and so forth). [Regarding the phrase "thirty-three bodies and nineteen preachings," one should specifically indicate their combinations and separations;
however, as the summary is brief, it simply lists nineteen, such as the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly, which are each summarized into a single mention. II. General Response.
Akṣayamati (up to) "wandering through various lands to deliver sentient beings.

This is a transition from the specific to the general. The specific text is extensive while its meaning is narrow; the general answer is concise while its meaning is vast. △ Third, the exhortation to make offerings.
Herein, because one has seen his form and heard the Dharma, there is an exhortation to make offerings. Part two: First, the exhortation.
Therefore, you all [should know that] he is universally titled "The Bestower of Fearlessness.
△ Next, receiving the mandate:
Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] ...roaming throughout the Sahā world.
There are six ways of receiving [the offering]: first, accepting the command; second, not accepting; third, respectfully accepting;

fourth, being exhorted by the Buddha; fifth, accepting immediately; sixth, the conclusion (all as in the text). [Supplementary note: Regarding "accepting immediately," Avalokiteśvara accepts out of compassion, yet because of his wisdom, he divides it into two parts—this is accepting while not accepting.

Furthermore, when Akṣayamati offers the jeweled necklace of the Dharma-gift, this gift is the true cause of the reality-mark (*dharmatā*). Avalokiteśvara then divides it to offer to Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna; this acceptance is the true fruit of the reality-mark. Cause and fruit are non-dual; the Wheel of Dharma is of a single characteristic. △

Two verses in verse form. The *Xu seng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) states: "These verses were translated by Jñānagupta; as there was no text in the Qin translation, there is likewise no commentary on the phrasing.
Now, following the *Huìyì kēzhù* (Commentary on the Classified Annotations), I shall provide an exegesis based on the topical divisions established by the Venerable Ciyun.
The main outline is divided into three parts: first, the double verses on the two questions; second, the double verses... [text continues].
There are two responses and three pairs of verses that provide two exhortations. This is the first.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse:
"World-Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask you again: For what cause and condition, O Son of the Buddha, is he named Avalokiteśvara?"
The first line praises the Buddha’s virtues; the second line contains both questions; and the final two lines specifically versify the first question.

△ Second, the dual versification of the two answers has two parts: first, the supplementary versification of the general praise of practice and vows; second, the specific versification of the two answers.
Now, first:
"Endowed with wondrous marks, the Honored One" (up to) "arouse a great, pure vow.
The first two lines are the introductory narration by the scribe; the subsequent six lines are the Buddha’s formal praise. △ Second, the separate verses on the two [aspects].

The answer consists of two parts: first, a verse summarizing the preceding answer; second, a verse for the subsequent answer. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a verse summarizing the general answer; second, a verse for the specific answer. This is the first [of those].
I shall explain this briefly for you: hearing the name, seeing the body, and recollecting in the mind—these do not pass in vain, for they can extinguish all suffering within the realms of existence.
"Briefly explained" means to state the essentials. Hearing the name constitutes the vocal karma; it is the instrument [of practice].

Seeing the body constitutes the bodily karma; it is the instrument. Recollecting in the mind constitutes the mental karma; it is the instrument. (A supplementary note states: hearing the name answers the former question; seeing the body answers the latter question. △

The two verses provide separate answers to two [sets of questions]: the first verse addresses the seven perils, and the second verse addresses the three poisons and the two types of seeking. Within the first [section], there are twelve [perils];
the first verse addresses the first peril, the fire, up to the twelfth verse, which adds the peril of thunder and rain. Now, the first [verse].

Even if one should give rise to a harmful intent (up to: the fire pit transforms into a pond)—regarding such matters as the danger of fire, one must explain them in terms of the retribution of evil karma and afflictions (the same applies to all such dangers).

Regarding the phrase "those who call upon that Avalokiteśvara": if spoken from the perspective of the Buddha, Avalokiteśvara is "that" and the practitioner is "this," thus provisionally distinguishing between self and other based on the relationship of teacher and disciple.
If spoken from the perspective of sentient beings, "calling upon that Avalokiteśvara" provisionally distinguishes between self and other based on the principle of resonance and response (*ganying*).

This resonance and response between teacher and disciple is nothing other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). While the subject and object appear distinct, they are ultimately severed; as sentient beings call upon him, they themselves [realize this].
The Avalokiteśvara within one's own mind responds to the sentient being within that same mind;
this mutual resonance between cause and effect is inconceivable. △ Second, a verse on the second peril of water.
Or if drifting upon the vast ocean, beset by the perils of dragons, fish, and various ghosts—by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, the waves cannot submerge them.
△ Third, an added verse on the peril of falling from Mount Sumeru.
"Or if one were on the peak of Mount Sumeru and were pushed over by someone, by virtue of the power of that Avalokiteśvara, one would abide in the void like the sun.
Regarding the literal sense, this is a figurative expression; even if one were to fall from Mount Sumeru, one would not be harmed, let alone from any other mountain.
Regarding the perspective of contemplative understanding, it refers to the fundamental nature and merit of the Middle Way and True Reality (dharmatā), which is like the King of Mountains, Sumeru.

Ignorant and wicked people are pushed into the sea of the two deaths; yet by recollecting Avalokiteśvara’s three wisdoms and three virtues, they immediately become equal to all Buddhas, abiding in non-abiding.
△ Fourth, adding a verse on the peril of falling onto a mountain of diamond: this may be understood by analogy with the difficulty of [climbing] Mount Sumeru.
Or if pursued by evil men and cast down Mount Vajra, by virtue of recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed.
△ Fifth, this verse transcends [the description of] the seventh peril of hostile bandits.
Or if one encounters hostile bandits surrounding them, each wielding blades to inflict harm; by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a heart of compassion.
△ Sixth, a retrospective verse on the fourth peril: the danger of blades and staves.
Or if one encounters the suffering of royal peril, facing execution as life draws to its end, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, the blade shall immediately shatter into pieces.
△ Seventh, a retrospective verse on the sixth difficulty: the hardship of shackles and fetters.

"Sovereignty" refers to the unity of principle. "Spiritual powers" refer to the unity of practice. "Majestic virtue" refers to the unity of the person.
"Renown" refers to the unity of the teaching. Furthermore, sovereignty is permanence; spiritual powers are bliss; majestic virtue is...

By the power of purity, flowers rain down; by the power of bliss, music is played; by the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), the earth trembles;
and by the power of mastery, it rains according to one's will—raining wherever one goes, and playing music wherever one moves. It is, for example, like this:
The great dragon flies without ceasing; clouds and rain surround its body, flowing forth inexhaustibly.

Samantabhadra and his retinue, assuming the bodies of bodhisattvas, arrive by means of the power of the four virtues to exhort the realization of the "Four Ones. At every place they pass through, they personally present the highest offerings;

such are their deeds. (Regarding the phrase "following along" and so forth: "going" and "moving" merely signify coming and going. As for "following," it means that the rain does not wait for prior accumulation before falling, nor does the music wait for prior storage before being performed.)

Therefore, it is illustrated by the analogy of the dragon’s rain. This is brought about by the power of the mind, the power of the Dharma, the power of sentient beings, the power of responsive transformation, and the power of the inconceivable. △ Second, the downward transformation.

therefore, he requested once more that the True Teaching be expounded. By encouraging others toward awakening, he requested the propagation of the teaching; by encouraging others toward awakening, he encouraged the transformation of others. Thus did the Tathāgata...

△ Next, the explanation:
first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; (up to) fourth, giving rise to the mind to rescue all sentient beings.
The names of the four dharmas are listed separately as in the text. Since they were requested in pairs, the Tathāgata skillfully answered by briefly citing four to encompass all.
This is truly because the essentials of these four dharmas comprehensively include and pervade the correct and the provisional. Why is this?

Although the Buddha is without partiality, if one can distance oneself from evil and follow what is good, turn back from delusion toward the correct, and open up provisional knowledge and vision to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then—
It accords with the holy mind and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas. When the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, Prajñā manifests before one.

This is the planting of the roots of all virtues, and it is also entry into the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). It is neither distracted nor savoring; it is neither grasping nor abandoning.

It is also the arousal of the resolve to rescue sentient beings. Furthermore, one should know that these four [aspects] and the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real" differ in name but are identical in essence.

They are non-dual and without distinction. That which is protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; that which plants the roots of all virtues is the revealing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

that which gives rise to the salvation of sentient beings is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and that which enters the stage of right determination is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
These four essentials of the "Trace Gate" are thus complete. Furthermore, the Trace has its Origin; from the Origin, there is the opening and revealing.

Awakening and entry. Thus, there is the revelation, instruction, awakening, and entry within the traces (*śeṣa*). Now, by revealing the traces, the fundamental reality (*mūla*) is manifested; the fundamental and the trace are non-dual and without distinction.
By means of these four dharmas, his request is answered correctly; the meaning is thus clear. Furthermore, he answers the request for its circulation with these same four dharmas.
Regarding the method of circulation, it consists only of three or four [aspects]: to give rise to the salvation of sentient beings is to enter into the Tathāgata.
The chamber. Entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and being protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha—this is donning the robe of the Tathāgata.

Planting the roots of all virtues—this is sitting upon the seat of the Tathāgata. This is the essential method for widely proclaiming [the Dharma]; it is three yet fourfold. To resolve to rescue sentient beings is the practice of peaceful conduct through vow;
entering the stage of right determination is the practice of peaceful conduct through mind; planting the roots of all virtues is the practice of peaceful conduct through speech.

The Practice of Peaceful Abiding (*sukha-vihāra*). Protecting and mindfulness of this body is the practice of peaceful abiding. One should know that the latter four [sections] are precisely the former four practices.

First, he answers his two requests and presents the four [practices] as a canopy covering the entire sutra. This is the re-enactment of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the re-proclamation of this scripture.

The exhortation for those who have come from afar has its meaning in this way. (Regarding "only three" and "only four": the four are simply the four practices of peaceful abiding; the three are simply...)

"Good sons and good daughters (up to) shall certainly obtain this sutra. Question:

How much more so for those who have previously been able to accomplish the four dharmas; even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they shall still obtain this sutra, let alone while the Tathāgata is currently present preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.

"To cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision. This is indeed the essence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The authentic text states: "If one can practice these four dharmas, one will certainly attain this understanding; thus, this understanding is called a 'sūtra' (scripture).

This concludes the inquiry regarding the request for the correct teaching. If one can apply this understanding and practice to transmit it to others, and those others attain such faith and understanding, they become the first person of reliance who is able to attain true understanding.
They then become the second, third, and fourth persons of reliance. This concludes [the section].

Regarding the question of requesting the circulation [of this teaching], this intent is not seen; have you perhaps offered a superficial interpretation? (To offer a "superficial interpretation" means:

if someone were to reject this interpretation, they would be rejecting one's own practice and the transformation of others; they would be rejecting the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering; they would be rejecting the three—room, robes, and seat.

If one says it is not a rejection but merely lacks textual evidence, then if the sutra lacks it, that is a rejection of the essential repetition. If it were not so, by what means could one grasp the main body of this present sutra and treat its arrival here as a repetition? [Supplementary Note: Those who practice these four dharmas are likewise...]

One gives rise to the bodhicitta and formulates the Four Great Vows. To say "to give rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings" refers to the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. To say "to enter the assembly of those fixed in rightness" refers to the vow to sever inexhaustible afflictions.

To say "to plant the roots of all virtues" refers to the vow to study immeasurable Dharma-gates. To say "to be protected and remembered by all Buddhas" refers to the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed path of the Buddha. Indeed, the bodhicitta is the Buddha-mind.

One attains the mind of the Buddha. That is, one immediately hears the revelation of the provisional to reveal the real (*kai-ken gen-jitsu*) and the revelation of the traces to reveal the fundamental (*kai-seki gen-hon*). Once these two gates of revelation have been clearly elucidated, the formal teaching is complete. Furthermore, by means of these four dharmas, one transmits and clarifies them for others, with clarity being passed down in succession.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if there are sentient beings who obtain these four dharmas, there are none who do not obtain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; this is precisely the inexhaustible circulation [of the Dharma]. (The first inquiry and exhortation to practice are concluded.)
△ Second, the exhortation to fulfill the vow. The text is divided into two parts: first, protecting persons; second, protecting the Dharma.
Protecting persons consists of six sections. First, warding off external difficulties. This has two parts. The first is the general warding off of difficulties;
thus it says, "so that no one seeking an opportunity shall find an advantage. This is it.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "those who seek an opportunity shall find none.

whether it be Māras or the sons of Māras, [up to] those who afflict people, none shall be able to gain an advantage.
△ Second, protecting his inner Dharma. There are three successive instructions. First, he practices standing and reciting;
riding upon a six-tusked white elephant, he brings comfort to his mind.
Whether this person is walking or standing (up to the point mentioned), it is also for the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Next, while sitting in contemplation, they again mount the six-tusked elephant, who instructs them in the sutra and bestows upon them samādhi.
If this person sits and contemplates this sutra, they will attain such *dhāraṇīs* as these:

△ Third, he covered [them] with supernormal power.
"World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas... (up to) all this is through the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra."
Whether hearing it or upholding it, this is none other than the power of spiritual efficacy. △ Fourth, showing the superior causes:
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this]... (up to) all Tathāgatas will stroke their heads with their hands."
If there are those who uphold [this teaching], even to the point of understanding its meaning and practicing according to what is taught, they will possess the five virtues of a Dharma teacher.
Such persons have, for the Buddhas of the three periods of time, performed the acts of planting, ripening, and liberating.

Because these individuals attain liberation together with the future Buddhas, it is said that their conduct is identical to that of Samantabhadra. Because these individuals have already planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas, it is said...
Having deeply planted roots of goodness, this person has been ripened by the Buddha appearing before them; therefore, it is said that he strokes their head with his hand.
△ Fifth, showing the proximate fruit:
"If one merely transcribes [this]... up to "...there are such merits and benefits as these."

If one can merely transcribe [the text], one will be reborn nearby in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. If one possesses the qualities of the five types of Dharma-preachers, one will next be reborn in Tuṣita, as described in the text. [Supplementary Note:

If a person merely transcribes the text but cannot receive, uphold, read, recite, or even understand its meaning and intent, nor practice according to the teaching, they will be born in Trāyastriṃśa and remain within the Desire Realm.

However, if one possesses the virtues of the five types of Dharma-preachers, one will be reborn in Tuṣita to personally attend upon Maitreya, surrounded by the great Bodhisattvas, and together hear the wondrous Dharma. Furthermore, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial maidens who are reborn together; these are those of like vision and like practice who have joined in advance.]
Those who have entered the stream of the noble ones are not the celestial maidens of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. △ Six: Summary of the Two [Points]. First, the summary of those protected:
"Therefore, the wise person... (up to)... practices according to the teaching."

[Supplementary Note: To "protect others" means to rely solely on the act of copying [the scripture], thereby being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by the power of that merit and enjoying the pleasures of the five senses. Once that merit is exhausted, one sinks back into the cycle of suffering; such a person is not a wise one. If one can understand its meaning and practice according to the teaching, that is true wisdom.]
Possessing the virtues of a Dharma Master, he is first called "the Wise One" (Zhìzhě). △ Second, the conclusion of the vow to protect the Dharma:
"World-Honored One, by means of my supernatural powers... [until] I shall cause it to be widely disseminated so that it never ceases."
(The second exhortation concludes. △ Third, the description of the arousal [of the mind] has six parts. First, the description of protecting the Dharma:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... until "...protecting those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva."
"It is said that you are thus able to provide great benefit externally and accumulate compassion internally.
Furthermore, having provided such protection for many eons, I too shall, by the power of my supernatural faculties, protect those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra."
This is also like Samantabhadra’s protection of the Dharma. △ Second, describing his protection of people:
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra]... (up to) they shall be covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha."

[Supplementary Note: Second, regarding those who protect people. If a person possesses the virtues of a Dharma Master, they are as one who has heard the sutras directly from the Buddha’s own mouth; they are as one who personally makes offerings to the Buddha, for whom the Buddha praises their goodness, strokes their head with his hand, and covers their body with his robe.]

By virtue of the merit of the *dharmatā*, they are equal to the Tathāgata and equal to Samantabhadra. This constitutes the wisdom and compassion of the same essence, which circulate throughout the *dharmadhātu*. Their natures are mutually related; their resonance occurs spontaneously, not through deliberate mental intention.
△ Third, describing the cause for their manifestation.
Such a person (up to) is able to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.

This extensively illustrates that, being free from all faults and evils during the causal stage, possessing few desires and contentment, and cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra, they are thus able to receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, practice, and transcribe this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. △ Fourth, describing its proximate fruit.
Samantabhadra, whether after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa [or even in the present life], one shall obtain the retribution of such merit.
Such a person shall go to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and will certainly achieve the distant fruit; how much more so the near fruit!
They shall also obtain the near fruit in the present life, enjoying it spontaneously and without attachment. △ Fifth, describing their ability to ward off external calamities.

If there are those who speak words of contempt and disparagement—up to the point of calling them "evil and grievous illnesses"—the Buddha extensively reveals the transgressions of such disparagers so that they may recognize their faults and surely reform, thereby not causing mutual affliction and disorder.

It is not only that the upholder of the sutra does not suffer from such disparagement, but it also causes merit to arise for the disparager. Free from both blame and praise, both parties shall abide in peace.
Joy. To save all extensively and without partiality is the ultimate of compassion. △ Sixth, describing the merit of those who establish faith:
"Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, as if honoring a Buddha."
(Third, the conclusion of the exposition of the arousal [of the mind]). △ Fourth, the benefits of the arousal [of the mind], in two parts. First, the benefit of hearing this chapter:
When this "Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Exhortation to Arouse the Mind" was being preached... until "...one is endowed with the path of Universal Worthy."
The *Pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī* corresponds to the first stage (*bhūmi*). Being endowed with the path of Samantabhadra corresponds to the tenth stage.
△ Second, the benefit of hearing the sutra: the great assembly rejoiced.
When the Buddha had spoken this sutra (up to the point where they) received and upheld the Buddha’s words, paid homage, and departed, all were filled with great joy.
This means that at the single assembly on Vulture Peak, having finished hearing the Dharma, all attained the great joy of the Tathāgata’s four immeasurable minds;
it pervaded their dharma-bodies and circulated throughout the dharma-realm, flowing on through eternity, forever and ever.
It is inexhaustible. Question: Why is it still called "śrāvaka" (voice-hearer) here? Answer: This is because the compiler of the sutra preserved its outward appearance;
the underlying intention is that these are Mahāyāna śrāvakas. By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, they cause all to hear—this meaning is thereby made even more manifest.
The Venerable Jingxi said: "As for the traces of the Tiantai teachings, those in the land of Chu (India) longed for them with admiration, yet they could not be obtained in Zhendan (China).
In this region, however, those who truly understand them are few, like the people of Lu. Only those who have planted the roots of virtue in previous lives [can comprehend them]."

Only now do we begin to understand its direction. We respectfully exhort all students to praise it according to their capacity; they should know that practicing this for oneself while guiding others is a rare encounter once in vast eons.
Whether one speaks or listens, the realm and wisdom remain present. Whether in obscurity or in manifestation, the ripening of the seeds may be expected.

This is entirely because those who propagate the sutras possess skillful means. If propagating the sutras were merely a matter of lecturing and explaining, why would there be the three admonitions regarding robes, seats, and dwellings?
How could that which was dispatched by the Tathāgata be treated with such casualness? As I examine myself and reflect upon my own views, I am personally filled with much shame.

Yet, constrained by various circumstances, I have forcibly composed this outline once more. Even if it contains points of establishment or refutation, it is intended to serve as a foundation for further growth.
The Perfect Vehicle enables those of like mind to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is ultimately free from partiality and does not follow mere conjecture.
I hope that all who read this will fully discern my humble sincerity. May even a single phrase permeate the spirit, forever becoming a seed of Buddhahood, to be contemplated and cultivated.

Deeply resonating with the Buddha-mind, may all who see or hear this rejoice; may we always be as principal and attendant, whether grasping or relinquishing, so that even what passes through the ears becomes a condition for awakening.

Whether favorable or adverse, may it ultimately lead to liberation through this cause. On the day of our liberation, may the primary and secondary retributions constantly proclaim the wondrous sutras;
may every land and every speck of dust be nothing other than a means to benefit sentient beings. We pray only that all Buddhas will secretly infuse their power and provide their protection.
All Bodhisattvas secretly borrow their majestic spiritual power; wherever [the Dharma] has not yet been preached, they all offer exhortations and requests.

Wherever it is preached, they personally receive and make offerings. With every single phrase, every single verse, every color, and every fragrance, they advance toward Bodhi, never regressing for eternity.
